audubon-birds-1-wild-turkey: The opening plate of Birds of America presents a male Meleagris gallopavo striding through cane, painted at Beechwoods Plantation in West Feliciana Parish. The towering double-elephant folio format permitted Audubon to render the bird at life size, with iridescent body plumage built up in layered aquatint.
audubon-birds-10-brown-titlark: Plate 10 of Birds of America depicts two Brown Titlarks, now known as the American Pipit, shown among dark ground cover and mushrooms. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell from Audubon's watercolour, the plate records the male and female of the species with characteristic attention to plumage detail.
audubon-birds-100-marsh-wren: Plate 100 of The Birds of America shows the Marsh Wren clinging among reedy stems of its nesting habitat. Engraved and aquatinted by Robert Havell Jr. from Audubon's watercolor, the life-size composition pairs species portrait with carefully observed wetland setting.
audubon-birds-101-raven: Plate 101 presents the Common Raven at full life size, perched on a branch laden with hickory nuts, its beak open. Glossy black plumage is rendered through Havell's hand-coloured aquatint, and the male is labelled on the plate as Corvus corax.
audubon-birds-102-blue-jay: Plate 102 of Birds of America depicts three Blue Jays — labelled male, female, and a third — gathered on a leafy branch bearing tubular red and orange flowers. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell from Audubon's watercolour, the composition shows the vivid blue-and-white plumage and crested head of Cyanocitta cristata.
audubon-birds-103-canada-warbler: Plate 103 shows the Canada Warbler among the foliage of a flowering plant, the yellow breast and necklace of streaks rendered with diagnostic precision. Audubon's habit of pairing each species with botanically accurate vegetation is on full display.
audubon-birds-104-chipping-sparrow: Plate 104 depicts the Chipping Sparrow perched on a flowering branch, its rufous crown and clean breast carefully delineated. The aquatint preserves the soft gradations of the small songbird's plumage achieved in Audubon's original watercolor.
audubon-birds-105-red-breasted-nuthatch: Plate 105 depicts two Red-breasted Nuthatches on a broken dead tree trunk, one bird in its characteristic head-down posture. The slate-blue back, rust-orange underparts, and bold black-and-white facial striping are rendered at life size in this plate from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
audubon-birds-106-black-vulture-or-carri: Plate 106 presents two Black Vultures at a carcass, a subject that gave Audubon the chance to depict carrion-feeding behavior alongside the species' bare gray head and broad wings. The composition fills the double-elephant sheet with its scavenging pair.
audubon-birds-107-canada-jay: Plate 107 depicts two Canada Jays among the lobed leaves of a White Oak (Quercus alba), one bird tending a nest at the lower centre of the composition. The soft gray and white plumage is conveyed through selective hand-colouring over the aquatint, and the plate labels the tree as White Oak (Quercus alba).
audubon-birds-108-fox-coloured-sparrow: Plate 108 shows two Fox-coloured Sparrows among mossy ground cover with ferns, berries, and low vegetation. The rich rufous tail and heavily spotted breast of the species are carefully rendered, set against the dense groundscape typical of Audubon's life-history compositions from Birds of America.
audubon-birds-109-savannah-finch: Plate 109 depicts two Savannah Finches (Savannah Sparrows) perched on branches and slender stems among grasses and flowering plants including red tubular blooms. Audubon's composition captures the species' open-country habitat, and the streaked brown plumage is rendered with characteristic precision in this plate from Birds of America.
audubon-birds-11-bird-of-washington: Plate 11 presents Audubon's so-called Bird of Washington, a large brown eagle depicted on a rocky perch. Audubon claimed it as a distinct species, but recent scholarship has demonstrated that the image was based on copies of earlier drawings rather than an original specimen, making it one of the more contested plates in Birds of America.
audubon-birds-110-hooded-warbler: Plate 110 shows the Hooded Warbler, the male's black hood framing a vivid yellow face. Audubon places the bird among the foliage of an understory plant, in keeping with the species' preference for shady eastern woodlands.
audubon-birds-111-pileated-woodpecker: Plate 111 fills the double-elephant sheet with four Pileated Woodpeckers on a tree trunk entwined with grape vine. The birds' flaming red crests are a vivid accent against the dark plumage and bark, and the composition showcases Audubon's signature pairing of life-size scale with active, behaviour-driven groupings.
audubon-birds-112-downy-woodpecker: Plate 112 depicts a male and female Downy Woodpecker on a branch covered with a flowering vine bearing red buds and yellow blossoms. The crisp black-and-white plumage and the male's small red nape patch are precisely rendered, and the plate title notes both sexes from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved by Havell.
audubon-birds-113-blue-bird: Plate 113 shows the Eastern Bluebird (Sialia sialis) in three figures: a male in mid-flight above, and a male and female on a leafy branch below, the female appearing to pass food to her mate. The vibrant blue plumage, achieved through hand-colouring over the aquatint, made this plate from Birds of America a perennial favourite.
audubon-birds-114-white-crowned-sparrow: Plate 114 depicts two White-crowned Sparrows among the broad leaves and dark berry clusters of a grape vine. The boldly black-and-white striped crown and clean gray breast are crisply rendered in this plate from Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
audubon-birds-115-wood-pewee: Plate 115 shows the Eastern Wood-Pewee perched among the blossoms of swamp azalea (then Azalea viscosa, now Rhododendron viscosum). The pairing of small flycatcher and flowering branch is typical of Audubon's union of ornithology and botanical record.
audubon-birds-116-ferruginous-thrush: Plate 116 depicts three Ferruginous Thrushes (now Brown Thrasher) in a dramatic defensive scene around a nest with eggs, while a black snake coils through the oak-leafed branches toward them. The long tail and rich rusty back of the species are clearly rendered, and the multi-figure composition is among the most narratively charged in Audubon's Birds of America.
audubon-birds-117-mississippi-kite: Two Mississippi Kites perched on lichen- and moss-draped branches, the male above with wings partially spread and the female below. The slate-grey plumage and pointed wings characteristic of the species are carefully rendered in Audubon's Plate CXVII from Birds of America (1827–1838), credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-118-warbling-flycatcher: A study of the small olive-toned songbird known today as the warbling vireo, perched amid foliage. The plate exemplifies Audubon's habit of pairing each species with a botanical setting drawn from direct field observation.
audubon-birds-119-yellow-throated-vireo: The yellow-throated vireo is shown among leafy branches, its lemon breast and white spectacles picked out in fine line and watercolour wash. Engraved by Robert Havell Jr. from Audubon's life-size original.
audubon-birds-12-baltimore-oriole: Baltimore orioles — adult male, female, and immature — arranged across flowering branches, their pendulous woven nest at the centre of the composition. Audubon pairs the birds' bold black-and-orange plumage with the pale rose-centred blooms of the host plant in Plate XII of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-120-pewit-flycatcher: Two Eastern Phoebes — here under their older name Pewit Flycatcher — perched on the stems of a cotton plant in full boll. One bird is alert with open bill, the other below with wings spread. Plate CXX from Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-121-snowy-owl: A pair of Snowy Owls perched on the limbs of a dead tree against a dark, cloud-streaked sky, the more heavily barred individual in the foreground and the paler bird above. Audubon differentiates male and female by the density of their dark markings in Plate CXXI of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-122-blue-grosbeak: Male, female, and immature Blue Grosbeaks in the branches of a leafy dogwood, a nest visible at the centre of the composition. The deep cobalt male contrasts with the warm amber-brown female in Plate CXXII of Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-123-black-yellow-warblers: A study of magnolia warblers, formerly called black and yellow warblers, arranged on a flowering branch. Audubon's compositional habit of stacking multiple individuals across a single bough allowed him to display plumage variation within a species.
audubon-birds-124-green-black-capt-flyca: The Wilson's warbler, here under an obsolete name, perched on a slender stem. The black-capped male and plainer female demonstrate the sexual dimorphism Audubon was careful to record.
audubon-birds-125-brown-headed-nuthatch: A southern pine specialist shown clinging head-down to bark in the species' typical pose. The plate captures the small nuthatch's sharp bill and stubby tail, characters Audubon emphasised through tight, descriptive line work.
audubon-birds-126-white-headed-eagle: An immature Bald Eagle — labelled 'Young' on the plate — depicted in full three-quarter view, its dark brown plumage and mottled tail filling the composition. The plate is among the most imposing in Audubon's double-elephant folio, Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-127-rose-breasted-grosbeak: Multiple Rose-breasted Grosbeaks — adult male, female, and birds in autumn plumage — arranged across spruce branches bearing small red berries. The adult male's vivid crimson bib and bold black-and-white wings anchor the composition in Plate CXXVII of Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-128-cat-bird: A pair of grey catbirds among bramble, named for their mewing call. Audubon situates the birds within thorny undergrowth typical of their breeding habitat, a recurring strategy for grounding species in ecological context.
audubon-birds-129-great-crested-flycatch: The great crested flycatcher poised on a forked branch, its rufous tail and lemon belly delicately laid in. Audubon notes the species' habit of weaving shed snake skins into its nest, an ethological detail typical of his accompanying writings.
audubon-birds-13-snow-bird: Male and female dark-eyed juncos — then called the Snow Bird — perched on leafless winter branches hung with small dark berries. Audubon's spare, uncluttered staging suits the species' winter familiarity in Plate XIII of Birds of America (1827–1838), University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-130-yellow-winged-sparrow: Grasshopper sparrows, under an older name, posed low among grass stems. Audubon's spare composition reflects the cryptic, ground-dwelling nature of the bird, whose flat-headed silhouette he renders with characteristic precision.
audubon-birds-131-american-robin: American robins at a nest in a leafy tree, an adult arriving with food while open-mouthed nestlings beg from the cup below. A second adult perches nearby. The plate documents the species across life stages and is Plate 131 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-132-three-toed-woodpecker: Three woodpeckers cling to a deciduous tree trunk, each displaying the yellow crown patch that distinguishes the three-toed species. The plate groups male and female birds of differing plumages and is Plate 132 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-133-black-poll-warbler: Three blackpoll warblers perch on a fruiting branch bearing clusters of small dark berries, the male's black cap and white cheek contrasting with his streaked flanks. The plate is from Audubon's Birds of America (Plate 133) and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-134-hemlock-warbler: Two warblers — now considered synonymous with the Blackburnian warbler — perch among the broad lobed leaves of a deciduous shrub bearing small hanging flowers. The plate reflects the unsettled state of warbler taxonomy in the early nineteenth century and is Plate 134 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-135-blackburnian-warbler: A male Blackburnian warbler perches on a stem of pink-flowering phlox, his flame-orange throat vivid against the black-and-white body plumage. The plate is Plate 135 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-136-meadow-lark: Eastern meadowlarks posed in tall prairie grass, the yellow breast and black V boldly displayed. The composition links the species firmly to the open agricultural country in which Audubon most often observed it.
audubon-birds-137-yellow-breasted-chat: Yellow-breasted chats around a nest set among wild-rose branches bearing soft pink blossoms, with birds shown in flight and perched. Audubon plays the chat's lemon-yellow breast against the pale-pink roses in a composition that integrates bird and habitat. The plate is Plate 137 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-138-connecticut-warbler: Two Connecticut warblers perch among stems bearing large blue flowers, the upper bird showing the olive-green upperparts and the lower displaying yellow underparts typical of the species. The plate is Plate 138 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-139-field-sparrow: A field sparrow rests on a mossy rock amid a low composition of wildflowers and berry-bearing stems, the bird's pale pink bill and warm-toned crown characteristic of the species. The plate is Plate 139 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-14-prairie-warbler: Two prairie warblers perch among flowering branches, their yellow underparts and side streaking carefully delineated. The plate is typical of the early Havell numbers, in which Audubon paired songbirds with the specific vegetation in which he had observed them feeding.
audubon-birds-140-pine-creeping-warbler: Pine warblers, under an older common name, posed on a pine bough heavy with cones. Audubon ties the species inseparably to its host tree, reflecting the strict habitat fidelity that gives the warbler its name.
audubon-birds-141-i-goshawk-2-stanley-ha: Three raptors occupy a single composition: an immature goshawk perched atop a stump, a dark-mantled adult goshawk below, and the Stanley hawk — now identified as the Cooper's hawk — shown at right. The plate allowed Audubon to document multiple plumage stages of these accipiters and is Plate 141 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-142-american-sparrow-hawk: American kestrels — formerly called sparrow hawks — shown in a leafy tree, one male holding prey while others display the distinctive rufous back and slate-blue wing of this small falcon. The plate is Plate 142 of Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-143-golden-crowned-thrush: Two ovenbirds — depicted under their older name, the Golden-crowned Thrush — are shown near a mossy log beside water, one perching on a branch with red berries above. Audubon renders the olive back and streaked underparts of this ground-dwelling warbler with characteristic precision. The plate is Plate 143 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-144-small-green-crested-fl: Two Small Green Crested Flycatchers are shown among leafy branches laden with dark berries in this plate from the Havell edition of Birds of America. One bird is perched in an alert posture while the other is depicted with wings spread, together demonstrating the species' lively character. Audubon's botanical setting is rendered with the careful observation that distinguishes the double-elephant folio from earlier ornithological prints.
audubon-birds-145-yellow-red-poll-warble: A pair of Yellow Red-poll Warblers perch on a flowering plant bearing yellow daisy-like blooms in Plate 145 of Audubon's Birds of America. The warm brownish-rufous streaking on the crowns and the yellow-tinged underparts are rendered with precision by the colourists working under Robert Havell Jr. in London. The birds are shown in complementary attitudes — one upright and alert, the other at a lower angle — capturing their natural deportment.
audubon-birds-146-fish-crow: Two Fish Crows are shown perched among the feathery compound foliage and hanging seed pods of what appears to be a mimosa tree in Plate 146 of Birds of America. The glossy black plumage is rendered through the layered tonal work characteristic of Audubon's engraved plates. Audubon distinguished this species from the larger American Crow chiefly by voice and habitat, as he documented in his Ornithological Biography.
audubon-birds-147-night-hawk: Nighthawks wheel and rest in this composition, their long pointed wings and cryptic mottled plumage shown in multiple attitudes. Audubon characteristically combined several individuals on a single sheet to display sex differences and flight posture in one image.
audubon-birds-148-pine-swamp-warbler: Two Pine Swamp Warblers are shown among the broad leaves and ripe red berry clusters of a deciduous shrub in this plate from the Havell edition of Birds of America. The birds' greenish and grey-blue plumage is set off against the warm reddish-brown berries and large linden-like leaves. The plate was etched and hand-coloured in London by Robert Havell Jr. after Audubon's original watercolour studies.
audubon-birds-149-sharp-tailed-finch: Three Sharp-tailed Finches are depicted in a marsh setting of grasses and reeds in Plate 149 of Birds of America: one bird sings from the tip of a bare twig, a second perches in the grass, and a third tends a nest at the base of the composition. The streaked breast and buff face pattern of the species are clearly rendered against the muted greens of the wetland vegetation. Audubon associated the species with the low coastal marshes of eastern North America.
audubon-birds-15-blue-yellow-backed-warb: The diminutive Northern Parula is shown working through lichen and blossom, its blue-grey back and yellow throat picked out in delicate washes. Audubon's botanical setting reflects the bird's preference for Spanish-moss-laden southern woodlands.
audubon-birds-150-red-eyed-vireo: A Red-eyed Vireo perches on a bare branch above a spray of compound foliage in Plate 150 of Birds of America, with a large spider suspended from its web prominently depicted in the upper left of the composition. The bird's olive-green back, white eyebrow stripe, and diagnostic eye are carefully rendered by the Havell workshop colourists. Audubon's inclusion of the spider reflects his broader interest in recording the natural relationships of his subjects.
audubon-birds-151-turkey-buzzard: Two Turkey Vultures are shown in Plate 151 of Birds of America: a large individual perches upright on a heavy branch, its bare red head and dark brown plumage dominating the upper composition, while a second bird below holds its wings partially spread. Audubon's observations on this species fed his celebrated dispute with Charles Waterton over whether vultures locate carrion by sight or smell, a controversy he documented in the Ornithological Biography.
audubon-birds-152-white-breasted-black-c: Nuthatches descend a tree trunk head-first in their characteristic posture, the bark texture engraved with fine aquatint grain. The composition records the bird's habitual foraging behaviour rather than presenting it as a static museum specimen.
audubon-birds-153-yellow-crown-warbler: Three Yellow-crown Warblers are arranged on an iris plant entwined with a berry-bearing vine in Plate 153 of Birds of America. The birds display their yellow crown patches and streaked plumage in varied attitudes — one with wings fanned, one perched alertly on the iris stalk, and one lower on the vine. Audubon frequently grouped several individuals on a single plate to illustrate plumage variation across sex or age.
audubon-birds-154-tennessee-warbler: A Tennessee Warbler perches among slender twigs, its olive-and-grey palette modelled by selectively applied aquatint. The species was named by Alexander Wilson from a migrant collected on the Cumberland River, and Audubon retained the regional epithet.
audubon-birds-155-black-throated-blue-wa: A male Black-throated Blue Warbler — its slate-blue upperparts, black face and throat, and white underparts rendered in vivid colour — perches on a Canadian columbine plant bearing red pendant flowers in Plate 155 of Birds of America. The composition shows a single bird, and the columbine setting places the warbler in the woodland habitat it frequents during migration. The plate was engraved and hand-coloured in London by the Havell workshop.
audubon-birds-156-american-crow: An American Crow perches on a branch among compound foliage and clusters of green round fruits — consistent with black walnut — in Plate 156 of Birds of America. The bird's glossy black plumage fills the lower portion of the composition, its bill directed toward the fruit. Audubon's corvid imagery often records the crow's association with cultivated or woodland food sources while affording the species a dignified formal portrait.
audubon-birds-157-rusty-grakle: Four Rusty Grakles are shown in autumn plumage among bare branches bearing clusters of dark blue berries and yellow-turning leaves in Plate 157 of Birds of America. Three dark males and one warm-brown female are arranged across the composition, the brownish edging to their feathers giving the group the rufous cast for which the species was named. The Havell workshop colourists captured the subtle contrast between the female's warm brown tones and the iridescent black of the males.
audubon-birds-158-american-swift: Two Chimney Swifts are shown in flight against a plain ground, their dark cigar-shaped bodies and swept-back wings captured in different attitudes. Below the aerial figures Audubon includes a detailed study of the species' characteristic nest of twigs and a grass fragment. Plate 158 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-159-cardinal-grosbeak: A pair of Northern Cardinals are arranged on a fruiting branch, the male's vermilion plumage carried by a saturated red wash applied over the engraved ground. The plate's vivid colouring relies on the brilliant cochineal- and madder-based reds available to the Havell workshop.
audubon-birds-16-great-footed-hawk: A male and female Peregrine Falcon — here called the Great-footed Hawk — contend over freshly killed waterfowl identified on the plate as Green-winged Teal and Gadwall, blood-flecked feathers scattered around them. The two raptors face each other with wings spread, making this one of the most dynamically charged predator compositions in Birds of America. Plate 16 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-160-black-capped-titmouse: A Black-capped Chickadee hangs from a slender twig, its bold cap and bib reduced to crisp shapes against the understated background. Audubon often illustrated tits and chickadees in acrobatic feeding postures observed at close range.
audubon-birds-161-brasilian-caracara-eag: Two Crested Caracaras face each other in a confrontational posture, their bare red facial skin, dark crests, and barred breast plumage carefully rendered against a plain ground. One bird is shown from above with wings partially spread, emphasising the bold patterning of the tail and flight feathers. Plate 161 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-162-zenaida-dove: A pair of Zenaida Doves perch on a fruiting branch, their warm cinnamon plumage and iridescent neck patches finely modelled. Audubon studied this West Indian species on his 1832 expedition to the Florida Keys, the principal source for several plates in this section.
audubon-birds-163-palm-warbler: Palm Warblers are placed among low foliage with their characteristic tail-pumping posture suggested by the bird's downward-curved attitude. The plate reflects Audubon's habit of incorporating diagnostic behaviour into otherwise still compositions.
audubon-birds-164-tawny-thrush: A Veery is shown among understorey foliage, the warm cinnamon back and faintly spotted breast realised through restrained washes. Audubon followed nineteenth-century usage in calling this woodland thrush the Tawny Thrush.
audubon-birds-165-bachmans-finch: A single Bachman's Sparrow — here called Bachman's Finch — perches on a flowering branch bearing pink blossoms and developing buds, its streaked brown back and plain buff underparts described with restrained precision. The species was named in honour of Audubon's friend and co-author the Reverend John Bachman. Plate 165 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-166-rough-legged-falcon: A single male Rough-legged Falcon clings to the top of a weathered stump, bending forward to grip a small dark bird in its talons, its wings raised in a sweeping arc above. The feathered tarsi that give the species its name are visible against the pale buff and dark-streaked plumage. Plate 166 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-167-key-west-dove: A pair of Key West Doves face each other in a billing posture on a fallen log, their rich rufous-brown plumage and iridescent eye-rings rendered against a backdrop of morning glories and low coastal vegetation. The ground-level composition emphasises the species' terrestrial habits. Plate 167 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by R. Havell.
audubon-birds-168-fork-tailed-flycatcher: A Fork-tailed Flycatcher perches on a flowering branch — bearing large white blossoms — its two greatly elongated central tail feathers hanging straight downward in a striking vertical line. The grey upperparts, black cap, and rufous crown patch are crisply rendered. Plate 168 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, depicting a species then known as a rare vagrant to the eastern United States.
audubon-birds-169-mangrove-cuckoo: The Mangrove Cuckoo perches in dense coastal foliage, its buff underparts and black ear-patch picked out against tropical leaves. Audubon recorded the species during his Florida Keys expedition, where he distinguished it from the more familiar Yellow-billed Cuckoo.
audubon-birds-17-carolina-turtle-dove: Carolina (mourning) doves grouped on a flowering branch, their pinkish-buff plumage set against delicate blossoms. The composition uses overlapping figures to create the multi-bird tableaux Audubon favoured for sociable species.
audubon-birds-170-gray-tyrant: A Gray Kingbird perches alertly on a slender stem, its pale grey upperparts and stout black bill rendered with restrained tonal washes. Audubon associated the species with the Florida coast, where it occupies the same exposed perches as its more northerly relative the Eastern Kingbird.
audubon-birds-171-barn-owl: Two barn owls occupy a dramatic nocturnal composition, one perched with a small rodent clasped in its talons. Audubon's hand-coloured aquatint highlights the species' distinctive heart-shaped facial disc and softly mottled buff-and-white plumage against a dark, atmospheric sky. The plate is Plate 171 of Birds of America, engraved by Robert Havell Jr. and held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-172-blue-headed-pigeon: Three Blue-headed Pigeons (Columba cyanocephala) are shown on rocky ground amid low grasses, the male's iridescent blue cap and white throat-stripe contrasting with the chestnut body. Native to Cuba and the Caribbean, the species is depicted here in the sparse, open setting Audubon often reserved for ground-dwelling birds. This is Plate 172 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
audubon-birds-173-barn-swallow: A pair of barn swallows tend their mud-and-grass nest in Plate 173 of Birds of America, one arriving with wings spread and the other perched at the nest entrance. The deep rust-orange throat, steel-blue upperparts, and forked tail are precisely rendered. Audubon's focus on the nesting behaviour rather than isolated specimen poses is characteristic of his approach throughout the folio.
audubon-birds-174-olive-sided-flycatcher: Two olive-sided flycatchers — male above, female below — are shown on a conifer branch bearing blue-grey cones in Plate 174 of Birds of America. The species' characteristic large-headed silhouette, dark flanks, and pale central breast are carefully recorded. The aquatint, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., reflects Audubon's standard practice of depicting both sexes on the same plate.
audubon-birds-175-nuttall-s-lesser-marsh: Marsh wrens perched among reedy stalks, named here for the naturalist Thomas Nuttall. The plate places the small passerines within a habitat vignette, a hallmark of Audubon's life-size approach to ornithological portraiture.
audubon-birds-176-spotted-grous: Four Spotted Grouse (Tetrao canadensis) — three males displaying their vivid red eye-combs and a brown female at left — are grouped among low foliage bearing red berries in Plate 176 of Birds of America. The bold barred and scaled patterning of the males' black-and-white plumage contrasts with the female's streaked brown colouring. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
audubon-birds-177-white-crowned-pigeon: Two White-crowned Pigeons (Columba leucocephala) perch among the dark green foliage and vivid orange trumpet-shaped blossoms of a tropical shrub in Plate 177 of Birds of America. The species' white cap and deep slate-grey body are precisely rendered, with iridescent greenish neck feathers visible on the upper bird. Audubon documented the species from its Caribbean and Floridian range, and the plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
audubon-birds-178-orange-crowned-warbler: Two orange-crowned warblers cling to the slender stems of a flowering shrub bearing small pink-white blossoms in Plate 178 of Birds of America. The species' uniform olive-green plumage and inconspicuous head-stripe are characteristic, the hidden orange crown patch not prominently displayed. The plate was engraved, etched, and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
audubon-birds-179-wood-wren: A single Wood Wren picks its way across a mossy ground-level bank set with red berries and broad botanical leaves in Plate 179 of Birds of America. The bird's tail is raised in the alert posture typical of the family, and its barred brown plumage blends with the earthy setting. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. and depicts one male (Troglodytes americanus).
audubon-birds-18-bewick-s-wren: A single Bewick's Wren perches on a slender leafy branch in Plate 18 of Birds of America, its cocked, barred tail and pale supercilium clearly delineated. Named for the English engraver Thomas Bewick, the species was closely observed by Audubon across the eastern United States. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell and represents the male.
audubon-birds-180-pine-finch: Pine finches (now pine siskins) perched among conifer foliage, with streaked plumage and yellow wing-flashes precisely registered. The plate exemplifies Audubon's dual interest in scientific accuracy and decorative botanical setting.
audubon-birds-181-goldon-eagle: A female adult Golden Eagle grips a white Northern Hare in its talons, wings fanned wide against a stormy mountainous backdrop, in Plate 181 of Birds of America. The plate label reads 'female adult — Northern Hare,' and the composition focuses on the close confrontation between predator and prey at ledge level rather than a mid-air stoop. Audubon's treatment of large raptors favoured dramatic scale, and the plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
audubon-birds-182-ground-dove: Five Common Ground-Doves (Columbina passerina) — two males, a female, and young — are arranged across a leafy branch bearing round green fruits in Plate 182 of Birds of America. The species' small scale, spotted breast, and rufous wing-flashes are accurately recorded across the different plumage stages. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr.
audubon-birds-183-goldon-crested-wren: Two Golden-crested Wrens (kinglets) perch on the stems of a broad-leaved plant bearing grey flowering spikes and large paddle-shaped leaves in Plate 183 of Birds of America. The vivid orange and yellow crown stripes of the male and female are sharply rendered against the birds' olive-green plumage. The plate was engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr. for Audubon's double elephant folio.
audubon-birds-184-mangrove-humming-bird: A mangrove hummingbird hovering at tropical blossoms, its iridescence captured through the layered aquatint process. The plate reflects the broader nineteenth-century fascination with the dazzling plumage of New World hummingbirds.
audubon-birds-185-bachman-s-warbler: Bachman's warbler depicted on a flowering branch, named after Audubon's friend and collaborator the Rev. John Bachman. Once a southern wetland species, the bird is now feared extinct, lending the plate added documentary weight.
audubon-birds-186-pinnated-grous: Pinnated grouse (greater prairie chicken) depicted in a lively group: a male in full display with neck-sacs inflated and pinnae raised, alongside females and a chick, set against an open prairie landscape with yellow lilies. Plate 186 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents the species' courtship behaviour and prairie habitat across male, female, and young plumages.
audubon-birds-187-boat-tailed-grackle: Boat-tailed grackles shown in male and female plumage on a live oak branch bearing acorns and trails of Spanish moss — the plate's own caption names the tree Quercus virens. The iridescent blue-black male and the smaller, warm-brown female are contrasted in size and colouring in Plate 187 of Audubon's Birds of America.
audubon-birds-188-tree-sparrow: Two American tree sparrows perch on fruiting branches hung with small red berries, their rufous caps and characteristic breast-spots carefully rendered. Plate 188 of John James Audubon's Birds of America shows both birds in characteristic poses, foregrounding the plumage study that defines the series.
audubon-birds-189-snow-bunting: Three snow buntings are shown in a coastal or upland setting with hills in the background: one adult in flight displaying bold black-and-white wing pattern, one perched adult in white-and-buff plumage, and one younger, browner bird on the ground. Plate 189 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents adult and immature plumages of this circumpolar species.
audubon-birds-19-louisiana-water-thrush: Parkesia motacilla shown probing along a streamside branch, rendered with the characteristic streaked underparts and bold supercilium. Engraved by Robert Havell Jr. from Audubon's double-elephant folio watercolour, with delicate aquatint tonal washes evoking damp woodland habitat.
audubon-birds-190-yellow-bellied-woodpec: Two yellow-bellied sapsuckers are shown on a branch laden with dark berries, one perched upright and one in a descending posture, both displaying the red crown and strongly patterned black-and-white head that identify the species. Plate 190 of John James Audubon's Birds of America places the birds in a fruiting tree setting rather than on a trunk.
audubon-birds-191-willow-grous-or-large-: A willow ptarmigan male in full summer rufous-and-white plumage stands beside a mottled brown female sheltering a brood of downy chicks on mossy, flower-strewn ground. Plate 191 of John James Audubon's Birds of America captures the species in breeding season, showing male, female, and young together and documenting the feathered legs and feet that are a key adaptation to Arctic conditions.
audubon-birds-192-great-american-shrike-: Four northern shrikes are arranged on a hawthorn branch bearing clusters of red berries, their grey, black, and white plumage precisely recorded across different postures. Plate 192 of John James Audubon's Birds of America presents multiple individuals of the species known as the Butcher Bird, combining naturalistic observation with the compositional drama Audubon favoured for larger passerines.
audubon-birds-193-lincoln-finch: Lincoln's sparrow depicted on a flowering branch, named for Audubon's young Labrador-expedition companion Thomas Lincoln. Subtly streaked plumage and a buff malar stripe distinguish the species from related sparrows.
audubon-birds-194-canadian-titmouse: Boreal chickadees, then called Canadian titmice, are shown clinging to deciduous berry-bearing branches in various active postures. Plate 194 of John James Audubon's Birds of America records the species' distinctive brown cap — which distinguishes it from the black-capped chickadee — across male, female, and young plumages.
audubon-birds-195-ruby-crowned-wren: Ruby-crowned kinglets shown among slender sprigs, the male displaying the scarlet crown-patch usually concealed beneath olive feathers. The miniature scale required especially fine aquatint work in the Havell engraving.
audubon-birds-196-labrador-falcon: Two Labrador falcons — a dark morph of the gyrfalcon — are shown on bare branches, one perched compactly from above and one with wings partially spread looking upward, both rendered in very dark grey-black plumage. Plate 196 of John James Audubon's Birds of America shows male and female adults and reflects observations Audubon made during his 1833 Labrador expedition.
audubon-birds-197-american-crossbill: Red crossbills feeding among conifer cones, the unique mandible crossing essential to their seed-extraction technique clearly visible. The composition unites diet, habitat and anatomy in a single life-size study.
audubon-birds-198-brown-headed-worm-eati: A worm-eating warbler perched on slender vegetation, the bold dark head-stripes that identify the species precisely registered. The plate shows the typical aquatint-and-watercolour layering of the Havell-engraved double elephant folio.
audubon-birds-199-little-owl: Two owls are depicted: one perched on a bare branch in three-quarter view, and a second shown on a rocky outcrop with wings spread wide, securing a small mammal in its talons. The plate is labelled Plate CXCIX of Birds of America by John James Audubon, with the Latin Strix acadica identifying the North American species Audubon called the Little Owl, now the Northern Saw-whet Owl. Hand-applied colour over aquatint models the warm brown upperparts and streaked white underparts characteristic of the species.
audubon-birds-2-yellow-billed-cuckoo: Two Yellow-billed Cuckoos are depicted among the large leaves and ripening fruit of a pawpaw, with a tiger swallowtail butterfly resting on the foliage. The elongated S-curve formed by the birds' bodies became a hallmark of the early Birds of America plates. Plate 2 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-20-blue-winged-yellow-warb: Two Blue-winged Yellow Warblers are arranged on the stems and blooms of a rose mallow (Hibiscus grandiflorus), the large pale-pink flowers providing a bold counterpoint to the birds' yellow underparts and dark wings. The pose, with one bird clinging to a stem and the other perched below, reflects Audubon's practice of wiring fresh specimens into lifelike attitudes. Plate 20 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-200-shore-lark: Four Shore Larks in varying plumages—adult male with black facial mask and horns, a winter-plumage adult, and juveniles—are shown in and around a nest set in dense green low vegetation. The composition illustrates the species' life history rather than a single field pose. Plate 200 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-201-canada-goose: A large Canada Goose fills the sheet in a near-vertical composition, its black neck extended and bill open, set against marsh reeds and willow foliage. A second bird is partially visible in the lower foreground. The crisply rendered black head and neck, white chinstrap, and soft brown body plumage are characteristic of Audubon's treatment of large waterfowl. Plate 201 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-202-red-throated-diver: Four Red-throated Divers in different plumages are depicted: a large standing bird in spotted winter dress beside marsh plants including pitcher plants, two swimming birds showing summer breeding plumage with the distinctive rust-red throat patch, and a fourth turning away. The arrangement across breeding and non-breeding plumages makes Plate 202 of Birds of America by John James Audubon a comprehensive reference for the species, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-203-fresh-water-marsh-hen: King rail, Rallus elegans, drawn skulking among reeds with neck extended in characteristic cautious gait. Fine etched lines build the barred flank pattern, while aquatint shading establishes the dim, vegetated marsh interior.
audubon-birds-204-salt-water-marsh-hen: Rallus crepitans set within tidal cordgrass, the long bill and laterally compressed body conveying its furtive habits in salt marshes. Subtle tonal aquatint distinguishes the muted ochre and grey plumage suited to coastal camouflage.
audubon-birds-205-virginia-rail: Three Virginia Rails are depicted at a marsh edge among reeds: one adult strides forward, a second raises its bill sharply skyward, and a juvenile crouches in the lower right. The plate captures different ages and postures of the species, with the characteristic long reddish bill and barred flanks carefully rendered. Plate 205 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-206-summer-or-wood-duck: Aix sponsa shown in arboreal habit suggested by overhanging foliage, the drake's iridescent crest and bold facial striping rendered in saturated hand-applied watercolour over aquatint. A favoured Audubon subject for its colour and behaviour.
audubon-birds-207-booby-gannet: Sula leucogaster perched in profile, the wedge-shaped bill and dark mantle contrasted against pale underparts. The composition reflects observations from Audubon's Florida and Gulf coast voyages aboard the Marion in the 1830s.
audubon-birds-208-esquimaux-curlew: Numenius borealis shown probing tundra ground, the slender decurved bill carefully traced. The species was already in steep decline during Audubon's lifetime and is now likely extinct, lending the plate documentary value.
audubon-birds-209-wilson-s-plover: Two Wilson's Plovers—identified by the plate label as male and female—are shown on a sandy coastal margin, one standing upright and the other crouching to probe the ground. The species' heavy black bill and single dark breast band are rendered with precision against the pale sandy setting. Plate 209 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-21-mocking-bird: Mimus polyglottos engaged with a coiled rattlesnake amid yellow jessamine vines, one of Audubon's most narrative compositions. The dramatic encounter drew scientific criticism over snake-climbing accuracy but established the plate's enduring fame.
audubon-birds-210-least-bittern: Three Least Bitterns are shown in marsh reeds: one adult to the left in a low horizontal stance, and two central birds adopting the species' characteristic alarm posture with bills pointed skyward and streaked buff plumage blending into the surrounding stems. The composition illustrates both typical foraging and concealment behaviours. Plate 210 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-211-great-blue-heron: Ardea herodias rendered at full life size by bending the long neck and legs to fit the double-elephant folio sheet. Aquatint and watercolour build the slate-grey body and shaggy plumes, with marshland horizon barely indicated.
audubon-birds-212-common-gull: Larus canus, as Audubon labelled the species, shown as an adult and a young bird standing on a grassy rise, the adult's soft grey mantle and yellow bill described in muted aquatint washes. A relatively restrained composition typical of plates devoted to widespread coastal species.
audubon-birds-213-puffin: Atlantic puffin, Fratercula arctica, shown with breeding-season bill ornament and orange feet. The plate likely draws on observations from Audubon's 1833 expedition to Labrador, where he studied seabird colonies first-hand.
audubon-birds-214-razor-bill: Alca torda depicted in two figures — male and female — swimming on choppy water before a cliff coastline, with the species' characteristic laterally flattened bill and white vertical stripe faithfully rendered. The dark upperparts and clean white underparts show the sharp tonal contrast of breeding plumage. Plate 214 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-215-hyperborean-phalarope: Phalaropus hyperboreus (red-necked phalarope) shown in three individuals: one in flight with wings spread and rufous neck markings visible, one swimming among marsh debris, and one wading in shallower water. The plate illustrates both sexes and the species' aquatic habits, with the needle-thin bill prominent in each pose. Plate 215 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-216-wood-ibiss: Mycteria americana (wood stork) shown stooping over a log at water's edge, the long decurved bill directed toward the ground and the bare, darkly scaled head characteristic of the species clearly delineated. White body plumage contrasts with black flight feathers, set against a wetland background of cypress and water. Plate 216 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-217-louisiana-heron: Tricolored heron, Egretta tricolor, captured in a sinuous wading pose with white belly stripe set against slate body. The dynamic curve of the neck typifies Audubon's preference for active, narrative postures over static specimen views.
audubon-birds-218-foolish-guillemot: Common murre, Uria aalge, shown in profile with the pointed bill and dark upperparts of breeding plumage. The plate reflects observations from Audubon's Labrador voyage among dense seabird cliffs.
audubon-birds-219-black-guillemot: Cepphus grylle in breeding plumage, the sooty body relieved by a striking white wing patch and red feet rendered in saturated watercolour. The cliff-perched composition evokes North Atlantic colony habitat.
audubon-birds-22-purple-martin: Several purple martins gather around a hollow gourd nest, the glossy blue-black males and duller females shown in the cooperative groupings typical of the colony-nesting swallow. The plate documents an early form of artificial nest box used by southern planters, embedding ethnography within ornithological observation.
audubon-birds-220-piping-plover: Charadrius melodus on pale sand, the bird's sandy-buff back and partial neck band described with minimal etched line. The sparse beach setting reflects the species' preference for open Atlantic shoreline.
audubon-birds-221-mallard-duck: Anas platyrhynchos shown in a group of males and females amid tall marsh vegetation, the drakes' bottle-green heads and chestnut breasts contrasting with the streaked brown plumage of the hens. A blue speculum is visible on the foreground female. Plate 221 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-222-white-ibis: Eudocimus albus rendered in two individuals: a white adult with long pink decurved bill, black wingtips, and pink legs, facing a heavily brown-plumaged immature bird with a yellowish bill. A small crayfish at lower left adds habitat context. Plate 222 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-223-pied-oyster-catcher: Haematopus palliatus depicted in active running pose along a surf-washed shoreline, the long vivid-red bill, black hood, and white underparts rendered with bold tonal contrast. Waves and a sandy beach constitute the entire background, placing the bird firmly in its coastal habitat. Plate 223 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-224-kittiwake-gull: Rissa tridactyla rendered with the species' clean grey mantle and black wingtips, perched on rocks suggestive of ocean cliffs. The plate's restrained palette emphasises the kittiwake's pelagic, colony-nesting life.
audubon-birds-225-kildeer-plover: Charadrius vociferus shown in two figures on a rocky shore: one standing upright and alert, the second in a spread-wing distraction display that exposes the vivid russet rump. The double black breast bands are clearly depicted on both individuals. Plate 225 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-226-hooping-crane: A whooping crane bows its long neck to seize a young alligator from a marshy Louisiana shoreline, with additional hatchlings scattering through the grass. Composed in stages between 1821 and 1822, the plate combines on-the-spot field study with a later background, and depicts the bird at full life-size by twisting its neck downward.
audubon-birds-227-pin-tailed-duck: A drake northern pintail and his mate are paired against a watery margin, the male's chocolate head and slender tail-spike contrasted with the hen's softer scalloping. The aquatint records the species' elegant body line and the fine vermiculation across the flanks that Audubon studied closely from skinned specimens.
audubon-birds-228-american-green-winged-: Drake and hen green-winged teal stand on a rocky bank, the male's chestnut head marked by an iridescent green eye-mask and the speculum displaying its metallic green patch. The hen shows the species' typical brown, finely scalloped plumage. Plate 228 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-229-scaup-duck: A drake and hen scaup rest on a bank before marsh grasses, the male's dark iridescent head and finely vermiculated back contrasted with the female's brown plumage and pale facial patch. The blue-grey bill and compact body typical of the species are clearly rendered. Plate 229 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-23-yellow-breasted-warbler: A small yellow-breasted warbler perches among slim foliage, its citron underparts and olive back rendered with fine stipple. The plate reflects Audubon's effort to document the still-unsettled nomenclature of North American wood-warblers, several of which were known by names that have since been revised.
audubon-birds-230-ruddy-plover: Two sanderlings, here called Ruddy Plover, are shown on a rocky coastal slope in pale transitional plumage, with islands visible across the water behind them. Audubon rendered the species' compact form and scalloped upperparts against a broad shoreline setting. Plate 230 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-231-long-billed-curlew: Two long-billed curlews stand among tall marsh reeds, their enormous decurved bills and cinnamon-buff plumage rendered at close range against a distant view of Charleston harbour. Audubon's use of a recognisable city skyline as backdrop is unusual for the series. Plate 231 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-232-hooded-merganser: A drake hooded merganser raises his fan-shaped black-and-white crest while the hen stands alongside on a rocky bank, her shaggy rust-coloured tuft erect. The plate emphasises the saw-edged bill and the bold pied pattern of the breeding male. Plate 232 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-233-sora-or-rail: Three soras — male, female, and young — are shown on a fallen log amid marsh grasses, the adults displaying the species' yellow bill, dark facial mask, and barred flanks, while the young bird shows plainer buff tones. Audubon used the dense reed setting to suggest the species' preference for dense cover. Plate 233 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-234-tufted-duck: A drake and hen tufted duck stand on low grassy ground, the male's drooping black crest and golden eye contrasted with his bold black-and-white body, while the brown hen rests alongside. Plate 234 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838, depicts this Eurasian diving duck.
audubon-birds-235-sooty-tern: A sooty tern banks in flight, its dark upperparts and white underparts and forehead resolved against a pale clouded sky. The plate captures the species' deeply forked tail and swept-back wings in a spare, aerial composition. Plate 235 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-236-night-heron-or-qua-bir: An adult and an immature black-crowned night heron stand side by side in dense marsh vegetation, the sleek slate-and-white adult leaning toward the water and the streaky brown juvenile standing upright nearby. The plate presents the species' dramatic age-related plumage change in a single composition. Plate 236 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-237-great-esquimaux-curlew: An Eskimo curlew stands on open ground amid coastal grasses, its slender decurved bill raised, the streaked buff-and-brown plumage rendered at life-size. The plate is a significant record of a species that was abundant in Audubon's day and is now feared extinct. Plate 237 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-238-great-marbled-godwit: Two marbled godwits stand among coastal grasses, their long slightly upturned bicoloured bills and rich cinnamon plumage with barred upperparts clearly shown. Audubon's composition presents both birds against a backdrop of reeds and low vegetation. Plate 238 of Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-239-american-coot: An American coot strides along a muddy bank before a stand of reeds, the white frontal shield and ivory bill conspicuous against the slate-black plumage. Its large lobed toes are prominently displayed, distinguishing the species from the ducks with which it shares its habitat. Plate 239 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-24-roscoe-s-yellow-throat: A small yellow-throated warbler perches on a slender twig, the throat and breast a saturated lemon yellow against an olive back. The name Roscoe's Yellow-throat reflects nineteenth-century nomenclatural confusion that ornithology later resolved by folding the bird into established species.
audubon-birds-240-roseate-tern: A roseate tern plunges in a steep dive against a blue-grey ground, its deeply forked tail and long wings spread wide. The pale grey mantle and faintly pink-flushed underparts distinguish it from related species, while the orange-red bill — tipped dark — is clearly rendered in Audubon's hand-coloured aquatint. Plate 240 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by R. Havell, London.
audubon-birds-241-black-backed-gull: A great black-backed gull is shown with wings fully spread and bill open wide, its glossy slate-black mantle contrasted with white underparts and a heavy yellow bill marked by a red gonys spot. The dynamic composition — the bird calling or landing on a grassy coastal bank — conveys the formidable scale of the world's largest gull. Plate 241 of John James Audubon's Birds of America; a small overhead view of the bird in flight appears in the upper right.
audubon-birds-242-snowy-heron-or-white-e: A snowy egret in full breeding plumage stands on a muddy bank amid marsh vegetation, its golden-yellow feet prominent against dark ground and the long aigrette plumes cascading from back and breast. A distant background shows a plantation landscape with buildings and a river. Plate 242 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Egretta thula and drawn from a South Carolina locality.
audubon-birds-243-american-snipe: Three American snipe are shown on a muddy bank among reeds, with a riverside landscape visible behind. One bird stands alert with bill raised, while the others crouch low, their cryptic striped-and-barred plumage blending against the vegetation. Plate 243 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Male 1, Female 2, 3 and identified as Scolopax Wilsonii.
audubon-birds-244-common-gallinule: A common gallinule strides across a rocky bank at the water's edge, its bright red frontal shield and yellow-tipped bill catching the eye against dark slate plumage. The long greenish legs and splayed toes that adapt the species to wetland habitats are clearly delineated. Plate 244 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Gallinula chloropus.
audubon-birds-245-thick-billed-murre: A thick-billed murre is shown in low flight over an open sea, its black-and-white plumage and stout bill captured mid-wingbeat above choppy water. The horizontal flight pose was a compositional choice that emphasises the species' powerful, rapid flight over northern oceans. Plate 245 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Uria Brunnichii.
audubon-birds-246-eider-duck: Several common eiders are grouped on land among dense reeds: drakes display bold black-and-white plumage with the pale green nape characteristic of the species, while a brown hen is visible among them. Plate 246 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Male 1, Female 2 and identified as Fuligula Mollissima.
audubon-birds-247-velvet-duck: A white-winged scoter, here called Velvet Duck, floats on coastal water, the drake's velvety black plumage broken by a white wing patch and a knobbed orange bill. Aquatint reproduces the matte quality of the breeding plumage that gave the species its old name.
audubon-birds-248-american-pied-bill-dob: A pied-billed grebe sits on calm water, the short dark-banded ivory bill and stub-tailed silhouette giving the species its archaic name. The plate emphasises the lobed feet barely visible below the surface, the same structural feature shared with coots and other grebes.
audubon-birds-249-tufted-auk: Two birds occupy the plate: a large tufted puffin stands in profile on rocky ground, its white facial plumes, pale eye, and large orange-and-yellow bill clearly rendered; beside it a second, smaller bird is shown face-on. Plate 249 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Tufted Auk and identified as Mormon Cirrhatus, Male 1, Female 2.
audubon-birds-25-song-sparrow: Song sparrows perched on a flowering branch, their streaked breasts and warm brown backs picked out in fine engraved line. Audubon places the birds in active poses that suggest the territorial singing for which the species is named across North America.
audubon-birds-250-arctic-tern: An Arctic tern hovers with deeply forked tail and short red legs trailing, the blood-red bill held downward as it scans for fish. The plate captures the proportions of the famously long-distance migrant, whose annual journey between polar oceans Audubon could only have suspected.
audubon-birds-251-brown-pelican: A brown pelican perches on a mangrove branch, its huge gular pouch slack and the chestnut-and-cream nape of breeding plumage clearly registered. Audubon studied the species at close range during his 1832 Florida voyage, allowing the life-size composition to bend the bird into a natural resting posture.
audubon-birds-252-florida-cormorant: A Florida cormorant perches on a broken stump above open water, its neck arched and bright orange gular pouch fully exposed in an alert, calling pose. The dark iridescent plumage and hooked bill are precisely rendered, with a flock of cormorants visible on the water in the distance. Plate 252 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, identified as Carbo Floridanus in spring plumage.
audubon-birds-253-jager: A jaeger perched on a grassy coastal mound, an open oyster shell beside it and icy peaks visible in the distant background. The bird's dark brown upperparts and pale streaked breast are rendered with characteristic precision. Plate 253 of Audubon's Birds of America documents this pelagic seabird, known for its habit of pursuing other birds to steal their catches.
audubon-birds-254-wilson-s-phalarope: Two Wilson's phalaropes depicted in contrasting poses: one bird in flight displaying the chestnut and rufous tones of breeding plumage, the other crouching near reedy water. Audubon's Plate 254 captures both male and female, their needle-fine bills clearly detailed. Wilson's phalarope is notable among shorebirds for its reversed sex-role display during the breeding season.
audubon-birds-255-red-phalarope: Red phalaropes depicted in their rust-coloured summer dress, slender bills probing at the water's edge. Hand-coloured aquatint by Robert Havell Jr. brings out the contrast between the rich plumage and the muted tones of the Arctic-tinged habitat.
audubon-birds-256-purple-heron: Two herons fill Plate 256: an adult in dark breeding plumage with a striking rust-orange neck and shaggy crest, and a white-plumaged bird standing beside lush tropical foliage. The dark bird's vivid blue legs and upright, alert stance contrast with the quieter posture of its companion. Audubon based the plate on Ardea refescens, the reddish egret, recording both colour morphs of the species.
audubon-birds-257-double-crested-cormora: A double-crested cormorant perched on a rocky coastal outcrop, its two wispy nuptial tufts fanned above a glossy green-black head. The bird faces left against a background of cliffs and distant water. Plate 257 of Birds of America presents the male in adult spring plumage, the iridescent dark plumage and long hooked bill clearly articulated.
audubon-birds-258-hudsonian-godwit: Two Hudsonian godwits share the plate: the left bird in rich cinnamon breeding plumage with wings raised, the right in plainer brownish non-breeding dress. The slightly upturned bill characteristic of the species is evident on both. Audubon's Plate 258 of Birds of America records male, female, and seasonal plumage in a single composition, set against a bare tidal flat.
audubon-birds-259-horned-grebe: Two horned grebes appear side by side in Plate 259: the left bird in vivid breeding plumage with golden ear tufts, chestnut neck, and dark cap, the right in sober winter dress of dark grey above and white below. Both birds are shown at the water's edge against a backdrop of reeds. Audubon's treatment of the species captures the dramatic seasonal transformation in a single plate.
audubon-birds-26-carolina-parrot: Carolina parakeets clustered on a cocklebur branch, their green bodies and yellow-and-orange heads brilliantly hand-coloured. Audubon's plate is now bittersweet documentation of the only parrot native to the eastern United States, driven to extinction by the early twentieth century.
audubon-birds-260-fork-tail-petrel: Two fork-tailed petrels are shown banking over breaking ocean waves in Plate 260, their dark brown plumage contrasting with white rump patches and pale underwings. The forked tail of the upper bird is clearly visible as it crests a wave. The Birds of America plate — engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr. — conveys the stormy pelagic conditions this small storm-petrel inhabits.
audubon-birds-261-hooping-crane: A young whooping crane stands on open grassland in Plate 261, its grey-brown plumage and red forehead patch identifying it as an immature bird; white adults are visible in the distant marsh background. The bird's great height fills the double-elephant sheet, bill open and neck arched. Audubon chose to depict the juvenile plumage, a species already declining during his lifetime and now the subject of intensive conservation efforts.
audubon-birds-262-tropic-bird: A tropicbird rendered with elongated tail streamers trailing behind a stout white body. The plate evokes the species' offshore wanderings across warm seas, where it plunge-dives for squid and flying fish far from any coast.
audubon-birds-263-pigmy-curlew: A pygmy curlew, today known as the curlew sandpiper, depicted with its decurved bill probing at the tide line. Audubon's aquatint records a Eurasian visitor to North American shores, in transitional plumage between the rufous breeding dress and pale winter coat.
audubon-birds-264-fulmar-petrel: A fulmar perched on a moss-covered rock in Plate 264, its white head and underparts contrasting with pale grey wings against a stormy sky and choppy sea. The bird's yellow tube-nosed bill is clearly shown in profile. Audubon's plate of Fulmarus glacialis presents the male in adult summer plumage, capturing the stocky, gull-like form of this North Atlantic seabird.
audubon-birds-265-buff-breasted-sandpipe: Two buff-breasted sandpipers appear in Plate 265, one walking on a sandy shore and one perched on a rock with wings partly raised. Both show the soft ochre tones, plain dove-like face, and yellow-orange legs that typify the species. Audubon's hand-coloured plate presents male and female, the upright bearing and open-country habitat well conveyed.
audubon-birds-266-common-cormorant: Plate 266 depicts a great cormorant nest scene on a cliff ledge: one adult leans over a nest of seaweed to feed two gaping chicks, while a second adult stands upright beside the nest calling with bill agape. The iridescent dark plumage, white facial patch, and yellow gular skin of the adults are finely rendered. Audubon's composition is one of his most animated breeding scenes in Birds of America.
audubon-birds-267-arctic-yager: A long-tailed jaeger shown over open water, the slender central rectrices streaming behind a sharply patterned body. The plate documents a high-Arctic breeder that follows seabird colonies south, robbing them of their catch in piratical chases.
audubon-birds-268-american-woodcock: Three American woodcocks are shown among tall reeds and marsh grasses at the water's edge, with one bird rising in a wing-spread display. Audubon captures the mottled brown-and-buff plumage that provides cryptic cover in wetland vegetation, and the long bill and high-set eyes adapted for probing damp ground. Plate 268 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-269-greenshank: A greenshank standing tall on its namesake olive-green legs, slightly upturned bill held alert. The aquatint records a Eurasian wader that occasionally appears on American shores, with the soft grey-and-white winter plumage carefully picked out.
audubon-birds-27-red-headed-woodpecker: Plate 27 depicts adult red-headed woodpeckers — crimson head, white belly, and ink-black wings with bold white secondaries — attending young birds at a nest cavity in a weathered dead tree. Audubon records both flying adults and nestlings at different stages, documenting the species across its life cycle. The plate is from Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-270-stormy-petrel: A storm petrel skimming low over the waves, its small dark form and white rump patch finely engraved. The plate captures the swallow-like flight by which these tiny seabirds patter across the surface, picking at oily morsels in open water.
audubon-birds-271-frigate-pelican: A male magnificent frigatebird fills the plate in Audubon's characteristic close-up style, its deeply forked tail and angular wings spread wide against a plain ground. The long, hooked bill and iridescent black plumage are recorded in detail, with two isolated feet depicted as anatomical references at the top of the sheet. Plate 271 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-272-richardson-s-jager: A parasitic jaeger, here under its older name honouring the Arctic naturalist Sir John Richardson, shown as a pale-bellied adult alongside a barred young bird in September plumage. The plate captures the falcon-like wings and pointed central tail feathers used in agile aerial pursuits of terns and small gulls.
audubon-birds-273-cayenne-tern: A Cayenne tern stands on a sandy shore beside a large pink crab, its shaggy black crest and distinctive orange-red bill rendered in careful profile. The species — now treated as a subspecies of the Sandwich tern — is shown in adult breeding plumage with pale grey upperparts and white underparts. Plate 273 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-274-semipalmated-snipe-or-: A willet in breeding plumage, the long straight bill and grey-brown body opening to reveal the striking black-and-white wing pattern in flight. Audubon's plate shows both standing and flying postures to record the field marks that emerge only when the wings unfold.
audubon-birds-275-noddy-tern: A brown noddy with its sooty body and pale cap, perched on a tropical branch. The plate reflects the species' colonial nesting on warm-water islands, where birds build flat platforms in low trees rather than scraping in the sand like most terns.
audubon-birds-276-king-duck: Audubon pairs a male king eider — slate-blue crown, vivid green cheek patches, and bulbous orange-pink forehead shield — with a soberly barred brown female against an Arctic coastal backdrop. The dramatic sexual dimorphism of the species is the plate's central subject, with the male standing tall on a rock and the female resting at the water's edge. Plate 276 of Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-277-hutchins-s-barnacle-go: A small Canada goose form, then named for naval officer Thomas Hutchins, depicted standing alert on tundra ground. The plate captures the compact body and short neck that distinguish this northern subspecies, now generally treated as a cackling goose by ornithologists.
audubon-birds-278-schinz-s-sandpiper-res: A small sandpiper attributed to Schinz, with the streaked breast and decurved bill that fit it equally to a dunlin or white-rumped sandpiper. The plate stands at the centre of a long taxonomic confusion stretching from Brehm's 1822 description through Bonaparte and Coues.
audubon-birds-279-cabot-s-tern: A Cabot's tern with shaggy black crest and yellow bill tip, rendered in clean profile against the page. The aquatint marks this American population of what was long considered a Sandwich tern, whose taxonomic status has shifted between subspecies and full species over time.
audubon-birds-28-solitary-flycatcher-or-: A small olive-and-white songbird with bold white spectacles, perched among foliage. Now known as the Blue-headed Vireo, the plate captures the deliberate, gleaning movements that distinguish vireos from the more aerial true flycatchers.
audubon-birds-280-black-tern: Plate 280 pairs an adult black tern in full sooty breeding plumage, perched on a rock, with a pale grey-and-white non-breeding or juvenile bird shown diving overhead. Audubon's composition records both seasonal plumages in a single sheet, documenting the species' distinctive transformation between its dark summer coat and the pale winter dress. From Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-281-great-white-heron: A towering all-white heron with a heavy yellow bill grasps a fish on a sandy bank, with water and a distant shoreline behind it. Audubon treated the Great White Heron as a species distinct from the Great Blue Heron, and the bird's dramatically arched neck — required to fit the double-elephant folio sheet at near life size — gives the plate its striking silhouette. Plate 281 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-282-white-winged-silvery-g: Two pale grey-and-white gulls are shown on rocky ground — one leaning forward as if foraging, the other at rest — against a dark cloudy sky. The White-winged Silvery Gull, now known as the Iceland Gull, was among the northern species Audubon documented in the later numbers of Birds of America. Plate 282, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-283-wandering-shearwater: A dark-backed, white-bellied shearwater stands on a low rocky ledge beside calm water, with mountains visible in the distance. The contrast between the bird's dark upperparts and white underparts — a characteristic of the species — is clearly rendered in the plate. Plate 283 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-284-purple-sandpiper: Three Purple Sandpipers in varying plumage are shown on rocky outcrops by the water's edge, their dark, mottled backs and yellowish-orange legs clearly depicted against the pale stone. The species favours wave-washed rocky shores along North Atlantic coasts, and Audubon's composition captures several individuals in close proximity on such a habitat. Plate 284 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-285-fork-tailed-gull: A Fork-tailed Gull with a dark grey hood and forked tail perches on a rock, while a smaller shorebird forages on the sandy ground nearby. The gull's pale grey mantle, white underparts, and distinctive tail are faithfully rendered against a calm riverine background. Plate 285 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-286-white-fronted-goose: A male and female White-fronted Goose are shown together in a marsh setting, both displaying the species' characteristic white facial blaze, barred belly, and pink bill against dark brown-grey plumage. The standing male faces left while the female stretches her wings with a boldly patterned dark flight feather spread. Plate 286 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-287-ivory-gull: Two Ivory Gulls — an adult in pure white plumage and a juvenile with dark spotting — stand on rocky, lichen-covered ground beside scattered shells, against a grey overcast sky. The adult's black legs and yellow bill are clearly rendered, with the lobed feet of the juvenile also visible. Plate 287 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-288-yellow-shank: A single Yellow Shank with bright yellow legs stands among tall grasses at the edge of a wide river, surrounded by moss-draped trees in a richly coloured southern landscape. The species, now called the Greater Yellowlegs, is shown in the wooded wetland setting where Audubon observed it along the coasts and rivers of North America. Plate 288 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-289-solitary-sandpiper: Two Solitary Sandpipers are shown in a marshy setting among reeds and broad-leaved plants, one with wings raised in display and the other alert on the opposite bank. The species' spotted, dark-backed plumage and white eye-ring are well rendered in Audubon's composition. Plate 289 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-29-towhe-bunting: A male Towhe Bunting with a black hood, rufous flanks, and white belly perches on a thorny branch above a brown-hooded female in a tangle of brambles and flowering shrubs. The plate corresponds to the Eastern Towhee, and Audubon's two-bird composition shows the strong sexual plumage dimorphism of the species. Plate 29 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-290-red-backed-sandpiper: Two Red-backed Sandpipers are shown on a rocky shore: a winter-plumaged bird in grey on the left and a breeding-plumaged bird with brick-red upperparts and a black belly patch on the right. The pairing to show both seasonal plumages was a characteristic device in the later plates of Birds of America. Plate 290, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-291-herring-gull: An adult Herring Gull with grey mantle and yellow bill soars overhead while a mottled immature bird stands on a rocky shore below, its brown-streaked plumage contrasting with the adult's clean grey and white. The composition illustrating multiple age plumages in a single plate is a recurring feature of Audubon's gull sequences. Plate 291 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-292-crested-grebe: Two Crested Grebes ride choppy waves, one calling with bill raised and chestnut-and-black head plumes fanned in display, the other holding a lower posture with neck curved. A careful study of the lobed foot is inset in the upper right corner. Plate 292 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-293-large-billed-puffin: A Large-billed Puffin stands on a low flat rock at the water's edge while a second bird floats on the sea behind it, with a mountain headland visible in the distance. The species' deep, ridged orange-and-yellow bill and black-and-white plumage are rendered in detail. Plate 293 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-294-pectoral-sandpiper: Two Pectoral Sandpipers stand on a sandy, shell-strewn coastal shore with water and low hills behind them, the male slightly larger than the female. The species' sharply demarcated streaked breast band and warm brown-and-chestnut upperparts are clearly depicted. Plate 294 of Birds of America by John James Audubon, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-295-manks-shearwater: Plate 295 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a Manks Shearwater perched on the sea surface, dark brown-black above and white below, with a rocky coastal headland visible in the background. The species — a transatlantic pelagic seabird — is rendered in profile, its pale underparts contrasting sharply with the deep colouring of the back and wings.
audubon-birds-296-barnacle-goose: Plate 296 of Birds of America shows two Barnacle Geese on open rocky terrain, each displaying the species' distinctive white face, jet-black neck and breast, and silvery grey barred back. Audubon's text noted the medieval legend that the birds hatched from goose-barnacles, a belief the plate's natural-history framing quietly refutes by grounding the species in its actual coastal and grassland habitat.
audubon-birds-297-harlequin-duck: Plate 297 of Birds of America presents three Harlequin Ducks — a brilliantly marked adult male in full breeding plumage, a second male in duller eclipse dress, and a soberly mottled brown female — arranged on a rocky shore with a coastal cliff visible beyond.
