The adult male's slate-blue, chestnut, and white markings are rendered with characteristic precision, illustrating the sexual dimorphism of a species associated with turbulent mountain streams and surf-washed coastlines.
audubon-birds-298-red-necked-grebe: Plate 298 of Birds of America depicts two Red-necked Grebes on a grassy bank with a landscape of cliffs and water behind them. The left-hand bird is in rich breeding plumage — a deep chestnut neck and dark cap with small reddish eye — while the right-hand bird shows the greyer winter dress, its yellow-tipped bill clearly rendered. The contrast between the two seasonal plumages is the plate's central ornithological subject.
audubon-birds-299-dusky-petrel: Plate 299 of Birds of America depicts a Dusky Petrel in low flight above open ocean, the bird's dark upperparts and pale underparts silhouetted against a coastal headland backdrop. The slender wings are held straight and the tail is fanned, capturing the effortless gliding posture characteristic of petrels in flight. Audubon included the species in the double-elephant folio as part of his effort to document the full range of North American seabirds.
audubon-birds-3-prothonotary-warbler-res: Brilliant golden-yellow warblers move through a tangle of cane and creeper at the edge of a southern swamp. Audubon drew the species in the bottomland habitat where it nests in flooded tree cavities, a detail he stressed in the accompanying Ornithological Biography.
audubon-birds-30-vigor-s-warbler: Plate 30 of Birds of America depicts a single Vigor's Warbler — a small, yellowish wood warbler — perched on a broad-leaved plant bearing purple-red blossoms, identified in the plate caption as Virginia spiderwort. Audubon named the species in honour of British zoologist Nicholas Aylward Vigors; the bird is now regarded as a probable hybrid or misidentified specimen, making the plate a notable artefact of early American ornithological taxonomy.
audubon-birds-300-golden-plover: Plate 300 of Birds of America presents three American Golden Plovers in different plumages and attitudes — one standing bird in mottled transitional plumage, one in crouching summer dress with dark belly patches, and one bird in flight overhead showing the spangled gold-and-black upperparts. Audubon documented this long-distance migrant whose vast autumn flocks were heavily hunted throughout the nineteenth century, and the multi-pose composition conveys both seasonal variation and the species' dynamic behaviour.
audubon-birds-301-canvas-backed-duck: Plate 301 of Birds of America depicts three Canvas-backed Ducks — two males with their rich chestnut heads, black breasts, and pale grey backs, and one brown female — arranged at the water's edge with a distant harbour and city skyline in the background, generally identified as Baltimore on the Chesapeake Bay. Audubon's plate documents the species whose taste for wild celery made it highly prized by nineteenth-century market hunters.
audubon-birds-302-dusky-duck: Plate 302 of Birds of America shows two Dusky Ducks on a grassy bank beside open water, one standing and one with wings raised and spread. Both birds display the species' uniformly dark brown mottled plumage, yellow-green bills, and a flash of iridescent blue-purple on the secondaries — the features Audubon used to distinguish what is now called the American Black Duck from the closely related Mallard.
audubon-birds-303-bartram-sandpiper: Plate 303 of Birds of America depicts two Bartram's Sandpipers in dynamic action — one in mid-air with wings fully spread, bill open as it pursues an insect, and one crouching at the water's edge before a backdrop of flowering tropical vegetation. The species, now called the Upland Sandpiper, was named by Audubon in honour of the Philadelphia naturalist William Bartram, and the plate's energetic composition is among the more animated in the series.
audubon-birds-304-turn-stone: Plate 304 of Birds of America shows two Ruddy Turnstones: one in vigorous flight, wings fully spread to display the striking orange-chestnut, black, and white pattern that distinguishes the species, and one standing on a sandy shore in slightly duller plumage. The hand-coloured aquatint captures the harlequin boldness of the breeding male's markings, making this one of the most visually striking shorebird plates in the folio.
audubon-birds-305-purple-gallinule: Plate 305 of Birds of America presents a single adult Purple Gallinule striding along an open bank with a river and distant marsh vegetation behind it. The bird's iridescent blue-violet plumage, green-tinged back, red-and-yellow bill with a pale blue frontal shield, and long yellow-green toes are rendered with precision in the hand-coloured aquatint. Audubon depicted the species in adult spring plumage, as noted in the plate's caption.
audubon-birds-306-great-northern-diver-o: Plate 306 of Birds of America depicts two Common Loons: a large adult in full breeding plumage — iridescent dark green head, white-spotted black back, and striped neck — standing upright among reeds with bill open, and a smaller winter-plumaged or immature bird floating on the water in the left background. The life-size rendering of the two birds across the double-elephant folio sheet conveys both the adult's dramatic patterning and the contrast with the greyer immature plumage.
audubon-birds-307-blue-crane-or-heron: Plate 307 of Birds of America depicts a Little Blue Heron in adult spring plumage, standing tall and alert on a muddy bank with reeds and a broad marshland backdrop. The slate-blue body and darker bluish head and neck are precisely rendered, with the long wispy crest feathers visible behind the crown and a small white egret visible in the far background. The plate's caption identifies the subjects as adult in spring plumage and a young bird, reflecting the species' striking seasonal and age-related variation.
audubon-birds-308-tell-tale-godwit-or-sn: Plate 308 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Greater Yellowlegs — then called Tell-tale Godwit for the alarm calls that warned hunters of an observer's approach. One bird stands alert with wings slightly raised while the other probes the mud below, both showing the bright yellow legs that give the species its modern name. A background of coastal marsh with distant buildings situates the birds in their tidal habitat.
audubon-birds-309-great-tern: Plate 309 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a single tern — labelled Great Tern but corresponding to what is now the Common Tern (Sterna hirundo) — in a dramatic near-vertical diving posture against a grey ground. The black cap, red bill, red feet, and white body are rendered with sharp detail; the deeply forked tail is spread at the apex of the plunge. Audubon favoured these dynamic flight studies for seabirds, composing them from freshly shot specimens wired into lifelike attitudes.
audubon-birds-31-white-headed-eagle: A Bald Eagle stands over a freshly killed catfish, gripping the pale belly of the prey with one taloned foot. The grim, unsentimental treatment of carrion and predation is characteristic of Audubon's approach to North American raptors.
audubon-birds-310-spotted-sandpiper: Two Spotted Sandpipers occupy a rocky shoreline, their breeding plumage carrying the heavy round spots that vanish in winter. Audubon often paired adults to compress life history into a single sheet of the Birds of America.
audubon-birds-311-american-white-pelican: An American White Pelican fills the folio sheet, its vast bill resting along the breast and the breeding-season horn rising from the upper mandible. The compressed pose was Audubon's standard solution for fitting outsized waterbirds within the double-elephant format.
audubon-birds-312-long-tailed-duck: Long-tailed Ducks, then called Old-squaws, are shown in winter pied plumage with the drake's slender tail trailing behind. Audubon studied them on the Atlantic coast where they wintered in noisy rafts.
audubon-birds-313-blue-winged-teal: Plate 313 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a pair of Blue-winged Teal in flight, the large powder-blue forewing patch that names the species prominently displayed on both birds. The drake below presents his blue-grey head with its white facial crescent and richly spotted cinnamon breast; the hen above shows the more cryptic brown plumage typical of the species. A coastal landscape with water and distant hills forms the background.
audubon-birds-314-black-headed-gull: Plate 314 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Laughing Gulls (Larus atricilla) standing on a flat surface: a breeding adult with a dark hood, red bill, grey mantle, white underparts, and red legs, accompanied by a smaller immature bird with duller, brownish plumage and a dark-tipped bill. The Laughing Gull is a common North American coastal species, breeding from the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
audubon-birds-315-red-breasted-sandpiper: The Red Knot, here under its older common name, is shown in the rust-coloured breeding plumage that earns the species its alternative title. Audubon paired it with a winter-plumaged bird to record the dramatic seasonal change.
audubon-birds-316-black-bellied-darter: Plate 316 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Anhingas perched on a dead tree above a southern swamp. The upper bird displays its wings fully spread in the drying posture characteristic of the species, showing the silver-white streaking on the dark scapulars and the long serpentine neck; the lower bird, with its rich cinnamon-brown neck, sits with wings folded. Audubon worked the species from southern swamp habitat, capturing its distinctive pose and plumage contrasts.
audubon-birds-317-black-or-surf-duck: Plate 317 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a male and female Surf Scoter (then called Black or Surf Duck) on a rocky coastal shore. The drake perches on a rock, his largely black plumage offset by white head patches and the species' distinctive multicoloured orange, red, and yellow bill; the darker brown female rests on the sand below beside open clam shells. The plate represents Audubon's interest in coastal sea ducks of the New England shore.
audubon-birds-318-american-avocet: An American Avocet wades on stilt-like blue legs, the upturned bill sweeping water for invertebrates. The cinnamon head and neck mark breeding plumage; the plate uses a low horizon to emphasise the bird's improbable proportions.
audubon-birds-319-lesser-tern: Plate 319 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Lesser Terns (now Least Tern, Sternula antillarum) in flight against a dark sky. The adult below displays the black cap, yellow bill, and white forked-tail form of the breeding bird; the upper figure, in speckled brownish plumage, represents an immature or autumn bird. The Least Tern remains one of the smallest terns in the Americas, nesting colonially on sandy beaches and riverbanks.
audubon-birds-32-black-billed-cuckoo: Plate 32 of Audubon's Birds of America places two Black-billed Cuckoos among the large white flowers and glossy dark leaves of the Great Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora), one bird perched above and one hovering to the right with wings spread. The cuckoos' long graduated tails and slender bills are set off against the prominent white blooms, with smaller insects visible near the centre. The botanical backgrounds in Audubon's early plates were typically contributed by assistants such as Joseph Mason.
audubon-birds-320-little-sandpiper: Plate 320 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Least Sandpipers on the rocks of a rushing stream, one with bill tilted upward and one leaning forward near the water's edge. The species' warm brown-and-buff spotted upperparts and pale underparts are carefully rendered, and the yellowish legs that distinguish it from the otherwise similar Semipalmated Sandpiper are visible on the foreground bird. Plate 320 of the Birds of America is credited to the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-321-roseate-spoonbill: A Roseate Spoonbill bends its spatulate bill to feed, the deep pink wing coverts and orange tail set against a Florida backwater. The plate is among the most flamboyant in Birds of America and helped fix the species in the public imagination.
audubon-birds-322-red-headed-duck: A Redhead drake and female stand on a bank, the drake's deep chestnut head and pale grey back clearly distinct from the closely related Canvasback. Plate 322 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the two sexes to document the species' strong plumage contrast.
audubon-birds-323-black-skimmer-or-shear: A Black Skimmer cuts low over rough, wave-tossed water, its outsized lower mandible slicing the surface in the characteristic feeding flight. The asymmetrical bill, longer below than above, is unique among North American birds and is rendered with precision in Plate 323 of Audubon's Birds of America.
audubon-birds-324-bonapartian-gull: Plate 324 of Birds of America depicts three Bonaparte's Gulls: an adult in breeding plumage with its distinctive dark brown hood, a second adult in flight shown from behind, and a juvenile with mottled grey-brown wings. Audubon named the species for the ornithologist Charles Lucien Bonaparte, and the plate captures the bird across plumage stages.
audubon-birds-325-buffel-headed-duck: A Bufflehead drake displays the puffy white-and-iridescent head pattern that gives the species its old name. Audubon paired the small diver with a more sober female to document the strong sexual dimorphism.
audubon-birds-326-gannet: Plate 326 of Birds of America depicts two Northern Gannets: a standing adult with its characteristic buff-yellow head and vivid blue eye-ring, and a large brown-and-white immature beside it on a rocky shore with open sea behind. Audubon visited breeding colonies on the Gulf of St Lawrence and drew the species across age classes.
audubon-birds-327-shoveller-duck: A Northern Shoveler drake and female face each other on a rocky bank in a courtship display, both birds upright with bills open to reveal the broad, spatulate shape that gives the species its name. The drake's iridescent dark green head, chestnut flanks, and blue wing patches are vividly rendered in Plate 327 of Audubon's Birds of America.
audubon-birds-328-long-legged-avocet: The Black-necked Stilt, here depicted under the older name Long-legged Avocet, stands on rocks against an open coastal horizon, its sharply contrasting black-and-white plumage supported by improbably long reddish-pink legs. Plate 328 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a single bird, and the near-vertical composition emphasises the slender, stilted form.
audubon-birds-329-yellow-breasted-rail: A Yellow Rail crouches in dense sedges, the buff-and-black striping providing camouflage that made the bird notoriously hard to flush. Audubon's plate is among the earliest detailed depictions of this secretive marsh species.
audubon-birds-33-american-goldfinch: Goldfinches in summer yellow perch among thistle, the seedhead Audubon repeatedly used to characterise this species' diet. The plate is among the earlier engravings in the series, executed initially by W. H. Lizars before Havell took over production.
audubon-birds-330-ring-plover: Plate 330 of Birds of America depicts two Semipalmated Plovers on rocky ground beside water: an adult in breeding plumage with its distinctive black breast-band in a distraction display, and a juvenile in plain brownish-grey plumage. The sourceDescription confirms the species as Charadrius semipalmatus, long grouped with the Eurasian Ringed Plover.
audubon-birds-331-goosander: Plate 331 of Birds of America shows a Common Merganser drake standing on a riverbank before a sweeping waterfall, its glossy dark green head and white flanks contrasting with a female swimming in the foreground with her rusty-brown crested head. The serrated bill, adapted for gripping slippery fish, is clearly rendered on both birds.
audubon-birds-332-pied-duck: The Labrador Duck, extinct since around 1878, appears here in piebald drake plumage and brown female dress. Audubon's plate is now a historical document of one of the first North American birds lost to human pressure.
audubon-birds-333-green-heron: Plate 333 of Birds of America depicts two Green Herons amid lush vegetation — one bird in a dramatic bill-raised posture and a second in a calmer stance — against a backdrop of broad-leaved tropical plants rather than open reedy water. Audubon's composition captures the species' hunched, cryptic shape and the rich chestnut-and-green plumage.
audubon-birds-334-black-bellied-plover: Plate 334 of Birds of America shows three Black-bellied Plovers on rocky coastal ground: an adult male in full breeding plumage with jet-black underparts and silvery-dappled upperparts, a non-breeding adult above it, and a juvenile on the right. The arrangement documents the species' striking seasonal plumage variation.
audubon-birds-335-red-breasted-snipe: Long-billed dowitchers, then known as red-breasted snipe, probe a shoreline in postures observed during Audubon's wetland field studies. The plate uses Robert Havell Jr.'s aquatint and engraving to render the streaked, cinnamon-toned breeding dress.
audubon-birds-336-yellow-crowned-heron: Plate 336 of Birds of America shows an adult and an immature yellow-crowned night heron perched together on a gnarled tree branch above a coastal waterway. The adult displays the species' distinctive black-and-white head pattern and long white facial plumes, while the heavily streaked juvenile perches above. The composition, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-337-american-bittern: Plate 337 of Birds of America depicts three American bitterns among marsh reeds, one with neck stretched upward in the species' characteristic freeze posture and two others in lower, active stances. The streaked brown and buff plumage that serves as camouflage in wetland vegetation is rendered in fine tonal gradations across all three figures. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-338-bemaculated-duck: Plate 338 of Birds of America shows a single bemaculated duck — a mallard-like bird with a green-glossed head, chestnut breast, and yellow feet — standing alert on a grassy bank with reeds behind it. Audubon recorded this bird as a distinct species, though it is now considered a variant or hybrid rather than a full species. The plate was engraved and hand-coloured by R. Havell and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-339-little-auk: Plate 339 of Birds of America shows two little auks (dovekies): one swimming at the surface with a small fish in its bill, and one standing on a coastal rock in bold black-and-white breeding plumage. The compact, stub-billed auk is depicted against a backdrop of open sea and distant cliffs. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-34-worm-eating-warbler: Plate 34 of Birds of America depicts two worm-eating warblers — buff-toned birds with bold black head stripes — among fruiting and leafy branches. The lower bird clings horizontally to a twig in the posture characteristic of this ground-foraging species. Engraved, printed, and coloured by Robert Havell, the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-340-least-stormy-petrel: A tiny pelagic petrel skims a wave trough, wings raised in the fluttering flight that earned the family its name. Audubon shows the species over open ocean, a setting rare in the folio and demanding extensive aquatint tone for the swell.
audubon-birds-341-great-auk: Plate 341 of Birds of America depicts two great auks — one swimming in choppy coastal waters and one standing upright on a rock — rendered at full scale against a dramatic backdrop of sea cliffs. The flightless North Atlantic bird was already declining when Audubon's plate was published and went extinct in 1844, making this one of its most widely reproduced likenesses. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-342-golden-eye-duck: Plate 342 of Birds of America shows a drake and hen common goldeneye in flight, wings fully spread against a grey sky. The drake's bottle-green head, white cheek spot, and bold black-and-white wing pattern are rendered at full scale, while the brown-headed female is shown banking above him. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-343-ruddy-duck: Plate 343 of Birds of America presents four ruddy ducks in different plumages: a breeding male standing tall on a rock with chestnut body, black cap, and bright blue bill; a female; and two birds in intermediate or non-breeding dress. The stiff-tailed posture of the breeding male, with bill tilted upward, is characteristic of the species' courtship display. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-344-long-legged-sandpiper: Plate 344 of Birds of America shows two long-legged sandpipers — now identified as the stilt sandpiper — standing on rocky ground above a coastal shoreline. Both birds display a pinkish-rufous wash on the neck and breast consistent with breeding plumage, and the patterned upper parts are rendered with careful tonal gradation. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-345-american-widgeon: A drake American wigeon displays the white forecrown and green eye-stripe that distinguish it from its Eurasian cousin. The bird is set on still water, with reflections built up by selective biting of the aquatint plate.
audubon-birds-346-black-throated-diver: The black-throated loon, called diver in British usage, is shown in breeding plumage with its striped neck patch. The vermiculated back pattern is achieved by very fine engraved cross-hatching beneath the aquatint tone.
audubon-birds-347-smew-or-white-nun: Plate 347 of Birds of America depicts two smews against a mountainous coastal background: a drake in flight showing his crisp white plumage with black markings, and a rufous-headed female riding the waves below. The smew is a small Eurasian sawbill that occasionally strays to North America, and the plate records both sexes to illustrate the marked sexual dimorphism of the species. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-348-gadwall-duck: Plate 348 of Birds of America shows a pair of gadwall standing on coastal rocks above open water. The drake, on the right, displays the subtly vermiculated grey flanks and black tail coverts that distinguish the species from other dabbling ducks, while the brown-patterned female stands beside him. Engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell Jr., the plate was produced between 1827 and 1838 and is held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-349-least-water-hen: Two least water-hens stand at a marshy shoreline, one rufous-backed and one dark-plumaged, with reeds rising behind them. Plate 349 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts Rallus jamaicensis against a low-lying coastal marsh landscape with clouded sky.
audubon-birds-35-children-s-warbler: A small wood-warbler named after John George Children of the British Museum, now considered a juvenile yellow warbler rather than a distinct species. The plate is a record of the taxonomic uncertainty that surrounded many small migrants in Audubon's day.
audubon-birds-350-rocky-mountain-plover: A mountain plover forages on a rocky alpine slope against a backdrop of craggy peaks. Plate 350 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the pale, unmarked underparts and the bird's characteristic posture, placing it in the mountain terrain for which it was named.
audubon-birds-351-great-cinereous-owl: A great grey owl perches on a broken branch, the concentric facial discs rendered through circular sweeps of aquatint tone. The plate captures the disproportion between the species' enormous head and its relatively slight body.
audubon-birds-352-black-winged-hawk: Two black-winged hawks — the white-tailed kite of later nomenclature — are shown against a pale sky: one bird in an open-winged flight pose above, and a second perched on a broken branch below. Plate 352 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the species' grey and white plumage and sharply contrasting dark wing patches.
audubon-birds-353-i-chesnut-backed-titmo: Multiple chestnut-backed, black-capped, and chestnut-crowned titmice are arranged around a large hanging moss nest suspended from leafy branches, with additional birds perched on lower stems. Plate 353 of Audubon's Birds of America presents a nest-building scene that allows comparison of the three closely related western and boreal forms.
audubon-birds-354-i-louisiana-tanager-2-: Four tanagers occupy leafy branches: two Louisiana tanagers (western tanager) showing the male's red head, yellow body, and black wings alongside a duller individual, a vivid all-red scarlet tanager male in flight, and a greenish female below. Plate 354 of Audubon's Birds of America places these species together as a comparative study of the two most colourful North American tanagers.
audubon-birds-355-macgillivray-s-finch: Two small streaked sparrows perch among upright salt-marsh reeds, with two pale butterflies included in the composition above them. Plate 355 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts MacGillivray's Finch — now considered a seaside sparrow — named by Audubon for the Scottish naturalist William MacGillivray, his collaborator on the Ornithological Biography.
audubon-birds-356-marsh-hawk: Three marsh hawks are presented: a large brown bird perched prominently at top, a grey male on a branch below it, and a third bird at the bottom feeding on prey amid marsh grasses near water. Plate 356 of Audubon's Birds of America captures multiple plumages of the northern harrier, known for the white rump patch visible in the grey male.
audubon-birds-357-american-magpie: Two American magpies are depicted: one bird in full flight with wings spread wide, displaying striking iridescent green and blue flight feathers, and a second perched below on a small branch showing the long graduated tail. Plate 357 of Audubon's Birds of America renders the corvid's bold black-and-white plumage alongside its brilliant iridescent wing and tail coloration.
audubon-birds-358-pine-grosbeak: Three pine grosbeaks are arranged on pine branches: a crimson-red male at lower left, a grey-brown bird at centre right, and an olive-green individual at top. Plate 358 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the species' marked sexual dimorphism, with the heavy bill characteristic of these large boreal finches clearly visible across all three figures.
audubon-birds-359-i-arkansaw-flycatcher-: Five tyrant flycatcher figures are distributed across multiple branches: Arkansaw flycatchers (western kingbird) at top, scissor-tailed flycatchers with their distinctive elongated outer tail feathers in the middle register, and a Say's flycatcher at lower right. Plate 359 of Audubon's Birds of America groups three western species in a comparative arrangement, with butterflies included as compositional elements.
audubon-birds-36-stanley-hawk: A Stanley Hawk in dynamic flight — shown as a young male — sweeps across the composition above a second hawk perched on a weathered post, while a small eastern bluebird appears at upper right. Plate 36 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two plumages of this Cooper's Hawk, known under an older vernacular name, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
audubon-birds-360-i-winter-wren-2-rock-w: Four wrens are depicted in a naturalistic setting of mossy ground, lichen-covered branches, and low herbage: the Winter Wren figures perch on branches and among ground-level vegetation, while the Rock Wrens appear near rocky elements at right. Plate 360 of Audubon's Birds of America presents the two species with careful attention to the fine barring that marks the plumage of both.
audubon-birds-361-long-tailed-or-dusky-g: A dark male and a brown-barred female dusky grouse stand on open mountain terrain with rocky peaks and a distant valley visible behind them. Plate 361 of Audubon's Birds of America captures the species' sexual dimorphism, with the male's dark plumage and reddish eye-comb contrasting against the female's cryptic patterning.
audubon-birds-362-i-yellow-billed-magpie: Plate 362 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts four western corvids — Yellow-billed Magpie, Steller's Jay, Ultramarine Jay, and Clark's Crow — arranged on branches of sweetgum amid palmate leaves and spiky seed-balls. The California-endemic Yellow-billed Magpie occupies the lower left, its yellow bill and grey-and-black-green plumage distinct from the deeply blue Steller's Jay above. Published between 1827 and 1838, the plate is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-363-bohemian-chatterer: A pair of Bohemian Waxwings perched on a fruiting branch, their silky cinnamon plumage punctuated by red sealing-wax tips on the secondaries. The aquatint tone captures the smooth, almost powdered quality of waxwing feathers.
audubon-birds-364-white-winged-crossbill: Plate 364 of Audubon's Birds of America shows White-winged Crossbills working the seed-bearing stems of a broadleaf shrub, with crimson males and olive-yellow females arranged to display the species' sexual dimorphism. The crossed mandibles, adapted for extracting seeds, are clearly delineated in profile on several birds. The plate was engraved and hand-coloured for the double elephant folio, published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-365-lapland-long-spur: Plate 365 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts Lapland Longspurs on bare ground before a lake and mountain backdrop. Three birds are shown: a breeding male with a black face and chestnut nape stands prominently, while two more streaked, sparrow-like individuals illustrate alternate plumages. The plate appeared in the double elephant folio published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-366-iceland-or-jer-falcon: Plate 366 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two Iceland or Gyrfalcons, both in the pale white morph, against a dark teal background. One bird is shown in mid-flight with wings spread wide, its white plumage marked with dark barring, while the other perches below. The composition emphasises the circumpolar raptor's impressive wingspan and the near-white colouration characteristic of its northern populations.
audubon-birds-367-band-tailed-pigeon: Plate 367 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts a male and female Band-tailed Pigeon perched on a branch of flowering dogwood, its white blossoms and red berries filling the upper portion of the composition. Both birds display the species' broad dark terminal tail-band and yellow-tipped bill. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-368-rock-grous: Plate 368 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Rock Ptarmigan in an alpine landscape: a male in white winter plumage stands upright at right, its red eye-comb prominent against a snowy mountain backdrop, while a second bird in brown mottled summer plumage crouches at lower left. The contrasting seasonal coats on a single plate illustrate the species' dramatic moult cycle. The plate appeared in the double elephant folio published between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-369-i-mountain-mocking-bir: Plate 369 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the Mountain Mockingbird (now Sage Thrasher) with male and female Varied Thrushes on a flowering shrub branch. The thrashers show the plain grey-brown streaked upperparts and faintly spotted breast distinctive of the species, while the Varied Thrush male displays its rich orange breast and black breast-band. The plate was published between 1827 and 1838 as part of the double elephant folio.
audubon-birds-37-golden-winged-woodpecke: Plate 37 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two male and two female Northern Flickers — then called Golden-winged Woodpeckers — around a large weathered tree stump. The bright yellow wing and tail-shaft feathers, visible on the bird shown in flight with spread wings, give the species its Audubon-era common name. The composition appeared early in the double elephant folio, published from 1827 onwards.
audubon-birds-370-american-water-ouzel: Plate 370 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two American Dippers perched on rocks beside a rushing cascade, with an open mountain valley behind. The birds show the species' characteristic rufous-brown crown contrasting with slate-grey body plumage. The rushing water in the composition alludes to the dipper's habitat along fast-flowing mountain streams. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-371-cock-of-the-plains: A male Greater Sage-Grouse in lek display, air sacs inflated over a white ruff while the spike-tailed female crouches nearby. The plate documents a sagebrush species Audubon never saw alive, drawn from Townsend specimens.
audubon-birds-372-common-buzzard: Plate 372 of Audubon's Birds of America shows a Common Buzzard diving upon a hare in an open landscape, its dark brown wings spread and talons extended as it descends on the prey. A lighter-breasted second view of the bird appears below, conveying the species' plumage variation. The Eurasian bird was included in the folio on the basis of a single American specimen, a record now generally considered erroneous.
audubon-birds-373-i-evening-grosbeak-2-s: Plate 373 of Audubon's Birds of America shows Evening Grosbeaks and Spotted (Black-headed) Grosbeaks perched on bare grey branches. The male Evening Grosbeak at the top displays its bold yellow body and black-and-white wings, while the Black-headed Grosbeak below shows the species' black hood and deep cinnamon-orange breast. The contrasting massive seed-cracking bills of both species are a visual focus of the composition.
audubon-birds-374-sharp-shinned-hawk: Plate 374 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts two Sharp-shinned Hawks perched on a curved branch, one of which grips a small prey item in its talons. Both birds show the slate-blue upperparts and rusty-barred underparts of adults, with strongly banded tails. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-375-lesser-red-poll: Plate 375 of Audubon's Birds of America shows two Lesser Redpolls (Common Redpolls) perched on a flowering shrub bearing small white blossoms and pale berries. Both birds display the species' distinctive red forecrown, and the male shows a rosy-pink flush on the breast. The plate was published in the double elephant folio between 1827 and 1838 and is held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-376-trumpeter-swan: An adult Trumpeter Swan arches its neck to drink from a marsh pool, the long body filling almost the full sheet of the double elephant folio. The plate is one of the largest single-bird compositions in the series, exploiting the format for North America's heaviest waterfowl.
audubon-birds-377-scolopaceus-courlan: A Limpkin strides across an open rocky bank, its straight pointed bill carried forward and its long legs extended mid-step. The brown plumage shows white streaking on the neck and breast. Plate 377 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-378-hawk-owl: Two Hawk Owls appear on a bare tree stub: one perches upright at the top, displaying the barred underparts and long tail that give the species its falcon-like silhouette, while a second bird below spreads its wings wide. Plate 378 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-379-ruff-necked-humming-bi: Several Ruff-necked (Rufous) Hummingbirds surround a tall flowering plant, the males' copper-and-flame gorgets catching the light as they hover near the blooms; a fourth bird tends a small lichen-covered nest lower on the stem. The plate gathers multiple postures and sexes to document the species' plumage variation. Plate 379 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-38-kentucky-warbler: Two olive-and-yellow warblers with bold black sideburns perch on a flowering magnolia branch. The composition pairs an eastern songbird with a southern bloom, a habit Audubon used to compress habitat and season into one engraved sheet.
audubon-birds-380-tengmalm-s-owl: Two Tengmalm's (Boreal) Owls share a plain composition: one perches on a bare stub facing away, showing the spotted back and rounded facial disc, while a second bird spreads its wings below in a contrasting posture. The background is plain paper with no foliage. Plate 380 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-381-snow-goose: An adult white-morph Snow Goose stands beside a dark-morph (Blue Goose) individual, the latter showing a dark body with white head and neck, together contrasting the two recognised colour forms of the species. The black wingtips of the white bird and the pink bill and feet of both are rendered against a stormy coastal sky. Plate 381 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-382-sharp-tailed-grous: Two Sharp-tailed Grouse walk across open ground before a mountain and river landscape, the pointed central tail feathers and pale spotted underparts clearly shown. A small berry-bearing shrub appears at lower left. Plate 382 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-383-long-eared-owl: A Long-eared Owl perches on a single bare gray branch against an open background, its elongated ear tufts and orange-tinted facial disc clearly visible as it turns its head to one side. The mottled brown, buff, and cream plumage is rendered in detail. Plate 383 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-384-black-throated-bunting: A pair of Dickcissels on grain stalks, the male's yellow breast crossed by a black bib reminiscent of a meadowlark in miniature. Audubon set them in cultivated grasses to allude to the species' preference for grain fields and old prairie.
audubon-birds-385-i-bank-swallow-2-viole: A Bank Swallow at a sandy burrow entrance is paired with the western Violet-green Swallow, contrasting brown plumage against iridescent green and purple. The grouping aligns nesting habit with geographical range across one sheet.
audubon-birds-386-white-heron: A Great Egret in breeding plumage stands amid coastal vegetation, long aigrette plumes cascading down its back. The plate documents the species before late nineteenth-century plume hunting nearly drove it to extinction.
audubon-birds-387-glossy-ibis: A Glossy Ibis probes a wetland margin, the curved bill and mahogany body washed with green-bronze iridescence rendered through layered aquatint and watercolour. Audubon based the figure on a Florida specimen of this then-uncommon coastal wader.
audubon-birds-388-i-nuttall-s-starling-2: Three species share a cascade of bare branches: Nuttall's Starling at the top with its black plumage and scarlet shoulder patch, the Yellow-headed Troopial below with its striking yellow head and chest, and Bullock's Oriole at the bottom showing orange and black. A smaller female or immature figure also appears to the right. Plate 388 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-389-red-cockaded-woodpecke: Three Red-cockaded Woodpeckers cling to a single smooth-barked trunk: one bird near a cavity at the top, another mid-trunk with the male's tiny red cockade visible behind the eye, and a third lower on the tree. The bold black-and-white ladder pattern of the back and the white cheek patch are the key marks rendered at life size in the double elephant folio format. Plate 389 of Audubon's Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838 and credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-39-crested-titmouse: A pair of tufted titmice work over a white pine branch hung with elongated cones, their upright crests and dark eye-patches giving each a sharp, inquisitive profile. Plate 39 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, captures the species in its preferred eastern conifer habitat.
audubon-birds-390-i-lark-finch-2-prairie: Three birds of the Great Plains are arranged on twigs and grassy ground: the Lark Finch with its rufous-marked head perches above, the dark Prairie Finch clings to a twig mid-plate, and a pair of Brown Song Sparrows forage at the base. Plate 390 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838, gathers species representative of the interior grassland and Pacific slope.
audubon-birds-391-brant-goose: Two brant geese face one another in a tense display on rocky ground, one spreading its wings upward while the other lunges forward with bill open, both showing the species' dark head and neck and pale barred flanks. Plate 391 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the male and female engaged in territorial behaviour, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-392-louisiana-hawk: A Louisiana Hawk — now known as Harris's Hawk — perches alert on a broken stump, its dark plumage contrasting with the rich chestnut shoulder patches that distinguish the species. Plate 392 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by J. Smyth from Audubon's drawing, presents the bird in the composed lateral profile typical of his raptor studies.
audubon-birds-393-i-townsend-s-warbler-2: Five western birds representing three recently described species share a branch bearing red blossoms: Townsend's Warbler with its yellow and black head, two vivid blue Arctic Blue-birds, and two Western Blue-birds with blue backs and rusty breasts. Plate 393 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838, drew on Pacific Northwest skins supplied by John Kirk Townsend.
audubon-birds-394-i-chestnut-coloured-fi: Four small seed-eaters are arranged across twigs and grassy ground: the bright yellow Chestnut-coloured Finch with black head, a streaked finch catching an insect near a pink flower, a rufous-breasted bird at mid-ground, and a dark, rufous-sided Arctic Ground Finch at the base. Plate 394 of Audubon's Birds of America groups newly described western species that reached Audubon as study skins during the later phases of the folio's production.
audubon-birds-395-i-audubon-s-warbler-2-: Three western wood-warblers perch across a deciduous branch hung with round red berries: Audubon's Warbler with its yellow crown patch, the Hermit Warbler, and the boldly patterned Black-throated Gray Warbler at the base. Plate 395 of Audubon's Birds of America introduced these Pacific species to subscribers, drawn from specimens collected during Townsend and Nuttall's western expedition.
audubon-birds-396-burgomaster-gull: An adult Burgomaster Gull in pale grey-and-white plumage stands alongside a mottled brown immature bird on a rocky shore, the adult's yellow bill conspicuous against the dark coastal background. Plate 396 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts this large gull — now classified as the glaucous gull — in two age-plumages, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-397-scarlet-ibis: A vivid scarlet adult ibis stands beside a brown, immature individual on a muddy coastal bank, both birds showing the species' long decurved bill against a pale open-water sky. Plate 397 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the two plumage stages, published by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-398-i-lazuli-finch-2-clay-: Three western finches share a branch of pink-flowering shrub: the Lazuli Finch above with its blue head and orange breast, the plain Clay-coloured Finch at centre, and the darker Oregon Snow Finch below. Plate 398 of Audubon's Birds of America groups these birds of the western interior, assembled from study skins for the folio's later numbers.
audubon-birds-399-i-black-throated-green: Five warblers are arranged along a deciduous branch bearing broad leaves and pendant acorns: two Black-throated Green Warblers at the top, the warm-throated Blackburnian in the middle, and two Mourning Warblers below. Plate 399 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Havell, groups these eastern wood-warblers in a single composition for the folio's closing numbers.
audubon-birds-4-purple-finch: Two raspberry-red males and a streaked brown female Purple Finch cling to a pine branch hung with small cones, the males' rich crimson heads set against the sparse needles. Plate 4 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the species' marked sexual dimorphism and was among the earliest plates engraved and published by Havell from 1827 onwards.
audubon-birds-40-american-redstart: Black-and-orange flycatching warblers spread their tails through a tangled branch, flashing the pigment patches that give the species its name. Audubon shows the male in the fan-tailed display posture used to startle insects from leaves.
audubon-birds-400-i-arkansaw-siskin-2-me: Five birds are arranged across bare twigs and a grassy bank: the yellow-green Arkansaw Siskin at upper left, the streaked red-crowned Mealy Red-poll above, a yellow-green Louisiana Tanager at centre, and two finches — the boldly patterned Townsend's Finch and a Buff-breasted Finch — at the base. Plate 400 of Audubon's Birds of America marks the folio's four-hundredth number and was compiled largely from western study skins.
audubon-birds-401-red-breasted-merganser: A female Red-breasted Merganser flies overhead with wings fully spread while the drake swims below, his ragged green crest, white collar, and rust-washed breast contrasting with the female's brown head and white chin. Plate 401 of Audubon's Birds of America pairs the sexes in action against a wetland setting of pitcher plants and reeds, engraved and coloured by Havell between 1827 and 1838.
audubon-birds-402-i-black-throated-guill: Four North Pacific alcids — Black-throated Guillemot, Nobbed-billed Auk, Curled-crested Auk, and Horned-billed Guillemot — are arranged against an arctic seascape of ice floes and distant snow-capped mountains. Plate 402 of Audubon's Birds of America brings together species collected on the Northwest Coast and largely unknown to Atlantic subscribers.
audubon-birds-403-golden-eye-duck: A single drake common goldeneye rides open water, its iridescent purple-green head and circular white cheek-patch rendered with close attention to gloss and form. Plate 403 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the male in breeding plumage, the orange-yellow feet and black-and-white flanks clearly delineated beneath the surface.
audubon-birds-404-eared-grebe: Two Eared Grebes are shown on a muddy bank beside open water, one in full breeding dress with the species' distinctive golden ear-tufts and red eye, the other in plain grey-and-white winter plumage. Plate 404 of Audubon's Birds of America presents the striking seasonal contrast between the two plumages of the same species.
audubon-birds-405-semipalmated-sandpiper: Two Semipalmated Sandpipers forage along a rocky shore littered with small shells, one probing low at the water's edge and the other walking at a higher point. Plate 405 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., shows the streaked brown-and-white plumage of this common Atlantic shorebird in detail.
audubon-birds-406-trumpeter-swan: A massive white swan arches its neck along the full height of the double elephant folio sheet, snapping at a small moth. Audubon bent the bird's neck into a tight curl so it could stand at life size on a page just over a metre tall — one of his most-discussed compositional solutions.
audubon-birds-407-dusky-albatros: A uniformly dark-brown Dusky Albatros stands on a rocky coastal ledge, the sea and breaking waves visible behind it. Plate 407 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts this sooty-plumaged seabird in a perched pose, its pale-yellow feet and hooked bill carefully rendered.
audubon-birds-408-american-scoter-duck: A jet-black drake American Scoter with its distinctive orange-knobbed bill rides a low swell in the foreground, a brownish hen visible behind. Plate 408 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the strong sexual dimorphism of this sea duck, a species that winters in rafts along North American coasts.
audubon-birds-409-i-havell-s-tern-2-trud: Havell's Tern and Trudeau's Tern perch together on a rocky, grass-covered coastal headland, a wide estuary and distant shore stretching behind them. Plate 409 of Audubon's Birds of America features two tern species named by Audubon, distinguishable by bill colour and cap pattern, with scattered shells arranged at their feet.
audubon-birds-41-ruffed-grouse: Two male Ruffed Grouse fan their black-banded tails and erect their dark neck ruffs in courtship display while a female stands nearby amid dense foliage with large broad leaves and clusters of dark berries. Plate 41 of Audubon's Birds of America shows the species' dramatic sexual display within the leafy undergrowth of the eastern hardwood forest.
audubon-birds-410-marsh-tern: A Marsh Tern plunges steeply downward against a pale blue sky, wings raised and bill angled sharply toward a small insect below. Plate 410 of Audubon's Birds of America — labelled Sterna anglica on the plate — depicts the bird in a dramatic diving attitude, rendered in summer plumage with a full black cap.
audubon-birds-411-common-american-swan: A Common American Swan (Tundra Swan) glides across a still pond bordered by water-lily pads and yellow flowers, the small reddish spot at the base of the dark bill visible in profile. Plate 411 of Audubon's Birds of America depicts the species Audubon distinguished from the Trumpeter Swan by its smaller size and bill markings.
audubon-birds-412-i-violet-green-cormora: A Violet-green Cormorant and a Townsend's Cormorant stand on a flat rocky ledge with the open sea behind them, the smaller Violet-green displaying brilliantly iridescent blue-green plumage and a red facial patch, while the larger Townsend's shows a pale buff chest and yellow bill. Plate 412 of Audubon's Birds of America presents two Pacific cormorant species drawn from specimens collected on the West Coast.
audubon-birds-413-california-partridge: A male California Partridge stands upright on an open hillside, its forward-curling black topknot and blue-and-chestnut flanks conspicuous, while a female crouches below in a foraging posture. Plate 413 of Audubon's Birds of America introduces one of the West Coast's most distinctive game birds to the folio, set against a broad valley landscape.
audubon-birds-414-i-golden-winged-warble: Several Golden-winged and Cape May Warblers perch among leafy branches, the Golden-winged individuals showing their black throat patch and bold yellow wing bars, the Cape May birds displaying the warm chestnut-orange cheek patches and streaked yellow underparts. Plate 414 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., presents multiple specimens of each species for comparative study.
audubon-birds-415-i-brown-creeper-2-cali: A Brown Creeper fans its wings in mid-flight to the left while two Californian Nuthatches cling to a lichen-covered tree trunk in their characteristic head-up and head-down poses. Plate 415 of Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell Jr., contrasts two bark-foraging species of the western forests.
audubon-birds-416-i-hairy-woodpecker-2-r: A composite study of five woodpecker species posed on dead snags, comparing crown patterns, barred backs and tail bracing across eastern and western North America. Such grouped plates appeared in the later supplementary numbers of the folio, accommodating species Audubon received from western expeditions.
audubon-birds-417-i-maria-s-woodpecker-2: Six woodpecker forms are stacked on a single trunk, several of them now treated as regional races of the Hairy and American Three-toed Woodpeckers. The plate reflects the taxonomic optimism of 1830s ornithology, when subtle plumage variants were routinely described as full species.
audubon-birds-418-i-american-ptarmigan-2: Two high-latitude grouse are posed on a rocky alpine slope against a mountain sky: the American Ptarmigan (left) shown in transitional plumage with mottled brown-and-white markings, wings partially spread, and the White-tailed Grouse (right) in near-complete white winter dress with a red eye-comb. Plate 418 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-419-i-little-tawny-thrush-: Three forest birds share a sprig of foliage: the russet Hermit Thrush form, Townsend's Solitaire with its pale eye-ring, and the soft grey Canada Jay. The grouping pulls together species new to science from John Kirk Townsend's Columbia River collections.
audubon-birds-42-orchard-oriole: Several Orchard Orioles — including a yellow-green female and a brick-red adult male — animate a thorny locust branch bearing compound foliage and a suspended woven nest. Plate 42 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-420-prairie-starling: Two birds perch on a slender budding branch: a male with jet-black plumage and a prominent red-orange shoulder patch, consistent with Audubon's Prairie Starling (now identified as the Red-winged Blackbird), and above it a smaller streaked brownish female. Plate 420 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-421-brown-pelican: A Brown Pelican stands on a rocky coastal ledge with its long bill held wide open and the pouch fully extended, its chestnut-brown plumage rendered at near life size against a coastal waterway background. Plate 421 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-422-rough-legged-falcon: Two Rough-legged Hawks — a dark morph and a light morph — perch on a forked branch facing each other, their feathered tarsi and barred underparts clearly displayed against a plain ground. Plate 422 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-423-i-plumed-partridge-2-t: Two western quail are figured together: the Mountain Quail with its long straight head plume, and the Scaled Quail showing its distinctive crescent-edged feathering. The plate draws on specimens from Townsend and Nuttall's overland expedition to the Pacific.
audubon-birds-424-i-lazuli-finch-2-crims: Six finch-like passerines crowd a single branch, ranging from the turquoise Lazuli Bunting to the heavy-billed Evening Grosbeak. Such crowded composite sheets close the folio, making efficient use of the costly copper plates as Audubon hurried to incorporate western discoveries.
audubon-birds-425-columbian-humming-bird: Multiple hummingbirds with iridescent red gorgets and green backs hover around and perch on a tall stem of large pink mallow-type flowers, while a fifth bird sits on a small nest at the base. Plate 425 of Audubon's Birds of America, labelled Columbian Humming Bird and produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-426-californian-vulture: A California Condor perches on a weathered log, its bare brownish-orange head and blue neck patch contrasting with jet-black body plumage and a bold white stripe along the underwing coverts. Plate 426 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838 from skins rather than a living specimen, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-427-i-white-legged-oyster-: Two dark-plumaged oystercatchers are shown on a rocky shore: the Slender-billed Oyster-catcher (standing, with a bright red bill and red legs) and the White-legged Oyster-catcher (prostrate, probing among small bivalves with an orange-yellow bill). Both names are now subsumed into the Black Oystercatcher of the Pacific coast. Plate 427 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-428-townsend-s-sandpiper: Two Townsend's Sandpipers are shown in flight above a misty waterway, their wing patterns and underparts displayed in dorsal and ventral views. First described from a single specimen collected by John Kirk Townsend, the taxon is now regarded by modern ornithologists as aberrant or hybrid rather than a valid species. Plate 428 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-429-western-duck: Two male Steller's Eiders — shown under the name Western Duck — stand on a rocky reed-fringed shore, displaying their white heads with iridescent green patches, black backs, and warm buff-orange underparts. Plate 429 of Audubon's Birds of America, produced between 1827 and 1838, held by the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-43-cedar-bird: Two Cedar Waxwings perch on a branch of eastern red cedar laden with blue-grey berries, their silky fawn plumage, black masks, and red wing-tip wax drops rendered with close attention to texture. Plate 43 of Audubon's Birds of America, published by Robert Havell, London, credited to the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-430-slender-billed-guillem: Two Slender-billed Guillemots stand on a rocky coastal ledge, one showing the brownish scalloped upperparts and pale belly of its plumage, the other darker with a contrasting white underside, a grey sea and clouds receding behind them. Plate 430 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-431-american-flamingo: A single flamingo bows its long neck almost to the ground, its body filling the double-elephant sheet vertically so the entire bird could be shown life-size. Audubon studied the species in the Florida Keys in 1832 and the plate is among the most graphically daring of the folio.
audubon-birds-432-i-burrowing-owl-2-larg: Five small owls are arranged across a grassy open landscape: the Burrowing Owl and Large-headed Burrowing Owl perch on branches at left, while the Little Night Owl and Columbian Owl share a central branch, and the large Short-eared Owl crouches on the ground at centre-bottom. Plate 432 of John James Audubon's Birds of America presents a comparative study of head shape, leg length, and wing form across these related species, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
audubon-birds-433-i-bullock-s-oriole-2-b: An assortment of bright passerines crowds a leafy branch: two oriole species, a Lesser Goldfinch, a Varied Thrush and a Northern Waterthrush. Such mixed plates were a practical way to publish western specimens that reached Audubon late in the project.
audubon-birds-434-i-little-tyrant-fly-ca: Six small insect-eaters share a single twig, several of them species known only from a handful of skins and never reliably observed since. The plate has long fascinated ornithologists as a possible record of birds now extinct or never validly described.
audubon-birds-435-i-columbian-water-ouze: Two Water Ouzels (American Dippers) are depicted on rocky cliff ledges above a rushing waterfall, one leaning forward as though about to descend toward the water below. Plate 435 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents the Columbian and Arctic Water Ouzel, western specimens associated with Townsend's Pacific collecting expeditions, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell.
audubon-birds-44-summer-red-bird: Three Summer Tanagers share a fruiting branch bearing dark grapes: the adult male in full scarlet perches at the top, a transitional bird with mixed red and olive-green plumage appears at lower left, and an olive-yellow female occupies the centre. Plate 44 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-45-traill-s-flycatcher: A small olive-brown Empidonax flycatcher named after the Edinburgh naturalist Thomas Stewart Traill perches alertly on a sprig. Modern taxonomy splits the original Traill's into the Alder and Willow Flycatchers, two near-identical species separable mainly by song.
audubon-birds-46-barred-owl: A Barred Owl spreads its wings dramatically on a mossy branch, turning its head downward toward a grey squirrel perched below it — Audubon's characteristic predator-and-prey narrative composition. The horizontal barring across the upper breast and vertical streaking below are clearly differentiated, and the squirrel's bushy tail adds counterweight to the composition. Plate 46 of Birds of America, engraved and coloured by Robert Havell, credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-47-ruby-throated-humming-b: Multiple Ruby-throated Hummingbirds hover and perch around trumpet-creeper blossoms, the iridescent throats catching light at different angles. Audubon used the plate to advertise the species' status as the only hummingbird breeding east of the Mississippi.
audubon-birds-48-azure-warbler: Two Azure Warblers — now generally identified with the Cerulean Warbler — are shown among red berries and mixed foliage, their vivid blue-and-white plumage contrasting with the seasonal colouring of the branch. Plate 48 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-49-blue-green-warbler: A single Blue-green Warbler perches among the large leaves and rounded pink-and-red berry clusters of a tall fruiting plant, its blue-grey and greenish plumage matched to the species' name. Plate 49 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, drawn life-size in the double-elephant folio format and engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell, credited to the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-5-bonaparte-s-flycatcher: A small flycatcher named for the ornithologist Charles Lucien Bonaparte perches among slender branches. The bird is no longer recognised as a distinct species and is generally considered a misidentified or aberrant specimen, surviving only in this plate.
audubon-birds-50-black-yellow-warbler: A Black and Yellow Warbler — now identified as the Magnolia Warbler — perches on an oak branch bearing developing acorns, its tail spread to reveal the distinctive white tail-band pattern. Plate 50 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, engraved and hand-coloured by Robert Havell for the double-elephant folio, held in the University of Pittsburgh collection.
audubon-birds-51-red-tailed-hawk: Two hawks grapple over a hare in a dramatic mid-air struggle, talons interlocked and wings braced against one another. The double-elephant folio's full sheet is exploited to show the raptors at life size, a scale unprecedented in ornithological publishing of the period.
audubon-birds-52-chuck-will-s-widow: Two Chuck-will's-widows confront a vividly banded coral snake draped across a branch of a flowering vine in Plate 52 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The cryptic brown-mottled plumage of both birds is rendered with fine tonal gradations, set against the vine's tubular red flowers. Audubon's preference for staging behavioural encounters rather than isolating specimens against blank grounds is fully evident here.
audubon-birds-53-painted-finch: The painted bunting, called the Nonpareil for its blue, green and crimson plumage, is shown with several individuals on a sprig of wild almond. The plate demonstrates the colourists' ability to register multiple unmixed pigments through the aquatint ground without muddying the saturated hues.
audubon-birds-54-rice-bird: A breeding male bobolink in his striking inverted black, white, and buff plumage perches at the top of a red-maple branch, while a streaked olive-brown female occupies a lower spray of the same tree in Plate 54 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The plate documents the species under the agricultural name 'Rice Bird,' reflecting the damage migrating flocks caused to Carolina grain fields. The red-maple setting, labelled in the plate text, gives the composition its warm autumnal tones.
audubon-birds-55-cuvier-s-regulus: A tiny crested kinglet sits on a leafy branch, its identity now considered a probable hybrid or unrepeatable observation. The plate honours Georges Cuvier and exemplifies the speculative species occasionally included from single field encounters.
audubon-birds-56-red-shouldered-hawk: Two red-shouldered hawks — male above, female below — perch on lichen-draped oak branches draped with Spanish moss in Plate 56 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. The male's strongly barred rufous breast and boldly banded tail are carefully differentiated from the broader, browner female. Spanish moss festooning the branches grounds the composition in the Louisiana lowland habitat where Audubon first observed the species.
audubon-birds-57-loggerhead-shrike: A pair of shrikes occupies the spiny branches of a green-briar, the predatory songbird's hooked bill and black mask carefully delineated. The botanical setting accurately records a thicket habitat where shrikes impale prey on thorns.
audubon-birds-58-hermit-thrush: Two hermit thrushes perch on the wiry branches of a berry-laden shrub in Plate 58 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, their warm rufous tails and spotted breasts rendered against clusters of small orange-red fruit. The pair composition — labelled Male and Female in the plate text — allows comparison of the species' characteristic spotted underparts and contrasting tail colour. The open branch setting gives full prominence to the birds' clean silhouettes.
audubon-birds-59-chestnut-sided-warbler: Two warblers move through a flowering shrub, their yellow crowns and chestnut flanks picked out against fresh green leaves. The aquatint records a species that became more common as nineteenth-century clearing created the second-growth scrub it favours.
audubon-birds-6-wild-turkey: A large female wild turkey strides across grassy ground accompanied by a brood of young poults in Plate 6 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the plate caption reading 'Female and Young.' The hen's iridescent dark plumage and blue-grey head fill the composition, while the alert, scurrying chicks animate the foreground. The double-elephant folio's full sheet is exploited to show the female near life size, establishing the monumental scale that distinguishes Birds of America from all earlier ornithological publications.
audubon-birds-6-wild-turkey-2: A male wild turkey strides across the ground, iridescent body feathers and bare blue head turned in profile. The bird occupies almost the full sheet of the double-elephant folio, a deliberate scaling that opens the publication's prospectus and signals American subject matter.
audubon-birds-60-carbonated-warbler: Two male Carbonated Warblers — a species known only from Audubon's single reported encounter and now considered of uncertain identity — perch on a branch of a fruiting may-bush in Plate 60 of John James Audubon's Birds of America. Their greenish-yellow plumage is marked with dark streaking on the crown and back. The plate stands as the sole pictorial record of a bird that has never been confirmed by another observer.
audubon-birds-61-great-horned-owl: A pair of great horned owls perches on a lichen-covered branch in Plate 61 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, their prominent ear tufts erect and yellow eyes directed toward the viewer. The warm brown and buff barring of their plumage is finely graduated against a pale ground, showing the Havell workshop's control of tonal colour printing. The plate is one of the larger raptors in the series and presents both birds nearly face-on to emphasise the species' intense, forward-facing gaze.
audubon-birds-62-passenger-pigeon: A male and female passenger pigeon are shown in an allofeeding interaction on a branch in Plate 62 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the male's slate-blue head and rich rufous breast contrasting with the olive-brown upperparts of the female above. The intimate pose documents a social behaviour of a species then numbering in the billions but driven to extinction by 1914. Audubon's composition captures both the beauty and the vitality of a bird whose loss he could not have foreseen.
audubon-birds-63-white-eyed-flycatcher-o: A single white-eyed vireo perches on a tall flowering plant in Plate 63 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the pale iris that gives the bird its name clearly visible beside a small spider rendered nearby. The botanical setting — a slender stem with delicate clustered blooms — gives the composition an airy openness quite different from the denser foliage of many plates. The title reflects the unsettled early-nineteenth-century taxonomy that grouped vireos among the flycatchers.
audubon-birds-64-swamp-sparrow: A swamp sparrow perches on the arching stem of a may-apple in Plate 64 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, the bird's rusty cap and streaked back set against the plant's large lobed leaves and single white flower. The plate text identifies the botanical subject as May Apple, Podophyllum peltatum. The single-bird composition keeps the focus on the sparrow's subdued but carefully differentiated plumage.
audubon-birds-65-rathbone-warbler: A small warbler named in honour of the Rathbone family of Liverpool, patrons during the artist's English subscription drive. Now considered an immature or variant yellow warbler rather than a distinct species, the plate preserves a name otherwise lost from ornithology.
audubon-birds-66-ivory-billed-woodpecker: Four ivory-billed woodpeckers — male, female, and two immatures — are shown clinging to a lichen-covered dead trunk, the male's vivid red crest and both sexes' distinctive ivory bills rendered at life size. Plate 66 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838), it stands as one of the most celebrated images of a species now widely regarded as extinct, last reliably documented in the old-growth bottomland forests of the American South.
audubon-birds-67-red-winged-starling-or-: Red-winged blackbirds in graded plumages — adult male, young male, and female — are shown on a blossoming branch bearing small pink flowers, the male's scarlet-and-yellow epaulet conspicuous in display. Plate 67 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) uses the older common names 'Red-winged Starling' and 'Marsh Blackbird' current before the species was universally grouped among American blackbirds.
audubon-birds-68-republican-or-cliff-swa: Cliff swallows are shown alongside their gourd-shaped mud nests built under a rocky overhang, several birds entering and leaving the colony. The plate documents the colonial nesting biology that earned the bird its alternative name of Republican Swallow.
audubon-birds-69-bay-breasted-warbler: Two bay-breasted warblers move through the foliage of a flowering branch, the male's chestnut throat and crown contrasted with creamy neck patches. The plate captures spring breeding plumage rarely encountered south of the boreal forest.
audubon-birds-7-purple-grakle-or-common-: Common Grackles cluster on a maize stalk, ears split open to expose the kernels they raid. The composition links the species directly to its reputation as an agricultural pest, with iridescent plumage rendered through layered hand-colouring over an aquatint base.
audubon-birds-70-henslow-s-bunting: Henslow's sparrow — placed among the buntings in Audubon's classification — is shown at ground level among rocks and flowering plants, the streaked brown plumage blending naturally with the low-growing vegetation. Plate 70 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) honours the Cambridge professor John Stevens Henslow, for whom the species was named.
audubon-birds-71-winter-hawk: A Winter Hawk — now understood as an immature red-shouldered hawk — is shown in active flight, stooping to seize a large frog amid a marshy, grass-filled setting. Plate 71 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) records a name once believed to designate a separate species, before juvenile and adult plumages of the red-shouldered hawk were correctly correlated.
audubon-birds-72-swallow-tailed-hawk: A swallow-tailed kite (called Swallow-tailed Hawk by Audubon) banks on long pointed wings against a plain background, a garter snake gripped in its bill — illustrating one of the reptilian prey items the species takes in flight. Plate 72 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) exploits the double-elephant folio's generous format to convey the dramatic wingspan of this raptor of southern North America.
audubon-birds-73-wood-thrush: Two wood thrushes — male above, female below — perch on a branch of fruiting dogwood (Cornus florida), the bold round breast spots of the lower bird contrasting with the deep rufous upperparts of the upper. Plate 73 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) pairs the species with one of the most characteristic trees of eastern deciduous forest, depicted here in berry-laden autumn condition.
audubon-birds-74-indigo-bird: Three indigo buntings — two full-blue males and a brownish female — are shown on a climbing vine with pendant small flowers and berries, the males' saturated blue plumage capturing one of the most vivid colours in North American ornithology. Plate 74 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) employs the common name 'Indigo Bird' current before the species was reclassified among the cardinal-grosbeak family.
audubon-birds-75-le-petit-caporal: Le Petit Caporal — labelled in the plate as Falco temerarius — is shown as a single small hawk perched on a dead stump entwined with ivy, the banded tail and body shape suggesting an accipiter type. Plate 75 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) preserves a vernacular French name used in Louisiana that never entered standard ornithological nomenclature.
audubon-birds-76-virginian-partridge: A covey of Virginian (Northern Bobwhite) Partridges scatters in panic as a hawk strikes from above, the dynamic composition exemplifying the dramatic narrative staging that distinguishes Birds of America from earlier ornithological plates. Hand-coloured aquatint after a watercolour drawn from life-size specimens.
audubon-birds-77-belted-kingfisher: Three belted kingfishers — one male and two females, one of the females tossing a fish — are depicted against a richly painted river and mountain landscape in Plate 77 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838). The composition highlights the sexual dimorphism of the species, with the female's diagnostic chestnut breast band clearly rendered alongside the slate-blue and white plumage shared by both sexes.
audubon-birds-78-great-carolina-wren: Two Carolina Wrens — male above, female below — perch on the flowering stem of a Dwarf Buckeye (Aesculus parva), the warm cinnamon plumage and prominent white supercilium characteristic of the species clearly rendered. Plate 78 of John James Audubon's Birds of America (1827–1838) presents the birds at life size on the double-elephant folio sheet, with careful botanical detail devoted to the plant's clustered tubular flowers.
audubon-birds-79-tyrant-fly-catcher: An Eastern Kingbird is shown defending its territory, the species' aggressive behaviour toward larger raptors having earned it the name Tyrant Fly-catcher. Hand-coloured aquatint engraving by Robert Havell Jr. of London, working from the original watercolour study.
audubon-birds-8-white-throated-sparrow: Two White-throated Sparrows perch on a flowering dogwood branch bearing white blossoms, the boldly striped head and bright white throat patch of each bird clearly differentiated. Hand-coloured aquatint from Plate 8 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-80-prairie-titlark: A single Prairie Titlark (American Pipit) stands on the ground among low vegetation with pink blooms, reflecting the species' terrestrial habits. Plate 80 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-81-fish-hawk-or-osprey: An Osprey grips a large silvery fish in its talons as it rises above a coastal waterway, wings dramatically spread across the composition. Plate 81 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-82-whip-poor-will: Three Eastern Whip-poor-wills are depicted among lobed oak foliage: two roosting on branches and one in flight catching a large moth, its gaping bill and bristled rictus conveying the nocturnal nightjar's hunting behaviour. Plate 82 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-83-house-wren: Two House Wrens animate an old hat repurposed as a nesting cavity, a domestic vignette underscoring the species' readiness to nest in human-made objects. Plate 83 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-84-blue-grey-fly-catcher: Two Blue-grey Gnatcatchers perch on branches of a black walnut, their slender forms and long tails characteristic of the species. Plate 84 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-85-yellow-throated-warbler: A single Yellow-throated Warbler perches on a chinquapin branch bearing spiny burrs, the bold yellow throat patch and facial striping rendered from Audubon's life-size study. Plate 85 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint from the double-elephant folio, held at the University of Pittsburgh.
audubon-birds-86-black-warrior: Two Black Warrior hawks (Falco harlani, now classified as Harlan's Hawk), male above and female below, are shown in contrasting dark plumages on bare branches. Plate 86 of John James Audubon's Birds of America documents this dark-morph raptor, which Audubon treated as a distinct species before it was later subsumed into Buteo jamaicensis.
audubon-birds-87-florida-jay: A pair of Florida Jays (Florida Scrub-Jays) perches on a persimmon branch laden with golden fruits, the vivid blue-and-white plumage rendered against the autumnal foliage. Plate 87 of John James Audubon's Birds of America, hand-coloured aquatint engraved by Robert Havell Jr., held at the University of Pittsburgh.
