Madame Molé-Reymond, actress of the Comédie-Italienne, turns toward the viewer in a purple dress and broad blue hat trimmed with feathers, a fur muff clasped at her side. Vigée Le Brun captures the sitter's animated half-turn with a quick, energetic brushwork characteristic of her informal portraits of the late Ancien Régime. The work entered the collection of the Louvre's Department of Paintings and is dated 1786.

The young sitter stands in three-quarter view wearing a wide-brimmed straw hat and a dark bodice over a red skirt, a lace shawl draped across her shoulders. She holds a wicker basket of grapes and other fruit, lending the portrait a pastoral informality favoured by Vigée Le Brun in the 1780s. The painting, dated 1784, is held by the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City.

A double portrait set out of doors, the Marquise de Pezay seated beside the Marquise de Rougé, whose two young sons press in beside her. Painted on the eve of the Revolution, the canvas blends the natural settings and tender maternal grouping that Vigée Le Brun had refined in her portraits of Marie Antoinette and her circle.
collection-of-beauty-elisabeth-vigee-le-: An allegorical pair: Peace, in classical drapery, gently leads forward Abundance, who carries a sheaf of wheat and a cornucopia. The painting was Vigée Le Brun's reception piece for the Académie Royale, accepted in 1783, and shows her combining Neoclassical subject matter with the warm flesh tones and silken finish of her portrait practice.
collection-of-beauty-elisabeth-vigee-leb: Emma Hamilton turns in the studio with a turbaned head and parted lips, posed as the prophetic Sibyl of Cumae. Vigée Le Brun carried the resulting composition through her exile from Naples to Vienna and Russia as a calling card of her Italian period.

Madame du Barry is portrayed in a formal silver-white silk gown with lace-trimmed ruffled sleeves and a pink sash, her powdered hair crowned with a wreath of white feathers and flowers. She stands before a garden backdrop, holding a garland of colourful blooms. Vigée Le Brun painted this three-quarter-length portrait in 1782; it is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

The countess is shown seated, wearing a blue silk gown with olive-green sleeves and a gold sash, a white veil draped over her curling auburn hair. A pearl necklace and a small hand mirror complete the composition, which has the smooth, polished finish characteristic of Vigée Le Brun's court portraits. The work is dated 1790, painted during the artist's émigré years.

The Parisian actress Hyacinthe-Gabrielle Roland — mistress and, from 1794, wife of Richard Wellesley, Earl of Mornington, which later made her Marchioness Wellesley — sits informally with loosened, ribboned hair against a stormy sky. Vigée Le Brun painted her in Rome in 1791, during the Italian years of her emigration from revolutionary France; the portrait now hangs in the Legion of Honor, Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.

Emma Hamilton is depicted standing and turning, her right arm raised to hold a tambourine above her head, long dark hair streaming behind her. She wears a loose classical robe with a gold belt, and Vesuvius rises in the background — an allusion to her famous 'attitudes' performed in Naples. The portrait, dated circa 1790, is held by the Lady Lever Art Gallery.

Vigée Le Brun holds her young daughter Julie in a close embrace, the artist dressed in a blue silk gown with long sleeves against a dark ground. Painted in 1789, the canvas adopts the Madonna-and-Child compositional type to express ideals of maternal sentiment fashionable in the late eighteenth century.
collection-of-beauty-elizabeth-vigee-leb: Muhammad Dervish Khan stands full-length against an open sky, wearing white robes and an elaborately embroidered outer garment, a curved sabre held at his side. Vigée Le Brun painted this monumental portrait in Paris in 1788, presenting her subject with the formal gravity of state portraiture.
collection-of-beauty-emmanuel-joseph-sie: The abbé Sieyès, theorist of the Third Estate and architect of the Brumaire coup that brought Napoleon to power, sits in dark coat against a plain ground. David painted the portrait in Brussels, where both artist and sitter were exiled after the Bourbon Restoration of 1815.
collection-of-beauty-enbu-by-hayami-gyos: Moths of varying colours — white, cream, spotted, and pale blue-green — spiral upward through tongues of flame against a deep dark ground. Hayami Gyoshū painted this work in 1925, fusing nihonga pigments with a decorative, rhythmic energy that reflects the Taishō-era modernism of his circle; the work is held in the Yamatane Museum, Tokyo.
collection-of-beauty-enoshima-in-the-sag: The tidal causeway to the sacred island of Enoshima opens before pilgrims as Mount Fuji rises in the distance. From Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, the print exploits imported Prussian blue and the bold diagonal of the sandbar to organise its broad sea view.
collection-of-beauty-enrique-viii-de-ing: Henry VIII appears half-length in a richly embroidered gold doublet with dark puffed sleeves set with jewels, a heavy jewelled collar across his broad shoulders. Dated 1540 and now in the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica at Palazzo Barberini in Rome, the panel is among Holbein's autograph small-format Tudor portraits produced for diplomatic and courtly circulation.
collection-of-beauty-entree-d-alexandre-: Alexander, clad in gold and laurel, rides in a triumphal chariot as he enters Babylon, surrounded by a throng of soldiers, supplicants, and captives bearing spoils. Le Brun painted the canvas between 1664 and 1665 as part of his celebrated Alexander cycle for Louis XIV; it hangs in the Louvre and served as the basis for the Gobelins tapestry series.
collection-of-beauty-entree-de-cimetiere: A wrought-iron gate opens onto a hushed graveyard, its crosses and weathered stones receding into mist. Friedrich treats the cemetery as a threshold between visible world and the beyond, his characteristic Romantic meditation on mortality rendered in muted earth tones and silvery atmosphere.
collection-of-beauty-epes-sargent-a13818: A man in a grey coat and white wig leans beside a stone pedestal, his hands folded at his chest, with a landscape glimpsed to the right. Painted by John Singleton Copley around 1760 and now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, the portrait exemplifies the young Copley's command of European compositional formulas adapted for his American clientele.
collection-of-beauty-erasistratus-the-ph: The court physician Erasistratus takes the pulse of the lovesick prince Antiochus as his stepmother Stratonice enters the chamber, revealing the cause of his illness. West painted the Hellenistic anecdote, drawn from Plutarch, in 1772. The canvas is in the Birmingham Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-erasmus-quellinus-i: A winged Cupid lies on his back in deep slumber, his nude body draped against rich red fabric, a candle or lamp glowing above him. The motif of the disarmed and sleeping god of love was a favourite of the Flemish Baroque tradition; this painting is linked to the Museo del Prado and dateable to around 1630.

Europa, in a red drape, clings to the horn of a white bull as it carries her through turbulent waves, her hair streaming in the wind. Erasmus Quellinus II painted this interpretation of Ovid's myth in 1635; the canvas is in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-ernst-ludwig-kirchn: Two figures raise a single large bow in a vivid, light-filled landscape of yellows and greens, a target visible in the distance, while a third figure at lower right holds a clutch of arrows. Kirchner painted this work between 1935 and 1937 during his final years near Davos, applying the flattened, bold contours characteristic of his late style.

A woman — identified as Kirchner's model Dodo — is shown bust-length in a boldly painted portrait, the collar around her neck rendered in slashing strokes of yellow, white, and red against a blue garment and flickering background. Painted around 1906 and now in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid, the canvas is an early statement of the chromatic intensity Kirchner would develop with the Brücke group.

A nude figure is shown hunched over in what appears to be a tub, the body reduced to bold white forms cut against a black ground. Kirchner produced the woodcut in 1908, while the Brücke group was working in Dresden, and an impression is held in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

A soldier and a young woman stand in a wooded clearing under a rising moon, the figures pressed close in the half-light. Painted in 1905 during Kirchner's Dresden student years, the canvas entered the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston as accession number 98.286.

Trams curve around the Berlin square of Nollendorfplatz under a steep, tipped-up perspective, with hurrying figures pressed against the kerb. Kirchner began his Berlin street pictures shortly after the Brücke group relocated from Dresden; the canvas is now held by Stiftung Stadtmuseum Berlin.

The Sertig valley unfolds in autumn brilliance, its forested slopes ablaze in ochre and orange beneath jagged peaks rendered in Kirchner's angular Expressionist palette. A foreground railing anchors the panoramic view down to a cluster of valley buildings. The canvas belongs to the alpine body of work Kirchner produced near Davos after his wartime breakdown, where mountain geometry tempered the urban intensity of his Brücke years.

Three naked figures move through a sun-dappled outdoor setting beneath a large tree, their bodies rendered in broad, flat planes of orange, red, and green typical of Kirchner's Brücke idiom. The canvas, dated 1910, grew out of the group's summers at the Moritzburg lakes near Dresden, where communal bathing in nature served both as lived practice and programmatic subject.
collection-of-beauty-escola-de-atenas-va: Painted for Pope Julius II's private library in the Stanza della Segnatura, this fresco assembles the philosophers of antiquity beneath a vast coffered vault, with Plato and Aristotle striding through the central arch. Raphael's lucid one-point perspective and idealised figures became a touchstone of High Renaissance harmony.
collection-of-beauty-espagnole-et-agneau: A Spanish woman's face is overlaid with the lamb and other contour images in superimposed line. Made in 1928, the work belongs to Picabia's Transparencies series, begun the previous year, in which he alternated paint with resinous varnish so that motifs drawn from Renaissance frescoes, Catalan murals and popular sources could coexist without fully merging.
collection-of-beauty-etretat-george-inne: Inness looks down from a hillside above Étretat across green meadows where sheep and cattle graze, with the village and the famous white chalk cliffs visible in the middle ground and the grey Channel beyond. Two figures pause in the foreground pasture beneath a gathering, dramatic sky. Dated 1875 and held at the Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford, the canvas reflects Inness's atmospheric approach to European landscape during his sojourns abroad.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-de-blaas-the-: Two young women are seated on a stone bench against a brick wall while a bare-footed young man leans toward them in easy conversation, a basket of fruit at his feet. De Blaas captures a familiar moment of Venetian working-class sociability, dressed in the colourful regional costume he favoured, rendered with the lustrous academic finish that brought him success at Edwardian salons. The painting is dated 1904.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-bil: Arthur Graf Berchtold (1843–1929), hereditary member of the Hungarian Upper House and deputy to the Hungarian Reichstag, is portrayed in a half-length format wearing a dark fur-trimmed ceremonial coat with elaborately jewelled clasps. The dark ground and three-quarter gaze lend the portrait the gravity expected of official commissions. De Blaas signed and dated the canvas 1882.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-der: A young woman leans on a windowsill, her gaze meeting the viewer directly while she holds a vivid red fan loosely at her side. The single warm accent of the fan against her white dress and dark interior backdrop typifies de Blaas's skill at turning a simple prop into a focal point. The panel is signed and dated 1892.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-pla: Three women engaged in needlework and lace-making are gathered in a vine-shaded courtyard while a young man seated backwards on a chair addresses them with an animated gesture, a basket of fruit on the ground nearby. De Blaas lavishes attention on the women's colourful Venetian costume and the varied textures of fabric, setting the lively exchange against a sun-warmed brick wall. The canvas is signed and dated 1905.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-sha: A woman pauses at a washboard to look up at her companion, who stands smiling and holds a letter she has just received. The exchange between the two figures, set against a worn brick wall, captures the small social moments de Blaas drew from Venetian working life and polished with the slick academic technique that won him wide Edwardian popularity. The canvas is dated 1904.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-the: A smiling young woman leans against a column as a working man — carrying a large bundle of straw and a wicker basket on his back — bends close to whisper something to her. Copper vessels lie at her feet on the cobblestones. De Blaas constructs a knowing courtship scene from working-class Venetian street life, rendered with his characteristic academic precision. The canvas is signed and dated 1889.
collection-of-beauty-eugen-von-blaas-two: Two women are depicted in close half-length format: one in white lace with fair colouring and pearl jewellery, the other in a black gold-dotted veil with a coral necklace. Together they hold a single white rose. The intimate double-portrait format and refined costume place this work in de Blaas's more elevated register, distinct from his working-courtyard genre scenes. The canvas is dated 1898.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-de-blaas-a-p: A young woman in Venetian costume sits sideways on a low brick parapet, her gaze directed across the lagoon toward a distant cityscape, her hands resting loosely in her lap. A straw hat hangs at her back, a basket of fruit sits below on the ground, and a discarded sandal lies nearby. De Blaas uses the open waterside setting to give the figure an air of reverie. The canvas is dated 1896 and held by the Art Renewal Center.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-de-blaas-cur: Two young women climb a wooden ladder propped against a stone wall, both craning to see what lies on the other side. The painting's title and the evident delight on their faces make the subject plain: the curiosity is directed outward, not shared between them. The high academic finish and genre charm are hallmarks of de Blaas's Venetian figure painting, dated 1892.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-de-blaas-day: A young woman stands at the water's edge, her gaze turned towards the horizon while she rests on a long shepherd's staff. Two wicker baskets of market goods — one holding live poultry — sit at her feet, suggesting a brief pause on an errand. De Blaas renders her yellow dress and embroidered bodice with the precise textile attention characteristic of his genre work, here set against a wide, silver-toned lagoon sky. Signed and dated 1895.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix: Delacroix portrays himself in three-quarter view, curly dark hair framing a face of intense, searching expression. He wears a dark coat with a visible green collar, against a warm ochre-brown background that merges with his silhouette. Painted in 1837, when the artist was in his late thirties, this self-portrait is now in the Louvre.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-a-: A bandit, slumped in a rocky landscape, drinks from a stream as his life ebbs away, the body twisted in a pose that recalls Delacroix's study of Géricault. The picture distils the young Romantic's taste for outsiders, suffering, and Byronic violence into a single charged moment.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-ch: In this Romantic interpretation of the Gospel storm narrative, Christ lies asleep amid the boat's huddled figures while the disciples gesture in fear and the sea churns around them. Painted in 1841, it is one of several versions Delacroix made of the subject, each exploring the contrast between divine calm and human terror.

Christ sleeps in the stern of a fishing boat while terrified apostles wrestle the sail against a green wall of water. Delacroix returned to the Gospel subject repeatedly in the 1850s, each version intensifying the chromatic clash between the storm and the calm figure asleep in its centre.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-co: Delacroix drew on his 1832 North African journey with Count de Mornay's diplomatic mission to evoke the violent equestrian games of the Moroccan court. The clashing horses and flying robes display the saturated, almost vibrating palette he developed after seeing Maghreb light at first hand.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-fr: Delacroix painted this portrait of Frédéric Chopin in 1838 as part of a larger double portrait that also depicted George Sand; the canvas was cut into two separate works after the artist's death, leaving only this fragment of the composer. Chopin appears in three-quarter view, his auburn hair loosely framing an introspective face rendered against a warm brown ground. The fragment is now in the Louvre.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-le: A Natchez couple cradles their newborn on the banks of the Mississippi, fugitives from a colonial massacre, after Chateaubriand's 1801 novel 'Atala'. Delacroix turns the literary source into a sombre meditation on indigenous extinction, exhibited at the Salon of 1835 and now in the Metropolitan Museum.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-ov: The exiled Roman poet Ovid reclines on the grass of the Black Sea steppe, offered milk and bread by Scythian herdsmen while their horses graze in the background. Delacroix exhibited a smaller version at the 1859 Salon and returned to the subject in 1862, the year before his death; the painting is now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-ri: A jaguar springs from a thicket onto the haunches of a rearing horse, its rider thrown back as the predator's claws sink into the animal's flank. Delacroix borrowed the motif from Rubens and the Stubbs lion-and-horse tradition, condensing the struggle into a tight vertical of intersecting muscle.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-sh: A small craft is overwhelmed by churning surf beneath a leaden sky, figures barely visible amid the spray. The late Delacroix returns again to the shipwreck motif as an emblem of human helplessness before nature, treated with a freer, almost atmospheric brush.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-st: A scarlet lobster, hare, game birds, and a tartan bag are arranged on an open ground with weapons, while mounted hunters appear in the distant landscape behind. The painting was exhibited at the Salon of 1827–28 alongside the Death of Sardanapalus and is now in the Louvre. Delacroix's handling of the lustrous shell and limp game anticipates the chromatic ambitions of his larger Romantic canvases, dated 1826–27.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-delacroix-th: Ophelia clings to a willow branch as it splits above the brook, her white shift catching on the bark while her wreath of flowers drifts away. Delacroix's first version of the subject, drawn from Gertrude's speech in Act IV of Hamlet, was painted in 1838 and is now in the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.

The Assyrian king Sardanapalus reclining on his bed as his slaves, horses and treasures are destroyed at his command, a writhing mass of bodies in red and gold. Oil on canvas, about 3.9 by 5 metres, in the Louvre, Paris, shown at the Salon of 1827. The subject derives from Byron's verse drama, and the picture drew sharp criticism for its turbulent composition.

Victorious Central Asian troops stand among severed heads and abandoned weapons after the action, the celebration unsettling rather than triumphant. Paired with 'After a failure', the picture insists that battlefield outcomes share a single moral landscape of slaughter.

Delacroix records the ecstatic Aissaoua brotherhood spilling through the streets of Tangier, a procession he had witnessed during his 1832 Moroccan trip. The swirling crowd and sun-bleached architecture exemplify his lifelong fascination with North African religious spectacle.
collection-of-beauty-eugene-ferdinand-vi: An Arab horseman in a white burnoose tends to his chestnut horse, reaching up to adjust the animal's bridle while it stands restless beside him. A pistol and red cloth lie on the ground in the foreground. Painted in 1855, the work draws on sketches from Delacroix's 1832 journey to Morocco and is catalogued under the title 'Arab saddling his horse.'
collection-of-beauty-eugene-murer-hyacin: The pastry cook and collector Eugène Murer, born Hyacinthe-Eugène Meunier, shown bust-length in a dark coat. Renoir painted the portrait in 1877; Murer eventually gathered some 122 Impressionist works, including fifteen by Renoir, and the canvas is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-evening-landscape-a: A reaped wheat field with stacked sheaves lies under a swollen orange moon rising from behind the hills of the Alpilles. Van Gogh painted the canvas, also known as Landscape with Wheat Sheaves and Rising Moon, in the summer of 1889, working from the walled field he could see from his room at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy. It is held by the Kröller-Müller Museum in Otterlo.
collection-of-beauty-evening-snow-at-ter: A snow-covered village street at night, with electric poles cutting through a deep blue sky and warm light glowing from the windows of low-roofed houses on either side of a canal. A solitary figure with an umbrella makes their way along the path in the distance. Kawase Hasui produced this shin-hanga woodblock print in 1920, depicting Terajima Village on the outskirts of Tokyo.
collection-of-beauty-faded-laurels-by-ed: An elderly, laurel-crowned nobleman sits apart on stone steps while a lively medieval court celebration unfolds behind him, his isolation conveying the melancholy of faded dignity. Edmund Blair Leighton, working in his characteristically precise late-Victorian academic style, frames the chivalric subject with antiquarian attention to costume and architecture, 1889.
collection-of-beauty-famille-de-paysans-: A peasant family pauses around a sparse table in a dim cottage interior, each face turned outwards with quiet directness. The Le Nain brothers' rare empathetic treatment of rural poverty, painted in a sober earthen palette, anticipates the realism of Courbet two centuries later.
collection-of-beauty-fantomas-juan-gris: A Synthetic Cubist still life of pipe, newspaper and glass, with the words FANTOMAS and LE JOURNAL legible across the fragmented planes. Painted in 1915 and held in the Chester Dale Collection at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, the title cites the popular pulp anti-hero of Souvestre and Allain's serial novels.
collection-of-beauty-felicien-rops-porno: A blindfolded nude woman in stockings and heeled shoes leads a pig on a leash along a pedestal, above a frieze of prostrated allegorical figures labelled Sculpture, Musique, Poésie, and Peinture, while three winged putti hover overhead. Félicien Rops's 1878 satirical drawing, housed in the Musée provincial Félicien Rops, personifies the dominance of carnal appetite over the arts in a characteristic Decadent indictment of bourgeois culture.
collection-of-beauty-female-nude-with-fo: A standing female nude is rendered in loose, rapid strokes of warm pink and green against a background of dappled foliage, the figure's surface dissolved into coloured patches of reflected light. Painted in oil on cardboard in 1905 and held in the Kirchner Museum Davos, the work predates the formal founding of Die Brücke later that year in Dresden.
collection-of-beauty-femenine-wave: A massive, circular wave curls inward on itself, its deep indigo interior flecked with white and its outer rim dissolving into swirling foam, filling the composition from edge to edge. Katsushika Hokusai's 'Feminine Wave' (c. 1845) was conceived as the companion to his 'Masculine Wave', and together they demonstrate his late-career treatment of water as pure dynamic form within the ukiyo-e tradition.
collection-of-beauty-femmes-d-alger-dans: Three women lounge with a servant in a tiled Algerian harem chamber, surrounded by hookah, slippers and richly patterned textiles. Painted after Delacroix gained rare access to a domestic interior in 1832, the Louvre canvas became a foundational source of the nineteenth-century Orientalist imagination.
collection-of-beauty-ferdinand-victor-eu: A single rider in red, mounted on a grey horse, struggles to control a rearing brown horse in the surf at the edge of a North African shore, a coastal town visible on the distant headland. Painted in 1860 — three years before Delacroix's death — the canvas distils decades of the artist's Maghreb sketchbooks into a concentrated motif of animal energy and human mastery; it is now in the Phillips Collection, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-fernand-khnopff013: Khnopff portrays his sister Marguerite, a recurring presence in his work, with the cool, hieratic detachment that defines his Symbolist portraiture. The pale palette and flattened space distil her into an emblem of withdrawn, idealised femininity rather than likeness alone.
collection-of-beauty-fernand-le-quesne-l: A pale-skinned nude woman reclines on a large shell-like rock at the shoreline while a dark-skinned standing male nude leans over her against an open seascape with a distant sailboat. Fernand Le Quesne's 1889 academic painting, exhibited in the orbit of the Paris Salon, pairs the two nude figures in a sun-lit coastal setting, the title casting their contrasting forms as twin pearls.
collection-of-beauty-fiesta-campestre: Two clothed musicians and two nude women sit in a wooded clearing near Venice, a shepherd driving his flock past in the middle distance. Long attributed to Giorgione, the Pastoral Concert is now generally given to the young Titian and entered the French royal collection by 1671 before passing to the Louvre.
collection-of-beauty-figure-studies-met-: A bearded, heavily draped man stands gesturing on a rise of ground, surrounded by figures who kneel, crouch, and sprawl around him — a sheet of studies for a crowded religious composition. Ricci worked it up in pen and brown ink with gray wash over traces of red and black chalk, letting rapid hatching stand in for landscape. Such fluent study sheets were the working currency of Venetian painters of his generation; this one is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-file-ivan-aivazovsk: A storm breaks over the headland of Cape Sounion on the southern tip of Attica, the ruined columns of the Temple of Poseidon picked out above churning sea. Aivazovsky, court painter to the Russian navy, treated the Aegean coastline as a stage for Romantic seascape rather than archaeological record.
collection-of-beauty-fin-d-arabesque-edg: A soloist holds a final triumphant pose, one arm raised and the other lowered with a flower bouquet, her gaze inclined downward while a group of other dancers cluster in the background. Degas's 1876 work, held in the Musée d'Orsay, captures a moment of stage performance in his characteristic combination of pastel and other media on paper.
collection-of-beauty-finches-and-bamboo-: Two finches perch on the arching stems of teal-green bamboo beside a weathered rock, observed with the minute feather detail characteristic of the imperial court bird-and-flower idiom. The handscroll, attributed to the Northern Song Emperor Huizong (r. 1100–1125) and held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, exemplifies the exacting naturalism and calligraphic elegance of the gongbi tradition.
collection-of-beauty-five-egrets-descend: Five egrets glide through falling snow toward a quiet shoreline, their white forms dissolving against the pale ground. Koson, the leading kachoga (bird-and-flower) printmaker of the shin-hanga era, captures the species' winter behaviour with delicately graded woodblock impressions.
collection-of-beauty-flaming-june-by-fre: A young woman sleeps curled in a translucent orange-saffron gown, one arm thrown over her head, a sprig of oleander above her. Leighton painted the oil in 1895; after decades of neglect it was bought for the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico in the 1960s. The folded pose fills a square format, the fabric worked in deep orange against a marble parapet and sea.
collection-of-beauty-floorpolishers-male: Two labourers scrub a parquet floor, their bodies rendered as bold, block-like volumes in yellow and red against a loosely painted interior. Catalogued as Nakov F-196, the gouache on paper is dated 1911 and is held by the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.
collection-of-beauty-flora-tristan-1838: Portrait of the French socialist and feminist writer Flora Tristan (1803–1844), shown in half-length with arms crossed and dark curling hair. A lithograph published by Aubert in 1838, the print appeared in Le Charivari no. 53 on 22 February 1839.
collection-of-beauty-flowering-meadow-wi: Gnarled pine trunks rise from a meadow thick with long grass and dandelions, some in yellow bloom and some gone to seed, in the garden of the Saint-Paul asylum at Saint-Rémy. Van Gogh painted it in the spring of 1890, during his final weeks there, cropping the view to the ground plane so the flowering grass fills the canvas. Kröller-Müller Museum, Otterlo.
collection-of-beauty-flowers-in-a-rococo: A mixed bouquet of roses, anemones, and other flowers spills from an ornate Rococo vase with blue scrollwork, set against a pale grey-blue ground. Paul Cézanne painted this still life around 1876; it is now in the collection of the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-foggy-morning-at-po: Mist swallows the Norman cliffs above Pourville, where Monet spent the summer of 1882 pursuing the dissolving effects of marine atmosphere. Pale lavenders and silvered greens are knit together in short, parallel strokes, leaving the horizon as little more than a suggestion.
collection-of-beauty-follower-of-rogier-: A close adaptation of Rogier van der Weyden's celebrated Descent from the Cross, with the limp body of Christ lowered amid a tightly grouped frieze of mourners. The sharp Netherlandish drawing, jewel-toned drapery, and shallow gilded space follow the prototype's compressed, sculptural staging.
collection-of-beauty-fourth-muscle-man-b: A woodcut from Andreas Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica, the fourth in the famous sequence of muscle men that strip away the body's musculature layer by layer; here dissected muscles hang loose from the figure's arms as he stands in a landscape of hills and buildings that continues from plate to plate across the series. The blocks, cut for the book's first edition of 1543 and attributed to artists in Titian's circle, transformed anatomical illustration. This impression comes from the 1555 second edition and is in the Wellcome Collection, London.
collection-of-beauty-fox-in-the-snow-cou: A red fox bounds through a snow-covered winter landscape, its body caught in mid-motion against granular whites and a dark sky. Gustave Courbet painted this canvas in 1860; it is now in the collection of the Dallas Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-coresus-s: The high priest Coresus plunges a dagger into his own breast before the altar to save the maiden Callirhoe from the sacrifice Bacchus had demanded, the temple filled with collapsing onlookers. Fragonard's morceau d'agrément for admission to the Académie Royale in 1765, the canvas was bought immediately by Louis XV and hangs in the Louvre.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-francois-: A half-length portrait of François-Henri d'Harcourt (1726–1802), dressed in a loosely painted dark costume with a white lace collar and swirling red and blue drapery. Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted the oil on canvas around 1769 in the manner of his figures de fantaisie, in which sitters appear in theatrical or Renaissance-inflected dress.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-swing: A young woman in a pink silk gown swings forward through a garden bower, kicking off one slipper as a hidden suitor peers up from the bushes below. Commissioned by the Baron de Saint-Julien for his château, Fragonard's canvas became the defining image of Rococo libertinage.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-the-reade: A young woman in a yellow silk dress sits absorbed in a small book, her head inclined and a cushion visible beside her. Fragonard's oil on canvas, dated 1770, is held at the National Gallery of Art in Washington and is among the most refined of his intimate figure studies.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-the-see-s: A young woman in a red and green skirt swoops upward on a garden seesaw while a young man and two children look on below, surrounded by a leafy parkland setting. Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted this playful outdoor scene between 1750 and 1752, early in his career.
collection-of-beauty-fragonard-woman-w-d: A woman in an elaborate silk and lace gown holds a small white lapdog on a blue ribbon, raising the animal before her in a formal three-quarter pose. Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted this oil on canvas around 1769; it is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-fragonardsisters: Two young girls in yellow and pink silk dresses sit close together, their powdered hair and rosy cheeks lit against a dark background, with theatrical masks visible at the lower left. Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted this double portrait, known as The Two Sisters, in 1769.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-056: Samson stands upright over the fallen lion, his powerful torso bare and a drape gathered at his waist, gazing downward at the defeated beast in a wooded landscape. Francesco Hayez painted this monumental canvas in 1842, applying the academic Romantic manner he developed in Milan.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-oda: A nude woman sits in profile seen from behind, reading an open book against a deep crimson drapery, her dark hair falling loose around her shoulders. Francesco Hayez painted this Odalisque reading between 1866 and 1867; it is held at Villa Carlotta on Lake Como.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-rit: The novelist Alessandro Manzoni, author of I Promessi Sposi, sits in sober dark dress against a neutral ground, fixing the viewer with a measured gaze. Hayez treats the literary patriot of the Risorgimento with the restrained likeness and crisp drawing of the Italian Romantic portrait tradition.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-sel: Hayez places himself at the centre of a close-knit group that includes the painters Giuseppe Molteni and Giovanni Migliara, the sculptor Pelagio Pelagi, and the writer Tommaso Grossi. The five figures are pressed together in a tight cluster, with Hayez looking directly at the viewer from behind round spectacles. Now in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli, Milan, the small canvas records the intimate Lombard circle that shaped Italian Romanticism.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-sus: The biblical Susanna twists modestly at her bath, surprised by the elders whose presence is implied beyond the frame. Hayez handles the polished nude in the National Gallery, London, with a sculptural finish indebted to Canova and the warm tonalities of his Venetian training.
collection-of-beauty-francesco-hayez-the: A crowd of Greek refugees streams toward the shore as smoke rises from the hilltop town of Parga above them, dramatising the 1819 exodus before Ottoman rule. Men, women, children, and clergy fill the foreground, carrying possessions and looking back at the burning city. Hayez orchestrates the crowded shoreline as a Romantic tableau of exile and loss, in keeping with his patriotic history paintings.
collection-of-beauty-francis-brooks-chad: A loose bust-length oil sketch of the painter Francis Brooks Chadwick on a small panel measuring 13.75 by 10 inches. Sargent painted his friend in 1880, inscribing the location and date directly on the canvas. The work is held in a private collection.
collection-of-beauty-francis-osborne-5th: Francis Osborne, 5th Duke of Leeds, is shown as a young man in white ceremonial robes trimmed with gold lace over a red undergarment, the dress of a Knight of the Garter or similar order. Benjamin West painted the portrait before his death in 1820; it was given to the National Portrait Gallery, London in 1888.
collection-of-beauty-francis-picabia-191: The terraced hills above Cassis stack up in flat patches of pink, ochre and pine green under a Mediterranean light. Painted in December 1911 in oil on canvas at roughly 50 by 62 cm, the landscape belongs to the brief Fauve-derived phase Picabia ran through before swinging into the Section d'Or Cubism of 1912.

A near-square canvas of nearly two and a half metres on each side, resolving a mountain spring into broad interlocking facets of terracotta, brown, and dark grey. Picabia showed La Source at the 1912 Salon d'Automne in Paris; the picture later entered the Museum of Modern Art, New York.

Robed penitents and processional banners pulse through a Sevillian street in a Cubist-Orphist lattice of cones and curves. Inspired by Picabia's travels in Spain, the square canvas was shown at the 1912 Salon de la Section d'Or and travelled to the 1913 Armory Show; it now hangs at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

Three metres square, the canvas threads abstract bands of yellow, blue, grey, and orange around a remembered encounter between a dancer and a cleric observed during Picabia's Atlantic crossing. The invented title interleaves the French words étoile and danse; the picture was shown at the 1913 Armory Show and is now at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Curving metallic planes and tubular forms hurtle across a near-square canvas almost three metres on each side. Picabia painted Udnie in 1913 after watching Polish dancer Stasia Napierkowska perform on the ship carrying him to the Armory Show; the picture now hangs at the Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou, Paris.

A mechanical schematic rendered in ink, its interlocking gears, cog-wheels, and abstract structural elements arranged across the sheet with the title 'RÉVEIL MATIN' inscribed below. Made in 1919 and held by Tate, London, the drawing belongs to Picabia's machinist Dada period, when technical diagrams served to satirise human behaviour as mere mechanism.
collection-of-beauty-francis-picabia-192: Concentric black and white rings form a target across the sheet, with a reclining female nude figure laid diagonally over them, part coloured in watercolour wash. The title 'OPTOPHONE' is inscribed at the lower left. Made around 1922 in ink, watercolour, and pencil on board (72.1 × 60 cm), the work belongs to Picabia's Dada period.
collection-of-beauty-francis-picabia-ici: Alfred Stieglitz is portrayed as a bellows camera apparatus with a gearshift lever, its mechanism reaching toward the word 'IDEAL' printed at the top. Picabia's mechanomorphic portrait appeared on the cover of issue No. 1 of the New York review 291 in 1915, and is signed 'F. Picabia / 1915 / New York.'
collection-of-beauty-francis-picabia-tra: Overlapping semi-abstract figures are interwoven in warm ochres, reds, and dark browns, their contours dissolving into one another across the surface in a dense, gestural composition. The work belongs to Picabia's Transparences series, in which he layered figural forms to produce images readable at multiple depths, a direction he pursued from the late 1920s.
collection-of-beauty-francisco-de-goya-s: From the Black Paintings Goya applied directly to the walls of his Quinta del Sordo, the titan Cronus tears into one of his children, eyes blazing in a void. The savage handling, sooty palette, and private setting belong to the bleak, late vocabulary now reassembled in the Prado.
collection-of-beauty-francisco-de-zurbar: A bound lamb lies on a grey ledge against a dark ground, an Agnus Dei meditation on Christ's sacrifice rendered with extraordinary fleecy detail. The picture, in the Prado, distils Zurbarán's ascetic Sevillian piety into one of the most economical still lifes of the Spanish Baroque.

Saint Luke, traditionally credited with painting the Virgin's likeness, leans on a palette and gazes up at the crucified Christ, conflating the evangelist with the artist's own self-portrait. The sober brown ground and clipped lighting are characteristic of Zurbarán's monastic Sevillian commissions.

A life-size crucified Christ emerges from impenetrable darkness, the body modelled with sculptural tenebrism that fooled at least one early viewer into thinking the work a polychrome carving. Painted for Seville's Dominican monastery of San Pablo, it announced Zurbarán's austere devotional manner.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-00: A painter in a red coat sits at an easel working on a landscape in a dark, cluttered studio. Boucher painted this small genre scene between circa 1730 and 1735, in the years immediately following his return from Rome, where he had studied at the French Academy.

Pastoral figures — a woman leaning on a fence, a drover above with cattle — are disposed around a ruined stone arch bridge over a mill pond, with tall trees massed behind. Boucher signed and dated the canvas 1751, placing small staffage figures within a lush, theatrically composed landscape that draws on the decorative pastoral tradition he had absorbed in Rome.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-17: A thatched watermill with a turning wheel stands at the centre of a wooded river scene; washerwomen crouch at the bank while a standing figure pauses nearby, and a stone bridge appears at right middle distance. Boucher signed and dated the canvas 1755; the work is now in the National Gallery, London (NG6374).
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-dr: A shepherdess in a pink silk bodice reclines against a mossy bank with her crook and a basket of flowers beside her, her sheep dozing in the background. Painted around 1763, the canvas exemplifies Boucher's pastorale galante, the courtly fantasy of country life that filled the boudoirs of Madame de Pompadour and her circle.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-la: Jupiter, disguised as the chaste Diana, leans toward the nymph Callisto with the seducer's eagle hidden above a pink satin curtain. Signed and dated 1759 and acquired by the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City through the William Rockhill Nelson Trust, the small canvas concentrates the late Rococo into a tight palette of pinks, greens and blues.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-sk: Madame de Pompadour stands in a gilded interior wearing an elaborate green silk gown trimmed with flowers, holding a fan, with a tall looking-glass partially visible behind her. Boucher made the study around 1750 as a preparatory work for the formal portraits he produced for his principal patron; the painting is now at Waddesdon Manor, Buckinghamshire, in the National Trust collection.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-th: Venus rises from the sea attended by Tritons and Nereids, doves wheeling above the rococo curl of foam. Boucher painted the canvas in 1740 for the Swedish ambassador Carl Gustaf Tessin, who carried it back to Stockholm where it now hangs in the Nationalmuseum.

Venus is borne across the swell on a surge of nereids, tritons, and dolphins, while putti tumble through the air trailing a great loop of rose-patterned silk above her head. Painted in 1740, the canvas is Boucher's definitive statement of the mythological marine fantasy — flesh, spray, and drapery dissolving into a single silvery-blue arabesque. It was acquired by Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, the Swedish ambassador in Paris, and hangs today in the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm.
collection-of-beauty-francois-boucher-yo: A barefoot peasant girl raises her skirts and lifts a tambourine as she dances, painted in the late 1760s for a private Paris client. Boucher's pastorale prettifies rural labour into a courtly entertainment, and the picture passed through the Marchioness of Cholmondeley's collection.
collection-of-beauty-francois-joseph-nav: François-Joseph Navez painted this half-length portrait of his teacher Jacques-Louis David in Brussels in 1817, the year Navez joined David in Belgian exile. The sitter is shown in a dark coat with a white cravat and a red boutonnière, his direct gaze conveying the authority of the leading French Neoclassical painter.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snijders-keuk: A loaded kitchen table heaves with game, fruit and copper vessels in the lavish Antwerp manner that Snyders developed alongside Rubens. Strong diagonals and life-size scale push the still life toward decorative grandeur, intended for the dining halls of patrician collectors.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-a-gre: A white greyhound pins a young wild boar to the ground in an open landscape of rolling hills and scattered vegetation, a cloudy sky above. The work displays the precise animal anatomy Snyders brought to hunting subjects, and dates to the first half of the seventeenth century.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-and-w: Hounds tear at a cornered boar in a churning Baroque mêlée, the kind of large hunting piece Snyders supplied with workshop assistance for aristocratic galleries. Sweeping diagonals, splayed limbs and a bruised sky echo the dynamic compositions he had honed beside Rubens.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-conce: An owl serves as conductor while a riot of songbirds reads from a sheet of music, a witty allegorical conceit Snyders treated repeatedly. The tightly observed plumage of finches, parrots and birds of prey reflects his standing as Antwerp's premier animal specialist.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-cook-: A cook stands at a table laden with dead game birds — a peacock, pheasants, partridges and smaller fowl — raising a knife while a cat tugs at a peacock tail feather on the floor below. Additional birds hang from a hook at upper left. Painted between 1634 and 1637, the work is in the Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-lying: A lioness lies collapsed against a wooded rocky ground, her head turned toward the viewer with mouth slightly open, in a large-format oil attributed to Frans Snyders now held at the Liechtenstein Museum. Snyders, the leading Flemish Baroque animal painter, brought close observation and confident brushwork to his animal subjects throughout his career in Antwerp.
collection-of-beauty-frans-snyders-orphe: Orpheus charms a menagerie of beasts and birds with his lyre, the Ovidian subject becoming a pretext for Snyders's encyclopaedic display of fur, feather and scale. The composition crowds exotic species into a forested clearing in the Flemish Baroque manner.
collection-of-beauty-franz-von-stuck-004: A nude woman emerges from deep shadow with a large serpent coiled around her body in Franz von Stuck's iconic painting The Sin (1893). The frontal composition, strong chiaroscuro, and femme-fatale imagery are hallmarks of von Stuck's Symbolist manner and were sufficiently celebrated that he produced several versions of the subject.
collection-of-beauty-franz-von-stuck-by-: A late self-portrait on board, signed and dated 1923, presents the Munich Secession founder in dark dress against a neutral ground. The clipped scale and sober finish reflect von Stuck's habit of treating his own image as part of his public persona as artist-prince.
collection-of-beauty-franz-von-stuck-sal: Salome is depicted alone, mid-dance, against a deep black background within von Stuck's characteristic gilded architectural frame, a platter bearing the Baptist's head resting at her side. Painted in 1906, the work belongs to the fin-de-siècle Munich Symbolist tradition in which von Stuck repeatedly staged the biblical temptress with jewelled ornament and theatrical shadow.
collection-of-beauty-franz-von-stuck-the: Two nude male figures grapple aggressively in the left half of the canvas while a pale, red-haired female nude stands apart on the right, an impassive witness to the contest over her. Signed and dated 1905, the painting is held at the Hermitage Museum and exemplifies von Stuck's use of mythic-primeval allegory to explore erotic rivalry within the Symbolist idiom of the Munich Secession.
collection-of-beauty-franz-von-stuck-wou: A helmeted Amazon writhes in a circular composition of billowing red drapery, her nude torso bearing a wound while arrows and a fallen adversary appear at the edges of the canvas. The work, dated 1904 by the Van Gogh Museum, demonstrates von Stuck's use of classical warrior iconography to produce images of intense physical drama charged with Symbolist eroticism.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-00: A direct self-portrait set against a dark ground, the painter holding his palette and brushes. Oil on canvas, 108.9 by 71.1 cm, executed in 1865 to 1866 and held by the Art Institute of Chicago, which purchased it in 1962. Bazille was in his mid-twenties when he painted it.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-ba: The painter's studio at 9 rue de la Condamine in the Batignolles quarter of Paris, hung with canvases and peopled by his circle, Bazille himself shown at the easel. Painted in 1870; Manet contributed the figure of Bazille, and the work has been in the Musée d'Orsay since 1986.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-na: A still life of fish laid out on a kitchen table. Oil on canvas, painted in 1866 and held by the Detroit Institute of Arts. Bazille took up still life repeatedly in the mid-1860s, treating fish, game and a heron in turn.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-po: A bust-length portrait of a young man costumed as a medieval troubadour, his collar and cap evoking the Romantic revival of the type. The sitter is identified as the poet Paul Verlaine; Bazille painted the canvas in 1868, and it is now in the Dallas Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-th: A boy in white breeches, a pink shirt and a boater stands in a planted garden under a bright sky. Oil on canvas, about 128 by 169 cm, painted in 1866 to 1867 and held by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. Bazille left the foreground unfinished, the bare canvas still visible.

A young woman in a pink-and-white striped dress seen from behind, seated on a wall and looking out over the sunlit village of Castelnau near Montpellier. Oil on canvas, 147 by 110 cm, painted in 1864 and now in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris. The sitter is Bazille's cousin Thérèse des Hours.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-bazille-yo: A Black woman holding out a bouquet of pink-and-white peonies beside a basket of tulips, roses and lilac, posed as a flower seller. Oil on canvas, 60 by 75 cm, painted in 1870 and now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington; a related version is at the Musée Fabre.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-leighton-b: Frederic Leighton seated in his Academician's gown, left elbow hooked over the chair back, hands loosely clasped. Watts painted this oil from sittings in 1881, the year Leighton sat for the work now in the National Portrait Gallery, London (NPG 1049). It is one of three portraits Watts made of his friend across their long acquaintance.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-leighton-c: A long procession bears Cimabue's altarpiece of the Madonna through Florence toward Santa Maria Novella, the painter Cimabue leading with the boy Giotto. Leighton painted this over two metres tall and more than five metres wide in Rome between 1853 and 1855; Queen Victoria bought it on the opening day of the 1855 Royal Academy exhibition for 600 guineas.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-leighton-k: A reclining woman in pale drapery plays with a litter of kittens, her arm stretched along a couch. Leighton's canvas measures roughly 119 by 79 cm and treats a domestic subject far removed from the classical and mythological scenes for which he was known.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-leighton-p: May Sartoris, about fifteen, stands in a dark riding habit with a red scarf and a wide black hat, a felled tree at her side. Leighton painted the portrait around 1860; the oil measures 152.1 by 90.2 cm and is held in the Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-leighton-t: Three nymphs recline beneath an apple tree, the serpent Ladon coiled around its trunk to guard the golden fruit that was Hera's gift. Leighton painted the tondo about 1892; it is held by the Lady Lever Art Gallery in Port Sunlight. The circular format sets the sleeping figures within the curve of the tree's foliage.

Hermes lifts Persephone up from the underworld toward her mother Demeter, who reaches down through a gap of light at the cave mouth. Leighton painted the oil in 1891 and it hangs in Leeds Art Gallery. The figures form a single rising diagonal from the dark earth into the bright opening above.
collection-of-beauty-frederic-lord-leigh: Andromeda is chained naked to the rocks while the dragon spreads dark wings over her and Perseus dives in from above on the winged horse Pegasus. Leighton painted the oil in 1891; it entered the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool. The arched composition wraps the monster's body around the upper edge like a canopy.
collection-of-beauty-frederick-law-olmst: Sargent painted the landscape architect of Central Park during work on the Biltmore Estate grounds, posing him among the rhododendrons he had laid out. Loose, plein-air handling of the foliage gives way to a tighter likeness of the sitter, knitting Realist portraiture to Impressionist surface.
collection-of-beauty-frederick-leighton-: A close head-and-shoulders study of a fair-haired young Italian girl, her white blouse laced with a dark bodice, titled with the Italian for the blonde one. The oil belongs to the Hamburger Kunsthalle and is dated by the museum to 1879.

A half-length young woman in a black and gold dress turns to one side, her head resting against her hand. The model was Edith Pullen, sister of Leighton's regular model Dorothy Dene; the picture dates to 1883. Leighton kept his contours smooth and his palette restrained in the manner of his classicising portraiture.

A single draped woman seated on a rock above still water in a deep mountain hollow. Oil on canvas painted around 1890; Leighton described the setting as a place worn so deep that absolute silence holds. The picture is now in the Maryhill Museum of Art, Washington State.
collection-of-beauty-frederik-hendrik-15: Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange (1584–1647), is shown in three-quarter length wearing full burnished armour and a blue sash of office against a red draped curtain. This posthumous workshop portrait, produced in 1650 by the atelier of Gerard van Honthorst, is held in the Rijksmuseum collection.
collection-of-beauty-fritillaria-imperia: A crown imperial (Fritillaria imperialis) with its ring of pendent orange bells beneath a tuft of upright leaves, drawn life-size against a plain ground. Plate from Redouté's Les Liliacées, the eight-volume folio issued in Paris between 1802 and 1816. The image is a colour stipple engraving after Redouté's watercolour on vellum, finished by hand.
collection-of-beauty-frosty-morning-mont: A broad autumn or late-season meadow stretches beneath bare trees, with sheep grazing in the middle distance and a shepherd figure visible under an overcast sky. George Inness signed this canvas in 1885 and associated it with the New Jersey landscape around Montclair, where he spent his later years developing the atmospheric, tonal manner of his mature work.
collection-of-beauty-fujiwara-no-yasumas: A late triptych by Yoshitoshi shows the Heian courtier Fujiwara no Yasumasa playing his flute on a moonlit moor while the bandit Hakamadare, disarmed by the music, looks on. Long stretches of muted ground and the cool autumnal palette demonstrate Yoshitoshi's reformed late style for the Meiji woodblock market.
collection-of-beauty-fuseliartistmovedto: A small artist figure slumps on a plinth dwarfed by colossal antique fragments — a great foot and an outstretched hand — in this pen, ink and wash drawing by Henry Fuseli made during his Roman years (1778–1779). The sheet, now at the Kunsthaus Zürich, encapsulates the Romantic sense of awe and inadequacy before the ruins of classical civilisation.
collection-of-beauty-futsuka-zuki-by-kaw: A thin crescent moon (futsuka-zuki, the two-day moon) hangs in a luminous dusk sky above a misty riverbank, where figures with horses or cattle move through swirling ground fog beside a silhouetted tree and distant mountains. The work, executed in sumi and colour on silk as a hanging scroll, won first prize at the 1907 Tokyo Industry Exhibition and is held in the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo.
collection-of-beauty-g-caillebotte-le-ja: A snow-blanketed view of the painter's own riverside garden across the Seine from Argenteuil, where Caillebotte spent his final years tending plants and painting boats. The muted whites and bare branches show the late, looser brushwork he developed after retreating from Paris's Impressionist circle.
collection-of-beauty-g-caillebotte-nastu: A close, plunging view of nasturtium leaves and blossoms painted in Caillebotte's Petit Gennevilliers garden. The unusual cropping and high vantage echo the steep perspectives he favoured in his urban scenes, applied here to a horticultural subject he cultivated himself.
collection-of-beauty-g-caillebotte-un-ba: Two men look down from the balcony of the artist's apartment at 31 Boulevard Haussmann — one in a top hat leaning on the railing, the other in a bowler hat standing at ease. The plunging view of a tree-lined Parisian boulevard and the modern bourgeois subject are characteristic of Caillebotte's engagement with Haussmann's reshaped city. The canvas, dated 1880, is now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-g-caillebotte-villa: Pastel seaside villas line the Normandy coast at Trouville, a fashionable resort favoured by Parisians on holiday. Caillebotte's looser handling and brighter palette here reflect his shift from urban scenes toward the open-air subjects of his later career.
collection-of-beauty-gaertner1: The southern segment of the 1834 Berlin panorama, recording rooftops, courtyards and chimneys spread out below the lantern of the Friedrichswerder church. Gaertner's six-part view was purchased by Friedrich Wilhelm III and a replica was later carried to Russia for Tsarina Alexandra Feodorovna.
collection-of-beauty-gaertner5: One panel from Gaertner's six-part angular panorama of Berlin, taken from the roof of Schinkel's Friedrichswerdersche Kirche in the summer of 1834. The architectural painter worked daily in a wooden booth atop the church, recording the new buildings of the Schinkel circle for King Friedrich Wilhelm III.
collection-of-beauty-gaertner6: A rooftop panorama of Berlin taken from the Friedrichswerdersche Kirche, showing monumental civic buildings — including a large domed rotunda and the broad forecourt of the Royal Palace — stretching to the horizon under a warm, hazy sky. Figures including an artist with a drawing board stand at the church parapet in the right foreground. The panel belongs to Eduard Gaertner's six-part panorama of Berlin executed in 1834.
collection-of-beauty-gainsborough-grace-: Full-length portrait of the courtesan Grace Dalrymple Elliott, known as 'Dally the Tall', in a yellow Van Dyck-style gown with a towering 1770s coiffure. Commissioned by her lover the Earl of Cholmondeley and shown at the Royal Academy in 1778, the canvas measures 234.3 by 153.7 cm and is now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-gainsborough-thomas: Elizabeth Linley stands at the left in a blue gown while her younger sister Mary sits beside her in an amber dress, holding a sheet of music. The two are posed in a wooded glade in Gainsborough's characteristic landscape setting. Painted around 1772 and retouched in 1785, the double portrait is in the collection of Dulwich Picture Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-galatskaya-bashnya-: The Galata Tower rises over the Golden Horn under moonlight, masts and rooftops picked out in silver across the water. Aivazovsky painted this view in 1845 after visiting Constantinople with Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolaevich; the oil measures about 52 by 80 cm.
collection-of-beauty-gamaun: The Slavic prophetic bird Gamayun perches on a bare branch above a blood-red dawn, woman-headed and crowned with dark plumage. Vasnetsov painted the panel in 1898 and exhibited it the following year; the imagery prompted Alexander Blok's 1899 sonnet of the same name.
collection-of-beauty-garcon-au-gilet-rou: The Italian model Michelangelo di Rosa in a red waistcoat, one of several studies Cézanne made of the boy around 1889 to 1890. This watercolour version, in the Barnes Foundation, Philadelphia, leaves the paper bare in places between washes. Cézanne used the repeated pose to test the figure against surrounding space.
collection-of-beauty-garden-at-bordigher: Painted during Monet's winter trip to the Italian Riviera, this view of a Bordighera garden captures the silvery light he found so disorienting after Normandy. Twisting olives and palms are rendered in feathery, near-pastel strokes, the morning haze softening every contour into vibrating colour.
collection-of-beauty-gathering-bamboo-sh: A color woodblock print by Suzuki Harunobu of a young woman in a wide straw hat digging in deep snow with a hoe, where a single bamboo shoot has broken the surface beneath snow-laden bamboo. The unseasonable subject evokes the Chinese filial-piety tale of Meng Zong, who dug for bamboo shoots in midwinter to feed his ailing mother, recast in Harunobu's fashion as a scene with an elegant contemporary beauty. The print, from about 1765, is in the Art Institute of Chicago.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-bretonne: A young woman in the white coif and dark dress of Pont-Aven posed during Gauguin's first Brittany sojourn. The simplified silhouette and reserved palette anticipate the cloisonnist flattening he would push further in following summers among the Breton peasantry.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-huttes-sous: Thatched cottages glimpsed through tree trunks, painted during Gauguin's stay in Martinique in 1887. The tropical light and broad colour areas mark his decisive turn away from Impressionist division of tone toward the synthetist style of Pont-Aven.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-nature-mort: Several exotic birds with brilliantly coloured plumage lie across a white cloth beside a dark ceramic vessel and a large gourd, with a gilt-framed sculptural idol presiding over the scene from the background. The canvas, signed and dated 1902, was painted during Gauguin's final years on Hiva Oa and exemplifies his late Polynesian still-life idiom. It is now in the Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-paul-sacred: Two Tahitian women sit cross-legged in the foreground beside a sacred pool — one in a dreaming reverie with her head resting on her hand, the other holding a small red flower. Behind them, additional figures move near the water's edge in a lush tropical landscape. Inscribed 'Nave nave moe' (Sacred Spring, Sweet Dreams), the canvas was painted in 1894 and entered the Hermitage Museum with the Shchukin collection.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-paul-still-: A bearded young man in profile crops the right edge of the canvas, staring at a ceramic pot the painter had thrown himself and a cluster of pears on a white cloth. Gauguin painted his friend and pupil Charles Laval in late 1886 after returning from Pont-Aven; the cut-off face nods to Degas's framing while the parallel strokes in the fruit pay tribute to Cezanne. Indianapolis Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-gauguin-selbstbildn: Gauguin portrays himself in strict profile against a deep reddish-brown ground, the face lit with warm, ruddy tones while the brushwork is reduced to its essentials. An inscription on the canvas reads 'à l'ami Daniel', identifying the work as a gift to Georges-Daniel de Monfreid, who supported the artist during his Tahitian years. The self-portrait is dated 1896.
collection-of-beauty-general-sir-david-b: A vast late history painting commemorating the British general's discovery of Tipu Sultan's body after the storming of Seringapatam in 1799. Wilkie staged the torch-lit scene with theatrical chiaroscuro, working in the grand manner he adopted following his travels in Spain.
collection-of-beauty-gentile-and-giovann: Saint Mark addresses a crowd of turbaned Mamluks and Venetian onlookers in a sun-bleached square dominated by a domed basilica conflating San Marco with Alexandrian architecture. Begun by Gentile Bellini around 1504 and completed by his brother Giovanni after 1507, the canvas was painted for the Scuola Grande di San Marco and now hangs in the Pinacoteca di Brera.
collection-of-beauty-gentileschi-allegor: A largely nude female figure is seen from behind, sprawling or bending low amid scattered painting implements on a studio floor, a canvas on an easel visible at the right edge. Attributed to Artemisia Gentileschi and dated 1620–1630, the work is held at the Musée de Tessé, Le Mans. The pose and setting connect the figure to allegorical representations of Painting, though the composition differs markedly from the artist's better-known upright self-portrait in the Royal Collection.
collection-of-beauty-gentileschi-artemis: The biblical queen swoons before the Persian king as she pleads for her people, a subject Gentileschi treats with operatic gesture and sumptuous fabrics. Painted during her Neapolitan years, it shows her assimilation of Caravaggesque drama into a more courtly, decorative key.
collection-of-beauty-gentileschi-lucrezi: A woman lies on a bed, restrained by a male assailant who threatens her with a knife while a second figure looks on from the left — a depiction of the rape of Lucretia rather than her subsequent suicide. Attributed to Artemisia Gentileschi and dated circa 1645–1650, the large canvas is held at the New Palace (Neues Palais), Potsdam. The dramatic chiaroscuro and forceful physical confrontation are characteristic of Gentileschi's Baroque manner.
collection-of-beauty-george-augustus-eli: A bust-length portrait study of George Augustus Eliott, 1st Baron Heathfield, in scarlet uniform with a plumed bicorn hat, set against a loose, smoky background. Copley painted this study in 1787 in connection with his large Siege of Gibraltar composition; the work is held at the National Portrait Gallery, London. Eliott's role as defender of Gibraltar during the Great Siege (1779–1783) is the subject's defining distinction.
collection-of-beauty-george-frederic-wat: Orlando lunges after the fleeing sorceress Fata Morgana, a scene drawn from Boiardo's epic 'Orlando Innamorato'. Watts began the canvas in Italy in 1846 and finished it in London by 1848; the oil, 165 by 120 cm, was given by the artist to the Leicester Museum and Art Gallery in 1888.

The Minotaur leaning on a parapet and gazing out to sea, a small bird crushed in his fist. Watts painted the oil in 1885 as a protest against the child prostitution exposed that summer by W. T. Stead in the Pall Mall Gazette. It entered the Tate in 1897 (N01634).
collection-of-beauty-george-frederick-wa: The artist at seventeen, with loose hair and a fixed gaze, the face firmly modelled while the clothing is left as bare canvas. Watts painted this oil, his first self-portrait, in 1834; it measures 53.3 by 38.1 cm and remains at the Watts Gallery in Compton, Surrey.
collection-of-beauty-george-inness-home-: A farmhouse and barn sit half-screened by bare trees on a damp New Jersey hillside, with figures and livestock dissolved in soft brown and ochre. Inness painted the view from his own property in Montclair where he settled in 1885, and the canvas now belongs to the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute.
collection-of-beauty-george-inness-in-th: A traveller with a horse pauses on a rocky path through the Massachusetts hills as a dramatic sunset breaks through storm clouds, illuminating dense foliage in the middle ground. George Inness painted the picture between 1848 and 1850, early in his career when he was working close to the Hudson River School manner. The work is held in the Colección Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza on deposit at the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-george-inness-milto: A solitary figure sits on a fallen log at the edge of a placid stream, surrounded by dense woodland under a grey, overcast sky. George Inness made this sketch-like work around 1856, approaching the more atmospheric, tonally restrained manner he would develop after his European study trips. The work is held at the Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven.
collection-of-beauty-george-inness-the-h: A heron stands almost lost in a marshy thicket of yellow reeds and dark pools, the whole scene veiled in golden mist. Inness painted the canvas in 1893, the final full year of his life, and the work now belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.
collection-of-beauty-george-inness-the-l: A seated figure in a red jacket and hat rests on a hillside above the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad roundhouse outside Scranton, Pennsylvania, watching a locomotive trail steam through a cleared valley dotted with stumps. George Inness painted the panorama around 1856, commissioned to celebrate the new railroad while embedding industrial expansion within a pastoral Hudson River idiom. The work is now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-george-spencer-2nd-: George Spencer, 2nd Earl Spencer, faces the viewer in a brown coat and white stock, his powdered hair above the blue sash and breast star of the Order of the Garter. Copley painted the portrait around 1800, while Spencer served as First Lord of the Admiralty under William Pitt, overseeing the Royal Navy through Camperdown and the Nile.
collection-of-beauty-george-washington-1: Washington faces the viewer in a black coat with white stock, his powdered hair brushed back from a high forehead. The 1795 canvas at the Metropolitan Museum (accession 07.160) belongs to the so-called Vaughan type, the first of three Washington portrait formats Stuart developed from life sittings.
collection-of-beauty-georges-de-la-tour-: Mary Magdalene sits in candlelit profile, one hand resting on a skull in her lap, before a candle whose flame is reflected in a gilt-framed mirror; pearls are scattered on the table beside her. Georges de La Tour's Penitent Magdalene at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (inv. 1978.517), dated 1625–1650, is one of several versions the artist made of this subject, each exploring how a single flame renders flesh, fabric, and vanitas objects in near-total darkness.

An angel appears to the sleeping Joseph in a candlelit interior, the standard Lorraine nocturne formula put to a religious end. The shielded flame, smooth modelling and quiet psychology are characteristic of La Tour's mature devotional pictures.

A standing woman in a red robe holds a candle close to a seated, half-naked bearded man who bows his head — La Tour's depiction of Job mocked by his wife. The wife's gesture and downward gaze over the hunched figure convey both contempt and proximity, the single candle she carries casting warm light across both figures in a deep nocturnal field. The work is dated 1625–1650 and is attributed to Georges de La Tour.

A tightly cropped nocturne in which a woman shields a candle as another presents a swaddled child, often read as a Nativity in contemporary dress. The smooth, sculptural surfaces and concealed flame are hallmarks of La Tour's late Lorraine candlelit manner.

Itinerant street musicians come to blows over a hurdy-gurdy, one wielding a knife as a companion squeezes a lemon to feign a wound. La Tour stages the brawl in cool daylight, his earlier Caravaggesque manner before he fully turned to candlelit nocturnes.

A young man in a dark cap leans forward and blows on the glowing tip of a burning stick or coal, the ember's light illuminating his cheek and jaw against a near-black ground; a long pipe is held in his other hand. Georges de La Tour's Le Souffleur à la pipe (1646) depicts the act of kindling a pipe rather than smoking one, reducing the subject to an intimate nocturne built around a single point of combustion. The work is held at the Tokyo Fuji Art Museum.

A naive young man has his palm read by an old gypsy while her accomplices pick his purse and cut his medal chain. La Tour stages the swindle in cool daylight rather than candlelight, exploiting fixed sidelong glances to spell out the deception.

The penitent saint sits in shadow, her cheek resting on her raised hand as she gazes at a smoking oil lamp whose wick trails a thin curl of smoke. A skull lies in her lap, and books are arranged on the table beside the lamp. One of several Magdalen meditations La Tour painted, this version — now at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art — reduces the vanitas iconography to flame, flesh and darkness.

The Magdalen sits in near-total darkness, her face faintly lit as she rests her cheek on her hand and contemplates a skull placed before her on a ledge. A candle provides the sole source of light, and a mirror to her left reflects its glow. La Tour pares the vanitas iconography to its essentials, letting the single flame model her features with calm geometry, in a composition dateable to circa 1635–1640.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-019: Seurat's last, unfinished canvas captures a circus performance with a bareback rider, ringmaster and tiered audience. The arabesque rhythms and yellow-blue contrasts apply Charles Henry's theories of expressive line and colour, pushing pointillism toward decorative stylisation.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-026: Painted in 1888 at the same stretch of the Seine that had inspired his monumental Grande Jatte, this canvas shows the river's surface dissolved into patiently calibrated dots of complementary colour, with sailboats and a leaning tree composing the scene. Now in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, it demonstrates the optical mixing at the heart of Seurat's divisionist method applied to an intimate, familiar location.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-048: Labourers at work levelling earth, a subject from the industrial fringes of Paris that Seurat tackled in his early career. The broad balayé brushwork and sober palette precede the ordered dots of his pointillist maturity.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-c-18: An early still life painted while Seurat was still absorbing Barbizon and Impressionist precedents. The dense impasto and earthy palette show him before the systematic divisionism of dots that would define his mature work later in the decade.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-land: An early landscape from the industrial outskirts north of Paris, painted before Seurat formulated his pointillist method. Loose, almost Corot-like brushwork registers river, sky and bank in muted tones, a quiet rehearsal for the rigorous technique to come.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-les-: Three views of the same studio model — facing, in profile and from behind — set against the painter's own Grande Jatte. Seurat used the picture as a programmatic demonstration of pointillism applied to the academic motif of the nude.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-seat: A seated nude figure seen in profile, rendered in Seurat's characteristic conté crayon technique, with tonal gradations built from the grainy texture of the paper rather than painted strokes. Made circa 1883 as a preparatory study for Bathers at Asnières, the work is held at the Scottish National Gallery and predates the systematised pointillist method Seurat would develop later that decade.
collection-of-beauty-georges-seurat-view: A coastal view from Grandcamp on the Normandy shore, part of the seaside campaigns Seurat undertook each summer to test his divisionist method against changing light. Tiny calibrated dots dissolve fortification, sea and sky into a luminous, near-abstract grid.
collection-of-beauty-georgianaofdevonshi: Georgiana Cavendish, Duchess of Devonshire, is shown three-quarter length in a pale lace dress and a wide black hat trimmed with a white feather, holding a rose. Gainsborough painted the Whig hostess between 1785 and 1787; the canvas was famously stolen from Agnew's gallery in 1876, recovered in Chicago in 1901, and is now at Chatsworth House.
collection-of-beauty-gerard-honthorst-gu: Engraved portrait of Gerard van Honthorst published in 1662 in Cornelis de Bie's Het Gulden Cabinet der edel vry schilder const, the Antwerp directory of painters. Pieter de Jode II cut the plate after a Honthorst self-portrait, with the print issued by Joannes Meyssens for an entry that placed the Utrecht master among the leading Northern painters of his century.
collection-of-beauty-gerard-van-honthors: Shepherds and attendant figures crowd around the manger, their weathered faces lit from below by the radiant Christ child, with Mary leaning tenderly over the swaddled infant and Joseph to the right beside an ox. Honthorst's 1622 canvas deploys the Caravaggist nocturne he had mastered in Rome, making the Christ child himself the sole source of light in a horizontal Nativity composition.

Caiaphas leans across the table to question Christ, the two faces lit only by a single candle set between them. Honthorst painted the canvas in Rome around 1617 for the Marchese Vincenzo Giustiniani, and the radical nocturne earned him the Italian nickname Gherardo delle Notti.

A candlelit group scene shows a young man in a plumed hat raising a drink toward a laughing woman who plays a lute, with further figures and a table strewn with books, cards, food, and a globe visible in the background. The Caravaggist chiaroscuro and moralising props — open manuscript, overturned glass — announce the squandered-learning theme typical of Honthorst's Utrecht tavern pieces. Catalogued as number 391 in the Bavarian State Painting Collections, the work dates to around 1622–1625.

The shepherd Daifilo reclines at the feet of the princess Granida, gazing up at her in a leafy pastoral setting with goats visible in the background. Signed and dated 1625, Honthorst's canvas takes its subject from Pieter Cornelisz Hooft's popular Dutch pastoral play Granida, which served as a vehicle for veiled court portraiture in the period.

The crowned and bearded David tilts his head back with eyes raised in song as he plays a wooden harp, his brocaded robe trimmed with spotted fur. Painted in 1622, the close-cropped composition shows Honthorst adapting his Caravaggist approach — strong modelling against a dark ground — to a single biblical musician after his return from Rome.

A young woman in a yellow-gold drape and a feathered cap holds a small stringed instrument, glancing to the side with a broad smile. The half-length single-figure format belongs to the series of Utrecht musician pictures Honthorst produced for the open market in the early 1620s, deriving from his study of Caravaggio's followers in Rome. The work is dated 1624.
