The forceful wave patterns and restricted blue-and-white palette recall the graphic intensity Hokusai had brought to the Great Wave in the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. The work is held in the Art Institute of Chicago.
collection-of-beauty-hokusai-1828-cuckoo: A cuckoo in swift flight soars above a dense mass of flowering azaleas in this woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, dated 1828. The composition pairs a vocal summer bird with the seasonally appropriate blossom, following conventions well established in Japanese kachō-e prints. Haiku text inscribed above the image reinforces the interplay of seasonal imagery and literary allusion central to the genre.
collection-of-beauty-hokusai-manga-01: A page from the first volume of the Hokusai Manga, the artist's sprawling printed sketchbooks that catalogue figures, animals, landscapes, and curiosities. Issued from 1814, the volumes circulated widely as drawing manuals and later became a key conduit of Japanese form into European art.
collection-of-beauty-hokusai-manga-02: Another page from the Hokusai Manga, the encyclopedic woodblock sketch compendium that eventually ran to fifteen volumes. The loose, observational lines were intended as study material for students, though they read today as a portrait of Edo's everyday visual world.
collection-of-beauty-holbein-danse-macab: The opening plate of Holbein's Dance of Death, designed in Basel in the 1520s, shows the Creation that frames the cycle's moral argument. Cut by Hans Lützelburger from Holbein's miniature designs, the series compresses scriptural and social satire into woodblocks scarcely larger than a thumbprint.

A plate from Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, in which Death intrudes upon a figure of contemporary estate, abbot, merchant, peasant or king. The miniature woodcuts, executed with Hans Lützelburger's exacting cutting, were an early printed vehicle for Reformation-era social critique.

A woodcut from Holbein's celebrated Dance of Death cycle, designed in Basel and cut by Hans Lützelburger. Each compact scene stages Death intruding upon a figure of medieval estate, satirising clerical and worldly vanity with razor-sharp draughtsmanship.

Part of the Dance of Death series first issued in Lyon in 1538, where Death visits every rung of the social ladder. The miniature woodblock concentrates dense narrative into a few square inches, a hallmark of Holbein's reformist printmaking.

Holbein's pocket-sized memento mori reduces a moral sermon to a single arrested gesture: the skeleton's grasp, the victim's surprise. Cut by Lützelburger from Holbein's drawings, the prints circulated widely in Reformation Europe.

The Abbot, plate XIV of Holbein's Dance of Death, shows a skeletal Death seizing a mitred prelate who clutches his crozier, dragging him away from an outdoor setting. The compact woodblock was designed by Hans Holbein the Younger and cut by Hans Lützelburger, combining sharp characterisation with a Reformation-era critique of ecclesiastical power. The series was first published in Lyon in 1538.

Another scene from the Dance of Death series, in which Death claims a representative of the medieval social order. Holbein's tightly composed woodcuts pair grim humour with precise observation of costume and gesture.

From the Dance of Death cycle published at Lyon, this plate confronts a worldly figure with the universal leveller. Holbein's drawing translates fluently into Lützelburger's miniature woodblock technique, reading clearly at thumbnail scale.

A plate from Holbein's Imagines Mortis, conceived in Basel in the late 1520s. Death's skeletal cameo within an ordered domestic or civic scene gave the series its lasting force as moral and social commentary.

From the Dance of Death cycle, Holbein stages Death as an active intruder rather than an emblem, lunging into a tableau of contemporary life. The series helped fix the iconography of the danse macabre for the print era.

The Advocate, plate XIX of the Dance of Death, finds the lawyer pocketing a coin while Death stands ready at his side. Holbein's reformist satire jabs at venal professions, the woodcut's miniature scale concentrating its sting.

The Temptation, the second plate of Holbein's Dance of Death, depicts the serpent in Eden as the origin of mortality. Holbein opens the cycle with the Fall before Death claims figures across society in succeeding plates.

A plate from Holbein's Dance of Death in which Death, wearing a leafy crown, insinuates himself between two standing men — one richly dressed — and asserts his claim. Cut by Hans Lützelburger from Holbein's designs, the series was published in Lyon in 1538 and became a landmark of Northern Renaissance printmaking.

In this plate from the Dance of Death, a priest preaches from a pulpit to a kneeling and seated congregation while Death observes from a lectern above. Holbein inserts the skeleton into the very act of spiritual instruction, undercutting clerical authority with quiet irony characteristic of the series.
Another plate in the Dance of Death sequence, joining its survey of estates from pope to peasant. Holbein's compositions remain models of pictorial economy, every line bearing narrative weight.

From the Dance of Death, Holbein again pairs the living with the cavorting skeleton, their gestures locked in a brief, fatal duet. The Lyon edition of 1538 became a model for memento mori imagery for centuries.

A scene from Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, in which Death steps into the everyday with grim levity. The series remains a high point of Northern Renaissance printmaking, sharpened by Reformation-era anticlerical wit.

Plate from the Imagines Mortis cycle, where Holbein's Death overturns hierarchies one estate at a time. The miniature woodcut format encouraged private meditation on mortality alongside its public satire.

Another tableau from the Dance of Death sequence, illustrating Death's universal claim. Holbein's draughtsmanship and Lützelburger's exacting cutting give the prints their crisp, almost engraving-like precision.

An astronomer sits at a table crowded with books and an armillary sphere while Death leans over his shoulder, interrupting scholarly inquiry with the same finality it brings to every estate. The image belongs to Hans Holbein the Younger's Dance of Death series, published in Lyon in 1538, in which no profession can purchase an exemption.

A Dance of Death plate carrying forward the cycle's procession through every rank of society. The format - small block, pithy scene, accompanying scriptural verse in the original edition - became the template for emblem books to come.

Holbein places Death amid the routines of trade or labour, reminding the viewer that no occupation provides exemption. The Imagines Mortis remained in print across multiple Lyon editions through the sixteenth century.

The Expulsion of Adam and Eve, the third plate in Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, follows the Temptation as the source of human mortality. The angel drives the pair into a thorny world while Death takes up his fiddle to lead them onward.
Another scene from the Dance of Death, marrying biting moral commentary to compact woodcut design. Holbein's cycle gave Reformation Europe its definitive picture of mortality stalking every estate.

From the Dance of Death series, Holbein renders Death as both companion and antagonist, mirroring the gestures of the living. The plates retain a draughtsman's vivacity despite the resistance of the woodblock.
A Dance of Death plate from Holbein's celebrated cycle, the figures locked in a brief contest of will and fate. Lützelburger's cutting captures every flicker of Holbein's pen-line at miniature scale.
Part of Holbein's Imagines Mortis, the small woodcut sets a skeleton against a figure of social rank, a formula the artist varies with inexhaustible invention across the series.
From the Dance of Death, Holbein uses the miniature woodcut as a stage for a quick, devastating morality play. The cycle pairs each image with a biblical citation underscoring its lesson.

From Holbein's Dance of Death, this plate depicts Death intruding on a sickbed in a well-appointed chamber, where skeletons attend a figure laid low in a carved four-poster bed. No rank or wealth can delay the summons. The woodcut belongs to Hans Holbein the Younger's celebrated cycle, designed in Basel and first published at Lyon in 1538.

A scene from the Dance of Death cycle, in which Holbein's skeleton mimics or mocks the trade of his victim. The miniature woodcut carries an outsized influence on later memento mori imagery across European print culture.

From the Imagines Mortis series, this plate continues Holbein's procession through the social order. Designed in Basel and printed in Lyon, the cycle balances religious gravity with sharp-edged worldly humour.

From Holbein's Dance of Death, this plate depicts a domestic interior where women tend a fire or cauldron while a skeleton approaches from the side. The scene belongs to Holbein's cycle of small woodcuts designed in Basel and first published at Lyon in 1538, in which Death intrudes on the routines of daily life regardless of station.

A woodcut from Hans Holbein the Younger's celebrated Dance of Death cycle, designed in the 1520s and first published at Lyon in 1538. Skeletons drag the living from every social rank, the moral message compressed into miniature scenes carved with extraordinary economy of line.

This plate from Holbein's Dance of Death cycle depicts a divine or eschatological scene: a enthroned figure presides above a celestial sphere while crowds of naked souls gather below, evoking the Last Judgement that frames the series. The woodcut was designed by Hans Holbein the Younger and cut by Hans Lützelburger in Basel; the series was first published at Lyon by the Trechsel brothers in 1538.

From Holbein's Dance of Death, an unsparing memento mori in miniature woodcut. Death intrudes on daily life with theatrical bluntness, the densely worked black lines reflecting the early sixteenth-century northern fascination with mortality and judgement.

A page from Holbein's Dance of Death, designed in Basel and printed at Lyon in 1538. The series subjected pope, emperor, merchant, and ploughman alike to Death's hand, channelling Reformation-era anxiety through tightly composed woodcut tableaux.

From Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, in which a capering skeleton interrupts the routines of medieval life. The print's terse narrative and crisp black-line carving exemplify the small-format moralising woodcut perfected in early sixteenth-century Basel.

Plate from Holbein's Dance of Death, a sequence of moral vignettes first issued at Lyon in 1538. Each scene confronts a different rank of society with mortality, the figures animated by Holbein's economical draftsmanship and the precision of Hans Lützelburger's cutting.

An image from Holbein's Dance of Death, the German painter's most widely circulated print cycle. Death is staged as both intruder and equaliser, a theme rooted in late medieval European tradition but rendered with Renaissance compositional clarity.

From Holbein's Dance of Death, a series of forty-one woodcuts in which Death appears as skeletal companion to every walk of life. The prints became a touchstone of Reformation-era moral imagery and shaped the iconography of mortality for centuries.

Plate from Holbein's Dance of Death, designed around 1526 and printed in Lyon a decade later. Crammed into a tight rectangular field, the scene typifies the cycle's blend of social satire and pious warning.

From Holbein's Dance of Death, where Death stalks every estate of society with grim impartiality. The miniature woodcut format favoured by Holbein concentrates psychological force into a few square inches of black line.

A late plate in Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, a programme of small woodcuts whose dark humour and moral urgency defined the German Renaissance memento mori. The figures are sharply observed, the architectural settings reduced to telling props.

Plate from Holbein's Dance of Death, the influential moralising sequence designed in Basel in the 1520s. Death descends without warning on princes and labourers alike, a theme intensified by the woodcut's confined format and emphatic shadows.

From Holbein's Dance of Death cycle, in which the skeletal figure of mortality breaks into an everyday scene with sardonic relish. The series helped fix the visual vocabulary of the danse macabre for European print culture.

An image from Holbein's Dance of Death, a Reformation-era meditation on mortality issued in Lyon in 1538. Death's intrusion is staged with theatrical compression, every gesture pared to its essential meaning.

Plate from Holbein the Younger's Dance of Death, where skeletons enact a mocking equality across every social rank. The cut is sharply contoured, drawing on the Basel woodcut tradition that Holbein elevated to a new pictorial intelligence.

From Holbein's Dance of Death sequence, designed about 1526 and widely reprinted across Europe. Death's grip is sudden and absolute; Holbein's command of small-scale figure groups gives each plate the punch of a self-contained drama.
collection-of-beauty-holbein-dead-christ: Christ's corpse lies life-size in a cramped tomb niche, emaciated, eyes and mouth still open, the wounds beginning to discolour — death observed without any visible promise of resurrection. Hans Holbein the Younger painted the panel in Basel in 1521-22, possibly as the predella of an altarpiece. Now in the Kunstmuseum Basel, it famously shook Dostoevsky, who has a character in The Idiot say a man could lose his faith looking at it.
collection-of-beauty-home-in-the-woods-1: A settler fishes at the edge of a wilderness lake while women and children tend to chores before a log cabin on the right bank, mountains rising behind. Thomas Cole painted this Hudson River School canvas in 1847; it is held at the Reynolda House Museum of American Art in Winston-Salem.
collection-of-beauty-homere-deifie-dit-a: Commissioned for a ceiling in the Louvre, this strictly symmetrical tableau enthrones the blind poet beneath a winged Victory while artists and writers from antiquity to the modern age gather as witnesses. Ingres treats the canvas almost as a bas-relief, marshalling Neoclassical contour and frieze-like balance to assert Homer's status as the wellspring of Western art.
collection-of-beauty-honjo-tatekawa-the-: From Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (no. 5), the print frames the distant peak behind a busy riverside timber yard at Honjo, where workers balance atop high stacks of lumber and planks. The composition contrasts the vertical mass of stored timber against the open sky and calm water, a characteristic Edo juxtaposition of urban labour and sublime landscape rendered in Hokusai's bold woodblock style.
collection-of-beauty-honthorst-solon-and: The Lydian king Croesus, enthroned and crowned, gestures toward his treasure — gold coins and silver vessels arrayed on the floor before him — as the aged, barefooted Solon stands at right, staff in hand. A chained captive kneels at the king's feet, amplifying the contrast between material power and moral wisdom. Signed and dated 1624 and now in the Hamburger Kunsthalle, Honthorst stages the Herodotean encounter as a full-length figure composition, each character individuated in his characteristic manner.
collection-of-beauty-horatiogatesbystuar: General Horatio Gates is shown in three-quarter length, wearing his dark blue Continental Army uniform with gold epaulettes and a large gold medal suspended from a blue ribbon sash — the Congressional Gold Medal awarded for his victory at Saratoga. Stuart painted the portrait between 1793 and 1794 and it is now in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-horatius-cocles-de-: Horatius Cocles stands full-length at the centre, sword raised in his right hand and shield in his left, while the battle at the Tiber bridge plays out in the background. Goltzius engraved the plate in Haarlem in 1586 as the second of eight numbered hero subjects within a ten-print series titled The Roman Heroes. The work is in the collection of the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.
collection-of-beauty-horror-from-le-brun: The plate depicts a bearded male head, brows heavily contracted and gaze cast downward in an expression of dark, brooding horror. It is a stipple engraving in red-brown ink, issued by Bowles around 1785 as part of his English edition of Charles Le Brun's lecture on the passions of the soul, a treatise that codified facial expression for academic painters for over a century.
collection-of-beauty-hovhannes-aivazovsk: Shipwrecked survivors cling to a makeshift raft of timbers and rigging as the towering ninth wave — said in Russian seafaring lore to be the most destructive of a storm — rises beneath a luminous dawn sky. Aivazovsky completed the painting in 1850 in Saint Petersburg; it has remained at the Russian Museum since the Imperial collection and is regarded as the defining canvas of Russian Romantic marine painting.
collection-of-beauty-hugo-van-der-goes-g: An unfinished panel by the Ghent master, depicting the three kings paying homage to the Christ Child amid a richly textured architectural ruin. Van der Goes builds the scene with sober psychological gravity and minute Netherlandish detail in the brocades, gold vessels, and northern landscape glimpsed beyond.
collection-of-beauty-hugo-van-der-goes-v: A small devotional diptych pairing the Fall of Man with a Lamentation, in which Van der Goes channels acute emotional weight through pale, exhausted flesh and the slumped diagonal of Christ's body. The meticulous Eyckian observation is carried by a temperament closer to mournful introspection than ceremonial display.
collection-of-beauty-hungry-ghosts-scrol: A late Heian-period handscroll depicting gaki, the emaciated hungry ghosts of Buddhist cosmology, condemned by past greed to wander among the living unseen. Ink and colour on paper carry the doctrine in plain pictorial narrative, the suffering specters set against scenes of human everyday life in twelfth-century Japan.
collection-of-beauty-hunt-awakeningconsc: A young woman starts up from her lover's lap in a cluttered London parlour, her face caught at the instant of moral recognition. Hunt loaded the picture with Pre-Raphaelite symbolism, every object on the patterned wallpaper, the discarded glove, the cat at the table chosen to spell out the cost of a kept woman's situation.
collection-of-beauty-hyacinthe-rigaud-gi: A late state portrait of the Genoese patrician and future doge, painted by the leading French portraitist of the age. Rigaud orchestrates a cascade of velvet, silk, and lace around the sitter's confident gaze, the formula of court magnificence he had perfected for Louis XIV transposed to a Ligurian nobleman.
collection-of-beauty-hyacinthe-rigaud-po: Dubois, tutor to the future Louis XV and chief minister under the Regent, sits enveloped in a voluminous wrap of scarlet silk topped by a short fur cape. Rigaud channels the swagger of Louis XIV-era state portraiture into a study of ecclesiastical and political power, the textiles handled with the sumptuous fluency that made him the Bourbon court's favoured face-maker.
collection-of-beauty-idylls-of-the-king-: A wood-engraved illustration to Tennyson's Arthurian cycle, showing Edyrn travelling to Arthur's court with his lady and dwarf, the party approaching a great castle perched on a rocky crag beneath a dramatic clouded sky. Doré builds the scene with the theatrical chiaroscuro and monumental architecture that characterise his illustrations for the 1868 Moxon edition of the Idylls of the King.
collection-of-beauty-igorsvyat: The slain warriors of Prince Igor Svyatoslavich lie scattered across the southern steppe among wildflowers and broken armour, while an eagle descends and a pale moon rises at the horizon. Vasnetsov drew the subject from the medieval Tale of Igor's Campaign and signed the canvas in 1882, building each figure from ethnographic studies into a meditation on the cost of defeat.
collection-of-beauty-ike-taiga-orchids-1: A literati-style study of orchids in ink on paper, drawn with the calligraphic spontaneity that defined Ike no Taiga's Nanga painting. The plant's sparse leaves and blossoms are set down in a few rapid strokes, a Confucian emblem of refined virtue rendered with Edo-period painterly freedom.
collection-of-beauty-ildefonso-altar-the: The reverse panel of the Ildefonso Altar shows the Holy Family at rest beneath a fruiting apple tree, accompanied by the infant St John and St Anne, with putti above. Rubens links Eve's tree of knowledge to Christ's redemption through warm Flemish flesh, billowing draperies, and a luminous sky. Executed between 1630 and 1632, the altarpiece is now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
collection-of-beauty-ilia-efimovich-repi: Eleven harnessed labourers heave a barge upstream across a vast, sun-bleached Volga sandbar, their faces individuated portraits of exhaustion and stoicism. Repin's early masterpiece announced the social conscience of the Peredvizhniki, marrying academic figure construction to a panoramic Russian landscape.
collection-of-beauty-ilja-jefimowitsch-r: A boisterous huddle of Ukrainian Cossacks dictates a profanity-laced letter to the Ottoman sultan, their laughter rolling across the tabletop. Repin worked on the picture for over a decade, building each character from ethnographic studies into a celebration of stubborn Slavic insolence and freedom.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-ceremoni: An immense official commission recording a centenary session of the Russian State Council in the Mariinsky Palace. Repin marshals more than eighty individual portraits into a coherent ceremonial space, his late brushwork looser and more atmospheric than the tightly modelled realism of his earlier work.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-cesar-cu: Repin's portrait of the composer and music critic César Cui, a member of The Mighty Handful, shows the sitter seated in a cane-backed chair, wearing a grey military coat with a red lining. The direct gaze, spectacles, and loose painterly brushwork are characteristic of Repin's intimate portraits of Russian cultural figures, painted in 1890.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-dragonfl: Repin's daughter Vera perches astride a wooden fence rail against a pale summer sky, arms spread and legs dangling in the pose that earned the portrait its nickname. She wears a patterned dress and a broad-brimmed hat; the high horizon and open outdoor light reflect Repin's engagement with plein-air practice in the intimate Russian family-portrait tradition. The work dates to 1884.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-sadko-go: Repin's graduation piece for the Imperial Academy of Arts depicts the Novgorod merchant-hero Sadko in the underwater kingdom of the Sea Tsar, choosing a bride from a procession of foreign maidens. Painted in Paris, it earned him a gold medal and signalled an early turn toward Russian folkloric subject matter.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-unexpect: A Siberian exile reappears in his family's drawing room, the household frozen mid-reaction in a moment of recognition. Now in the Tretyakov Gallery, the painting is a touchstone of Russian Realism, organising psychology along sharp diagonal sightlines that link the returnee to mother, wife, and uncomprehending children.
collection-of-beauty-ilya-repin-what-fre: A young gymnasium student and his companion dance in the surf of the iced-up Neva, the wave breaking around their boots while the boy throws open his coat to the wind. Painted in 1903 and now in the Russian Museum, Saint Petersburg, the canvas was Repin's ambivalent response to the new generation on the eve of the 1905 revolution.
collection-of-beauty-imaginary-tour-thro: A Southern Song handscroll, nearly four metres long, leading the viewer through the misted river country at the confluence of the Xiao and Xiang. Painted in monochrome ink on paper, it belongs to the contemplative literati tradition and is held by the Tokyo National Museum.
collection-of-beauty-in-the-conservatory: A fashionable Parisian couple — Monsieur and Madame Guillemet — pause among hothouse foliage, their hands almost meeting on a garden bench. Manet exhibited the canvas at the 1879 Salon, where its crisp drawing and modern subject bridged his Realist roots and Impressionist company.
collection-of-beauty-in-the-mountains-of: A woodblock print from Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, c. 1830-32. Sawyers rip boards from an enormous beam propped on trestles — one man saws from atop while another works beneath, a woman and child resting nearby — with Fuji framed in the triangle formed by the beam and its supports. This impression is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-in-the-water-by-eug: A nude young woman stands ankle-deep in shallow water, seen in three-quarter profile as she gazes downward, one arm extended slightly at her side. Eugene de Blaas rendered the figure with the smooth academic finish and delicate luminosity typical of his work; the canvas, signed lower left, is dated to around 1905 and measures 80.3 by 45 cm.
collection-of-beauty-inada-kyuzo-shinsuk: A sheet from Yoshitoshi's series Eimei nijūhasshūku (Twenty-eight Famous Murders with Verse), produced with Yoshiiku in 1866–67. The print exemplifies the late ukiyo-e taste for muzan-e — bloody, theatrical scenes drawn from kabuki and historical legend.
collection-of-beauty-indischer-maler-um-: A Deccani miniature of around 1615 depicting Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur standing in a garden, wearing golden robes over a white garment and a white turban, and holding a small object — likely a flower — at chest height. The refined Bijapur idiom is evident in the jewel-like colour, precise draughtsmanship, and lush landscape setting with a palace visible in the background. The work is attributed to Ali Riza.
collection-of-beauty-ingres-academic-stu: A youthful académie made in Jacques-Louis David's studio, drawn from a posed model with painstaking anatomical observation. Such exercises were the bedrock of Ingres's Neoclassical training and prefigure the sculptural torsos in his later history paintings.
collection-of-beauty-ingres-atelier-ange: A painted study from the Ingres atelier, held at La Piscine museum in Roubaix, depicting Angélique nude and chained to a sea-cliff, her long hair flowing and wrists bound to the rock above — the subject taken from Ariosto's Orlando Furioso. Dated 1819, the large-scale canvas (102 by 73.7 cm) reflects Ingres's sustained return to this mythological theme across several decades of his career.
collection-of-beauty-ingres-estudo-de-nu: An academic male nude executed during Ingres's training under David, when he was competing for the Prix de Rome. The figure's smooth modelling and elongated proportions already announce the linear classicism that would define his career.
collection-of-beauty-ingres-etude-bain-t: A preparatory drawing in the Louvre's Cabinet des dessins for Le Bain turc, the circular canvas Ingres completed at age 82. The sheet shows him reworking the languid female nudes he had drawn from life decades earlier into a single dense Orientalist tableau.
collection-of-beauty-ingres-mme-victor-b: Ingres portrays Mme Victor Baltard standing beside a stone balustrade, her young daughter Paule at her side. The inscription at lower left reads 'offert à son ami M. Ve Baltard / Ingres Del. Rom.', confirming the drawing was made in Rome. The face is rendered with Ingres's characteristic precision, while dress and background are lightly sketched in graphite.
collection-of-beauty-ingresodipusandsphi: Oedipus pauses on a rocky ledge to answer the riddle of the Sphinx, his polished nude profile set against deep shadow. Painted in Rome as part of Ingres's Prix de Rome obligations, it distils his Neoclassical doctrine of pure contour and idealised anatomy.
collection-of-beauty-inness-george-early: Tall Florida pines rise above a settlement of low buildings and a marshy foreground in the early morning light. George Inness painted this 1892 canvas during his winters at Tarpon Springs, applying the atmospheric diffusion and tonal subtlety characteristic of his late work.
collection-of-beauty-inness-george-the-r: A rainbow descends through parting storm clouds over a pastoral meadow, where cattle rest and graze in the foreground and a farmstead sits to the left. George Inness painted this canvas around 1878, combining dramatic meteorological observation with the Swedenborgian spiritual symbolism that pervades his later work.
collection-of-beauty-inness-sunset-on-th: The Passaic river spreads under a luminous orange and yellow sky at sunset, with boats on the water and a hazy industrial riverbank in the distance. George Inness painted this oil in 1891, and the canvas is now at the Honolulu Museum of Art; the glowing atmosphere and dissolved forms reflect his late Tonalist manner.
collection-of-beauty-irissen-rp-p-1999-5: Deep blue irises rise against a softly graded pale background in this colour woodblock print by Ohara Koson. Published by Watanabe Shōzaburō between 1925 and 1936, the print belongs to Koson's celebrated series of Shin-hanga flower subjects and is now in the collection of the Rijksmuseum.
collection-of-beauty-isaak-ilitsch-lewit: A whitewashed monastery sits on the far bank of a slow river at sunset, twin boats pulling toward the landing as bells ring across the water. Levitan combined memories of the Savvino-Storozhevsky monastery near Zvenigorod with the Krivoezersky monastery near Yuryevets, the canvas now in the Tretyakov Gallery.
collection-of-beauty-isaak-levitan-tihay: A small monastery rises above a bend in a forested river at evening, its golden domes reflecting in the still water as a plank footbridge leads toward the far shore. Isaac Levitan painted this canvas in 1890, and it is now held at the Tretyakov Gallery; the composition draws on sketches made near the Volga and exemplifies his lyrical approach to the Russian landscape.
collection-of-beauty-isenheim-altarpiece: A photographic record of the Concert of Angels panel from Matthias Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece (c. 1512–16), housed at the Musée Unterlinden in Colmar. The original shows angel musicians serenading the Virgin in jewel-coloured robes, part of the great folding altarpiece made for the monastery hospital of St Anthony.

This panel from the Isenheim Altarpiece depicts the Temptation of Saint Anthony: the hermit saint is overwhelmed by a writhing mass of grotesque demons and hybrid creatures in a rocky landscape, with a fiery sky above. Matthias Grünewald completed the altarpiece around 1516 for the Antonite hospital at Isenheim; the scene's raw depiction of bodily torment was designed to speak directly to patients suffering from ergotism. The work is now housed at the Musée Unterlinden in Colmar.

This panel from the Isenheim Altarpiece depicts the Meeting of Saints Paul the Hermit and Anthony Abbot in the desert: the two aged figures converse in a rocky wilderness landscape, with a palm tree and a lion visible to the right. Matthias Grünewald painted the scene as part of the altarpiece created around 1512–1516 for the Antonite monastery hospital at Isenheim; it is now at the Musée Unterlinden in Colmar.

Three scenes unfold across the altarpiece's second opening, from the Annunciation through the Nativity with its angel concert to the Resurrection, where Christ rises in a halo of incandescent yellow and red. Grünewald completed the polyptych around 1516 for the Antonite monastery at Isenheim, structuring the wings so successive feast-day openings revealed different cycles of the redemption story.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-aivazovsky-fog: A large sailing vessel lies at anchor in a coastal bay partially obscured by haze, while a group of figures with draught animals rest on the shore in the foreground and a small rowing boat crosses the calm water to the right. Ivan Aivazovsky painted this 1895 marine, one of many coastal scenes set against mountainous terrain that characterise his work from his studio at Feodosia.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-constantinovic: Ottoman ships burn in the bay of Cesme as the Russian fleet under Alexei Orlov destroys the Turkish line on the night of 25-26 June 1770. Painted in 1848 and now in the Aivazovsky National Gallery at Feodosia, the canvas belongs to the marine painter's cycle of naval victories commissioned during his years as official painter to the Russian Admiralty.

A boat carrying several Ottoman figures, including a veiled woman and attendants, glides along a narrow waterway bordered by lush vegetation and an ornate timber-framed building with arched windows. Ivan Aivazovsky painted this 1846 canvas during his travels in the Ottoman Empire, and the intimate garden setting and richly dressed passengers reflect the Orientalist mode he pursued alongside his marine subjects.

Figures in Ottoman dress gather at a waterfront coffee-house, smoking a hookah and playing music, with the Ortaköy Mosque and its minaret rising across the Bosphorus in the background. Painted by Ivan Aivazovsky in 1846, the canvas records the site during one of his Near Eastern travels, capturing the atmospheric haze and golden light typical of his marine and coastal work.

Sailboats drift on the still water of Lake Maggiore beneath an alpine evening sky, distant peaks fading into haze along the Italian shore. Painted in 1858 during one of Aivazovsky's tours abroad, the canvas trades his usual Black Sea storms for the softer Lombard atmosphere of the lake district.

A snowbound panorama of Moscow viewed from the Sparrow Hills, the city spreading toward the horizon beneath low winter cloud. Painted in 1872 on a 46 by 72 cm canvas, the picture is a rare urban subject from Aivazovsky, whose practice was overwhelmingly marine.

Black Sea Fleet warships ride at anchor in the roadstead of Sevastopol under a glassy sunset, the masts and yards of the squadron silhouetted against a pearl-coloured sky. Painted in 1846, the year Aivazovsky was appointed senior painter to the Russian Naval Staff and supplied with a studio at the fleet's home port.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-el-terrible-y-: The tsar cradles the dying son he has just struck down with his iron-tipped staff, blood smearing the Persian carpet. Held by the Tretyakov Gallery, the picture shocked contemporaries and was briefly banned by Alexander III for its raw psychological violence.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-k-ayvazovskiy-: The brig Mercury rejoins the Russian squadron after its 1829 escape from two Turkish line ships near the Bosphorus, sails crowding the horizon. Aivazovsky painted this commemoration in 1848, an oil of about 123.5 by 190 cm now in the State Russian Museum, St Petersburg.

A caravan of travellers and pack animals working along the precipitous mountain road that climbs from Mleta to Gudauri in the Caucasus, snow-capped peaks behind. Aivazovsky painted the oil in 1868, applying the atmospheric handling of mist and distance he is better known for in his sea pieces.

The Great Pyramid of Giza rising over the Egyptian desert under low warm light, with small figures at its base. Aivazovsky, better known for marine subjects, painted the oil in 1871; the canvas later passed through Christie's, London.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-konstantinovic: A moonlit coastal scene at Gurzuf on the Crimean shore, with a glowing disc of moon laid across the water and dark vessels near the foreground rocks. Aivazovsky painted the marine view in 1891; the canvas later passed through Heritage Auctions in Dallas. The Armenian-Russian painter produced thousands of seascapes from his studio at Feodosia on the Black Sea.
collection-of-beauty-ivan-krylov: Karl Bryullov's unfinished portrait of the Russian fabulist Ivan Andreyevich Krylov shows the heavy-set sitter in a dark coat, a small order just visible on his chest, facing the viewer with a weary directness. Begun in 1839 and left incomplete by Bryullov, the head and upper body are fully resolved; the canvas measures 102.3 by 86.2 cm and is held by the State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.
collection-of-beauty-j-l-gerome-the-wail: A lone figure in a green coat and tall hat stands in prayer before the vast Herodian ashlar courses of the Western Wall in Jerusalem, prayer book in hand. Painted in 1880 and now held by the Israel Museum, the composition is characteristic of Gérôme's Orientalist precision: a single human presence dwarfed by the ancient stonework, rendered with his polished academic finish.
collection-of-beauty-j-s-copley-paul-rev: The Boston silversmith sits in his shirtsleeves at a polished workbench, holding a teapot he is about to finish, engraving tools laid out before him. Copley shows Revere as an artisan rather than a gentleman, an unusually direct conception for a colonial portrait, now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-j-s-copley-samuel-a: Samuel Adams stands in a red coat, one hand resting on rolled documents and the other pointing toward them, in a pose that conveys civic resolve. Copley painted the portrait around 1772, capturing the leading Patriot politician at a moment of political tension; the work is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-jordaens-nake: An academic figure study of an aged male model, drawn from life with the meaty corporeality typical of the Antwerp Baroque. Jordaens repeatedly used such studies as a stockpile for the satyrs, river gods, and apostles populating his crowded canvases.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-jordaens-prom: Chained to the Caucasus, Prometheus writhes as the eagle of Zeus rends his liver — a punishment renewed each day. Jordaens treats the Titan with brawny, ruddy realism, working in the Rubensian Antwerp idiom of muscular flesh and dramatic chiaroscuro.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-jordaens-psyc: Jordaens arranges the gods of Olympus in a sweeping circular composition around a luminous central opening, with Psyche at the centre receiving the cup of immortality that will seal her union with Cupid. Painted around 1652 and now in the collection of The Phoebus Foundation, the large-scale work — 266.5 by 226 cm — deploys the warm flesh tones and dynamic figural groupings characteristic of the Antwerp Baroque.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-jordaens-selb: Jordaens presents himself in middle age wearing a green cloak with gold buttons over a dark garment, holding a rolled sheet of paper and turning to face the viewer with characteristic directness. Dated 1650, the portrait — inventory no. 12876 — is held by the Bavarian State Painting Collections in Munich.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-jordaens-the-: A boisterous Twelfth Night feast in which whoever finds the bean in the cake reigns as king while companions roar 'The king drinks!' Jordaens returned to the proverbial subject several times, packing the table with three generations and the wet-eyed comedy of overindulgence.
collection-of-beauty-jacob-wrestles-with: A wood-engraved illustration from Doré's English Bible (1866), depicting Genesis 32 — Jacob struggling through the night with a divine adversary at the ford of the Jabbok. The dense black hatching and theatrical lighting are hallmarks of Doré's Romantic graphic style.
collection-of-beauty-jacopo-tintoretto-c: A photographic record of Tintoretto's Creation of the Animals (c. 1551–52) for the Scuola Grande della Trinità, now in the Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice. God the Father sweeps across the sky propelling birds, fish, and beasts into existence in a single rushing diagonal.
collection-of-beauty-jacopo-tintoretto-m: A crowded banquet hall, coffered ceiling hung with chandeliers, frames the wedding feast at Cana, with Christ visible among the assembled guests and servants filling water jars in the foreground. Tintoretto animates the scene with strong diagonals, dramatic lighting, and a press of richly dressed figures. Dated 1561 and catalogued by the Web Gallery of Art, this canvas belongs to Tintoretto's intense Mannerist engagement with large-scale narrative subjects.
collection-of-beauty-jacopo-tintoretto-t: Painted for the chancel of San Giorgio Maggiore in the last year of Tintoretto's life, the scene tilts the table on a sharp diagonal and dissolves the upper room in smoky angelic apparitions. It marks the radical conclusion of his Mannerist experiments with light and off-axis composition.
collection-of-beauty-jacques-louis-david: Pope Pius VII sits three-quarter length before the viewer, clothed in richly embroidered red papal vestments over a white rochet, his hand resting on the gilded arm of a throne-like chair. Inscribed 'PARISIIS 1805', the portrait was painted by Jacques-Louis David in Paris while the pontiff remained in the city following Napoleon's coronation. A restrained and penetrating characterisation, it shows the measured authority that made David the pre-eminent portraitist of the Napoleonic era.

Stanisław Kostka Potocki reins in a grey horse and extends his arm in a saluting gesture, dressed in a white open-necked shirt with a blue sash and breeches, a hound crouching below the horse's hooves. The stone architecture in the background recalls the antique settings David absorbed during his Roman years. Painted in 1781, the portrait follows the tradition of the Baroque equestrian portrait while projecting an Enlightenment ideal of aristocratic ease.

A satyr in a spotted pelt leans over the reclining nude figure of Antiope, drawing aside a white cloth as she sleeps in a woodland setting. The work, dated 1771 and associated with the collection at Sens, was painted by David before his departure for Rome and belongs to his early Rococo phase — a sensual mythological subject he would later set aside in favour of Neoclassical severity. The composition echoes a long tradition of the Jupiter-and-Antiope theme in French painting.

The murdered Jacobin Jean-Paul Marat slumps in his medicinal bathtub, the bloodied knife on the floor and Charlotte Corday's letter still in his hand. David finished the canvas in October 1793, three months after the assassination, presenting it to the National Convention as a martyr's icon; it is now in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels.

Venus and the Graces undress Mars on a cloud-borne couch, removing his sword and helmet while Cupid unbuckles his sandal. David's last completed picture, finished in Brussels in 1824 and exhibited the next year to large crowds; it now belongs to the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium.

A muscular male nude is shown from behind, seated on red drapery against a dark rocky ground, his body turned away from the viewer in a classic académie pose. Painted in Rome in 1780 during David's pensionnat at the French Academy, the study is an exercise in heroic anatomy and the rendering of the back and shoulders from life. It is catalogued by the Web Gallery of Art as Patroclus, the Homeric hero whose death sets the Iliad's climax in motion.

The Comte de Turenne sits in a black fur-trimmed coat, a small medal ribbon at his lapel, his gaze directed at the viewer, one hand resting on his knee and the other holding gloves. A letter addressed to Brussels lies on the table beside him, suggesting David's exile context. Painted in 1816, the portrait is a characteristic product of David's Brussels years, calm and direct in its characterisation.

Suzanne Le Peletier de Saint-Fargeau, daughter of the assassinated Jacobin deputy whose deathbed portrait David had painted in 1793, sits in white empire dress against a plain ground. The commission came from her family some eleven years after the father's funeral picture had been destroyed by Suzanne herself in a royalist reversal of her loyalties.

Achilles draws his sword on Agamemnon as Iphigenia stands veiled for sacrifice, the four figures pressed into a shallow neoclassical frieze. David completed the picture in Brussels in 1819 and exhibited it the following year; it now hangs at the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth.

Joséphine kneels before Napoleon at Notre-Dame as he raises the crown to place it on her head, Pope Pius VII seated in the background. David's monumental canvas, painted between 1805 and 1807 and now in the Louvre, recasts the coronation as a spectacle of dynastic legitimacy, famously including Napoleon's mother Letizia in the gallery despite her absence from the actual ceremony — her presence a posthumous addition at Napoleon's request.

Telemachus, son of Odysseus, takes leave of the nymph Eucharis on Calypso's island, drawn from Fénelon's didactic novel. David painted the canvas in Brussels for Count Nikolai Demidov; it is now at the Getty Museum and shows the late, softened style of his exile years.

Joseph Bonaparte's daughters Zénaïde and Charlotte sit together reading a letter from their exiled father, who had fled to New Jersey after Waterloo. David painted the double portrait in Brussels in 1821; it is now at the Getty Museum.
collection-of-beauty-james-abbot-mcneill: Old Battersea Bridge looms in silhouette over the Thames at dusk, its piers stretched into a near-Japanese vertical. Whistler reduced river, sky, and timber to a few veils of blue and gold, treating the cityscape as an arrangement of tones in line with his Aesthetic credo.

A full-length portrait of a woman in an elaborate pink and grey gown and feathered hat, set against a muted grey-brown ground. Whistler's musical titles — here Nocturne in Rosa und Grau — subordinate the sitter to an overall harmony of tones, consistent with his Aestheticist programme. The work, dated 1881, is held by the Frick Collection, New York.
collection-of-beauty-james-abbott-mcneil: A small etching from Whistler's Venice set, produced after the artist arrived in the city following his bankruptcy. Sparing, calligraphic line on laid paper sketches a moored vessel against open water, the unworked paper standing in for sky and reflection.

Plate from the Thames Set, made when Whistler took rooms at the Angel Inn to study London's working riverfront. A balcony view crowded with rigging, mooring posts and a pair of seamen, etched with the dense, descriptive line he later abandoned for atmospheric suggestion.
collection-of-beauty-james-mcneill-whist: A small landscape from Whistler's late period, showing a broad green meadow with a lone figure in the middle distance and a low skyline of trees and rooftops beyond. Titled Green and Silver: Beaulieu, 1888, the work was painted during a French sojourn and is now in the Freer Gallery of Art, Washington. The title signals Whistler's characteristic insistence on colour harmony as the true subject of a picture.

Painted in London during Whistler's japonisme phase, the canvas dresses Christine Spartali in a loose kimono among Asian carpets and a folding screen. Frederick Leyland later acquired it and hung it in the dining room that became the Peacock Room, now reinstalled at the Freer Gallery.

An oil sketch for an unrealised group portrait, showing Whistler at the right holding a palette, with two female models — one seated in white, one standing in a pale gold robe — in a grey studio interior. The thinly brushed, almost monochrome handling demonstrates the tonal economy Whistler was formulating in the mid-1860s. The work, dated circa 1865–66, is held by the Art Institute of Chicago.

Several tall-masted vessels sit locked in ice along the Thames bank, their dark hulls contrasting with broken white floes in the foreground, where a lone figure stands on the shore. Painted in 1860, the picture belongs to Whistler's early Thames period and demonstrates the muted, near-monochrome palette he was developing for the river.

A large stone pier or mole occupies the foreground, with small figures walking along it; a single warship rides on a flat, cool-blue bay beyond, beneath a softly graded sky. Whistler painted the scene in Valparaiso in 1866, having travelled to Chile during the Spanish bombardment of the port. The atmospheric handling anticipates his Thames Nocturnes; the work is held by the Smithsonian American Art Museum.

A Thames-side view in which large furled red sails on a barge serve as the dominant vertical accents against a pearly grey river and overcast sky. Fashionably dressed pedestrians stroll along the embankment in the foreground, reduced to soft colour notations. Painted between 1871 and 1872, this work exemplifies Whistler's reformulation of landscape as tonal colour harmony.
collection-of-beauty-james-smith-benjami: A bust-length portrait of a young man in a dark green coat with gold buttons, set within a painted oval, against a dark ground. The sitter is identified as the American history painter Benjamin West, depicted here as a young man. The work is attributed to James Smith and dated 1770.
collection-of-beauty-jan-brueghel-de-oud: Jan Brueghel the Elder painted the abundant menagerie of Eden — peacocks, leopards, parrots, deer, and many other creatures amid lush vegetation — while Rubens contributed the figures of Adam and Eve at the Tree of Knowledge. The collaboration dates to 1615 and is now in the Mauritshuis, The Hague.
collection-of-beauty-jan-brueghel-i-pete: From the Five Senses cycle painted with Jan Brueghel the Elder for the Archdukes Albert and Isabella in Brussels. Brueghel laid in the encyclopaedic gallery interior crammed with instruments, music books and singing birds; Rubens contributed the figure of Venus listening to a concert of Cupids.

Sight, the most celebrated of the Five Senses series produced jointly with Jan Brueghel the Elder, sets Venus and Cupid in a kunstkammer crowded with paintings, scientific instruments and rarities. The picture doubles as an inventory of the Archdukes' collection in Brussels.

An outdoor garden setting overflowing with flowers, fruits, and foliage frames two figures — a woman and a winged putto — from the Five Senses series painted with Jan Brueghel the Elder for the regents of the Spanish Netherlands. Brueghel contributed the encyclopaedic floral abundance while Rubens supplied the figures. The panel is held at the Museo del Prado.
collection-of-beauty-jan-cossiers-narcis: The Antwerp Baroque painter Jan Cossiers depicts Narcissus nearly full-length, kneeling beside a pool and gazing at his reflection, a red drapery billowing behind him. A strong raking light models the flesh against a shadowy landscape. The work, dated to the seventeenth century, is held at the Museo del Prado.
collection-of-beauty-jan-van-der-hoecke-: Two armoured commanders on horseback dominate the foreground, surveying the sprawling engagement below as troops and banners mass toward the right and smoke rises over the distant plain. Jan van der Hoecke's large canvas, painted in 1634 and now in the Royal Collection at Windsor Castle (RCIN 400100), commemorates the Habsburg victory at Nördlingen — one of the decisive engagements of the Thirty Years' War — in the grand battle-piece manner Rubens established for court patronage.
collection-of-beauty-jan-vermeer-the-art: An allegory of painting in which an artist seen from behind sets brush to a portrait of Clio, the muse of history, identified by her trumpet and laurel. Vermeer kept the canvas in his Delft studio until his death, and the heavy map of the Seventeen Provinces above the model carries political weight.
collection-of-beauty-jan-vermeer-van-del: An early interior in which a young woman reads at a leaded casement, her face echoed in the panes. Recent restoration at the Gemäldegalerie in Dresden uncovered a painted Cupid on the back wall that had been overpainted after Vermeer's death, sharpening the picture's amorous subtext.

A courtship scene in which a man in dark cloak attentively stands beside a young woman in red who raises a glass of wine to her lips. At the upper left window a heraldic stained-glass roundel introduces a note of aristocratic propriety into the domestic interior. Painted between 1658 and 1660, the work is held at the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin (inv. 912C).
collection-of-beauty-jan-wierix-002: A bust-length profile engraving of the Antwerp painter Quentin Massys (Quintin Mesijs), identified by the Latin inscription below: QUINTINUS MESIUS ANVER PIANU[S] PICTOR. Johannes Wierix cut the plate, probably in the 1560s-1570s, as part of a series of artists' likenesses circulating in the late sixteenth century.
collection-of-beauty-japanese-anemones-h: Fantin-Latour built much of his reputation on still lifes painted in his Paris apartment for the English market. Here he sets autumn-flowering anemones in a glass vessel against a flat brown ground, modelling the petals with the cool, even illumination he preferred to the Impressionists' broken light.
collection-of-beauty-jaques-louis-david-: A three-quarter-length portrait of an unidentified officer in dark blue military uniform with gold epaulettes and a group of decorations on his chest, set against a warm neutral ground. The painting is signed and dated 1816 on the canvas, placing it in the period of David's Brussels exile, where the artist supported himself portraying fellow expatriates and visiting subjects until his death in 1825; the work is held at the Clark Art Institute.
collection-of-beauty-jean-auguste-domini: A society portrait of Louise de Broglie, comtesse d'Haussonville, that Ingres laboured over for three years and that now hangs in the Frick Collection. Mirror, ribboned slippers and porcelain are arranged with linear precision, while the sitter's improbably elongated arm exemplifies the artist's controlled anatomical license.

A seated nude seen from behind, her head wrapped in a patterned red-and-white turban, sits at the edge of a draped bath. Ingres painted this canvas in Rome in 1808 as part of his required submissions to the Académie, and its flawlessly modelled back — elevated to the surface as pure contour — became a touchstone for his later Turkish bath subjects. The work is now in the Louvre (RF 259).

A reclining concubine turns her head over a famously elongated back -- Ingres lengthened her spine by several vertebrae in pursuit of an ideal sinuous line. Commissioned by Caroline Murat for the Naples court, the picture was scandalised at the 1819 Salon for its anatomical liberties.

Joséphine-Élénore-Marie-Pauline de Galard de Brassac de Béarn, Princesse Albert de Broglie, is shown seated in a luminous blue satin gown against a grey-green panelled interior, a heraldic device visible at upper right. Painted by Ingres between 1851 and 1853 near the end of his career, the portrait is now a centrepiece of the Robert Lehman Collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

Ingres's exact-size copy of Titian's Venus of Urbino (1538), made during his Florentine years of 1820–1824 when he had access to the original at the Pitti Palace. The canvas was intended to serve as a model for his close friend, the sculptor Lorenzo Bartolini, who was working on a sculpture of the same subject. It is now in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (inv. 37.2392).

A standing nude pours water from an urn at her shoulder, an allegory of a freshwater spring. Ingres began the picture in Florence around 1820 and worked at it intermittently for decades; its porcelain-smooth contours epitomise his late Neoclassical ideal of feminine form.

An academic history piece showing Virgil reciting the Aeneid before the imperial family at the moment Octavia faints at the mention of her dead son Marcellus. The carefully balanced antique architecture and the chiselled outlines announce Ingres's lifelong allegiance to Davidian Neoclassicism.
collection-of-beauty-jean-francois-mille: Two men carry a newborn calf on a litter toward a farmhouse, the cow following at their heels. Millet painted this oil about 1860, a study of farm routine from his Barbizon years; the canvas is in the Princeton University Art Museum.

A herder driving cattle homeward at the close of day, the animals strung out along a low horizon. Pastel and Conté crayon on wove paper, about 55.9 by 41.3 cm, made around 1866 and held by the National Gallery of Art, Washington, in the Corcoran Collection. It comes from the William A. Clark holdings of Millet pastels.

A peasant couple pause over a basket of potatoes to pray as the Angelus bell sounds from a distant church spire. Millet painted the oil between 1857 and 1859; it measures 55.5 by 66 cm and hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris.

A standing woman draws thread from a distaff, her spindle turning at her side. Millet returned to spinners repeatedly in these years; the oil, painted about 1855 to 1860, belongs to the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute in Williamstown.

Three women stoop across a stubble field gathering fallen grain, a loaded harvest cart and stacks behind them. Millet painted 'Des glaneuses' in 1857; the canvas entered the Musée d'Orsay, Paris, where it remains.

A woman slides a loaf into an oven, sleeves pushed back, the dough and peel close to hand. Millet painted this domestic labour in 1854, one of the Barbizon peasant subjects that defined his mature work.

A young shepherdess stands knitting beside her flock in an open field, her back to the grazing sheep. Millet painted this oil about 1860 to 1862; it belongs to the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute in Williamstown.

A man and woman work a field together, he breaking the soil with a hoe while she drops seed potatoes, a basket and a donkey under a tree behind them. Millet painted this oil about 1861, pairing the two figures in the field labour central to his Barbizon work.

A shepherd stands wrapped in a cloak as his flock spreads across a flat plain under a wide, luminous sky. Painted in the early 1860s, oil on canvas, now in the Brooklyn Museum. Millet drew his rural subjects from life around Barbizon, where he settled in 1849.

A shepherd folds his flock into a hurdle pen under a low moon, the sheep crowding through the gap. Millet worked this nocturne between 1856 and 1860, the kind of dusk pastoral he favoured at Barbizon.
collection-of-beauty-jean-frederic-bazil: Figures gathering grapes in a Mediterranean vineyard, the left panel of a study Bazille made toward a grape-harvest composition. Oil on canvas, 38 by 46 cm, held at the Musée Fabre in Montpellier, the city near which the Bazille family kept their estate at Méric.

A young Italian girl in a headscarf shown at half length as a street singer. Oil on canvas, 131 by 98 cm, painted in 1866 and held by the Musée Fabre, Montpellier. Bazille worked the figure against a plain ground, concentrating the colour in the costume and complexion.

A female nude stretched full-length across the canvas, set against a dark ground. Oil on canvas, 70.5 by 190.5 cm, painted in 1864 and held by the Musée Fabre in Montpellier, Bazille's home city. The elongated horizontal format follows the academic odalisque tradition Bazille studied in Gleyre's Paris atelier.
collection-of-beauty-jean-honore-fragona: Aurora rides above the clouds scattering rose petals onto the sleeping figure of Night, lit by an upward-raking perspective. Painted around 1755-56 as an overdoor for a Parisian townhouse, the horizontal canvas was acquired by the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston at Sotheby's New York in January 2013.

A blindfolded young woman in a pink gown reaches outward on a garden terrace, flanked by flowers, trees and a young man seated to one side, in this early Fragonard painted around 1750–52. The scene pairs with a companion piece known as The See-Saw (Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum) as a pendant courtship subject, and reflects Fragonard's training in the Rococo pastoral manner under François Boucher.

Elegantly dressed women and children gather in a sunlit park, some reclining and others holding parasols, in a hazy golden landscape beneath flowering trees. Fragonard painted this pastoral garden scene between 1775 and 1780, during the period in which he produced numerous fêtes galantes in the Rococo tradition.

A young man in seventeenth-century costume looks upward from his writing desk, quill in hand, as if catching a passing thought. One of Fragonard's figures de fantaisie, the canvas was likely painted at speed in about an hour, an exercise in bravura brushwork over careful underdrawing.

Before a towering golden calf idol, a prophet raises his arm in denunciation while the king and his attendants react in agitation, the figures arranged in tense Baroque diagonals across a columned temple interior. Fragonard won the Prix de Rome with this composition in 1752 and it now belongs to the Académie des Beaux-Arts.

In a lush garden garden, a young man peers over a low wall while a young woman reclines below, gazing up at him beneath a stone statue of Venus and her attendant putto. Painted between 1771 and 1773 as the first of four panels in Fragonard's Progress of Love cycle, originally commissioned by Madame du Barry for her pavilion at Louveciennes, the suite is now held at the Frick Collection in New York.

A young woman cradles a bunch of grapes in her gathered skirt while squeezing juice over a baby at her feet. Painted around 1754-55, the canvas belongs to a set of four pastoral seasons at the Detroit Institute of Arts that Fragonard produced as overdoor or wall-panel decoration for an interior scheme.

A young woman at a writing table looks up from a sealed letter, a sprig of flowers tucked among the ribbons of her dress, a small dog beside her. Oil on canvas of about 1770, now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the picture is among Fragonard's most polished essays in the gallant tabletop scene.

A young woman in a silvery silk gown turns to receive a clandestine kiss in a doorway, the card party visible through the room beyond. Long attributed to Fragonard and now generally given to his sister-in-law and pupil Marguerite Gérard, the late-1780s panel passed through the Stanisław August collection to the Hermitage, where it still hangs.

A young mother and a visitor lean over a wicker cradle as a nurse holds an older child by the hand, the scene set in a sun-streaked country room. Fragonard painted the canvas around 1775, in the genre vein of domestic sentiment that Greuze had popularized. The National Gallery of Art in Washington holds it under accession 32685.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-01: A solo dancer raises her arms before seated Ottoman soldiers in a smoky tavern, the firelight glinting off brass and embroidered cloth. The almeh -- an Egyptian singing-dancer -- was one of Gérôme's recurring Orientalist motifs of the 1860s.

A large carpet — white ground with a blue-green medallion and red border — is displayed vertically in a Cairo courtyard while a group of buyers examines it from below and two men observe from an upper gallery. Gérôme's oil on canvas of about 1887, now at the Minneapolis Institute of Arts, deploys his tight academic finish to capture the textile's intricate geometry and the architectural ornament of the Mamluk-era setting.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ar: An Albanian irregular sits in an ornately latticed interior, drawing on a large hookah, his costume and surroundings rendered in Gérôme's characteristic academic precision. The small oil on canvas, dated 1865, is a single-figure ethnographic study of the kind Gérôme repeated across his Orientalist series of the 1860s.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-at: A solitary Muslim worshipper kneels on a prayer rug, the figure isolated against an austere architectural ground. The work belongs to Gérôme's earliest Orientalist forays, marked by his crisp draftsmanship and the smooth, almost lacquered surface he favoured throughout his career.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ba: A studio portrait of an Ottoman irregular soldier, painted from a model in Paris using costumes Gérôme had collected on his travels. Now in the Metropolitan Museum, the canvas is admired for the embroidered silk turban and the jewel-bright contrast against a dark ground.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-co: Now at the Musée d'Orsay, the canvas pictures the three crosses of Calvary as long shadows cast across Jerusalem at the moment of Christ's death. Gérôme adopts a striking near-aerial viewpoint, abstracting the Crucifixion to silhouette and shadow.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-di: The Cynic philosopher squats inside his earthenware tub, lighting a lamp by daylight to search Athens for an honest man. Gérôme surrounds him with the dogs that gave Cynicism its name, treating the anecdote with the archaeological literalism typical of his Greek subjects.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-eg: Painted after Gérôme's first journey up the Nile, the canvas shows conscripts being driven across the sand under guard. The high horizon, sharp shadows and ethnographic costume detail are characteristic of his fastidious Orientalist manner.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-el: In a richly appointed ancient interior, the queen of Lydia stands nude at the centre of the composition while King Candaules reclines on the bed and Gyges, having been brought to witness the scene, conceals himself in the shadows of the doorway at right. Gérôme painted the oil on canvas in 1859, drawing on Herodotus with his characteristic archaeological literalism; the work is held at the Museo de Arte de Ponce in Puerto Rico.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ev: Worshippers prostrate themselves on the flat roof of a Cairo mosque as the day's last light slants across the architecture. The picture belongs to Gérôme's prayer series of the 1860s, in which he applied his polished panel technique to ethnographic studies gathered on his Egyptian journeys.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-la: Greek warriors in plumed helmets perform the ancient pyrrhic war dance before a seated audience, swords and shields raised in unison. The carefully staged classical reconstruction is typical of Gérôme's late academic manner, in which archaeological detail is mobilised to bring antiquity to vivid life.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-le: An Orientalist hammam scene in which a black servant pours water over a seated bather. Gérôme returned often to the bathhouse subject after his travels to Cairo and Constantinople, exploiting marble, brass and steam for cool tonal contrasts and an air of ethnographic reportage.

A nude boy displays a python before a row of seated Ottoman soldiers, the tiled wall behind them rendered with archaeological exactitude. Long held up as the emblem of Saidian Orientalism after appearing on the cover of Edward Said's book, it shows Gérôme's appetite for stagecraft and luxurious surface.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-mo: A bather is attended by a dark-skinned servant in the steam of a hammam, the marble basin and brass ewer rendered with Gérôme's ethnographic precision. The subject became a recurring vehicle for him, combining Orientalist setting with academic study of the female nude.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-on: Commissioned by Baltimore collector William T. Walters, the small panel pictures a Nubian handler walking two slim sighthounds through a windswept desert. The trim silhouettes suggest Pharaoh hounds, a subject Gérôme studied during his Egyptian travels of the 1860s.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ph: Gérôme stages the legendary trial of the courtesan Phryne, disrobed by her advocate Hypereides to sway the Athenian judges. The single sweep of light on her body and the recoiling line of bearded jurors make a deliberately theatrical machine of his archaeological reconstruction.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-po: A staged Roman amphitheatre scene in which a victorious mirmillo stands over his fallen opponent and looks up at the Vestals' thumbs-down verdict. Gérôme drew on his own collection of antique armour for the gladiators' helmets and helped fix Hollywood's mental image of the arena.

Two nude women rest beside the pool of a tiled hamam interior, shafts of light falling through high vents in the vaulted ceiling. A dark-robed attendant stands in the foreground, carrying a long-stemmed pipe. Gérôme renders the Iznik-tiled walls, marble floor, and warm flesh with his characteristic near-photographic precision. The work, dated circa 1876, is held in the Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-pr: An Arnaut — a Balkan Ottoman irregular soldier in distinctive white kilt and red stockings — stands in prayer on a dark cape spread across the desert floor, his horse grazing behind him and a long caravan receding into the distance. Gérôme sets the solitary figure against a vast pale sky and open horizon, isolating devotion within the stillness of the desert. Painted in 1864 and informed by the artist's Near Eastern travels, the work is one of several prayer subjects in which Gérôme explores the intersection of landscape and ritual observance.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-py: The Cypriot sculptor embraces his ivory creation as she turns from cold stone to warm flesh from the hips upward. Gérôme also modelled the subject in polychrome sculpture in these years; the painting plays on his own dual practice as painter and sculptor.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ri: A horseman rests against the flank of his exhausted mount in the brassy heat of the desert afternoon, barren hills behind. Gérôme exploits a low horizon and brushed-smooth surface to evoke the still, shimmering air of his North African travels.

A substantial group of mounted and on-foot travellers crosses a sun-bleached desert plain, rust-coloured hills rising in the distance and a larger caravan trailing behind them in a haze of dust. Gérôme, painting after his 1868 Sinai expedition, deploys an oil-on-panel surface of great smoothness to convey the dazzling midday light. The 1870 work — 41 × 56 cm — exemplifies his frieze-like arrangement of colourful figures against an expansive desert landscape.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-se: A nude female captive stands on an auction platform, her back to the viewer, while a red-robed auctioneer addresses an assembled crowd of Roman buyers and onlookers. Gérôme renders the scene with the meticulous archaeological detail characteristic of his academic practice, distributing attention between the auctioneer's rhetoric and the varied responses of the bidders. The work, circa 1884, is one of six slave-market subjects Gérôme painted across ancient Roman and contemporary Ottoman settings, and is held in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-th: Gérôme avoids the assassination itself, instead showing senators streaming from the curia while Caesar's body lies abandoned in the foreground. The cool, measured composition and almost photographic finish drew contemporary comparison to a daguerreotype of the ancient world.

In a wintry Parisian park at dawn, the wounded Pierrot is supported by the red-robed Duc de Guise and a black-cloaked Domino, while to the right the victorious combatants — identifiable as Harlequin and another masquerade figure — confer at a distance. The work, painted between 1857 and 1859 and based on a composition Gérôme executed for the Duc d'Aumale, stages the aftermath of a carnival duel with the precise, theatrical finish of his academic manner. Oil on canvas, 39.1 × 56.3 cm, Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.

A solitary pasha in red and gold robes sits beside the body of his dead tiger, laid out on a blue carpet and strewn with flowers, two tall green candles burning at its head in the columned courtyard of a Moorish palace. The single figure's quiet grief and the ceremonial candlelight lend the scene the weight of an elegy. Gérôme's 1882 oil, held in the Joslyn Art Museum, Omaha, exemplifies his miniaturist precision in the rendering of tilework, carved stone, and animal anatomy.

A Black eunuch stands sentinel at the lattice of a waterfront kiosk while veiled women look out toward the Bosphorus. Gérôme's love of Ottoman tilework and his crisp architectural perspective shape the picture's mood of guarded retreat.

An outdoor slave market in the Ottoman world: several female captives in various states of undress wait against a whitewashed wall while a figure in white attends from an alcove above. Gérôme distributes figures across the scene with the detached ethnographic precision that marks his market pictures, rendering sunlit plaster, worn carpet, and shadow with equal care. The work, dated 1871, is one of several slave-market compositions by the artist and is held in the Cincinnati Art Museum.

On a dark, rain-wet night, a small winged Cupid stands at the heavy wooden door of a stone house, a line of firelight glowing beneath the threshold, while the bearded poet Anacreon leans out of an upper window to see who has knocked. Gérôme renders the exterior courtyard with archaeological care — rough-cut stone, climbing laurel, and the contrast of warm interior light against the nocturnal chill. The work, circa 1899 (oil on canvas, 60 × 81.5 cm), is the first in Gérôme's series illustrating the ode attributed to Anacreon.

The companion to the rainstorm scene: Anacreon has taken the shivering Cupid in and warms him by the hearth, just before the boy will draw his bow and pierce the host's heart. Gérôme stages the moral fable with the archaeological props and porcelain finish of his late manner.

Part of a late illustrative cycle Gérôme devoted to the Greek lyric poet Anacreon, the scene shows the mischievous Cupid escaping after warming himself at the poet's hearth. Drawn in Gérôme's tight academic line, it preserves the anecdotal charm of the original Anacreontic ode.

An oil painting from Gérôme's Anacreon series, showing the aged poet seated by a fire, head resting in his hand, as a luminous Cupid figure hovers in the smoke and light to his left. The classically furnished interior, rendered with Gérôme's characteristic precision, situates the literary reverie within an archaeologically detailed ancient setting. Oil on canvas, 60 × 81.5 cm, c. 1899.

A cavalryman tramples a tulip bed while soldiers behind him slash at the flower beds, an allegory of the Dutch tulipomania crash of 1636-37. Gérôme's choice of so eccentric an episode reflects his fondness for moral and economic anecdotes drawn from history.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-ti: A tiger sits alertly on a sandy desert ridge, turning its head toward a distant column of figures — soldiers or a caravan — winding across the plain below. Gérôme renders the animal with meticulous anatomical care, setting its warm stripes against the pale expanse of dunes and a clear desert sky. Completed in 1888, the work is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.
collection-of-beauty-jean-leon-gerome-yo: Two young Greek figures kneel on the polished marble floor of an Ottoman mosque interior while a standing figure in military dress looks on — a scene of cultural conversion rather than ordinary prayer. Gérôme renders the columned arcade and intricate architectural carving with Orientalist care. Oil on panel, 1865; Minneapolis Institute of Art (inv. 62.85).
collection-of-beauty-jean-louis-theodore: Survivors of the wrecked French frigate Méduse strain toward a distant ship, piling living and dead bodies into a single rising pyramid. Géricault interviewed actual survivors and modelled corpses in his studio for this Salon-shaking indictment of incompetent royalist command, now anchoring the Louvre's Romanticism galleries.
collection-of-beauty-jean-paul-flandrin-: Commissioned by King Wilhelm I of Württemberg, the picture reclines an odalisque before a garden vista while a servant plays the lute. Ingres designed and largely painted it, with the landscape backdrop entrusted to his pupil Paul Flandrin.
collection-of-beauty-jerome-bonaparte-by: Napoleon's youngest brother sits for an American portraitist while honeymooning in Baltimore with his first wife, Elizabeth Patterson. Stuart painted the 19-year-old Jérôme on canvas at 28 1/4 inches, the loose brushwork of the unfinished collar typical of his late Boston manner.
collection-of-beauty-jerusalem-artichoke: A large bouquet of yellow Jerusalem artichoke flowers fills a ceramic vase set on a round table, the blooms worked in feathery, broken touches of yellow and green against a flickering pink-grey ground. Monet signed and dated the canvas 1880; it is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington (inv. 1963.10.181).
collection-of-beauty-jeune-fille-au-pian: A young woman seated at an upright piano with a second woman sewing on a sofa behind her, in a domestic interior. Oil on canvas, about 57 by 92 cm, held by the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg under accession ГЭ-9166. The work carries the subtitle Overture to Tannhäuser, after the Wagner prelude.
collection-of-beauty-jeune-orpheline-au-: A young girl kneels beside a grave, her tear-streaked face turned skyward in mute appeal. Painted as a study for the Salon piece The Massacre at Chios, the work shows Delacroix's early Romantic instinct for raw psychological pathos rendered through loose brushwork and warm, earthen tones.
collection-of-beauty-jheronimus-bosch-01: A surviving fragment of a dismembered triptych depicting passengers crammed into a small boat, drinking, singing, and grasping at food while their craft drifts aimlessly. Bosch borrows the late-medieval Narrenschiff allegory to lampoon clerical vice, populating the scene with a lute-strumming nun and a tonsured friar.
collection-of-beauty-jheronimus-bosch-05: The right wing of the dismantled Wayfarer triptych, now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. A dying man hesitates between an angel at his pillow and a demon offering a sack of gold, while Death enters at the door — a memento mori rendered with the artist's cool, lapidary palette.
collection-of-beauty-jheronimus-bosch-de: The central panel of a triptych in the Prado, drawn from the Flemish proverb that the world is a haystack from which each takes what he can. Crowds claw at a giant cart of hay drawn by demons toward hell, Bosch's signature grotesques staging human greed with miniaturist precision.
collection-of-beauty-joachem-wtewael-ven: Vulcan drops his golden net over the naked lovers Mars and Venus in their bed while the Olympian gods crane down from the clouds to watch. Painted on copper in 1601, this Mauritshuis cabinet picture is one of several treatments Wtewael made of the Ovidian scene, prized in late Mannerist circles for its erotic-comic intricacy.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-anthonisz-w: Mars and Venus tangle naked in a curtained bed while Apollo, Diana and the rest of the Olympian gods sail in on clouds to mock them. Painted on copper between 1606 and 1610 and now in the Getty, the panel packs more than a dozen figures into a polished cabinet-sized surface intended for close, private viewing.

Sebastian is bound to a tree in an outdoor wooded landscape, his arms raised above and his body twisting, as figures around him prepare or discharge arrows. A winged putto descends from the upper right. Signed and dated 1600, the panel exemplifies Wtewael's Utrecht Mannerism, with elongated nude forms, restless poses, and vivid contrasts of flesh and foliage.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-patinier-te: Three demonic women in courtly dress press around the hermit Anthony at the lower edge while a vast world-landscape of rocks, rivers and burning towns recedes behind them. A documented collaboration: Quinten Metsys painted the figures and Joachim Patinir the panorama. The Prado panel carries inventory number P 1615.
