collection-of-beauty-joachim-patinir-010: Patinir fills nearly the entire sky and middle distance with the lurid orange glow of burning Sodom and Gomorrah, while pale rock formations rise at right and tiny figures — Lot and his companions guided by angels — appear at lower right. The work treats the Old Testament catastrophe as a panoramic landscape spectacle, with smouldering cities silhouetted against the inflamed horizon. Oil on panel, c. 1520; formerly Hermann Göring Collection.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-patinir-res: Mary is seated in a sunlit meadow nursing the Christ child while Joseph stands in the middle ground with the donkey, the Holy Family embedded in a sweeping Patinir world-landscape of green hills, rivers, and pale blue rock formations. The devotional subject serves as a vehicle for expansive landscape invention, layering warm foreground greens against cool rocky distances. Oil on panel, c. 1518–1520; Museo del Prado, Madrid (inv. P001611).
collection-of-beauty-joachim-patinir-st-: The giant ferryman wades a river bearing the Christ Child on his shoulder, the saint's labor dwarfed by Patinir's signature world-landscape stretching to a hazy blue horizon. The Antwerp master pioneered this compositional formula in which figures recede before vast geological panoramas.

The hermit saint bends in his makeshift wilderness shelter amid the craggy stratified landscape that is Patinir's hallmark, with a vast river valley and distant town dissolving into atmospheric blue behind him. Patinir uses the eremitic subject to display his trademark world-landscape, in which the human figure of penitence is dwarfed by enormous geological formations. Held in the Department of Paintings of the Louvre (RF 2429), the panel dates from between circa 1515 and 1520.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-wtewael-bac: The wine god is shown half-length, his head garlanded with vine leaves and full grape clusters, holding a large glass goblet in both hands while bunches of grapes trail across his bare torso. Wtewael, the Utrecht Mannerist who excelled in small cabinet pictures and mythological subjects, gives Bacchus a fleshy, ruddy vitality against a dark ground. The work is dated before 1638.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-wtewael-por: Christina van Halen, wife of the painter Joachim Wtewael, sits in a black gown with a wide millstone ruff, her right hand raised in a composed gesture beside a small table bearing jewellery. Signed and dated 1601, the panel is understood to be a pendant to Wtewael's own self-portrait of the same year, both associated with the Centraal Museum in Utrecht.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-wtewael-sel: The painter looks out in a white millstone ruff and black costume, holding his palette, brushes, and a maulstick as emblems of his craft. A coat of arms carved in relief is visible in the background. Signed and dated 1601, the panel is understood to be a pendant to the portrait of his wife Christina van Halen, both associated with the Centraal Museum in Utrecht.
collection-of-beauty-joachim-wtewael-the: Shepherds, animals, and attendant figures press in around the newborn Christ and the Madonna in a crowded scene set among crumbling brick ruins, with a fire illuminating the foreground and a goat prominent at right. Signed and dated 1598, the picture is a characteristic Utrecht Mannerist work by Wtewael, who specialised in large-scale scenes painted with intense colour and dynamic figure groupings.

A market woman arranges baskets of cabbages, plums, and gourds beside a copper bowl, with a small kitchen scene of Christ visiting Mary and Martha glimpsed through a doorway behind her. Wtewael painted several such genre pieces around 1618 in which the religious narrative is pushed to the background while still life dominates the foreground.
collection-of-beauty-johann-christian-ba: Portrait of the composer Johann Christian Bach (1735–1782), youngest son of J. S. Bach and known in England as the 'English Bach'. Gainsborough painted this likeness in 1776, showing the sitter in a buff coat and blue satin waistcoat, resting his hands on a sheet of music. The portrait was commissioned for the gallery of musicians in Bologna assembled by Padre Giovanni Battista Martini.
collection-of-beauty-johann-heinrich-fus: The Norse god Thor wrestles the Midgard Serpent in a churning sea, muscles knotted in the elongated, theatrical anatomy Fuseli favored. The Swiss-born painter mined Eddic and Miltonic mythology for charged subjects, exaggerating chiaroscuro and pose for sublime effect.

Odysseus steers his vessel between the six-headed Scylla and the whirlpool Charybdis, his crew contorted in heroic dread. The composition belongs to Fuseli's lifelong cycle of literary illustrations, where storms of muscular figures stage classical and Miltonic catastrophe.

A figure is overwhelmed and dragged down by an enormous serpent in a stormy outdoor setting, the attacker's coils filling the composition in a characteristic Fuselian display of overwhelming animal force. The work on paper, dating to circa 1800, draws on Mannerist precedents to push human anatomy into expressive distortion, and is titled 'Horseman Attacked by a Giant Snake' in the record.

The sea-nymph Thetis bends in mourning over the corpse of her son Achilles, her grief amplified by the painter's sinuous neoclassical line. Fuseli reinterprets the Homeric scene through the proto-Romantic lens of sublime emotion, giving the figures attenuated, almost weightless poise.
collection-of-beauty-johannes-jan-vermee: Vermeer's largest known painting and a rare history piece, made early in his career before he turned to domestic interiors. Christ gestures toward the seated, attentive Mary while Martha presents a basket of bread; the broad handling and warm reds anticipate the artist's mature poise.
collection-of-beauty-johannes-vermeer-a-: A young woman in a yellow ermine-trimmed jacket pauses at her writing table, lifting her gaze toward the viewer, an ink pot and pearl jewellery at her hand. Painted around 1665 and now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the small panel is one of Vermeer's most intimate evocations of the moment of address from writer to absent reader.
collection-of-beauty-johannes-vermeer-ge: A modest stretch of Delft brickwork, with figures absorbed in domestic chores in a doorway and an alley. One of only two surviving cityscapes by Vermeer, the picture distills the painter's quiet attention to weathered surface, mortar, and clouded northern light.
collection-of-beauty-johannes-vermeer-he: A sturdy kitchen maid pours a thin stream of milk into an earthenware bowl, the room hushed by daylight from a leaded window. Vermeer's pointillé highlights flicker on bread crusts and copper, and the lapis-derived blue of her apron exemplifies his costly pigment habits.
collection-of-beauty-johannes-vermeer-th: A scholar in a long robe leans over a celestial globe, his hand brushing its surface as if to set the cosmos turning. Painted as a pendant to The Geographer, the picture reflects Delft's culture of empirical inquiry, its still light and book-strewn study tuned to quiet concentration.

A scholar in a blue Japonse rok leans over a chart spread on a table, holding dividers, as morning light falls from a leaded window at left. A celestial globe rests atop the cabinet behind him and a sea-chart hangs on the wall at right. Dated 1668 and held at the Städel Museum, Frankfurt, the painting is the companion piece to The Astronomer and forms Vermeer's meditation on seventeenth-century Dutch scientific inquiry.

The smallest of Vermeer's surviving paintings, focusing tightly on a young woman bent over her bobbins and pins. Threads of red and white spill from a cushion in molten blurs that anticipate optical photography, while her concentrated face is rendered with the artist's signature stillness.
collection-of-beauty-john-adams-a18236: John Adams, in a black coat and powdered hair, faces the viewer in a half-length pose against a plain ground. Stuart began the portrait around 1800, when Adams was the sitting second president, and finished it about 1815 for the former president's son John Quincy.
collection-of-beauty-john-adams-by-john-: John Adams stands in a brown coat beside a globe and a draped table, one hand resting on a sword hilt, the other holding diplomatic papers. Copley painted Adams in London in 1783 as the Massachusetts minister was negotiating the peace that recognised American independence; the canvas is in the Harvard Art Museums.
collection-of-beauty-john-atkinson-grims: A wet Leeds thoroughfare at night, gas lamps casting warm amber light on glazed shopfronts and the glistening pavement below. Grimshaw built a career on these meticulously observed urban nocturnes, balancing precise architectural detail with a painterly command of artificial light and its reflections.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-1776: An intimate portrait of the painter's fiancée, completed shortly before their long-resisted marriage. Constable, primarily a landscapist, treats her face with a reserved tenderness, the muted palette and soft modelling reflecting the private nature of the commission.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-a-bo: A barge being lowered through the lock at Flatford Mill on the Stour, the lock-keeper leaning on the beam against a clearing sky. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1824 and sold on opening day, the picture was the only one of Constable's six-footers to find a buyer during the artist's lifetime.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-bran: A wide panoramic view across Hampstead Heath, with a sand or gravel excavation in the foreground where horses and workers with a cart are at work, a pond visible in the middle distance, and a vast, cloud-laden sky filling the upper half. Constable rented a house in Hampstead from 1819, and the heath's open terrain supplied him with the expansive sky studies he returned to throughout the 1820s, now held in the Cleveland Museum of Art.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-by-r: The young John Constable, then twenty-three, faces the viewer in dark coat and stock, his curling hair brushed forward. Reinagle painted the portrait in 1799, the year both men entered the Royal Academy Schools, and it now hangs in the National Portrait Gallery in London.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-flat: A view from a footbridge on the Stour, with a barge being unhitched in the foreground beneath open Suffolk sky. Painted largely en plein air on Constable's family land, the picture exemplifies the truth-to-nature creed that underpinned his six large 'Stour' canvases.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-hadl: The ruined fourteenth-century keep of Hadleigh Castle stands on the Essex shore above the wide grey mouth of the Thames, gulls wheeling in a clearing morning sky. Constable submitted the picture to the Royal Academy in 1829, the year of his election as an Academician and shortly after the death of his wife Maria; it now belongs to the Yale Center for British Art.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-harw: A breezy view of the Essex coast, with the squat Low Lighthouse anchoring a beach where small figures gather under a luminous, cloud-stacked sky. Constable's skies are scientifically observed, drawing on his sustained study of meteorology in oil sketches.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-parh: A working watermill at Gillingham in Dorset, its great wheel turning as water cascades over it into the stream below, with figures wading in the foreground and a stormy sky above. Constable painted the subject around 1826, working from studies made on visits to the area, and exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy that year.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-sali: The thirteenth-century spire of Salisbury Cathedral framed between tall trees in the Bishop's garden, cattle grazing at the edge of a sunlit meadow. Signed and dated 1826 and now in the Frick Collection, the picture was repainted by Constable at the request of Bishop John Fisher, who had objected to the dark sky of an earlier version.

The cathedral's spire rises through the screen of trees on a property owned by the painter's friend Bishop Fisher, who commissioned the picture. Constable renders the verdant grounds with characteristic flecks of white impasto — his 'snow' that animated foliage and water alike.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-sir-: A view from Haverstock Hill in rural Hampstead, looking south toward the dome of St Paul's, with Sir Richard Steele's cottage on the right and the Load of Hay inn on the left. Constable, who had lived in Hampstead since 1819, sketched the rise repeatedly; the cottage was demolished in 1867.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-ston: A late watercolour showing the prehistoric stones beneath a roiling sky split by a double rainbow. Constable, working in his final years, treats the monument as a meditation on time and weather, the broken trilithons set against the moving drama of the English heavens.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-the-: A wooden hay cart fords the millpond at Flatford on the Stour, with Willy Lott's cottage to the left and a slow bank of cumulus overhead. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1821, the six-foot canvas was shown at the 1824 Paris Salon, where it won a gold medal and influenced Delacroix and the young Barbizon painters.

A sweeping view east from Gun Hill over the River Stour to the tower of Dedham Church and the estuary beyond, painted with thickly worked impasto and white sparkle on the water. Dated 1828 and now in the Scottish National Gallery, the picture echoes Claude's Hagar and the Angel and helped secure Constable's election to the Royal Academy the following year.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-wate: Waterloo Bridge seen from the north bank of the Thames, its arches stretching across the river under a broad cloudy sky, with figures and rowing boats in the foreground. Constable worked on the Waterloo subject for nearly two decades, building from studies such as this toward the large 1832 exhibition picture commemorating the bridge's opening on the second anniversary of the battle.
collection-of-beauty-john-constable-wive: A panoramic estate view commissioned by Major-General Francis Slater-Rebow, balancing fishermen, swans, a grazing herd, and the distant house. Constable expanded the canvas at the patron's request to include a lawn and outbuildings, evidence of his pragmatic handling of the country-house genre.
collection-of-beauty-john-everett-millai: Titled from a song in Shakespeare's As You Like It, the painting shows a young woman huddled on a snowbound hillside in a bleak winter landscape, with a dog and a distant walking figure behind her. Painted in 1892 and held at the Auckland Art Gallery, the work exemplifies Millais's broader, more mood-driven late style, far removed from the close observation of his early Pre-Raphaelite years.

An autumnal Perthshire backwater under leaden skies, painted from a sandbank on the Tay near Murthly. Millais himself called this his first true landscape, and its damp, unromantic mood anticipates the meditative late landscapes that occupied his final decades.

A stone manor house glows with candlelit windows against a warm amber winter dusk, its bare trees and snow-covered grounds populated by crows foraging in the foreground. Painted in 1887, the work shows Millais's late landscape manner — meticulous in detail yet suffused with atmospheric colour — and is characteristic of the Scottish winter subjects he returned to in his final decades.

A lone figure walks away along a snow-dusted road lined with bare birch trees in the Perthshire glen near Birnam, the distant hills visible through the winter canopy. Painted in 1890, the work is characteristic of Millais's late Highland landscapes, rendered with the freer, broader brushwork of his maturity rather than the botanical precision of his Pre-Raphaelite youth.

Drawn from Tennyson's poem after the Shakespearean character, Mariana stretches wearily at her embroidery beside a stained-glass window, autumn leaves drifting onto the floor. Millais paints the heraldic glass and velvet gown with founding Pre-Raphaelite precision, every fibre and pane separately observed.

Shakespeare's drowning Ophelia drifts among meadow flowers along the Hogsmill River in Surrey. Millais painted the riverbank botany on site over five months, then posed Elizabeth Siddal in a heated bathtub for the figure. Each bloom carries Victorian floral symbolism for grief, innocence and madness.

A young Brunswick cavalry officer takes leave of his sweetheart on the eve of Waterloo, her hand braced against the door he is determined to open. Millais paired the black death's-head hussar uniform against shimmering ivory silk to heighten the parting. Charles Dickens's daughter Kate modelled for the woman.
collection-of-beauty-john-frederick-lewi: A young woman stands in a colonnaded doorway holding a tray, wearing richly layered Middle Eastern dress — embroidered jacket, striped sash and wide trousers — against a sunlit courtyard beyond. Lewis, who spent a decade in Cairo, renders the tilework floor, costume, and architectural detail with the miniaturist exactitude that distinguished his Orientalist work; the painting is held at Manchester Art Gallery.

A British traveller's tent camp pitched in the Sinai wilderness, with St Catherine's monastery faintly visible in the distance. Lewis drew on a decade of life in Cairo to render carpets, tasselled saddles and Bedouin retainers with miniaturist exactitude. The watercolour fuses Orientalist reportage with the topographical tradition.

A harem interior in Cairo, where a seated lady greets her guests amid mashrabiya screens and a sun-dappled mosaic floor. Lewis lived a decade in an Ottoman house in the city and made the filtered light through latticed windows his signature subject. Every textile, slipper and tile is rendered in jewel-bright watercolour clarity.

A late biblical genre piece taking its title from the Epistle of James, set within a sunlit Eastern interior. Lewis casts the scriptural episode in the Cairene domestic vocabulary he had perfected over decades. Mashrabiya light falls across patterned cushions and the bedside attendants in saturated colour.

A Scottish Highland interior from Lewis's early career, showing a group of men and women gathered around a central hearth in a rustic dwelling, with a spinning wheel to one side and dogs at their feet. Travellers or visitors are welcomed with food and drink by their hosts in Highland dress. Painted in 1832 and now held at the Yale Center for British Art, the picture belongs to the early nineteenth-century taste for Walter Scott-inflected genre subjects.

Two laden camels rest on a grassy bank beside the Nile, their ornate saddlery and tasselled trappings rendered in precise detail against a wide, cloud-filled blue sky. Waterfowl gather at the water's edge below, and a small figure with a basket appears among the reeds in the middle distance. Painted in 1876, long after Lewis's return to England, and now in the Yale Center for British Art, the composition draws on the Egyptian sketches he continued to mine throughout his later career.

A group of pilgrims is gathered inside a richly decorated basilica interior, its walls hung with devotional images and draped textiles, the floor spread with carpets. Women and children in regional Italian costume rest and pray amid the architectural splendour of the sacred space. Painted in 1854 and held at the Yale Center for British Art, the work applies the ethnographic precision Lewis would become famous for in his Orientalist pictures to the religious folk culture of Italy.
collection-of-beauty-john-hancock-painti: John Hancock sits at a writing table in a blue coat with his ledger open before him, the merchant and future signer of the Declaration of Independence painted at twenty-eight. Copley made the portrait in 1765 for the Hancock family in Boston, and it now hangs in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-john-henry-newman-b: Cardinal Newman, the theologian who led the Oxford Movement and later converted to Roman Catholicism, is shown in old age dressed in full cardinal robes — scarlet mozzetta, red zucchetto and a gold pectoral chain. Millais applies the assured, broadly brushed technique of his late portraiture to capture the aged cardinal's composed authority. Painted in 1881, the year after Newman received the cardinalate from Leo XIII, the portrait is held at the National Portrait Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-john-jay-gilbert-st: John Jay is seated in the distinctive black and orange judicial robes of the first Chief Justice of the United States, one hand resting against an upright book or document beside him. Gilbert Stuart painted Jay in 1794, the year he travelled to Britain to negotiate the commercial treaty that bears his name; the portrait is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. The handling is Stuart's characteristic blend of assured brushwork and dignified Neoclassical restraint.
collection-of-beauty-john-liston-byam-sh: A young woman in a dark dress stands lost in thought at the edge of an overgrown stream, the summer vegetation around her painted with Pre-Raphaelite exactness. The war of the title never appears: Byam Shaw shows only its cost at home, a woman mourning a loss in a conflict thousands of miles away, the indifferent lushness of the English countryside sharpening her grief. Painted in 1901 under the title The Boer War, the oil is in the collection of Birmingham Museums.

Eve stands at the centre of the composition, nude, eyes closed, as Adam reaches toward her from behind; to either side coils a great serpent amid an extravagant profusion of tropical flowers, foliage, and exotic birds. John Byam Liston Shaw's 1911 painting depicts the Garden of Eden temptation scene in a late Pre-Raphaelite idiom indebted to Burne-Jones, with saturated colour and densely patterned decoration filling every part of the canvas.
collection-of-beauty-john-singer-sargent: The painter Paul Helleu sketches outdoors beside his wife Alice, the canoe and grass rendered in broken Impressionist touch. Sargent painted the work at Fladbury during a summer of plein-air experiment under Monet's influence. The flushed greens and unfinished edges show him at his most explicitly Impressionist.

A circular ceiling painting for the rotunda of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, showing the Titan stooping under the celestial sphere while the nymphs of the western garden recline at his feet. Sargent took on the rotunda decoration as a late, demanding mural commission. The composition reads from any vantage on the floor below.

Women and children in Breton regional dress cross the sunlit tidal flats of Cancale carrying baskets of oysters, with sailboats and the harbour visible in the distance beneath a bright blue sky with billowing clouds. Shown at the Paris Salon in 1878, where it earned a second-class medal, the canvas — officially titled En route pour la pêche — brought the twenty-two-year-old Sargent to prominence. It is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

Two girls in white dresses light glowing Japanese paper lanterns amid tall white lilies and rose blooms in a garden at dusk. Sargent worked on the canvas over two consecutive summers in Broadway, painting only in the brief twilight each evening to capture the transient quality of the fading light. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1887 and now in Tate Britain, the picture is widely seen as the work that restored Sargent's reputation in England after the controversy over Madame X.

Lady Agnew sits in a carved and upholstered armchair, wearing a white muslin gown with a lavender sash, her dark eyes meeting the viewer directly and one arm resting loosely over the chair's side. Sargent painted the portrait in 1892 and it was exhibited at the Royal Academy the following year to considerable acclaim; the canvas is now the centrepiece of the Scottish National Gallery in Edinburgh. The relaxed pose and luminous handling of the white dress exemplify the command of character and painterly bravura for which Sargent's society portraits are celebrated.

A languid female figure reclines on a sofa, head turned away, wrapped in shimmering ivory satin and gauze. Sargent's niece Rose-Marie Ormond was the model for several such drapery studies in the years before the First World War. The picture is essentially a virtuoso exercise in painting white folds against deep shadow.

A personification of the defeated Synagogue, blindfolded and clutching a broken staff, painted for Sargent's Triumph of Religion mural cycle in the Boston Public Library. The medieval iconographic pairing with a triumphant Church drew sustained protest from Boston's Jewish community. The cycle was left unfinished, partly in the wake of that controversy.

Two friends bend over a board in a sun-shot garden during one of Sargent's Alpine summers in the Simplon. The painter spent these holidays sketching members of his travelling party in shawls, hats and Kashmiri textiles. The watercolour-like oil handling and high-keyed greens are typical of these informal late landscapes.

A young Venetian girl holds a long string of white onions, her dark shawl framing a white dress, while a view of the lagoon and a campanile opens through a window behind her. The canvas belongs to Sargent's early Venetian campaigns of 1880–82, when he sought out working-class subjects in the city's quieter quarters. Now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-john-singleton-copl: British soldiers surge around the fallen body of Major Francis Peirson after the French assault on Jersey in January 1781, the Union flag pressing forward through cannon smoke above the market square at St Helier. Copley undertook the large history painting on his own initiative and completed it in 1783; it now hangs in Tate Britain, London.

Admiral Duncan receives the sword of the defeated Vice-Admiral de Winter on the quarterdeck of HMS Venerable after the British victory off Camperdown on 11 October 1797. Copley finished the canvas in 1799 for the City of London, now in the National Galleries of Scotland (NG 2661).

Henry Pelham, Copley's half-brother, sits at a polished mahogany table with a flying squirrel tethered by a gold chain, a glass of water beside him. Shipped to London for the 1766 Society of Artists exhibition, the picture earned Copley election to the Society and Joshua Reynolds's qualified praise.

Thomas Mifflin, the Pennsylvania merchant and future first governor of the state, sits beside his wife Sarah Morris, who works at a small loom of fringed silk. Copley painted the double portrait in 1773, just before sailing for Europe, as a tribute to the non-importation movement that the Mifflins championed. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds it.

The Boston merchant and town clerk Ezekiel Goldthwait is shown three-quarter length in a dark red coat, holding a quill pen in one hand and a folded document in the other, with papers and an inkstand on the table beside him. Painted in oil on canvas in 1771, it is paired at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (accession 41.85) with Copley's companion portrait of his wife Elizabeth.

Hugh Montgomerie, later 12th Earl of Eglinton, stands in the full Highland dress of a British officer — red coat, tartan kilt, and feathered bonnet — his sword at his side and a battle in smoke behind him. Copley painted the full-length portrait in London in 1780 to mark Montgomerie's military service, including his years with the 77th (Highland) Regiment during the Seven Years' War.

Isaac Royall, the Massachusetts merchant and slaveholder, sits in a dark crimson coat with gold buttons, one hand gesturing toward an open document on the table beside him, a blue-green curtain providing the sole backdrop. Copley painted the portrait in 1769, and it is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (accession 39.247), one of several Cambridge sittings from the years before Copley's departure for Europe.

Two young daughters of the Medford merchant Isaac Royall Jr. are shown full-length in elaborate satin gowns — one blue, one yellow-green — one of them holding a small dark dog. Painted around 1758, when Copley was in his early twenties, the canvas is among his earliest known double portraits; the Loyalist Royall family fled to England in 1776 and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, acquired it in 1925.

Mary Toppan, wife of the Salem merchant Benjamin Pickman, stands in a blue satin gown trimmed with silver lace, holding a closed parasol at her side, with a stone balustrade behind her. Copley painted the portrait in 1763, and it is held at the Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven (accession 1966.79.3).

Mary Turner Sargent leans on a pedestal beside a fountain, water cupped in her hand, in a Boston society portrait of 1763. The conceit of the basin and the pose derive from English mezzotints after Reynolds, sources Copley studied avidly in colonial Massachusetts before his move to London.

Elizabeth Oliver Watson, wife of the Boston merchant George Watson, is shown in a red satin gown with lace cuffs, her hand resting on a blue-and-white vase of flowers beside her. Copley painted the portrait in 1765; it entered the Smithsonian American Art Museum as a family gift.

Mrs Humphrey Devereux, an older woman in a dark dress and white lace cap, leans forward with her elbow on a polished red table, her chin resting on her raised hand. Copley painted the half-length portrait in oil on canvas in 1771; it now hangs at the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tamaki.

A woman in a golden silk gown sits in three-quarter view, holding an open letter or document in both hands. Copley painted this half-length portrait in oil on canvas in 1771, during his Boston practice documenting the merchant class of pre-Revolutionary New England. The blue silk wrap edged in gold, the sitter's composed gaze, and the crimson chair back demonstrate Copley's command of textile and surface.

A bust-length study of a young Black man, painted by Copley around 1777–78 as a preparatory work connected to Watson and the Shark. The sitter wears a plain brownish garment and turns his head slightly, mouth open, his expression alert and individualised. The Detroit Institute of Arts holds the canvas, which presents its subject with a directness and dignity rare in British painting of the period.

Group portrait of the artist with his wife Susanna, their four children, and his Loyalist father-in-law Richard Clarke, painted in London after Copley departed Boston in 1774. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1777, the large canvas announced Copley's arrival on the London scene; it is now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

A naked Brook Watson founders in Havana harbour as a boat of rescuers strains toward him, with Morro Castle visible on the right and a Black sailor at the apex of the rescuing group. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1778 and now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, the canvas dramatises an attack Watson survived as a fourteen-year-old cabin boy in 1749.

A girl in a pink silk dress holds a blue ribbon tied to a parrot perched on a chairback, while a black-and-white spaniel stands at her side. Painted in Boston in 1767, before Copley's departure for Europe, the portrait entered the Toledo Museum of Art and shows his characteristic close observation of fabric, feather, and fur.
collection-of-beauty-john-trumbull-gilbe: The history painter John Trumbull, in a warm brown coat with fur collar and white stock, appears in three-quarter profile. Stuart painted his fellow American in 1818; the canvas is at the Yale University Art Gallery. Trumbull was then engaged on the four Revolutionary War scenes commissioned for the United States Capitol Rotunda.
collection-of-beauty-johnmontresorbycopl: Captain John Montresor, the British military engineer who surveyed Quebec and Detroit, sits in three-quarter view in his red officer's coat. Copley painted the portrait in oil on canvas around 1771, during his Boston practice before he left for London on the eve of the Revolution. The Detroit Institute of Arts holds the canvas.
collection-of-beauty-joseon-kang-huian-g: A Joseon scholar reclines on a rocky outcrop, overlooking water below — the scene identified by its title Gosagwansudo as a seonbi gazing from a high hill. Kang Hui-an was a fifteenth-century Korean court official and one of the earliest named painters in the Korean literati tradition. The work is small (15.7 by 23.4 cm) and executed in a gestural ink manner characteristic of his surviving output.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-brant-2: The Mohawk leader Thayendanegea, known to the British as Joseph Brant, appears bust-length in a red cloak, silver gorget, and feathered headdress. Stuart painted Brant in London in 1785 during the Mohawk leader's diplomatic mission to negotiate land grants for Loyalist Iroquois resettled in Upper Canada after the American war.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-mallord-will: Embarking passengers and fishwives crowd the French pier as a squall builds beyond the harbour mouth. Turner had himself crossed to Calais in rough weather in 1802, and he exhibited this large canvas to challenge the marine paintings of his French contemporaries.

A vessel lists at right, its masts steeply raked, against a pale luminous sky with warm yellow light on the horizon. Turner produced this painting between 1827 and 1828 as one of the Yarmouth sample studies intended to demonstrate his manner to engravers. It is held as part of the Turner Bequest, now at Tate.

A rainbow arcs over Buttermere following a Lake District shower, the slate fells doubled in the still water below. Turner exhibited the picture at the Royal Academy aged twenty-three, after a Cumberland sketching tour. It is one of his earliest essays in the sublime mountain weather effects that would define him.

Local fisherwomen, the poissards, dig for lugworm bait on the broad expanse of Calais beach as the sun sinks behind them. Turner returned to the Channel coast repeatedly, treating Calais as the symbolic threshold between England and the Continent. The sky and wet sand dissolve into a single shimmering field of low light.

Harvesters work an open field on the Earl of Essex's estate at Cassiobury in Hertfordshire. The painting was a private commission produced alongside a series of watercolours of the park. It shows Turner extending his Claudean pastoral mode to a contemporary English country-house setting.

A loose oil sketch toward the large Trafalgar canvas commissioned by George IV for St James's Palace. Turner stitched together multiple moments of the engagement onto a single mast-cluttered composition. The freedom of brushwork here, intended only as a working study, anticipates his later, looser exhibited manner.

Boats tow a damaged sailing ship into the imaginary Dutch harbour of Port Ruysdael, Turner's homage to Jacob van Ruisdael. Painted late in his career, the canvas dissolves rigging and breaking sea into broad sweeps of grey, white and salt. It is one of several pictures in which Turner used invented Dutch place-names as a critical tribute.

Grenoble lies between the Drac and the distant snowfields of Mont Blanc, drawn during Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens reopened France. The 1802 Alpine campaign permanently reshaped his sense of geological scale. The picture's stretched horizontal format prefigures his later panoramic mountain views.

A small, intimate study of a figure asleep, head sunk against bedding, kept in Turner's studio and bequeathed to the nation. The looseness of touch is closer to the colour-beginnings of his late watercolours than to anything he exhibited. It belongs to a private corpus of figurative sketches now in the Tate's Turner Bequest.

A broad panoramic view across the flat Roman Campagna, a winding river threading through an ochre plain toward a hazy mountain horizon. The near-abstract handling — thinly applied paint dissolving land, water, and sky — shows Turner working from sketches made during his time in Rome in 1828. The work is part of the Turner Bequest, now held at Tate.

A long horizontal sweep of Egremont's deer park with Tillington's spire pinning the horizon. One of the studies made in the Petworth studio Egremont set aside for him, the picture is structured almost entirely by golden, grazing light.

A view across the Earl of Egremont's lake, painted under the patronage that gave Turner the run of Petworth. Cool morning haze dissolves park, water and sky into the unified atmosphere typical of his Sussex landscapes.
An unpeopled stretch of cliff and surf treated as a study in elemental force. The thinly brushed sea and broken light show Turner's late shorthand for shoreline weather.

A turbulent marine scene from Turner's early career: a crowded rowing boat with figures in colourful dress occupies the foreground, making toward a large vessel grounded or moored in rough seas beside a dark breakwater, with smaller sailing craft to the left. The agitated handling and composition owe a clear debt to the seventeenth-century Dutch marine tradition. Dated 1798 and part of the Turner Bequest at Tate.

Sails crowd the Solent off East Cowes, where Turner stayed with the architect John Nash during the 1827 Royal Yacht Club regatta. The picture belongs to a series of studies generated by that summer visit.

An oil sketch on canvas worked up while Turner was Nash's guest at East Cowes Castle. The yachts beating against the wind would be reorganised into the finished regatta picture exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1828.

A second oil sketch from the East Cowes regatta campaign, broadly laid in to test the disposition of the racing yachts. Turner used these large studies almost as colour rehearsals before committing to a finished exhibition picture.

Form is reduced to bands of gold, rose and slate water in a late, near-abstract evocation of dusk. Pictures of this kind, left in his studio at his death, anticipate by half a century the dissolutions of Impressionism.

An English river caught at the end of the day, with rushes and a low bank silhouetted against burning sky. The work belongs to the loose Thames oil sketches Turner made from his boat around Walton and Windsor.

Teignmouth Harbour at sunset: two cattle and a wading figure occupy the shallow foreground, while a large ship's timber frame under construction dominates the right bank. In the middle distance the estuary opens toward the town, its masts and buildings dissolved in golden haze. Painted in 1812, the work is now at Petworth House in the care of the National Trust.

A close-quarters view of Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar, taken from the mizen-shrouds rather than the more conventional broadside vantage. Turner had boarded Victory on her return to the Medway and used the sketches he made there to anchor the smoke-wreathed scene.

Estuary shipping gathers where Thames and Medway meet, painted in the tradition of seventeenth-century Dutch sea pieces. Heavy cloud and a low horizon underline Turner's command of English coastal weather.

Night falls on the battlefield as women search the heaped dead by torchlight, three years after the engagement. Turner had walked the ground himself; the picture quotes Byron's Childe Harold and refuses any patriotic triumph.

A poet implores his muse in a cramped attic, an unusually literary genre subject for Turner. Exhibited at the Royal Academy with verses of his own composition, it shows him courting the hierarchy of history painting.

A vertiginous Alpine gorge on the St Gotthard road, with a narrow stone path clinging to the cliff face and cloud billowing through the chasm below. Turner painted the scene following his first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens reopened Europe in 1802, completing the oil between 1803 and 1804. The composition, in which sheer scale becomes the subject, is now held by Birmingham Museums Trust.

Storm and divine wrath sweep over a darkened Egyptian city as the firstborn die. An early bid for the prestige of Old Master history painting, the picture leans openly on Poussin's biblical compositions.

A quiet reach of the upper Thames painted from the boat Turner had fitted out as a floating studio. The fluid handling belongs to the Thames oil sketches in which he loosened his manner before the public ever saw it.

Most of the panel is given over to evening sky, with foliage massed at the lower edge and Guildford Castle barely indicated. The composition foreshadows Turner's later willingness to let weather dominate topography.

The Doge's Palace and the Riva degli Schiavoni shimmer through lagoon light in a late Venetian view. By his third trip to Venice in 1840 Turner was treating the city's stones as little more than coloured vapour.

The cliff-set Umbrian town floats above its golden plain in a picture begun and finished during Turner's second Roman stay. Exhibited at his studio on the Quattro Fontane, it greeted Italian visitors as a deliberate answer to Claude.
A pure marine, the canvas is given entirely to a churning sea raked by spray. Turner reportedly had himself lashed to a mast in storms; the picture's loose, scumbled paint claims that immediacy.
Cattle wade in the slow water below a country weir in one of Turner's pastoral Thames-valley sketches. The thin oil handling and silvery palette recall his admiration for Cuyp.

A screen of willows leans over still water in an unforced piece of Thames-side observation. It belongs to the group of Thames oil sketches on canvas that Turner kept in his studio rather than exhibiting; it entered the nation with the Turner Bequest in 1856.

The royal castle rides above the river on its chalk bluff, painted from Turner's boat on one of his summer Thames campaigns. Sky and water are set down in long, wet sweeps that leave the paint visibly mobile.

Fishermen drag a boat up onto a windswept beach beneath a heavy, scudding sky. Part of the Iveagh Bequest at Kenwood, the picture sits in Turner's lifelong dialogue with seventeenth-century Dutch marine painters such as van de Velde and Cuyp. Salt spray, wet sand and weather become as much the subject as the labour.

Agrippina steps ashore at Brundisium carrying the urn of her murdered husband Germanicus before a stage-set of imperial architecture. Conceived as the Ancient half of a paired Royal Academy exhibit, the canvas is built on Claudean perspective dissolved in Turner's own sun-soaked atmosphere.

The ruined Forum, then still grazed and known as the Campo Vaccino, glows under a luminous Roman evening. Painted as a pendant to Ancient Rome, it gave Turner one of his last great meditations on the city's layered time.

The Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp puts his ship about in heavy weather, a subject Turner returned to repeatedly in his last decade. The picture extends his admiration for the seventeenth-century Dutch marine tradition into a high-key, Romantic key.

The shattered piers of Caligula's pleasure-bridge at Baiae rise above a glassy bay in a moralised view of imperial vanity. Turner exhibited it at the Royal Academy with verses from his own Fallacies of Hope.

A tall-masted barge drifts past the island cemetery of San Michele in the Venetian lagoon. Painted alongside its Royal Academy companion the Dogano, the work converts a place of burial into a study of pearled morning light.

An early topographical watercolour from Turner's Cambridge tour, viewing Clare Hall and the soaring Perpendicular pinnacles of King's College Chapel across the Cam. A stone bridge arches over the river in the foreground, and the architecture is rendered with careful precision. Dated 1793, the sheet is now in the collection of the Yale Center for British Art.

A pastoral prospect along the Thames at Cliveden in Buckinghamshire, with cattle near the water's edge and trees softening the middle distance. Turner treats the open landscape with a warm, suffused light that dissolves firm outlines into haze. Painted in 1807, the oil sketch is held at Tate Britain (N01180).

An intensely abstracted figure — skeletal and monstrous, its claw-like hand outstretched — emerges from a vortex of dark ochre and deep red pigment against pale, vaporous ground. The near-formless handling makes this one of Turner's most extreme explorations of sublime terror and dissolution of form. Dated to circa 1825, the canvas is held at Tate Britain (National Gallery collection, N05504).

A glassy Dutch harbour bathed in golden morning light, paying open homage to Aelbert Cuyp, whose paintings Turner studied on his 1817 Low Countries tour. The becalmed packet boat anchors a luminous sky that occupies more than half the canvas.

Westminster's old Palace blazes against the night sky on 16 October 1834, watched by a crowd massed on the Thames. Turner sketched the fire from a hired boat and produced two oil versions, of which this is the Philadelphia canvas. The conflagration let him paint exactly the kind of incandescent yellow-and-red sky he had been pursuing for decades.

The thundering Rheinfall in Switzerland, its spray rising into a churning sky encountered on Turner's first Continental tour after the Peace of Amiens. The painting marks his early engagement with the Alpine sublime that would shape his Romantic vocabulary.

Fishing boats with furled sails crowd a working harbour foreshore beside stone cottages, rendered in monochrome wash with pen-like linear strokes. The sheet dates to circa 1790, placing it among Turner's earliest topographical studies produced in the picturesque watercolour tradition. It is held at the Yale Center for British Art.

Turner's first oil exhibited at the Royal Academy, depicting a fishing boat tossed beneath a cold moon off the Needles, Isle of Wight. The contrast of silver lunar light and orange lantern glow announces a lifelong preoccupation with luminous opposition.

Sailing vessels move through a choppy estuary beneath a luminous amber sky, the horizon loaded with incoming weather. The setting is the Blythe-Sand off the Suffolk coast, not the Thames, as the title records. Painted in 1809 and now at Tate Britain (National Gallery collection), the work reflects Turner's sustained engagement with Dutch seventeenth-century marine painting.

Tyneside coal-heavers loading colliers under a full moon at Shields, painted as a pendant to a Venetian scene to contrast industrial north and southern lagoon. The torchlit smoke and silvered water typify Turner's late nocturnes.

Linlithgow Palace rises through a warm golden haze above a wooded landscape, with bathers in the foreground pool and figures resting on the bank. The oil painting, dated circa 1806, translates a motif Turner drew on his Scottish tours into a richly atmospheric composition. It is held at the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool.

A panoramic survey of the capital seen from the hill at Greenwich, with the Queen's House and Wren's Royal Hospital below and St Paul's hazed in coal-smoke distance. The painting belongs to a series celebrating the Thames as the artery of empire.

The ruined arches of Newark Priory on the River Wey in Surrey appear as a faint silhouette through riverside trees at dusk, the foreground occupied by moored barges — one glowing with an interior fire — and quietly reflective water. Dated between 1806 and 1807, the canvas is held at the Yale Center for British Art, and exemplifies Turner's picturesque treatment of Gothic ruins in the English landscape.

Norham Castle on the River Tweed dissolves into a luminous haze of pale yellow and blue, the sun a glowing disc in the upper half of the composition and the castle keep just barely legible as a dark blue mass. A cow wading in the foreground water is all that anchors the scene to the tangible world. Painted in 1845 and held at Tate (National Gallery collection), this late oil is among the most radical of Turner's near-abstract works.

A house portrait commissioned by the third Earl of Darlington, set in his County Durham deer park with a hunt in the foreground. Turner devotes the upper canvas to a churning, dramatic sky, signalling his shift from topography to Romantic landscape.

A large warship stands silhouetted against a glowing, haze-wrapped sun on the left, while a smaller vessel with an ochre sail and a crowded rowboat labour through the rough swell in the foreground, with the Kent shore and Sheerness faintly visible to the right. Painted in 1808, the canvas was exhibited at Turner's own gallery and is now held at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

Working vessels labouring in the Thames estuary chop, sails braced against a low, weather-laden sky. The painting belongs to Turner's productive run of estuary subjects answering his rivalry with the marine tradition of van de Velde.

A paddle-steamer engulfed by a vortex of snow, smoke and sea, exhibited with Turner's claim that he had been lashed to the mast to observe it. Critics dismissed the canvas as 'soapsuds and whitewash', but it remains his definitive statement on the elemental sublime.

Two figures rest on rocks beside a cascading woodland stream in this early watercolour by Turner, dated 1794. The lush, overhanging trees and tumbling water reflect his training in the British picturesque tradition. The work is held at the Yale Center for British Art.

An eyewitness response to the conflagration that destroyed the medieval Palace of Westminster, watched by crowds along the Thames. Turner sketched the blaze from a hired boat and translated it into pyrotechnic yellows and reds against the cool Westminster Bridge.

Fisherfolk sell and sort their catch on the broad sandy beach at Hastings, with sailing vessels riding the surf behind them. Turner painted this scene in 1810, a period when Hastings served as both a working fishing port and a fashionable resort. The canvas is held at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City.

A bustling Norman harbour bathed in unnaturally Italianate light, criticised at the Royal Academy for its sun-drenched palette. The painting forms part of Turner's continental port series following his post-war travels to France.

Survivors clinging to lifeboats amid mountainous green seas, the doomed vessel rolling beyond. Engraved by Charles Turner, this was the first of the artist's canvases reproduced as a mezzotint, spreading his fame as a painter of catastrophe.

A lateen-sailed fishing boat departing the lagoon at dawn, its painted sail catching pink Adriatic light. Drawn from Turner's third Venetian visit, the canvas was accompanied by lines from his unfinished poem warning of storms ahead.

A reconstructed view of the Doric temple on Aegina, imagined intact above the Aegean, painted from sketches supplied by an architect-traveller as Turner himself never visited Greece. The canvas answered the British vogue for Hellenic antiquity stoked by the Elgin Marbles.

Nelson's flagship shown in three rotated views entering Sheerness with the admiral's body aboard, after Turner sketched her at anchor. The triple study reflects his marine fascination and the national mourning that followed Trafalgar.

Turner depicted the stone arch of Tummel Bridge spanning a turbulent Highland river, with dramatic storm clouds gathering over the mountains behind, painted between 1802 and 1803 following his Scottish tour. Cottages and cattle animate the middle ground beneath a brooding, weather-laden sky. The work is held at the Yale Center for British Art.

A fantastical pairing of the water-nymph Undine, drawn from de la Motte Fouqué's novella, with the Neapolitan fisherman-rebel Masaniello. Painted at seventy-one, the canvas dissolves narrative into a swirl of aquatic colour typical of Turner's late square-format mythologies.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-wright-an-ir: A nocturnal interior of a Midlands forge, the white-hot bloom illuminating the ironworker's family. Wright was the painter of the early Industrial Revolution, treating bellows and tilt-hammers with the same chiaroscuro reverence Caravaggio gave to saints.
collection-of-beauty-joseph-wright-of-de: A tall lighthouse with its lantern ablaze stands beside the Italian coast, its glow competing with a full moon rising through clouds in a teal nocturnal sky. Wright of Derby, painted in 1789, here applies his characteristic study of competing artificial and natural light sources to an outdoor coastal scene. The work is held at Tate, London.

A silvered view of the Derbyshire valley of Dovedale under a full moon, its limestone crags and quiet river rendered in a cool, near-monochrome palette. Wright pursued nocturnes throughout his career, applying the dramatic chiaroscuro he developed for candlelit interiors to the open landscape.

An aged alchemist kneels before a glowing flask as phosphorus ignites in his laboratory, alluding to Hennig Brand's 1669 discovery. Wright stages the scene with the theatrical single-source illumination that defined his Enlightenment subjects, balancing scientific wonder against gothic shadow.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-1915-natu: A guitar, wine bottle, grapes, and newspaper are arranged on a checked tablecloth in this oil on canvas by Juan Gris, painted in Paris in March 1915. The interlocking Cubist planes fragment and reassemble each object across the picture surface. The work entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art with the Leonard A. Lauder Cubist Collection in 2014.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-glass-and: A drinking glass and a checkerboard are resolved into interlocking geometric planes of green, terracotta, and cream in this Synthetic Cubist panel by Juan Gris, painted around 1917. The composition exemplifies Gris's method of beginning with abstract shapes and arriving at recognisable objects, rather than the reverse. The work is held at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-jose-vict: A table holding a Médoc bottle, fruit dish, glass and a copy of Le Journal stands before a window looking onto a Montmartre balustrade and the trees of Place Ravignan. Gris painted the 115-centimetre canvas in 1915 from his studio in the Bateau-Lavoir; it is held by the Philadelphia Museum of Art and counts among his Synthetic Cubist breakthroughs.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-portrait-: A Cubist portrait of Picasso seated with a palette, his face and jacket broken into pale blue and ochre facets. Painted in 1912 and now at the Art Institute of Chicago, Gris inscribed the canvas 'Hommage à Pablo Picasso', framing his own analytic style as both tribute and challenge to the older master.
collection-of-beauty-juan-gris-still-lif: A mandolin, fruit dish, and folded newspaper arranged on a patterned tablecloth in flat, interlocking planes of muted blue, ochre, and white. Painted in 1919, the canvas belongs to Gris's Synthetic Cubist maturity, when he composed by deduction from geometric scaffolds before adding the objects rather than fragmenting them in.
collection-of-beauty-juan-legua-1911-jua: A seated man in dark suit and stiff collar tilts back in his chair, face splintered into a small grid of facets while the body remains legible. Painted in 1911 at 55 by 46 cm, the canvas is one of Gris's earliest Cubist portraits, the sitter a Spanish journalist living in Paris who likely used Juan Legua as a pen name. It is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-judge-martin-howard: Judge Martin Howard sits in a green upholstered chair wearing the scarlet and gold robes of a colonial jurist, a powdered wig framing his steady gaze. A bound volume rests at his side. Copley's 1767 portrait, measuring 125.7 by 101 cm, is held by the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-judische-hochzeit-i: A woman dances before a crowd of seated guests in a whitewashed Moroccan interior, musicians playing at the centre of the room while onlookers press in from every side. Delacroix painted this scene of a Sephardi Jewish wedding in 1839, drawing on sketches made during his 1832 North African journey with the Comte de Mornay and translating direct observation into a Romantic study of colour and custom.
collection-of-beauty-judit-decapitando-a: The biblical heroine and her maidservant pin the Assyrian general to his bed, blade drawn across his throat as blood spurts onto the linen. Gentileschi heightens the Caravaggesque tenebrism with a tightly compressed composition and the unflinching, muscular cooperation of the two women.
collection-of-beauty-judith-and-her-maid: By candlelight Judith stands and turns, her hand raised near the flame, while Abra crouches at her feet tending to the severed head of Holofernes. A late work from Gentileschi's Naples period, dated circa 1645–1650, the painting is held at the Museo di Capodimonte and revisits the artist's signature subject in a quieter, nocturnal register, the single candle gilding the women's drapery against deep shadow.
collection-of-beauty-jupiter-and-antiope: The Haarlem master, better known as a virtuoso engraver, treats the mythological seduction with a sculptural nude and the warm flesh tones he absorbed from his late Italian journey. Jupiter approaches in satyr disguise, the composition borrowed from Northern Mannerist prints Goltzius himself had popularised across Europe.
collection-of-beauty-jupiter-and-juno-an: A section of Annibale Carracci's fresco decoration of the Farnese Gallery in Rome, painted for Cardinal Odoardo Farnese and completed around 1602. The panel shows Juno, half-draped, coming to Jupiter on his couch, his eagle gripping a thunderbolt at the bedside and her peacock looking on; the scene is framed like an easel picture within an illusionistic surround of nude youths and feigned stone atlantes. The cycle of the Loves of the Gods made the gallery one of the founding monuments of Baroque ceiling painting.
collection-of-beauty-kagesue-takatsuna-a: Across a three-sheet triptych, armoured samurai on horseback and on foot surge through the rapids of the Uji River in their celebrated race to lead the charge during the Genpei War. Kuniyoshi fills each panel with churning waves and straining figures, exemplifying the warrior-print genre (musha-e) he revived in the late Edo period. The work dates to 1849 and is held at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-kaigetsudo-ando-sta: A Yoshiwara courtesan stands alone in a richly patterned kimono, hip cocked in the languid S-curve that became the workshop's hallmark. As founder of the Kaigetsudō school, Ando concentrated entirely on monumental beauties, painted in fluid ink with broad swathes of color and gold on paper.
collection-of-beauty-kajikazawa-in-kai-p: Two fishermen work a line from a jagged green outcrop while Mount Fuji rises pale and triangular beyond the blue surf. The spare composition reduces landscape to interlocking geometric forms printed in the imported Prussian blue (bero-ai) that defines the series. First published around 1830, this is the forty-fifth design in Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, one of the nine additional views added to the original thirty-six.
collection-of-beauty-kalisz-rubens: Christ's body is lowered from the cross in a diagonal cascade of pale flesh and white shroud, supported by mourning saints. Rubens returned to this Counter-Reformation subject repeatedly after his Antwerp Cathedral altarpiece, modelling the dead Christ on classical sculpture studied during his years in Rome.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1915: A black-and-white cow grazes near a coastal shoreline, sailboats visible on the water behind it, the scene rendered in simplified flat planes of colour. This 1915 woodblock print by Kanae Yamamoto is held at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; Yamamoto was a pioneer of the creative-print movement in Japan, advocating that artists design, carve, and print their own blocks.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1926: A view at the foot of Mount Tokkō in oils, painted after Yamamoto's return from Europe where he absorbed Post-Impressionist palette and brushwork. Better remembered for woodblock prints, he pursued painting alongside his advocacy for the children's free-drawing and farmers' art movements in interwar Japan.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-1938: An oil painting of Mount Fuji seen from Kami-Ide, a village at the foot of the mountain, painted by Yamamoto Kanae in 1938. The snow-streaked cone rises under drifting clouds beyond a foreground of plowed fields and autumn-red trees. Yamamoto, a pioneer of the sosaku-hanga creative print movement, devoted much of his later career to oil painting; the work is held by the Kanae Yamamoto museum in Ueda, Nagano.
collection-of-beauty-kanae-yamamoto-dutc: A color woodcut by Yamamoto Kanae of a girl in Dutch folk dress standing on a sandy path before a flat river landscape of fields, trees and a distant cottage, the scene built from broad, simplified planes of green and ochre. Yamamoto, the founding figure of Japan's sosaku-hanga movement of self-carved, self-printed artist's prints, took up European subjects of this kind in connection with his years of study in Europe from 1912 to 1916. The print is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-kannon-riding-a-dra: The Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion rides a coiling dragon through cloudbanks, the figure modelled with the volumetric solidity of European academic painting. A Munich-trained pioneer of yōga (Western-style oil painting), Harada provoked debate by giving a Japanese religious subject the visual language of Counter-Reformation altarpieces.
collection-of-beauty-kano-eitoku-rakuchu: A panoramic bird's-eye survey of Kyoto in and around the capital, with thousands of tiny figures threading temples, markets and noble compounds amid gilded clouds. Eitoku codified the rakuchū rakugai zu format for the Momoyama elite; this pair was reportedly given by Oda Nobunaga to Uesugi Kenshin.
collection-of-beauty-kano-hideyori-maple: Groups of elegantly dressed figures gather beneath flame-red maples and beside a stream bridged by a stone arch, in a composition that spans the full width of a six-panel folding screen. Snow-capped ground in the upper left panel and flying cranes signal the transition of seasons across the composition. Attributed to Kanō Hideyori and dated to the sixteenth century, it is one of the earliest surviving Japanese genre paintings and is held at the Tokyo National Museum.
collection-of-beauty-kano-sansetsu-froli: Against an expansive gold ground, the gnarled, almost calligraphic branches of a flowering plum extend across the panels while birds perch among the blossoms; a large pine at the right shelters a bird of prey on a rocky outcrop. Kanō Sansetsu (1589–1651), the prominent Kyoto Kanō master, stylises nature into bold rhythmic forms that push the school's bird-and-flower repertoire toward a distinctive early-Edo elegance. Dated 1631, the work is held at Myōshin-ji Temple, Kyoto.
collection-of-beauty-karl-brullov-the-la: Citizens of Pompeii stumble through the streets as columns crack, lightning splits the sky and ash falls across the doomed city under Vesuvius. Painted in 1830-33 in Rome on commission from Count Anatoly Demidov, the vast canvas, 4.6 by 6.5 metres, won the gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1834 and now belongs to the State Russian Museum.
collection-of-beauty-karl-bryullov-bryul: Bathsheba, nude, reclines in a rocky garden setting as a dark-skinned child attends her, the two figures surrounded by lush foliage. Bryullov treats the biblical subject with the polished academic technique and warm flesh tones characteristic of his mature style. The canvas, dated 1832, remained unfinished; it is titled Bathsheba and was painted during the artist's years in Italy.
collection-of-beauty-karl-friedrich-abel: Carl Friedrich Abel is shown three-quarter length, holding his viola da gamba in one hand and its bow in the other, his expression easy and confident. Gainsborough, a close friend of the German-born composer and an amateur viol player himself, painted this portrait in 1765, the year the celebrated Bach-Abel concert series began in London. The instrument dominates the composition, underscoring Abel's renown as the foremost viola da gamba virtuoso of the era.
collection-of-beauty-karl-friedrich-schi: An allegorical tribute to the Prussian industrial reformer Peter Beuth, shown astride Pegasus as he soars over a panorama of human civilisation and progress. The composition fuses Romantic landscape with Enlightenment allegory, celebrating Beuth's role in the modernisation of the Prussian state.

An imagined Greek polis spreads along a rocky promontory, temples and stoa stacked up the slope toward a fortified acropolis. Schinkel painted the canvas in Berlin around 1806, years before his architectural career began, channelling his early training as a stage and panorama painter into archaeological reverie.

A grove of mature deciduous trees crowns a rounded hill, their canopies opening toward a luminous sky that suggests the pale light of morning. A few small figures linger at the hill's foot to the right, giving scale to the landscape without competing with the tranquil mood. Schinkel painted this canvas in 1813; titled Morning, it is held at the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin.

The Queen of the Night appears on a crescent moon beneath a vast hemispherical vault of stars, in Karl Friedrich Schinkel's set design for Mozart's Die Zauberflote. The gouache on paper, about 46 by 61 centimetres, was made around 1815 for the production staged at the Berlin Royal Opera in 1816 and is held in the Kupferstichkabinett of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. The starry hall became the most reproduced of Schinkel's stage designs and one of the most famous opera sets of the nineteenth century.

A spired Gothic cathedral rises atop a cliff above the sea, more vision than topography. The motif - architecture as sacred outcropping - belongs to the shared Romantic imagination of Schinkel and Friedrich, where the medieval church stands in for a yearned-for unity of faith, nation and landscape.

A vast Gothic cathedral towers over a riverside town at sunset, its silhouette dwarfing the mortal traffic on the quay. The motif of the imagined medieval Dom appealed to Romantic painters as both architectural dream and patriotic emblem after the Napoleonic Wars.

A fortified castle commands the bend of a broad river under a luminous, theatrical sky. The composition treats architecture scenographically, the way Schinkel did in his stage designs for Berlin, while the contemplative figures and burnished light belong to the wider Romantic landscape current.

A natural rock arch frames a distant view, conceived as the Nordic pendant to a sunlit Italian landscape. The pairing stages a Romantic dialogue between the sublime German wilderness and the classical south, a polarity that runs through the era's painting and through Schinkel's own architectural imagination.
collection-of-beauty-karl-joseph-stieler: The young daughter of a Greek War of Independence hero is shown in embroidered Greek costume, her dark hair loose beneath a tasselled cap. Stieler painted the portrait for Ludwig I of Bavaria's Schönheitengalerie, the Munich gallery of beauties in which the king collected idealised female likenesses.
collection-of-beauty-karolina-lizius: Karolina Lizius (1820–1872) gazes outward in a dark off-shoulder velvet gown against a neutral brown ground, painted by Joseph Karl Stieler in 1841. Stieler served as court painter in Munich and contributed numerous portraits to Ludwig I's Schönheitengalerie at Nymphenburg Palace. The smooth finish, restrained palette, and composed psychology are characteristic of his Biedermeier portrait formula.
collection-of-beauty-katsushika-hokusai-: Pilgrims bathe in the falls at Ōyama, where Rōben is said to have purified himself before founding the mountain's temple. From A Tour of the Waterfalls of the Provinces, Hokusai abstracts cascading water into ribbons of stylised line, treating each fall as a graphic emblem of place.

Yoshitsune's retainers wash their horses beneath the Yoshino falls, the cascade splitting into braided ribbons of pale paper. The plate from the Waterfalls series fuses warrior legend with landscape, characteristic of how Hokusai layered narrative into his late topographical print sets.

The Kirifuri ("falling mist") cascade on Mount Kurokami breaks into numerous white tendrils against dark cliffs, with tiny travellers gazing up from below. From Hokusai's Waterfalls series (c. 1833), the composition treats the sacred fall as a near-abstract decorative pattern, water rendered as flat stylised line rather than naturalistic spray.

Travellers and packhorses pause on the Kisokaidō highway beside the Ono falls, dwarfed by a smooth blue sheet of water. From the Tour of the Waterfalls, the print pairs Hokusai's stylised, almost geometric treatment of cascades with the everyday traffic of one of Edo Japan's great post roads.

The Amida Falls in the Far Reaches of the Kisokaidō Road depicts a great cascade falling from a circular pool — said to resemble the head of the Buddha Amida — above a group of seated figures in a lush mountain setting. The print belongs to Hokusai's Waterfalls series (c. 1833), now in the British Museum, in which each fall is treated as a near-abstract graphic emblem combining sweeping calligraphic line with flat planes of colour.

Cherry-blossom viewers gather on the bluff at Goten-yama overlooking Edo Bay, with Mount Fuji a faint cone on the horizon. Part of the Thirty-six Views, the print binds a popular hanami spot to the sacred mountain through Hokusai's careful balancing of human ritual and distant geology.

A canary alights on a bowed peony stem against a deep blue sky, accompanied by a haiku. From Hokusai's Large Flowers series for the publisher Eijudō, the print compresses the kachō-e bird-and-flower tradition into a tight diagonal, exploiting the new Prussian blue pigment for luminous backgrounds.

A polychrome woodblock print from Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published around 1830-32, known as Rainstorm Beneath the Summit (Sanka haku-u). While the peak of Fuji stands clear against drifting clouds, a storm breaks over the lower slopes and a jagged bolt of red lightning flashes across the darkened base of the mountain. The design is the stormy counterpart to the serene Fine Wind, Clear Morning, and ranks with the Great Wave among the most celebrated images of the series.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-ebisu-11: A snow-covered harbour at night, with buildings and their reflections spread across still water as flakes fall thickly from a dark sky. The print depicts the Port of Ebisu on Sado Island, published in December 1921 as part of Kawase Hasui's Souvenirs of Travel II series, and exemplifies the shin-hanga tradition's fusion of Edo woodblock technique with a modern sensitivity to atmospheric light and season.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-hasui-1931-s: Thick snow falls through a darkening sky onto a boat landing at Mukojima, on the bank of Tokyo's Sumida River: moored boats lie blanketed in white, a stilt-built boathouse glows from within, and a lone ferryman crosses the still water. The 1931 color woodblock print shows Hasui's shin-hanga manner at its most atmospheric, using graded blues and untouched white paper to carry the weight of the snowfall. Snow scenes such as this became the works for which he is best remembered.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-hasui-no-ser: Kawase Hasui's final print design, published in 1957, the year of his death. Snow-covered stone steps climb between snow-laden cedars toward the hall sheltering the Konjikido, the famed Golden Hall of Chuson-ji temple at Hiraizumi, while a lone figure ascends under an umbrella through the falling snow. The design is traditionally honored as the artist's zeppitsu, or last work.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-tenno-ji-27: A solitary figure with an umbrella stands before the multi-storeyed pagoda and snow-laden roofs of the ancient Shitennō-ji temple in Osaka. Published in 1927 as part of Kawase Hasui's Souvenirs of Travel III series, the print applies the shin-hanga woodblock tradition to a wintry scene, conveying the hush of falling snow through quiet tonal contrast.
collection-of-beauty-kawase-zojoji: View of the Tokugawa mortuary temple Zōjō-ji at Shiba, from the Twenty Views of Tokyo series. A solitary figure shelters under a paper umbrella as snow falls against the vermilion gate, a hallmark of Kawase's quiet, weather-soaked urban landscapes.
collection-of-beauty-kazimir-malevich-su: Coloured rectangles and bars float on a white field, freed from any object reference. Malevich exhibited his first Suprematist canvases at the Last Futurist Exhibition 0,10 in Petrograd on 19 December 1915, declaring painting's right to non-objective form; he hung the Black Square in the corner traditionally reserved for the household icon.
collection-of-beauty-keisai-eisen-wasser: A coiling water dragon, or mizuchi, from a late ukiyo-e series devoted to birds, beasts, insects and fish. Eisen, better known for bijin-ga prints of Edo women, here adapts the colour woodblock to a more decorative, naturalist mode in keeping with kacho-e tradition.
collection-of-beauty-kenko-shokei-shosho: Ink-painting from the Zen monk-painter's interpretation of the Eight Views of Xiao and Xiang, the canonical Chinese landscape suite of distant temples, mist and migrating geese. Shōkei trained in Kamakura under Geiami and brought a flecked, slightly nervous brush to the Muromachi suiboku tradition.
collection-of-beauty-khnopff-listening-t: A figure in black sits in a richly furnished interior, face buried in her hand, absorbed in music heard from the piano visible at the left edge of the composition. Fernand Khnopff painted this interior scene in 1883, capturing inwardness and emotional withdrawal with his characteristic muted palette and near-photographic stillness — hallmarks of his founding role in Belgian Symbolism.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-chuseon: Kim Hongdo's 1805 illustration of Ouyang Xiu's prose poem on the sounds of autumn presents a horizontal scroll pairing extensive calligraphic text on the left with a landscape at right — bare trees, a pavilion, and misty mountains rendered in delicate ink wash. Painted late in his career as Joseon Korea's leading court painter, the work fuses Chinese literary subject matter with Hongdo's characteristic atmospheric ink technique.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-feast-f: Officials and attendants are gathered in an open courtyard before the Pyongyang governor's pavilion, with performers arranged in the forecourt below the dais. The panoramic composition records the banquet in the descriptive mode of late Joseon court documentary painting. This is the first of a three-part series by Kim Hong-do depicting the feast.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-hwaseon: A scene from the Eight Views of Hwaseong attributed to Kim Hong-do, the fortress wall snaking along a ridge toward a hilltop command pavilion above the new royal city of Suwon. As court painter to King Jeongjo, Kim documented the fortress completed in 1796 in the ink-and-light-colour idiom of late Joseon topographic painting.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-kyujang: Kim Hong-do's view of Kyujanggak records the royal library founded on the grounds of Changdeokgung by King Jeongjo in 1776. The painting shows the complex of buildings nestled among trees against a mountainous backdrop, rendered in the bird's-eye topographical mode characteristic of Joseon court records. Kim Hong-do served as a designated court painter to King Jeongjo.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-samgong: A long horizontal handscroll in ink and colour on silk, Samgongbulhwando contrasts the freedom of nature with the burdens of office through scenes of recluses and scholars in mountain retreats. Kim Hong-do painted the scroll in 1801, measuring 133.7 by 418.4 cm and now held by the Leeum Samsung Museum of Art in Seoul.
collection-of-beauty-kim-hong-do-songhac: A solitary figure sits slumped beneath a towering gnarled pine, rendered in fluid ink brushwork on a pale ground. Kim Hong-do's composition, titled 'Drunken Monk under a Pine Tree' and dating to around 1800, merges genre humour with the literati ideal of the carefree sage. Calligraphic inscriptions and red seals occupy the upper right of the composition.
collection-of-beauty-king-lear-and-corde: The mad Lear, crowned in wildflowers, is reunited with the kneeling Cordelia at the French camp in Act IV, scene 7 of Shakespeare's tragedy. West painted the canvas in 1793 for John Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery; it now belongs to the Folger Shakespeare Library.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-1913-stree: Two cocottes in feathered hats and fur stoles stride down a Berlin pavement, a crowd of dark-suited men pressing past on either side. Oil on canvas, 120.6 x 91 cm, the picture belongs to Kirchner's Berlin Strassenbilder cycle of 1913-15 and is held by the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-farbentanz: Three nude female figures dance against a dark ground, their bodies rendered in flat planes of blue, yellow, and red separated by bold contour lines. Kirchner's Farbentanz (Colour Dance) belongs to his late period, when he reduced the figure to simplified, interlocking colour fields. Sunflowers at the base and circular forms above frame the composition in a decorative vertical format.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-sand-hills: Kirchner renders the sand hills near the Berlin suburb of Grünau in broad strokes of orange and ochre, with dark evergreen trees in the foreground and a pink-red sky above. The canvas, dated 1913, applies the chromatic intensity of Brücke Expressionism to a local landscape subject. A small tower or church is visible on the distant ridge.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-self-portr: Kirchner stands in his studio in army uniform with the bloodied stump of an amputated right hand, a nude model behind him in sickly yellow tones. The 1915 oil at the Allen Memorial Art Museum, Oberlin, references his service in the 75th Field Artillery Regiment and the breakdown that brought a provisional discharge; it was later included in the Nazi Entartete Kunst exhibition of 1937.
collection-of-beauty-kirchner-zwei-fraue: Two women in a colourful interior attend to a white washbasin, one in a pink coat bending her hands toward the water while the other in green looks on. Kirchner's bold use of pink and green complements, set against a warm red-orange ground, gives the domestic scene the visual tension of his Berlin period. The canvas is dated 1913 and bears the title Two Women with a Washbasin.
collection-of-beauty-kirgizskie-kibitki-: Kyrgyz felt tents (kibitki) pitched along the Chu river, which marks the border between present-day Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Vereshchagin recorded the encampment on his Central Asian travels of 1869 to 1870, the source material for his Turkestan series.
collection-of-beauty-kisokaido14-itahana: Snow-laden pine trees line the road at Itahana, the fourteenth station on the Kisokaidō, as travellers make their way through a deep winter landscape. The print belongs to the celebrated Sixty-Nine Stations of the Kisokaidō series; the artist recorded in the record is Keisai Eisen. A warm pink band at the horizon brightens the otherwise white and grey composition.
