collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-19-k: A scene of the towering Hōrai Rock rising from the Kiso River, drawn from Hasui's Souvenirs of Travel III. The print balances the cliff's bulk against soft atmospheric washes, a hallmark of the shin-hanga revival of traditional landscape woodblock.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-20-k: A nocturne depicting a quiet street in Kamezaki, Owari Province, with a large tree, a stone wall, and the warm glow of a lit window glimpsed through deep blue darkness. Kawase Hasui's woodblock print, from the series Souvenirs of Travel III, was published in 1928 and demonstrates the artist's skill in evoking atmosphere through dense, layered colour fields.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-22-k: Tall pines frame a wide bay view at Nishi Park in Fukuoka, with small islands and sailing boats on the calm water below a pink and blue sky. Kawase Hasui's woodblock print, from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (1928), uses the vertical rhythm of the pine trunks to draw the eye across an open coastal panorama.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-23-k: Moored boats rest in a Beppu harbour at dawn, their reflections held in still water beneath a crescent moon and a warm band of colour at the horizon. Tall hills press against the sky behind them. From the series Souvenirs of Travel III, the print demonstrates Hasui's mastery of bokashi gradation to render the cool, transitional light of early morning.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-25-k: From the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō, this print follows the Takinogawa River as it winds through suburban greenery. Hasui captures a quieter periphery of the modernizing capital, layering subtle woodblock washes for foliage and reflected water.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-26-k: A solitary figure with an umbrella picks their way along a rain-slicked path beside a large bare tree, with softly lit buildings and distant mountains receding into a dark, wet night. There is no coastal view; Hasui locates the scene in Beppu's streets rather than at the shore. From the series Souvenirs of Travel III (1929), the sheet uses bokashi to convey the deep-blue chill of a rainy evening.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-31-k: Part of Twenty Views of Tōkyō, the print shows the moon hanging over the rural fringes of Magome. Hasui builds the night scene from layered indigo blocks and a single luminous disc, demonstrating shin-hanga's debt to classical Edo landscape traditions.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586549-40-k: A shin-hanga woodblock print by Kawase Hasui of Ryusen-ji, popularly known as the Meguro Fudo temple, in Tokyo. Seen from beside the vermilion main hall, a woman in kimono pauses at the entrance while blossoms show beyond the gate roofs and dappled light falls across the stone steps and lanterns of the precinct. The print was published in 1931; this impression is preserved in the National Diet Library, Tokyo.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586550-07-k: A view of the Ōmori coast on Tokyo Bay, drawn from Twenty Views of Tōkyō. Hasui registers the meeting of urban edge and water in soft, overcast tones, the shin-hanga answer to Hokusai and Hiroshige's earlier capital views.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586550-50-k: A colour woodblock print by Kawase Hasui from a print collection published by Watanabe Shōzaburō's print shop in 1935 (Shōwa 10). Hasui's shin-hanga landscapes pair traditional ukiyo-e craftsmanship with naturalistic light and atmosphere, and this sheet is preserved in the National Diet Library's digital collection.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586550-58-k: A colour woodblock print by Kawase Hasui, issued in 1935 (Shōwa 10) through the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō as part of a collected print album. Like the rest of Hasui's shin-hanga output, it renders an atmospheric Japanese landscape with carved-block colour gradations; the copy digitised here belongs to the National Diet Library.
collection-of-beauty-ndl-dc-2586550-74-k: A colour woodblock print by Kawase Hasui from an album published by the Watanabe print shop in 1935 (Shōwa 10). Hasui, a central figure of the shin-hanga revival, supplied the watercolour design while Watanabe's carvers and printers produced the blocks; the impression shown is held by the National Diet Library.
collection-of-beauty-neapolitan-woman-18: A young Neapolitan woman sits turned away from the viewer, her elbow resting on a table and her chin supported on one hand, gazing downward in reverie. Repin renders her white lace-trimmed blouse and dark hair with direct, energetic brushwork characteristic of his Realist practice. The canvas, signed and dated Naples 1894, records a study made during the artist's travels in southern Italy.
collection-of-beauty-negro-boy-by-l-baks: Costume study of a boy attendant, drawn in pencil, watercolour and silver paint on laid paper, 29 by 15.5 centimetres. The 1910 sheet is held by the MAGMA collection and belongs to Bakst's high Ballets Russes period, when his orientalist costume designs for Schéhérazade and Cléopâtre were reshaping European stage design.
collection-of-beauty-nesterov-florensky-: A double portrait of theologians Pavel Florensky and Sergei Bulgakov walking in conversation through a quiet wooded landscape. Nesterov's pared composition and contemplative palette frame the encounter as an icon of Russian religious philosophy on the eve of revolution.
collection-of-beauty-nesterovmv-narusi20: An expansive procession of Russian people - peasants, monks, soldiers and intelligentsia - moves across a northern landscape in search of spiritual truth. Nesterov treats his pre-revolutionary allegory in luminous, restrained colour, blending Symbolist mood with Orthodox iconographic gravity.
collection-of-beauty-newport-castle-by-j: The ruined towers of Newport Castle rise from the water's edge on the river Usk, with several sailing craft and a rowboat moored alongside the ancient stonework. Turner made this watercolour around 1796 from sketches taken during his 1795 South Wales tour, combining topographical accuracy with the atmospheric washes that mark his early career.
collection-of-beauty-newton-williamblake: Blake's monoprint shows the natural philosopher hunched naked on a sea-floor rock, drawing geometric figures with a compass. The image reads as a critique of pure reason: Newton, absorbed in measurement, becomes blind to the imaginative cosmos beyond his diagram.
collection-of-beauty-niccolopaganini: A pencil portrait of the virtuoso violinist captured during Ingres's years in Rome. The drawing distils Paganini to crisp contour and minimal shading, exemplifying the precise linear style for which Ingres's portrait sketches of musicians and patrons remain prized.
collection-of-beauty-nichiren-bezweert-d: The Buddhist reformer Nichiren stands in a pitching boat off Kakuda, calming the waves with the Lotus Sutra during his exile to Sado. Kuniyoshi's woodblock print sets red robes against churning blue surf in the dramatic warrior-print idiom of late Edo Utagawa school design.
collection-of-beauty-nicholas-ii-of-russ: Tsar Nicholas II stands in the full dress uniform of the 2nd Dragoons, Royal Scots Greys, his bearskin tucked under one arm. Serov painted the portrait in 1902 for the regiment, of which the Emperor served as Colonel-in-Chief from 1894 until 1918, and it now hangs in the Royal Scots Dragoon Guards Museum in Edinburgh.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-de-largilli: Charles Le Brun is shown seated in an armchair in his studio, richly dressed in red velvet robes, his hand raised toward a large canvas behind him depicting a battle or mythological scene with horses and figures. Sculpted casts and drawings fill the foreground, attesting to his role as director of the Académie royale and the Gobelins manufactory. Largillière painted this homage between 1683 and 1686, near the end of Le Brun's tenure as First Painter to Louis XIV.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-poussin-fre: An Italianate landscape with a shepherd and goats in the foreground, a horseman near a rustic shelter at left, and a fortified villa reflected in the still waters of a pool. Poussin organises the composition with characteristic measure, placing each figure and architectural element for balance rather than picturesque incident. The work, dated 1650–51, is held at the J. Paul Getty Museum.

Venus rises from the sea attended by tritons, nereids and putti in a Baroque treatment of the Anadyomene theme. Poussin organizes the marine cortege into a frieze-like rhythm, marrying Ovidian mythology with the cool classical structure he distilled from antique relief sculpture.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-poussin-l-e: Roman soldiers seize Sabine women in a violent twist of bodies, framed by classicizing architecture. Poussin choreographs the abduction as a sculptural relief of opposing diagonals, applying his rigorous study of antique gesture to the legendary founding episode of Rome.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-poussin-le-: A soldier raises his sword to strike a mother who clutches her infant on the ground, while a woman in blue recoils in anguish at right. Poussin condenses the Massacre of the Innocents into a single searing triangle of figures, achieving maximum dramatic force through the stark confrontation of perpetrator, victim, and witness. The painting, dated between 1625 and 1629, is held at the Musée Condé, Chantilly.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-poussin-sto: Storm clouds boil over a vast Italianate landscape as the Ovidian lovers meet their tragedy beside a reflective lake. Poussin uses meteorological drama to magnify human catastrophe, with sheet lightning, fleeing horses and bowed trees orchestrated into a single classical machine.
collection-of-beauty-nicolas-poussin-the: Mary ascends heavenward in a deep blue mantle, borne aloft by a cluster of putti amid billowing clouds framed by classical columns. Below, an empty stone sarcophagus draped in white linen marks her departed tomb, while additional putti scatter flowers. Painted around 1630, the work belongs to Poussin's early Roman period and reflects his engagement with Baroque altarpiece tradition.

Christ gestures upward as he delivers the keys to a kneeling Peter, with the remaining apostles gathered around them in an open landscape setting. From Poussin's second series of the Seven Sacraments, painted between circa 1636 and 1640, the composition translates the scriptural moment of institutional founding into the artist's mature, archaeologically informed figure style. The work is held at the Kimbell Art Museum.
collection-of-beauty-night-bivouac-of-gr: Soldiers of Napoleon's Grande Armée huddle around guttering fires in a frozen Russian field during the catastrophic 1812 retreat. Vereshchagin, a battle painter known for unsparing realism, treats the scene with documentary cold rather than heroic rhetoric.
collection-of-beauty-nighthawks-by-edwar: Edward Hopper's oil on canvas of 1942 shows a late-night diner on a deserted New York street corner, its three customers and white-jacketed counterman sealed behind curving plate glass under harsh electric light. The painting's air of urban solitude has made it the most famous image of Hopper's career and one of the most widely recognized works of American art. The Art Institute of Chicago bought it from the artist within months of its completion in 1942, and it remains there in the Friends of American Art Collection.
collection-of-beauty-nihon-fukei-senshu-: The cliffside Kannon Hall at Abuto perches on snow-covered rocks as a blizzard sweeps across the composition, with a small glimpse of the Inland Sea visible at lower left. The bold vertical framing and diagonal lines of falling snow are characteristic of Hasui's shin-hanga handling of winter subjects. The print was published in 1922 as part of the Selected Views of Japan series.

A coastal view of Goryō on the Amakusa islands of Kyushu, from Hasui's Selected Views of Japan. The shin-hanga design pairs distant headlands with quiet anchorage, demonstrating the careful balance of woodblock colour and reserve that defined Hasui's travel sheets.

Terraced green fields stretch across the foreground, with a path winding toward the sea where a sailing vessel is just visible, and Mount Onsengadake rises in blue-grey tones across the water. The print belongs to Hasui's Selected Views of Japan series, published in 1922, and is held at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. The work exemplifies his integration of agricultural landscape with distant topographical landmark.

Morning light over the hot-spring town of Beppu, rendered in the muted blues and greys typical of Hasui's shin-hanga manner. Part of the Selected Views of Japan series, the print balances atmospheric mist against the orderly geometry of harbor architecture.

A large Japanese sailing vessel with billowing white sails occupies the centre of the composition, its hull reflected in the calm blue water, with rocky headlands rising behind. The print belongs to Hasui's Selected Views of Japan series, published in 1923, and depicts the coastal waters off Iwafune in the former Bingo Province. Hasui's characteristic clear sky and precise colour planes give the scene an air of quiet confidence.

White cherry trees in full bloom fill the centre of the composition before a backdrop of steep green cliffs, with thatched farm buildings nestled along a stone wall and a lone figure standing beneath the blossom. Issued within the Selected Views of Japan series in 1923, the print captures the brief spring flowering at Kakize in former Bungo Province, combining precise woodblock colour with a strong sense of mountain enclosure.

A monumental stone lantern tower dominates the foreground, with a woman in kimono and a child pausing beside it as sailing boats drift on the calm sea beyond. Published in 1922 as part of Selected Views of Japan, the print depicts the famous stone tōrō at Hakozaki in former Chikuzen Province, near present-day Fukuoka. Hasui's flat colour planes and open horizon give the scene a calm, meditative quality.

Dark volcanic rock walls enclose a deep pool of vivid turquoise water, with blazing orange autumn foliage crowning the cliffs above. The print belongs to Hasui's Selected Views of Japan series, published in 1922, and depicts the Kayagafuchi pool within Chōmonkyō Gorge in Yamaguchi Prefecture. The intense contrast of warm foliage, dark stone, and jewel-coloured water is among the most striking compositions in the series.

A night rain scene at Tochinoki Hot Springs in former Higo Province, with glowing windows piercing the dark while rain streaks fall against mountain silhouettes. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the print exemplifies the shin-hanga movement's capacity for atmospheric nocturnal landscape.

A coastal hillside at Kabeshima in Hizen Province, with thatched farmhouses, tall conifers, and flowering shrubs overlooking a calm sea with a distant island on the horizon. Part of Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1922 and held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the print exemplifies his ability to find intimate pastoral beauty in regional scenery.

A stone arch bridge spans a clear stream in Kanahama, Hizen Province, with two figures visible on the parapet and scattered boulders in the water below. Issued in 1923 as part of Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū) and held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the composition demonstrates the shin-hanga interest in regional architectural and natural detail.

The fishing village of Kyodomari in former Hizen Province, set into a sheltered cove of the Kyushu coast. Hasui uses softly registered color blocks and a low horizon line, in keeping with the contemplative pace of the Selected Views of Japan series.

A harbour scene at dawn in Mihogaseki, Izumo Province, with a stone jetty, a lantern post, moored sailboats, and a green headland reflected in still water. From the Selected Views of Japan series (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1925, the print is characteristic of Kawase Hasui's shin-hanga attention to specific times of day and coastal atmosphere.

A three-storied red pagoda at Kiyomizu-dera in Yasugi, Izumo Province, stands against a dark night sky while snow falls and settles on surrounding trees and stone walls. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1926, the print illustrates the shin-hanga mastery of winter atmosphere and architectural silhouette.

A full moon hangs over a multi-arch stone bridge on the Kōtsuki River in Kagoshima, with bare trees, street lanterns, and moonlit water in a quiet nocturnal scene. From the Selected Views of Japan series (Nihon fūkei senshū), created by Kawase Hasui in 1922, the print exemplifies the shin-hanga tradition of atmospheric night landscape.

Sakurajima rises in warm reddish-orange tones above the calm bay opposite Kagoshima, with numerous sailing vessels dotting the water in the foreground. Published in 1922 as part of Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), the print captures the iconic volcanic landmark using the bold colour and refined perspective of the shin-hanga movement.

A nocturnal canal scene at Kasuga-machi in Kumamoto, with white-walled storehouses and their reflections in dark water under a deep blue sky. Published in 1922 as part of Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), the print exemplifies his shin-hanga mastery of atmospheric night scenes with luminous architectural forms.

Nezame-no-Toko, the celebrated stretch of pale, water-sculpted rock along the Kiso River in Nagano. Hasui treats the famous gorge with crisp green water and bleached stone, placing the site within his Selected Views of Japan.

A view of Suhara, a post-station village along the old Nakasendo highway in the Kiso valley. Within Selected Views of Japan, Hasui sets clustered roofs against the surrounding mountains in his customary flat planes of color.

Lake Ezu in Kumamoto under summer rain, with lush green reed beds in the foreground, a solitary figure in a small boat, and tree-covered islets receding toward distant rain-veiled mountains. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1923, the print captures the atmospheric breadth of the lake using the layered colour gradations of shin-hanga printmaking.

The stone embankment and moat of Kumamoto Castle are reflected in calm water, with a small bridge visible in the middle distance beneath a soft dawn sky. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1923, the print pairs the castle's distinctive stonework with a tranquil waterside view in characteristic shin-hanga landscape style.

Three women in kimono stand before the sweeping vermilion halls of the Daigokuden at Heian-jingū Shrine in Kyoto, with spring-green trees framing the lacquered architecture against a pale sky. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), the print pairs the shrine's grand Tang-inspired architecture with figures that lend human scale to the composition.

Evening along the Kamo River in Kyoto, with low riverside buildings silhouetted against a graded dusk sky. Part of Selected Views of Japan, the print pairs Hasui's interest in city water with the long twilight of a Kyoto summer.

Nonomiya Shrine in Kyoto's Sagano district at night in winter, with tall tree trunks framing a snow-covered shrine building and stone wall under a deep blue starlit sky. From Kawase Hasui's Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), published in 1923 and held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the print renders the ancient shrine in a contemplative nocturnal atmosphere.

A view of Kanaya-machi, a hillside neighborhood overlooking the harbor of Nagasaki. Issued within Selected Views of Japan, the print sets stepped streets and tile roofs against the city's sheltered bay in Hasui's flat shin-hanga palette.

Sofuku-ji, an Obaku Zen temple in Nagasaki founded by Chinese merchants in the seventeenth century, recognizable by its red Ming-style gate. Hasui frames the precinct within Selected Views of Japan, marking Nagasaki's distinctive Sino-Japanese heritage.

A view of Okayama Castle, the sixteenth-century black-walled keep known as the Crow Castle, mirrored in the Asahi River. Hasui treats the silhouette in deep tonal blocks for his Selected Views of Japan.

The steep slope leading up to Senko-ji Temple in the port town of Onomichi, with rooftops descending toward the Inland Sea. From Selected Views of Japan, the print captures Onomichi's celebrated layered terrain.

A modest hot-spring village at Anraku in Osumi, southern Kyushu, set among low hills. The print is part of Hasui's Selected Views of Japan and reflects his persistent interest in regional bathing towns rendered in muted tones.

The volcanic Mount Mayuyama rising behind the harbor of Shimabara on Kyushu's Ariake coast. Within Selected Views of Japan, Hasui pairs working harbor and looming peak in a composition typical of his coastal landscapes.

Tsukumojima, the cluster of small islets near Shimabara in Nagasaki Prefecture, seen beneath billowing cumulonimbus clouds tinted rose and violet. From Selected Views of Japan (1922), Hasui places a rowboat with two figures in the calm foreground water, their reflections merging with those of the pine-covered islets and sky. A torii gate on the nearest island anchors the composition in the shin-hanga tradition of atmospheric landscape.

The Golden Pavilion of Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto under fresh snow, its gilded upper stories set against bare branches and a frozen pond. From Selected Views of Japan, this winter scene is among Hasui's most familiar treatments of a celebrated subject.
collection-of-beauty-nikko-kaido-hasui-k: A shin-hanga woodblock print depicting a quiet stretch of the Nikkō Kaidō, the historic highway leading to the Tokugawa mausoleum. Hasui captures the avenue's towering cryptomeria with the soft atmospheric tonality and precise gradation that define his landscape work.
collection-of-beauty-nikolaj-alexandrowi: A woman in dark dress and white head-covering reclines in a chair on a sunlit terrace, propped on pillows against a garden setting of oleander and green hills. Yaroshenko painted the work in 1890, titling it Im warmen Land (In a Warm Land). The composition conveys convalescent quietude, characteristic of the artist's empathetic approach to his subjects.
collection-of-beauty-nikolay-ii-of-russi: A formal portrait of Tsar Nicholas II, the last emperor of Russia, painted shortly after his coronation. Repin balances state-portrait dignity with the loose, vigorous brushwork that distinguished him among the Peredvizhniki realists.
collection-of-beauty-niobe-jacqueslouisd: Apollo and Diana descend from clouds to strike down the children of Niobe, who raises her arm in anguished supplication at the centre of the composition, surrounded by falling and dying figures. David painted this canvas in 1772 as one of his repeated unsuccessful entries for the Prix de Rome, a competition he finally won in 1774; the work now hangs at the Dallas Museum of Art. The dynamic groupings and mythological subject reflect the Neoclassical ambitions David pursued throughout his early career.
collection-of-beauty-nishikawa-sukenobu-: A page from the Ehon Asakayama (Picture Book of Mount Asaka) of 1739, a woodblock-printed book by Nishikawa Sukenobu, the leading Kyoto designer of pictures of beautiful women. Printed in ink monochrome, this sheet shows a woman at her toilette, her kimono slipped to the waist as she binds up her hair before a lacquer cabinet and a folding mirror stand. The book's two dozen studies of women rank among Sukenobu's most important contributions to the bijin-ga genre.
collection-of-beauty-nitta-yoshisada-tsu: A mounted samurai in full armour endures a barrage of arrows as he shelters beside a large tree, his white horse beneath him in a stormy landscape. The print depicts Nitta Yoshisada, the fourteenth-century warrior commander celebrated in medieval chronicles, and was published in 1900 by Tsuchiya Kōitsu. The dense arrow shower and theatrical composition are characteristic of the musha-e (warrior-picture) tradition.
collection-of-beauty-nmgrh-1455-adolf-lu: Adolf Ludvig Gustav Albert Couschi, known at the Swedish court as Badin, is shown holding a chess piece over a chessboard, wearing an elaborate feathered turban and ornate blue court costume with a white sash. Gustaf Lundberg drew the pastel portrait in 1775; it is held by the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm under inventory NMGrh 1455. Couschi had been brought to Sweden as a child and became a well-known figure at the court of Queen Lovisa Ulrika.
collection-of-beauty-nocturne-by-james-a: Part of Whistler's celebrated Nocturne series, in which the painter pared the Thames down to washes of dusky blue and pewter. The work treats landscape as a tonal arrangement, anticipating the abstract sensibilities Whistler championed in his Aesthetic writings.
collection-of-beauty-northeaster-by-wins: A lone outcrop of the Maine coast pummeled by a winter storm, rendered with the muscular realism Homer developed at Prout's Neck. The painting strips the marine subject to surf, rock, and spray, a meditation on raw natural force.
collection-of-beauty-notes-nocturne-lith: A lone boatman crosses the misty expanse of Chelsea Reach on the Thames, with the Battersea factories and a ruined tower dissolved into atmospheric grey washes on the far bank. Whistler executed this lithotint in 1878 — titled Nocturne: The River at Battersea — using scraping on a prepared half-tint ground with blue chine appliqué. The work is held in the British Museum, London.
collection-of-beauty-nuremberg-chronicle: A celebrated woodcut from Hartmann Schedel's Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493, showing capering skeletons in the late-medieval danse macabre tradition. Wolgemut's workshop produced one of the most ambitious printed-image programs of the incunabula period.
collection-of-beauty-nympheas-71293-3: One of the water-lily compositions Monet painted at his Giverny pond, dissolving the surface into floating pads, reflected sky, and submerged depths. The late series pushed Impressionism toward an immersive, near-abstract vision of light on water.
collection-of-beauty-o-soldado-esquecido: A monumental anti-war canvas by the Russian battle painter Vereshchagin, showing a fallen soldier abandoned on the battlefield as carrion birds gather. The work is part of the artist's unflinching cycle exposing the human cost of imperial conflict.
collection-of-beauty-ochanomizu-57588716: From Hasui's Twenty Views of Tokyo, this woodblock print shows wet snow muffling the rooftops along the Kanda River at Ochanomizu. The artist was renowned for his subtle differentiation of snowfall, here rendered as soft cotton-like accumulation.
collection-of-beauty-oeillets-et-clemati: A late still life painted in Manet's final months, when illness confined him to small flower pieces brought by visitors. Carnations and clematis are set in a faceted crystal vase, the brushwork economical yet luminous against a darkened ground.
collection-of-beauty-ohara-koson-gatto-e: A color woodcut of 1933 by Ohara Koson, the leading designer of bird-and-animal subjects in the shin-hanga print movement. A black-and-white cat wearing a red collar and bell crouches on the wooden floor, staring intently into a glass bowl in which orange goldfish circle, a small hand net lying beside it. An impression of the print is in the Cincinnati Art Museum.
collection-of-beauty-on-the-beach-two-ar: A wood engraving after Winslow Homer published in Harper's Weekly, depicting a flirtation interrupted on a New England beach. Homer's Reconstruction-era illustrations chronicled American leisure with a wry observational eye.
collection-of-beauty-ono-shindon-in-the-: From Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (no. 31), this woodblock print depicts farmers and heavily laden pack horses crossing the flat reclaimed lands of Ōno in Suruga Province, bundles of straw strapped to the animals' backs. Fuji's snow-capped peak rises serenely above the wide bay and marshes in the distance. First published around 1830, the composition uses bold horizontal bands of colour to balance the busy foreground activity against the mountain's still silhouette.
collection-of-beauty-ornament-with-owl-m: An engraving by Martin Schongauer in which an owl with outstretched wings perches at the base of a dense thicket of curling foliage, harried by the small day birds that dart through the scrollwork above. The owl mocked by daytime birds was a familiar medieval emblem of folly attracting scorn, and Schongauer works the motif into an ornament design of the kind used as a model by goldsmiths and other craftsmen. The sheet bears his monogram and belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-p-1948-sc-276-scale: A landscape from Monet's mature Impressionist period, catalogued as Wildenstein 1192. The painter's broken touch and high-keyed palette translate atmosphere and shifting light into the building blocks of the picture.
collection-of-beauty-p1110627wallraf-mus: A young woman in a cream satin gown and wide-brimmed hat stands beside a low chair draped in richly patterned fabric, on which a white Angora cat rears up on its hind legs. Painted between 1783 and 1785 and attributed jointly to Jean-Honoré Fragonard and Marguerite Gérard, the panel hangs in the Wallraf-Richartz Museum in Cologne (inv. WRM 3652). An older male figure is partially visible in the shadowed background, lending the intimate interior a note of quiet observation.
collection-of-beauty-painting-of-susanna: Susanna, surprised at her bath, twists away as two elders lean in over the garden wall — the apocryphal story from the Book of Daniel that let painters join a nude to a moral subject. Rubens painted this version in about 1606-07, during his years in Italy, and its compressed drama reflects his study of Italian models. Oil on canvas, Galleria Borghese, Rome.
collection-of-beauty-paisaje-con-san-jer: Patinir places the penitent Saint Jerome amid a sweeping panoramic landscape of crags, rivers, and distant towns. The Flemish painter is credited with elevating landscape to a primary subject in Western art, the figure dwarfed by the world he renounces.
collection-of-beauty-pallas-athena-by-re: A figure in gleaming helmet and gorget, traditionally identified as the goddess of wisdom and war. Rembrandt models the armour with thick, gilded impasto against deep shadow, a hallmark of his late chiaroscuro.
collection-of-beauty-pallasetlecentaure: Botticelli pairs Pallas Athena, dressed in a gown embroidered with interlocking rings and olive branches and holding a long halberd, with a subdued centaur whose hair she grasps. The tempera allegory, painted around 1482, is read as reason mastering brute instinct, and the olive-and-diamond-ring motifs on her garment connect the figure to Medici humanist symbolism. The work belongs to Botticelli's mature Florentine period and remains one of the most discussed mythological allegories of the Renaissance.
collection-of-beauty-pan-syrinx-rubens: Rubens stages the Ovidian myth of Pan pursuing the nymph Syrinx, who is moments from transformation into the riverside reeds that crowd the right of the composition. The figures rush through a lush, flower-strewn wetland, birds and frogs scattered at their feet. Painted between 1617 and 1619 and held by the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in Kassel (inv. GK 1229), the small panel is a characteristic Baroque fusion of mythological narrative and sensuous naturalism.
collection-of-beauty-panorama-vom-kreml-: Gaertner's 1839 panorama depicts the Cathedral Square of the Moscow Kremlin, with the white-walled Cathedral of the Archangel surmounted by a golden onion dome dominating the right, and a succession of Kremlin towers receding along the battlemented wall to the left. Figures in period dress cross the broad paved square in the middle distance. The picture is typical of Gaertner's meticulous topographical work recording imperial Russian architecture during his travels of the late 1830s.
collection-of-beauty-paolo-uccello-heili: Uccello's late panel of the chivalric saint lancing the dragon, with a tethered princess and a stylised storm gathering overhead. The artist's lifelong fascination with linear perspective is visible in the geometric grid of the cave and patterned ground.
collection-of-beauty-paolo-veronese-008: A reproduction documenting a painting by the Venetian master Paolo Veronese, photographed without its frame for archival study. Veronese's output spans grand religious cycles, mythologies, and ceiling allegories executed across sixteenth-century Venice.
collection-of-beauty-paolo-veronese-juno: A ceiling allegory painted for the Doge's Palace, in which Juno rains crowns, jewels, and ducal regalia onto a personified Venice. Veronese exploits the di sotto in sù viewpoint to send the goddess plunging through illusory clouds.
collection-of-beauty-paolo-veronese-lucr: Veronese's Lucretia presses the dagger to her breast in the Roman matron's act of self-destruction after her violation by Tarquin. The painter dresses the heroine in Venetian silks, fusing classical exemplum with sixteenth-century courtly elegance.
collection-of-beauty-paolo-veronese-the-: An early devotional canvas in which Christ raises the kneeling Magdalene from her former life. Veronese's Venetian instinct for sumptuous fabric, architectural staging, and silvery light is already evident in this youthful composition.

The defeated Persian queen and her household kneel before Alexander the Great after Issus, in a vast frieze-like composition acquired by London's National Gallery in 1857. Veronese fills the picture with contemporary Venetian costume, courtly architecture, and a noble gesture of clemency.
collection-of-beauty-paris-art-deco-boil: The sculptor Jean-Antoine Houdon at work in his studio, modelling a clay bust of the astronomer Pierre-Simon Laplace. Oil on canvas, about 1803, in the Musée des Arts décoratifs, Paris. Finished casts and tools fill the cluttered workshop behind the seated sculptor.
collection-of-beauty-parmigianino-004: A refined female bust by Parmigianino, likely a detail fragment, shows a young woman with downcast eyes, pearled headband, and elongated neck, rendered in the cool, polished manner that defines his Mannerist style. The figure's delicately idealised features and translucent drapery are characteristic of Parmigianino's work of the 1530s. The painting is associated with the title Madonna mit dem langen Hals in the record.
collection-of-beauty-parmigianino-madonn: Known as the Madonna of the Long Neck, this unfinished altarpiece is a touchstone of Italian Mannerism. Parmigianino elongates the Virgin's anatomy and tilts the spatial logic of the column and miniature prophet for an unsettling, refined elegance.
collection-of-beauty-parting-spring-by-k: The left panel of a pair of folding screens by Kawai Gyokudō, designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan. Working in the nihonga tradition, the artist evokes the melancholy of late spring through misty mountains and falling cherry blossoms.

The right panel of Kawai Gyokudō's Parting Spring screens, designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan, depicts steep rocky cliffs looming above churning waves, with two water-mill boats navigating the rough current. Working in the nihonga tradition, the artist renders the raw energy of the river gorge in close detail, completing the panoramic seasonal landscape begun in the left panel. The diptych is held by the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, and dates to 1916.
collection-of-beauty-patenierchristopher: Saint Christopher wades across a wide river bearing the Christ Child on his shoulder, dwarfed by a panoramic landscape of jagged rocks, distant towns and luminous water. The sweeping high viewpoint is characteristic of Patinir, often credited as the first specialist in Western landscape painting.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-1892-9: Two Provençal labourers face off across a wine bottle in Cézanne's most distilled treatment of the card-players theme. The Courtauld version reduces the cast to its essential pair, the figures built from the planar, faceted strokes that prefigured Cubism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-bather: A group of male nudes along a riverbank, some standing and some reclining, set into an open landscape. Oil on canvas of about 1890, part of the bather series Cézanne pursued from the 1870s onward, now in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris. The figures are built to structure the space rather than to display the flesh.

A group of nude bathers is arranged beneath arching trees that frame the composition like a vault, their bodies echoing the leaning trunks. One of three large Baigneuses Cézanne worked on between 1894 and 1905; this canvas is in the National Gallery, London. He sacrificed individual likeness to fit the figures to the triangular structure of the trees.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-boutei: A dark bottle, a glass carafe, a stoneware jug and a scatter of lemons stand on a draped table. Watercolour and graphite on paper of about 1902 to 1906, in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid. Cézanne left much of the sheet bare, letting the white paper carry the highlights between thin washes.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-french: Nude female figures arranged in two groups beneath a vault of leaning trees, the bodies pared to broad blue and ochre planes. The largest of Cézanne's Bather canvases, oil on canvas, about 210 by 251 cm, worked on over roughly seven years and left unfinished at his death in 1906. It entered the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1937.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-houses: Pale ochre houses clustered on a plateau above the Riaux valley, the rocky hillside built up in cool blues and greens beneath a high sky. Oil on canvas painted around 1883 near L'Estaque on the Mediterranean coast, now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. Cézanne worked the terrain in faceted planes of colour rather than line.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-le-gra: An adolescent boy mid-stride in a pale watery landscape, hands on his hips, his body slightly out of proportion. Oil on canvas of about 1885 based on a studio photograph of a posed model, now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York, from the Lillie P. Bliss Collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-madame: Hortense Fiquet, the painter's wife, sits in three-quarter view wearing a broad green hat, her hands folded in her lap. Oil on canvas of about 1891 to 1892, catalogued BF141 in the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia. Cézanne built the face and bodice from planes of dull violet, ochre and grey-green laid side by side.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-maison: A small ochre farmhouse, the Maison Maria, sits among pines on the road to the Château Noir near Aix-en-Provence. Oil on canvas of about 1895, in the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth. Cézanne worked the ground and foliage in parallel diagonal strokes of green, blue and orange.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-montag: Cézanne returned obsessively to the limestone ridge near his native Aix-en-Provence, structuring its slopes through patches of constructive brushwork. The painting treats landscape as an architecture of colour planes, foundational for early modernism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-pyrami: Four human skulls are stacked in a low pyramid on a bare tabletop against a dark ground. Oil on canvas painted between about 1898 and 1900, the only Cézanne to push the skulls so close to the viewer. He owned several skulls and returned to them in oil and watercolour in his final decade at Aix.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-the-mu: A violent scene in which two figures pin a third to the ground beside a body of water under a heavy sky. Oil on canvas, 64 by 81 cm, painted around 1870 and held by the Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool, under inventory WAG 6242. It belongs to the dark, dramatic subjects of Cézanne's early years.
collection-of-beauty-paul-cezanne-young-: A young woman in a striped blouse leans on a fabric-covered table, her head resting in her hand. Oil on canvas of about 1895 to 1900, accession 99.PA.40 in the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. Cézanne built her bulk from broad blocks of colour while the space behind her shifts and tilts.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-bull-su: A bull-baiting scene of the kind de Vos perfected in Rubens's Antwerp circle, with mastiffs lunging at a tethered bull's flanks. The diagonal tangle of muscle, horn and fang demonstrates the Flemish taste for animal combats as showcases of anatomical drama and tonal bravura.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-cats-fi: A pantry overturned by brawling cats among hanging game, fish and copper vessels, a kitchen-piece genre popularized by Frans Snyders and continued by his brother-in-law de Vos. The hissing animals serve as a moralized emblem of greed and chaos disrupting domestic order.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-jan-wil: A Flemish Baroque collaboration in which Jan Wildens supplied the wooded paradise landscape and Paul de Vos populated it with the assembled animals of creation. Such division of labor was standard practice in Antwerp's specialist workshops, here producing a dense menagerie set within a luminous park-like clearing.
collection-of-beauty-paul-de-vos-still-l: A monumental Flemish still life heaped with hanging game, poultry, fruit, and vegetables, attended by a servant figure at the left — likely contributed by a collaborating figure painter, possibly Cornelis de Vos. The composition exemplifies the Antwerp specialty of combining a Snyders-school animal painter with a figure specialist for sumptuous decorative ensembles. The work dates to before 1678 and is held by the Fundación Banco Santander.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-001: An academic life study from Gauguin's early years, predating the Tahitian primitivism for which he is now remembered. The figure is modelled with conventional tonal shading, evidence of the studio training he would soon discard for synthetism.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-004: Annah, the thirteen-year-old Javanese model Gauguin took in on his return to Paris, sits naked in a blue armchair with a small monkey at her feet. Painted in the Rue Vercingétorix studio in 1893 or 1894, the canvas carries the Tahitian inscription Aita tamari vahine Judith te parari and now hangs in the Stavros Niarchos collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-018-th: A swineherd stands in the foreground of a hilly Breton landscape above a village, a pair of pale yellow pigs grazing nearby and a horse at left. Painted at Pont-Aven in 1888, the canvas shows Gauguin moving from broken Impressionist touch toward broad, simplified zones of colour. The work is held in the Norton Simon collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-036: Four Breton peasant women in white coifs and dark dresses are gathered in an outdoor setting, their figures clustered against a background of foliage. Painted at Pont-Aven in 1886 during Gauguin's first Breton summer, the canvas records his early engagement with the rituals and costume of rural Brittany. The work belongs to the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen, on long-term deposit at the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-040: Vahine no te tiare shows a young Tahitian woman in a blue high-collared mission dress, holding a small pale tiare flower in her hands. Gauguin painted this, his first Polynesian portrait, in 1891, setting the sitter against a flat yellow ground animated by painted green foliage. The canvas is held in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-044: The Siesta shows several Tahitian women resting on a wooden veranda floor, two of them stretched out lengthways while others sit nearby. Painted between 1892 and 1894 during Gauguin's first stay in Tahiti, the canvas uses flat zones of colour and a high viewpoint to dissolve conventional depth. It is held in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-056: Two Tahitian women sit on a sandy beach, one in profile wearing a red patterned pareu, the other facing the viewer in a pink dress and working with something in her hands. The deep blue-green sea and a narrow strip of dark sky form a compressed background behind them. Gauguin painted the canvas in 1891 during his first Tahitian sojourn; it is in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-059: A snow-covered Paris garden seen from the window, the bare branches and low wall reduced to muted whites, blues and umbers. Gauguin painted the small canvas in 1879, still a stockbroker and Sunday painter under Camille Pissarro's tutelage; it now hangs in the Budapest Museum of Fine Arts.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-072: Marie Ginoux sits at a marble café table in Arles with a green absinthe glass and a soda siphon, while a billiard table and a row of slumped drinkers fill the back of the room. Painted in early November 1888 during Gauguin's two months sharing the Yellow House with Van Gogh, the canvas was acquired by the Pushkin Museum in Moscow from the Shchukin collection.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-085: Les Alyscamps depicts the ancient Roman burial ground at Arles: a canal path edged by tall flame-orange and green trees recedes toward a domed tower, with three dark-cloaked figures walking in the middle distance. Gauguin painted this during his stay with Van Gogh in autumn 1888, flattening the composition into saturated bands of colour. The canvas is held in the Musée d'Orsay, Paris.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-087: An early Martinique canvas from Gauguin's 1887 stay near Saint-Pierre, showing local women gathering fruit beneath dense tropical foliage. Painted before his Tahitian voyages, the work already shows his shift away from Impressionist brushwork toward flatter, decorative arrangements of figure and landscape.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-090: Three Tahitian women stand and sit against a luminous orange-red ground, one holding a bundle and another nursing a child, while a dog and a distant figure occupy the background. Gauguin painted the canvas in 1899 during his late Tahitian period, organising the figures as a frieze of broad, saturated silhouettes. The work is titled Women on the Seashore.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-091: Nevermore shows a nude Tahitian woman lying along a bed, her gaze turned towards the viewer, while a large dark teal bird occupies the upper centre of the canvas and two figures converse in the background. Painted in 1897 and titled after Edgar Allan Poe's raven, the work conveys an atmosphere of unease through its flattened pattern and cool colour. It is in the Courtauld Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-105: Riders on the Beach shows several horsemen seen mostly from behind moving across a pale sandy shore, tall bare trees framing the scene at left. Gauguin painted this canvas in 1902 on the island of Hiva Oa during his final years in the Marquesas, treating the figures as a decorative frieze against the muted beach and sky.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-106: The second version of Riders on the Beach shows a group of horsemen, including figures in white and red, moving across a vivid pink-lavender shore toward the sea, with a standing woman in the foreground. Painted in 1902 on Hiva Oa, the canvas distils the scene into a flat decorative frieze of saturated colour. It is one of two versions Gauguin painted that year.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-110: In this 1896 self-portrait titled près du Golgotha, Gauguin depicts himself bust-length in a white garment against a near-black ground, his expression grave and inward-looking. The canvas was painted in Tahiti during a period of severe illness and financial hardship, and the title's reference to Golgotha aligns the artist with the suffering Christ. It is held in the Museu de Arte de São Paulo.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-112: Gauguin paints himself in the role of Hugo's outlaw Jean Valjean, gaunt-cheeked against a wallpaper of pink flowers, with a small portrait of Émile Bernard pinned behind him. Sent to Vincent van Gogh in Arles in autumn 1888 as part of the exchange of self-portraits among the Pont-Aven group, the canvas now belongs to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-113: Mahana no atua, painted in Paris between Gauguin's two Tahitian sojourns, presents an idol of the moon goddess Hina flanked by ritual bathers. The lower foreground dissolves into pools of pure, mirror-bright color, an experiment in flat decorative abstraction that would influence Nabi and Fauve painters.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-121: This 1889 still life pairs two ceramic vessels — a pale mask-faced pot and a smaller head-shaped jug, both filled with cut flowers — on a pink surface before a yellow wall hung with a Japanese woodcut of a white-faced figure. Gauguin combined his interest in ceramic self-portraiture with the ukiyo-e prints circulating among the Paris avant-garde. The canvas is titled Still Life with Head-Shaped Vase and Japanese Woodcut.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-1880-t: Gauguin's wife Mette Sophie sits at a small table bent over her sewing, the dense brushwork drawn from Camille Pissarro's example. The 116 by 81 cm canvas, painted in 1880 while Gauguin was still a successful stockbroker, hangs at the Foundation E. G. Bührle in Zurich and is catalogued as Wildenstein 65.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-200: Gauguin, in his late twenties and still a Paris stockbroker, looks out from beneath a soft toque in muted browns and greys. Painted around 1875 to 1877, the small canvas is the earliest known self-portrait of an artist whose face would become one of the most painted subjects in his late Polynesian work; it is in the Harvard Art Museums.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-contes: Two young Tahitian women sit in a flowering grove while a crouching red-haired devil, an exaggerated likeness of the Dutch painter Meyer de Haan, lurks behind them. Painted in 1902 on Hiva Oa and now at the Museum Folkwang in Essen, the picture revisits Gauguin's old Pont-Aven companion as a demonic figure shadowing his Marquesan paradise.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-d-ou-v: A sleeping infant, a youth picking fruit, and an old woman crouched beside a blue idol stretch across nearly four metres of Tahitian forest. Gauguin painted the canvas in late 1897 as an intended summation before a suicide attempt, and it now anchors the collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-deux-t: Two bare-breasted Tahitian women stand close in the picture plane, one holding a tray of red fruit. Gauguin painted the canvas in 1899, and it is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-l-espr: Front and back covers of Gauguin's handwritten 1902 manuscript L'Esprit Moderne et le Catholicisme, with watercolour and gouache decoration of Tahitian figures and ornamental script. Written on Hiva Oa near the end of his life, the polemical text attacked the Catholic mission's authority over the Marquesans, an argument that earned Gauguin a libel conviction shortly before his death.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-la-ber: A young shepherdess sits barefoot on the grass with her flock in a sloping Pont-Aven pasture, the village rooftops in the middle distance. Gauguin signed and dated the canvas P Gauguin 86 at lower left, among the first works of his initial Brittany summer; it entered the Laing Art Gallery in Newcastle as a gift from the National Art Collections Fund in 1945.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-le-par: A nude woman with auburn hair stands with her back to the viewer near a central tree, while a large coiling serpent lies at the base and a pair of figures (Adam and Eve) walk away to the right. Painted around 1890, the canvas is titled Adam and Eve or Paradise Lost and is held at the Yale University Art Gallery.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-le-sor: A long-haired Marquesan in a short blue tunic and red cape stands frontally with a dog and bird at his feet, two veiled women shrinking behind a tree. Painted on Hiva Oa in 1902 and now at the Musée d'Art moderne in Liège, the figure is based on Haapuani, a local healer Gauguin had befriended in his final years.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-manao-: A nude Tahitian woman, Gauguin's companion Teha'amana, lies face down on a bed against a deep violet background, while the tupapau — the spirit of the dead — sits as a dark hooded figure behind her in the upper left. Painted in 1892 and now in the Albright-Knox Art Gallery (Buffalo AKG Art Museum), the title refers to Polynesian spirits believed to haunt the night.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-self-p: Gauguin sets his bespectacled face against a pale background, the gaze direct and the features marked by illness in his final months on Hiva Oa. Painted in 1903 and now at the Kunstmuseum Basel, this is considered the last known self-portrait of the artist.

Gauguin stares out from a flat red and yellow ground, a green snake coiling in one hand, three ripe apples floating beside his head and a thin golden halo above. Painted on a cupboard door at the Le Pouldu inn in 1889 and now at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the picture casts the artist as a sardonic Eden serpent and Christian saint at once.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-tahiti: A semi-nude Tahitian woman faces the viewer, a necklace across her chest, while a pale ghostly face with closed eyes hovers in the upper left behind her. The work is a print or monotype by Gauguin, dateable to around 1899–1900, and depicts his recurring theme of the spirit of the dead watching over the living.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-te-aa-: A young Tahitian woman sits nude on a patterned cloth, holding a sprouting mango seed against a field of flowering shrubs. Gauguin painted Te aa no areois, the Seed of the Areoi, in 1892 during his first Tahitian stay, casting his model Teha'amana as the mythic ancestress of the Areoi religious society; the canvas is now in MoMA.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gauguin-two-wo: An older Tahitian woman in dark blue clothing sits beside a younger woman in a red dress, the two figures close together against a green and ochre landscape. The canvas, titled Mother and Daughter, dates from around 1900 and is attributed to Gauguin's late Tahitian period.
collection-of-beauty-paul-gustave-dore-a: Gustave Dore's vision of Andromeda, the Ethiopian princess chained to a sea cliff awaiting Perseus's rescue. The composition exploits Dore's signature contrast of luminous flesh against turbulent rock and sky, a Romantic theatricality refined through years of book illustration. This file represents a digitally restored version of the image.
collection-of-beauty-paul-klee-1922-sene: A stylised head composed of geometric planes of yellow, orange, and pink, with two symmetrical round red eyes set within a circular form against a warm, textured ground. Painted in oil on gauze in 1922 during Klee's years at the Bauhaus in Weimar, the work reduces a human face to its essential geometry while preserving an uncanny expressiveness. It is held at the Kunstmuseum Basel.
collection-of-beauty-paul-klee-invention: A gaunt naked woman is draped across the bare branches of a gnarled tree, her elongated body rendered in precise etched line; a bird perches on a branch above. Part of the Inventionen series of etchings Klee produced in 1903, the print is held in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-peasant-family-goin: A peasant strides ahead on foot, laden with his gear, leading the horse on which his wife rides with a small child clinging on behind her; the road winds past a rocky crag toward a village with a church in the distance. One of Schongauer's secular genre engravings, it treats everyday rural life with the same fineness of line as his devotional prints. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
collection-of-beauty-pedro-pablo-rubens-: Susanna twists away from two leering elders who press in from the shadows of her garden bath, her startled body and rumpled drapery filling the canvas. Painted shortly after Rubens's return from Italy, the picture fuses Venetian colour with the muscular Roman figures he had studied there.
collection-of-beauty-peinturesmuseefabre: Venus, attended by putti and her swan, descends on clouds toward Vulcan who holds up completed armour, while workers labour in the forge at the right. Submitted as the painter's morceau de réception to the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture on 31 December 1734, the canvas is a polished demonstration of Rococo mythological painting. It is now in the Musée Fabre, Montpellier.
collection-of-beauty-pellegrinibydegas: Carlo Pellegrini, the Italian-born caricaturist who signed his Vanity Fair plates as Ape, is shown full-length in dark street clothes, his red-auburn beard prominent against a loose ochre ground. The sheet is inscribed 'à lui' and signed Degas, and dates to around 1876. It is a work on paper by Edgar Degas, produced circa 1876.
collection-of-beauty-perekochevka-kirgiz: A small party of Kyrgyz nomads crosses the grassy steppe, their camels loaded with carpets and household goods, the lead animal carrying a tall carpet-draped litter, while a rider on horseback brings up the rear and birds wheel overhead. Vereshchagin painted the scene in 1869-1870 for his Turkestan series; it is held in the Tretyakov Gallery.
collection-of-beauty-persus-and-andromed: Andromeda stands chained on a rocky shore, largely unclothed, while Perseus arrives on horseback from the upper right and a sea creature lurks in the middle ground, with a coastal town visible in the distance. The foreground is strewn with shells and sea-life rendered in Wtewael's characteristically minute detail. Joachim Wtewael, a leading Utrecht Mannerist, painted this version of the subject in 1611.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-ruben-s-: Four mounted soldiers strain over the standard of Anghiari, mouths open and horses crashing teeth-to-teeth in the central fight. Drawn around 1603 after Leonardo's lost mural for the Palazzo della Signoria, the sheet is the most authoritative surviving record of the composition Vasari painted over around 1560.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-0: Bathsheba sits at her bath while a black page delivers David's letter, the Old Testament narrative reframed as an excuse for sumptuous flesh, drapery, and still life. The painting now hangs in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden.

Salome presents the head of John the Baptist on a salver as Herod recoils at the banquet table. Rubens stages the gruesome moment with theatrical lighting and a dense crush of guests, balancing horror against the gleam of silver and silk.

An intimate, near-life-size portrait of Rubens's second wife Helena Fourment, draped only in a fur cloak. The picture's frank sensuality and tender naturalism mark it as a private image, kept in the artist's own household.

A panoramic view of the country estate Rubens purchased in 1635, with its turreted manor set among golden Brabant fields. The artist treats native landscape with vigorous brushwork and a low, glowing horizon, anticipating later Romantic vistas.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-1: Paris awards the golden apple to Venus while Juno and Minerva recoil in defeat, their nudes arranged in a graceful triad against an Arcadian landscape. Rubens revisited this mythological subject several times; the late Prado version is among his most assured.

A head-and-shoulders portrait of the young Vincenzo II Gonzaga, rendered with a large lace ruff collar and a richly embroidered golden doublet against a dark ground. Rubens painted the Mantuan duke around 1604 to 1605 during his years at the Gonzaga court, absorbing the courtly polish of his Italian models. The panel is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.

From the Decius Mus cycle, a tapestry-cartoon-scale battle scene in which the Roman consul plunges to his ritual death amid rearing horses and clashing standards. The composition is a swirling diagonal of armoured bodies, an early showcase of Rubensian dynamism.

A state portrait of Isabella of Bourbon, queen consort of Spain, in stiff black court dress and pearls. Rubens softens the rigid Habsburg formula with subtle modelling of the face and a discreet warmth in the flesh tones.

Hercules grapples the invulnerable Nemean lion in a knot of straining limbs, the hero's first labor reduced to its essential close-quarters violence. The Apsley House version follows a Rubens prototype that translates antique sculptural sources, especially the Belvedere Torso, into Baroque flesh and sinew.

A bust-length portrait of a man with moustache and pointed beard, wearing a large white ruff and a dark coat with a gold chain and pendant. The Colchester picture is an after-Rubens version, dated possibly c. 1650–1750, held in the Colchester and Ipswich Museums Service.

Cain raises a jawbone-club above his fallen brother in a violent, sculpturally compressed composition modelled on Michelangelo's Sistine ignudi. The Courtauld panel is a small but ferocious meditation on humanity's first murder, its diagonal locked into the surface like a relief.

Christ, robed in red and nimbed, extends the keys to a white-bearded Saint Peter, who bows to receive them, while a group of apostles bears witness behind. Painted in 1614 and now in the Gemäldegalerie Berlin, the composition translates the biblical grant of papal authority into Rubens's characteristic idiom of crowded, animated figures lit against a cool architectural ground.

The Virgin in red cradles the sleeping infant Christ on white drapery, while an elderly woman — Saint Anne — looks on from the upper left. The full English title recorded for this copy-after-Rubens work at Lady Margaret Hall is 'Madonna and Child with Saint Anne', and the three-figure grouping is central to the composition.

Diana and her companions recoil from leering satyrs at a forest pool in a late mythological invention treating chastity disturbed. Rubens entrusted much of the landscape and animal staffage to specialist collaborators, while reserving the warm, dimpled female nudes for himself.

Diana and a group of hunters drive deer with hounds across an open landscape, the central goddess lunging forward with a spear as the quarry leaps ahead of the pack. Dated 1632 and held in the Bode Museum, Berlin, the panoramic composition distributes the action across a wide frieze, with landscape, animals, and figures typical of Rubens's collaborative hunting scenes.

An oil head study, painted directly from a Antwerp model, of the kind Rubens kept on file for reuse as apostles, philosophers and patriarchs in larger compositions. The rapid wet-into-wet handling and ruddy flesh tones show his working method at its most direct.

Neptune, depicted as a venerable old man, is seated beside the standing nude Amphitrite at the centre of a monumental allegory populated by exotic animals — a lion, tiger, rhinoceros, and crocodile — flanking the divine pair. Painted in 1614 and held in the Gemäldegalerie Berlin (inv. 776A), the composition is Rubens's ambitious synthesis of mythological and allegorical traditions, here grouping the sea-deities with creatures symbolising the earth's continents and waters.

A three-quarter-length portrait of an elderly man in black robes with a large white ruff, shown in profile to the right, his grey beard framing a composed and authoritative face. A heraldic coat of arms appears in the upper left, confirming this as a formal commission; the work is dated 1623 and is in the Gemäldegalerie Berlin.

The dead Christ is supported between two mourners — a young man in red (Saint John) on the left and a woman in blue (the Virgin Mary) on the right — in a tightly focused composition of restrained grief. This school-of-Rubens Lamentation, dated c. 1610–1640, is in the collection of Durham University.

Saint Teresa of Ávila kneels in her Carmelite habit, hands raised and gaze lifted towards a dove descending from above in a burst of light. The finished painting of 1635, in the Fitzwilliam Museum, presents the saint's mystical vision with controlled drapery and luminous effect characteristic of Rubens's devotional works.

The corpulent Silenus staggers forward at the centre, supported by satyrs and a Black figure playing a tambourine, while maenads, putti, and grapes fill the scene in a riotous frieze of Bacchic excess. Dated 1619 and held in the Bode Museum, Berlin, the composition draws on antique precedents and Venetian colour to celebrate — rather than moralize — the pleasures of wine.

Saint Teresa of Ávila kneels in her Carmelite habit before a table bearing a skull, crucifix, and open book, her gaze lifted towards a luminous vision above. The work, dated c. 1614 and in the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, typifies Rubens's treatment of Counter-Reformation visionary subjects with controlled interior light and devotional symbolism.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-2: A three-quarter-length portrait of an unidentified man in black dress with a white lace ruff, standing before a large red curtain, his gaze direct and his bearing assured. Painted in 1630 and now in the Mauritshuis, The Hague, the portrait is typical of Rubens's formal likeness style in his mature Antwerp years.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-a: Rubens's homage to Titian, copied during his stay in Madrid where he studied the royal collection. The serpent-child reaches down to Eve as Adam grasps her arm; Rubens warms the Venetian palette and softens the contours toward his own fleshier ideal.

Shepherds press in around the manger, faces lit from below by the Christ child as Mary draws back the cloth. The diagonal massing of figures and theatrical lighting reflect Rubens's recent absorption of Caravaggio during his Italian years.

An ecorche drawing exposing the muscles of the male torso and limbs, made for the artist's own study of human structure. Such sheets fed the powerfully built figures of his history paintings and were later engraved as a teaching aid.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-c: The first murder rendered as violent close-quarters struggle, Cain's club raised above his fallen brother. Rubens compresses the action into a tight pyramidal group, exploiting contorted limbs and chiaroscuro for moral force.

The apostle is shown crucified upside down at his own request, his contorted, foreshortened body filling a tall altarpiece format. Commissioned for St Peter's Church in Cologne, the work was among the artist's last major altarpieces, completed shortly before his death and dispatched to the parish where his father had once lived.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-d: A young blonde child turns in profile, intently watching a small green bird perched on its hands. The intimate bust-length format and warm flesh tones place this panel within Rubens's circle of domestic portraits, a private counterpart to the grand commissions for which he is better known. The painting is held at the Gemäldegalerie Berlin (inv. 763), dated between 1614 and 1625.

A monumental Saint Jerome sits absorbed at his open book, lion at his feet and deep red drapery enveloping his powerful aged form, while two putti attend him. Rubens emphasises the hermit-scholar's muscular anatomy and the cardinal's scarlet, a saint central to Counter-Reformation imagery as an emblem of biblical orthodoxy. The painting, dating from 1608–09, is held at the Bildergalerie Sanssouci, Potsdam.

A solitary bearded figure, robed and sandalled, raises a lantern against a nocturnal sky marked by a crescent moon, his face turned upward in watchful attention. This tall outer wing of Rubens's Descent from the Cross triptych at the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekathedraal, Antwerp (1612–14), is identified as Saint Christopher, serving as the shuttered face the congregation would see when the triptych was closed.

Diana and her companions, returning from the hunt with hounds and game, are accosted by lecherous satyrs at the edge of a wood. The collision of nude bodies, fur and dead quarry typifies Rubens's late mythological mode.

Diana strides forward holding a long hunting spear, attended by two nymphs and accompanied by hounds, her quiver of arrows visible at her side. The composition presents the goddess of the hunt in motion, affording Rubens scope for studies of the female figure in varied poses. Painted between 1617 and 1620, the work is held at the Museo del Prado, Madrid (inv. P001727).

The Stoic philosopher stands in a basin while a physician opens his veins, his upturned head and outstretched arms recalling the antique sculpture Rubens had drawn in Rome. The picture distills the Baroque taste for Stoic exemplars of virtuous death.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-e: A peasant cart laden with felled timber rumbles down a rutted track as the day's last light catches clouds and treetops. The naturalistic Flemish countryside and warm low sun place this among the personal landscapes Rubens painted for his own pleasure.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-f: Prometheus, chained to a rocky outcrop, twists violently as the eagle of Zeus tears at his torso in a dramatically diagonal composition Rubens developed with Frans Snyders, who painted the bird. The torsion of the figure draws on Michelangelo and the Laocoön, fused with North-Italian colorism. This autograph version, begun around 1611–12, is held at the Philadelphia Museum of Art (inv. W1950-3-1).

Venus, partly nude, lifts the helmet from Mars as the fully armoured war-god yields to her embrace, while putti tug at his lance and scattered weapons and armour fill the foreground — an allegory of love's pacifying power over violence. The composition is set within a vaulted interior opening onto a background landscape with military activity. Painted around 1610, the work is held at the J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles (inv. 2000.68).

Four oil sketches of the same Black sitter, observed from different angles and in varied light, made as working material for finished compositions including the Adoration of the Magi. The studies are notable for their direct, dignified attention to an individual model.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-h: Mary and the infant Christ, supported by the elderly Joseph, gather in a semi-outdoor setting before a stone column and open landscape, while a large blue-and-gold macaw perches at left — a bird traditionally read as a symbol of the Virgin's purity. Rubens reworks the Renaissance devotional formula for the Holy Family with the characteristic warmth and fleshy vitality of his Flemish Baroque manner. The painting of 1614 is held at the Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp and displayed in the Rubenshuis.

A powerful, bearded Hercules raises his club with one hand while seizing a writhing female personification of Discord by the head with the other, as a winged putto looks on from above. Discord, depicted with serpents, is forced down beneath him in a cloud-filled setting that conveys the allegory of heroic virtue overcoming civil strife. Painted between 1632 and 1633, the work is in the collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
Hercules wraps the invulnerable lion in a strangling embrace, the hero's bunched muscles answered by the beast's twisting flank. The motif derives from antique sarcophagi Rubens had studied in Italy.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-i: A young woman, identified as Rubens's first wife Isabella Brant in the guise of Glycera, the ancient Greek flower seller, is shown in bust-length holding a garland of mixed blooms. She wears a pearl necklace and drop earring, and her braided hair is pinned up. The conceit fuses tender domestic portraiture with classical learning, and the work of circa 1616 is held at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-j: Judith, young and partially bare-shouldered, grasps the severed head of the Assyrian general Holofernes at mid-level while an aged maidservant assists beside her, both figures lit against deep shadow. Judith's sword is visible at left, reinforcing the immediate aftermath of the biblical act. Rubens treats the Old Testament heroine with the heightened drama of his early Italianate manner; the work of circa 1616–1618 is in the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, Brunswick.

A bust-length portrait of an unidentified young man wearing a distinctive black beret, rendered against a neutral dark ground and gazing toward the viewer. He is dressed in black with a white ruffled collar and wears a jewelled ring, the restrained palette and even lighting giving the work a sober, Northern character. Painted in oil on oak panel in the 1620s, the picture is in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich, within the Bavarian State Painting Collections.

Juno, in crimson robes, receives the eyes of the slain Argus — whose body lies at the lower right — and places them into the fanned tail of her peacock, which dominates the left of the composition. Female attendants and putti animate the open-air tableau, and a rainbow is visible in the upper sky. The Ovidian subject is drawn from the Metamorphoses and the painting of the 1610s is in the Wallraf–Richartz Museum, Cologne.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-k: A bound and crowned Christ is presented to the crowd, his torso lit against a brooding ground in the manner Rubens used to dramatize Passion scenes. The taut musculature and fall of light over the shoulders intensify the Counter-Reformation appeal to compassion.

In this intimate Lamentation, the dead Christ is supported by Saint John, who is dressed in vivid red, and the Virgin, whose green-draped figure bows over the body from the right. Rubens reduces the cast to its essential mourners, concentrating devotional intensity in the contrast of pale, lifeless flesh and richly coloured drapery. Painted circa 1614–1615, the work is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna (inv. GG 529).

An allegory of the four continents personified as river gods reclining beside their female consorts, traditionally identified with the Danube, Nile, Ganges and Rio de la Plata. Tigers, a crocodile and lush vegetation underscore the cosmographic ambition of the Vienna canvas.

A storm-drenched Ovidian landscape in which Jupiter and Mercury, sheltered by the pious Philemon and Baucis, unleash a deluge upon the surrounding valley. The boiling sky, falling trees and rain-swollen torrent show Rubens absorbing Venetian and Adam Elsheimer landscape models for cosmic moral drama.

Bishop Ambrose bars Emperor Theodosius from Milan Cathedral after the massacre at Thessalonica, a Counter-Reformation parable of clerical authority over secular power. Rubens stages the confrontation on the church steps with massed retinues, reworking a composition first treated by his Venetian model Veronese.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-l: The dead Christ lies on a sheaf of straw, his pallid body supported by a group of mourners that includes the Virgin in a dark hood, an older bearded man at left, and a young woman with loose hair at right. The sharply upturned face and foreshortened limbs intensify the grief of the surrounding figures, recalling Rubens's debt to Italian models of the Pietà. Painted 1617–1618, the work is in the Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (inv. 300).

A large, multi-figure Lamentation in which the dead Christ is laid out horizontally and surrounded by a dense group of mourners, including the Virgin, Saint John, and several other holy women and men. The warm, broadly lit composition conveys collective grief through varied expressions and gestures rather than chiaroscuro drama. Painted in 1612, the work is in the Liechtenstein Collections (inv. GE 62).

A broad Flemish countryside opens out under a sky cleared by a passing storm, a rainbow arching over fields, milkmaids and grazing cattle. Often paired with the View of Het Steen, it expresses Rubens's late identification with the land around his country house.

Roman ruins on the Palatine hill rise above figures and herds in a panoramic landscape conceived from sketches made during the artist's years in Italy. Antiquity is set in dialogue with a fertile, lived-in countryside.

Christ raises the bread at the centre of the long table while the apostles react in agitation; Judas turns toward the viewer with averted eyes. The picture concentrates on the moment of institution rather than the announcement of betrayal, in line with Counter-Reformation Eucharistic devotion.

Set in a rocky grotto with a distant fiery glow, Rubens depicts Lot flanked by his two daughters who offer him wine from an ornate golden vessel. Contrary to convention, Lot is rendered not as a passive victim but as a bearded yet physically vigorous man reaching actively toward the younger daughter. The canvas dates to circa 1610, shortly after Rubens's return from Italy, and is held at the Staatliches Museum Schwerin.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-m: The Virgin is borne aloft by a swirl of angels while the apostles cluster around her empty tomb below. The upward spiralling composition is a hallmark of Rubens's altarpieces for the Antwerp churches of the early seventeenth century.

In a wooded landscape, Mercury raises his sword to slay the sleeping Argus, who slumps at his feet exhausted. A white heifer — the transformed Io — stands to the left, the immediate object of this divine mission. Painted between 1636 and 1638, the composition draws on Ovid's Metamorphoses and exemplifies Rubens's late handling of mythological narrative in monumental outdoor settings.

Moses raises the bronze serpent on a pole as stricken Israelites writhe in the foreground, their wounds healed at a glance. The crowded, twisting figures provide a typological prefiguration of the Crucifixion familiar in Counter-Reformation imagery.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-n: This painted portrait depicts Nicolas Rubens as a young man, shown in three-quarter view wearing a broad-brimmed black hat and dark coat with a white collar, his long wavy hair falling to his shoulders. The confident bearing and direct yet composed expression distinguish it from the intimate childhood studies Rubens made of his children. The work is held at the Art Institute of Chicago (inv. 1954.299).
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-o: An aged woman shields a candle flame as a boy leans in to light his own taper from hers, the two faces modelled by the small light source. The picture belongs to the Northern tradition of nocturnal genre studies descending from Caravaggio and the Bassano workshop.

Three figures huddle in near-total darkness around a small pan of glowing coals: an old woman leans in from above while two children — one younger, one older — gaze intently at the light and warmth below. The chiaroscuro modelling of the upturned faces against the deep shadow is characteristic of the Northern nocturnal genre tradition. The painting, dated to the seventeenth century, is held at the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden.
