collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-p: Perseus, fresh from slaying the sea-monster, unbinds the nude Andromeda as putti and Pegasus crowd the rocky shore. The composition pairs heroic male armor with luminous female flesh in a swirling Baroque celebration of rescue and erotic deliverance.

Five full-length figures stand on a coastal shore beneath a cloudy sky as one of them — Peter — holds up a large fish from whose mouth a coin is to be retrieved, fulfilling the miracle of Matthew 17:27. The tall, narrow format of the panel reflects its function as an altarpiece panel in the Church of Our Lady across the river Dijle, Mechelen, for which Rubens painted it circa 1618–1619.

This close-up portrait of Clara Serena Rubens, the artist's eldest daughter, shows her as a young child with reddish-auburn hair neatly pinned, rosy cheeks, and an alert, slightly parted lips. The brisk yet affectionate handling — close in spirit to a rapid life study — is among the most intimate of Rubens's family works. Painted in 1616, it is now in the Liechtenstein Museum (inv. GE 105); Clara Serena died in 1623 at the age of twelve.

Kaspar Scioppius, the German Catholic controversialist, is shown in a three-quarter-length standing pose, wearing a dark cloak over a richly embroidered doublet with a white lace collar and holding a small object at his side. The direct, self-possessed gaze and the warm palette reflect the Venetian influence Rubens absorbed during his Italian years. Painted circa 1606, the portrait is now in the Galleria Palatina, Florence.

Ambrogio Spinola, 1st Marquis of the Balbases and commander of the Habsburg forces in the Low Countries, is portrayed in ornate gold-inlaid parade armor with a large white ruff and a red shoulder piece, his grey hair and composed expression conveying seasoned authority. Rubens, who knew the marquess personally during the Twelve Years' Truce negotiations, painted this portrait in 1625; it is now in the National Gallery Prague (inv. O 9688).
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-s: Saint Francis of Assisi kneels in ecstatic communion, his gaunt features and brown habit picked out against a darkened ground. The economy of means and devotional intensity reflect Counter-Reformation taste for affective images of penitent saints.

A workshop image of Democritus, the Greek thinker known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher, mocking the follies of humankind. His broad smile and weathered features draw on the Northern tradition of philosopher portraits revived by Rubens and his circle.

The painter, near sixty, presents himself in broad-brimmed hat, sword, and gloves — courtier and diplomat as much as artist. The dignified late self-portrait, withholding palette and brushes, asserts his ennoblement and standing among Europe's rulers.

A lean, elderly faun stands before a stone pedestal, one arm raised holding a pelt or cloth, the other hand carrying what appears to be a mask or severed head. The muscular yet weathered figure, painted by Rubens between 1636 and 1638, exemplifies the studio's engagement with antique subjects of Bacchic mythology.

Silenus slumbers in heavy intoxication while nymphs and attendants surround him amid an abundance of gold vessels, dishes, and luxurious still-life objects, a leopard resting at his side. Rubens painted this Bacchic scene in 1611, shortly after his Italian years, combining the antique subject of Silenus's drunken sleep with the lavish material culture of a princely feast. The work is held in the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna.

A chalk drawing of a crucified figure seen from below, arms extended upward and head thrown back with gaze directed to the heavens, the musculature of the torso rendered in crisp black-and-white contour and shading. Dated 1610, the study relates to Rubens's preparation for one of his major Antwerp altarpiece commissions, demonstrating his rigorous figure studies in drawn media before translating compositions to large-scale paint.

A bearded male head in strict left profile, the face deeply furrowed and lit from the left against a dark ground, with wavy grey-brown hair falling to the shoulder. Painted in 1616, the study belongs to the tradition of tronies — head studies used as reference for apostles, elders, and biblical figures in large-scale compositions. The work is held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

A sweeping Flemish landscape animated by peasants, cattle, and a laden cart making their way along a dusty road beneath a dramatic sky of breaking clouds and shafts of light. Rubens's Summer, dating to the 1620s and now at Buckingham Palace, situates the season's agricultural abundance within the long Flemish tradition of landscape painting, filling the foreground with the textures of rural life and the middle distance with a vast rolling prospect.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-t: A close head study of an aged, bearded man in strict profile, his white hair rendered with loose, fluent brushwork against a warm dark ground. The work belongs to Rubens's series of apostle heads and is held at the Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen, where it is catalogued under the broad date range of 1592 to 1640.

The infant Hercules, set to Juno's breast by Jupiter, draws milk so forcefully that the spilled stream becomes the Milky Way. Painted for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada, the canvas turns an Ovidian etiology into a swirl of cosmic drapery and divine flesh.

Moses raises the bronze serpent on a pole as Israelites writhe with snakebites below, looking up to be healed (Numbers 21). Rubens packs the foreground with anatomical contortions, a Counter-Reformation allegory of salvation through faith in the Crucified.

The dead Adonis lies outstretched on the ground while three mourning nymphs or Graces attend him, one cradling his head, as a grieving putto and a hound stand to the right. Rubens composed this Ovidian lamentation around 1614 with characteristic attention to the beauty of pale flesh against rich drapery; the work is held at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

The dead Christ is supported in the arms of a dark-robed figure — likely the Virgin — while two angels and Mary Magdalene attend in grief, the pale body dramatically lit against a storm-darkened sky. Painted in 1602 and held in the Galleria Borghese, this early Lamentation of Christ reflects Rubens's absorption of Italian models, particularly the lessons of Caravaggio and the Carracci encountered during his Roman years.

Muscular soldiers heave the cross upright on a steep diagonal, Christ's luminous body twisting against a stormy sky. Conceived for Antwerp's St. Walburga, the great triptych translates Italian heroic anatomy into a Flemish altarpiece of unprecedented physical force.

Christ's body is lowered onto the slab of anointing as the Marys and disciples crowd in grief. Rubens tightens Caravaggio's Vatican prototype into an oval of mourning figures, the dead flesh phosphorescent against the surrounding shadow.

Phaeton plummets from the chariot of the Sun as Jupiter's thunderbolt scatters the bolting horses and the Hours recoil through the zodiac. An early mythological tour de force, the picture shows Rubens already pushing Mannerist motion toward Baroque theater.

Worshippers garland a statue of Venus while putti, nymphs and satyrs dance in pagan revelry. Inspired by Titian's Worship of Venus and a passage in Philostratus, the late composition assembles Rubens's lifelong vocabulary of mythic celebration.

An aged hermit, drawn from Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, gazes upon the nude, sleeping Angelica against a dark, shadowy background. Rubens contrasts the ascetic gauntness of the clothed old man with the luminous flesh of the recumbent figure, transforming the chivalric romance into a Baroque meditation on temptation. The small panel, painted between 1626 and 1628, is held in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.

The Trojan prince Paris weighs the golden apple between Juno, Minerva and Venus while Mercury looks on. An early version of a subject Rubens revisited often, the composition arranges three nude goddesses to display Italianate disegno absorbed during his stay in Rome.

The Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier raises the dead and heals the afflicted before a toppling pagan idol, the converted crowding toward him in awe. Painted for Antwerp's Jesuit church, the altarpiece celebrates the global reach of Counter-Reformation evangelism.

Straining executioners heave the cross bearing Christ skyward in a violent diagonal of muscular labor. A late reprise of his Antwerp altarpiece, this version concentrates the drama into a tighter, more urgent gathering of bodies and tackle.

Europa clings to the white bull as he moves swiftly forward, her wind-blown drapery in red and pink behind her. This small oil sketch, dated 1636 and now in the Museo del Prado, is a modello related to Rubens's engagement with Titian's celebrated composition of the same subject, paying homage to Venetian colour in a rapid, fluid touch.

Christ hangs between the two thieves, the crosses set against a darkening sky in a tightly massed composition. Rubens compresses the Calvary scene into a vertical screen of straining bodies, a Counter-Reformation meditation on suffering and redemption.

Venus gazes at her own face in a large octagonal mirror held by a winged Cupid, while a dark-skinned attendant looks on from behind. Painted between 1614 and 1615 and now in the Liechtenstein Collection, the composition presents Venus seen from the back, her warm flesh contrasted against the cool reflective surface of the mirror, within the Venetian tradition of the toilette subject.

The Madonna and Child appear within an exuberant wreath of blossoms, painted in collaboration with the flower specialist Jan Brueghel the Elder. The conceit fuses Marian devotion with Antwerp's expertise in still life, the garland a votive offering of created beauty.

Two satyrs appear in close half-length view against a dark ground: the foreground figure, horned and wreathed, holds a bunch of white grapes and stares directly at the viewer, while the older satyr behind him drinks from a vessel with averted eyes. Painted between 1618 and 1619 and now in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich, the double tronie distils Rubens's vision of bacchic appetite into an arresting pair of bestial yet humanly knowing faces.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-v: Venus clings to the departing Adonis as he shoulders his spear and his hounds strain toward the fatal hunt. Rubens reworks Titian's Prado composition, heightening the embrace into a Baroque farewell of foreboding and tender resistance.

Rubens's own country estate near Mechelen lies under a low, golden dawn, with a hunter, hay wagon and far-flung fields stretching to the horizon. The expansive panorama, painted for personal pleasure, helped redirect Northern landscape toward atmospheric naturalism.
collection-of-beauty-peter-paul-rubens-w: An oil study of an armoured soldier, executed with the loose brushwork and ruddy palette Rubens reserved for working sketches. The figure's head and gleaming breastplate are modelled with rapid, confident strokes, capturing the swagger of a Baroque military type.

A half-length figure of a clothed woman in a dark dress with white collar and ruffled sleeves looks down at a small dark mirror held in one hand, her other hand raised to her hair. The composition, calm and interior in character, is held in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Kassel, and dated to around 1640.
collection-of-beauty-petergansevoortbyst: Peter Gansevoort, the defender of Fort Stanwix in 1777, wears the dark blue coat and gold epaulettes of a Continental general. Stuart painted the portrait in 1794, around the time Gansevoort was commissioned brigadier general of the New York militia; the canvas is now at the Munson-Williams-Proctor Arts Institute in Utica.
collection-of-beauty-philipp-otto-runge-: A portrait of the painter and writer Friedrich August von Klinkowström, Runge's close friend and a fellow figure in early German Romantic circles. The sitter is shown with a Nazarene-like clarity of contour and a steady, contemplative gaze.

Three young children of the Hülsenbeck family are depicted in a Hamburg garden dominated by tall sunflowers: the eldest stands to the right holding a hoop, the middle child brandishes a whip, and the youngest sits in a small wooden cart at left. Runge invests the scene with symbolic weight, treating childhood as a metaphysical state within his broader Romantic vision. The painting, dated 1805–06, is held at the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

A close study of a hound's head in chalk and lead, the breed's soft fur and alert eye observed with quiet precision. The drawing belongs to Runge's wider effort to ground his Romantic symbolism in patient natural observation.

Christ stretches out his hand to a sinking Peter on the Sea of Galilee, the figures reduced to clear, near-archaic outlines. Runge's interpretation of the Gospel episode reflects his ambition to fuse landscape, religion, and Romantic symbolism.

A black and white chalk drawing of the young Sophia Sieveking laid out in death, her features composed against a pale pillow. Runge made the sheet shortly before his own early death, lending its mortuary stillness an autobiographical weight.

This chalk and pencil study of 1809, now at the Hamburger Kunsthalle, shows a single nude infant kneeling among flowers and low plants, reaching towards a blossom. It is a preparatory sheet for Runge's ambitious but unfinished Great Morning, part of his cosmological Times of Day cycle, in which such child figures carry symbolic weight as embodiments of natural and spiritual renewal.

A detail from the unfinished Great Morning, showing the radiant central figure Runge devised as the embodiment of dawn within his Times of Day cycle. The hard-edged drawing and saturated colour reveal the artist's mystical, almost emblematic Romanticism.
collection-of-beauty-picabia-hera-2: Multiple female faces are superimposed in transparent contours across a ground of leaves and flowers in shades of yellow-green and blue, with hands and foliage woven throughout the composition. The work, dated around 1929, belongs to Picabia's Transparencies series, in which layered figures drawn from diverse visual sources are merged into a single ambiguous image. It is one of the series Picabia developed after his departure from the Paris avant-garde.
collection-of-beauty-picabia-stardancer: Abstract geometric shapes in red, black, grey, and white are stacked and interlocked across the surface of this 1913 watercolour, whose title — lettered at the top of the sheet — identifies the subject as a star dancer on a transatlantic liner. Painted during Picabia's crossing to New York for the Armory Show, the work translates movement into flat, interlocking forms rather than any legible figure. The source confirms it is a watercolour in a private collection.
collection-of-beauty-picture-anger-of-th: A small rowboat crowded with figures struggles through heavy swells beneath a vast, storm-torn sky; a towering wave rises on the left while broken light pierces the clouds above. Aivazovsky, who made the sea's power and human vulnerability his central subject, painted this canvas in 1886. The composition places human presence as a minor element against the overwhelming scale of the storm.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-auguste-reno: A bust-length study of Gabrielle with her chemise slipped from one shoulder, the flesh rendered in warm pinks against a sketchy ground. The sitter is Gabrielle Renard, cousin of Renoir's wife Aline and the family's nanny from 1894, who modelled often in his later years. Painted about 1907, oil on canvas.

The Comédie-Française actress Jeanne Samary is shown resting her chin on her hand, wearing a low-cut teal dress against a rosy, freely brushed ground. Renoir painted this intimate portrait in 1877, now held at the Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow; his feathery strokes give the sitter an air of warm, relaxed luminosity.

Ambroise Vollard leans over a small statuette of a kneeling nude, examining it as a connoisseur, his bald head and bulbous features softened by Renoir. The bronze is after the sculptor Aristide Maillol. Painted in 1908, oil on canvas, now in the Courtauld Gallery, London.

Charles and Georges Durand-Ruel, sons of Renoir's dealer, shown outdoors in three-piece suits against dense green foliage. Oil on canvas painted in 1882; Paul Durand-Ruel, who commissioned the double portrait, was reportedly displeased to find his sons painted out of doors. Charles holds a medallion, Georges a cigarette.

A double portrait of Renoir's friend the painter Alfred Sisley standing beside his companion, both in fashionable contemporary dress, the woman's arm through his. Painted in 1868 and now in the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum, Cologne, where it is catalogued as Das Ehepaar Sisley.

The art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel seated and contemplative, his dark coat set against a loosely brushed background. Durand-Ruel was the dealer who staked the Impressionists from the 1870s and a friend of Renoir for more than thirty years. Painted in 1910, oil on canvas.

Irène Cahen d'Anvers, daughter of a prominent Parisian banking family, is shown in three-quarter profile with long copper hair falling loosely to her waist and a blue ribbon at the back of her head. Renoir set her against a dark background of foliage and painted her in a pale blue-white dress, achieving the quiet reverie that characterises his best child portraits. The work dates to 1880 and was held in the Sammlung E.G. Bührle.

A bust-length self-portrait with unkempt hair and beard, the painter in a striped shirt and dark tie against a loosely brushed ground. Renoir made it in 1875, oil on canvas, and showed it at the second Impressionist exhibition the following year; it is now in the Clark Art Institute, Williamstown.

Two figures sit close to the bank of a river or lake, framed by overhanging foliage and dappled sunlight; a man in a straw hat faces left while a woman in lighter dress leans toward the water at right. Renoir painted this open-air scene around 1880, dissolving the surrounding vegetation into iridescent strokes of green, yellow, and violet in keeping with his Impressionist practice of that period.

Painted on the rocky beaches of Guernsey, where Renoir summered in 1883, the canvas shows small bathers playing among warm ochre boulders. The Channel light prompts a brighter, drier palette and the firmer drawing of his transitional period.

A couple dancing at an open-air ball, the woman in a red bonnet with a fan, a table of glasses behind them. Oil on canvas of 1883, Musée d'Orsay, Paris, paired with the contemporary Dance in the City. The models were Aline Charigot, later Renoir's wife, and his friend Paul Lhôte.

A nude woman holding a bow, a dead deer and an animal skin at her feet, cast as the huntress Diana. Oil on canvas, 197 by 132 cm, painted in 1867 and held by the National Gallery of Art, Washington. The model is thought to be Renoir's companion Lise Tréhot; the canvas was rejected by the 1867 Salon.

Renoir portrays his fellow Impressionist Frédéric Bazille at work before an easel, brush poised over a still life of a heron. The picture is a touching record of the early Batignolles circle, painted shortly before Bazille's death in the Franco-Prussian War.

A frieze of monumental nudes disports along a wooded bank, their crisp contours and pearly flesh marking Renoir's so-called Ingresque turn away from pure Impressionism. The picture occupied him for several years and now hangs at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Renoir's son Jean, aged fifteen, poses full-length with a borrowed gun and the family dog Bob, dressed in a jacket his father thought suited a huntsman. Painted at Les Collettes in 1910, oil on canvas, about 173 by 89 cm. The sitter later became the filmmaker Jean Renoir; the canvas is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

Renoir's friends gather on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise at Chatou, lingering over wine and fruit after a row on the Seine. The composition weaves portraiture, still life, and shimmering river light into one celebrated image of modern leisure.

A wooded landscape at La Roche-Guyon, a village on a bend of the Seine in the Val-d'Oise. Oil on canvas painted in 1887, two years after Renoir had spent a summer there working alongside Cézanne. The picture is now in the Pérez Simón collection.

Robert Nunès in a sailor suit standing before a loosely brushed beach, his father the mayor of Yport on the Normandy coast. Oil on canvas painted in 1883, when Renoir was commissioned to portray the Nunès children, now in the Barnes Foundation, Philadelphia (BF325).

A generous bouquet of spring garden flowers — peonies, lilac, iris, and wild blossoms — overflows a blue-and-white porcelain vase set on a stone ledge. Painted in 1866, the canvas belongs to an early period before Renoir's palette had fully lightened, the muted grey-green ground and dense paint surface recalling his pre-Impressionist formation. The work is held at the Fogg Museum, Harvard Art Museums.

Renoir's wife Aline stands with their eldest son Pierre, the young Jean held by a maid, and a neighbour's daughter gathered in front of a wall. Oil on canvas of 1896, catalogued BF819 in the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia. The painter set the figures close to the picture plane against a flatly brushed ground.

Renoir's view of Venice's central square dissolves the basilica's Byzantine facade into shimmering touches of pink, gold, and blue. Painted during his Italian journey, the canvas treats architecture as an Impressionist screen of light, with figures and pigeons scattered across the sunlit pavement.

A crowd under a canopy of umbrellas, a bare-headed milliner's assistant with her hatbox at the left edge. Renoir worked the canvas in two campaigns, the feathery right-hand figures about 1881 and the firmer left-hand pair around 1885, switching from cobalt to French ultramarine between them. Oil on canvas, National Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-cecile-puvis: A sleeping youth reclines beneath a pine tree at night, while three luminous allegorical female figures drift through the moonlit air above him, one reaching down with flowers or a garland. The muted, fresco-like tonalities and symbolic register are characteristic of Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, the leading French Symbolist painter of the nineteenth century. The work is known as Le Rêve (The Dream).

A young woman in a white dress sits on rocky ground, extending one arm to hold a small sprig, while behind her a broad landscape opens to reveal ruins and rows of grave crosses — an aftermath of war. Painted in 1872, the work is an allegory of Hope by Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, rendered in the pale, simplified tonalities he derived from fresco. It is housed in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
collection-of-beauty-pierre-puvis-de-cha: A gaunt fisher stands in his moored skiff while a woman gathers flowers and an infant sleeps on the bank, the scene reduced to chalky, almost frescoed planes of pale color. The austere composition and melancholic mood made the picture a touchstone for Symbolist painters and the young Picasso.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-d-a-: A teeming village square stages an allegorical joust between a barrel-riding Carnival, armed with a spit of meat, and a gaunt Lent on a church cart. Bruegel packs the panel with proverbs, Shrovetide revels, and Lenten almsgiving in a panoramic moral inventory of Netherlandish life.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-der-: The Holy Family threads a precipitous mountain path while a vast world landscape opens beneath them, with rivers, cliffs, and a shadowed pagan idol toppling on a column. Bruegel's panoramic Weltlandschaft tradition dwarfs the sacred travelers within Alpine and Flemish topographies.
collection-of-beauty-pieter-bruegel-the-: A ploughman, shepherd, and angler go about their work along a sunlit harbor while Icarus's legs vanish almost unnoticed into the sea at lower right. The composition reads as a quiet meditation on Ovid's myth and human indifference, later memorialized in Auden's poem.

Soldiers ransack a snowbound Flemish village in a transposition of Herod's biblical slaughter into the contemporary Low Countries under Spanish occupation. In the Royal Collection version many of the slain children were overpainted as bundles, geese, and game by later hands.

A line of six blind men stumbles diagonally across the panel toward a ditch, each face individually studied for the disfigurements of disease. Bruegel illustrates Christ's parable from Matthew 15 with clinical precision and an unforgiving rhythm of falling bodies.

The smaller of Bruegel's two surviving Babel panels shows the spiraling brick ziggurat looming over a coastal plain, swallowed by storm clouds at its summit. Painstaking architectural detail draws on Roman ruins Bruegel had studied in Italy.

King Nimrod inspects stonemasons in the foreground as the colossal tower rises above a Flemish port, its arcades modeled on the Colosseum. The painting marries Genesis with a sober warning about overreaching ambition, rendered with engineering exactitude.
collection-of-beauty-pinacoteca-querini-: Cardinal Angelo Maria Querini is shown seated in a gilded chair, dressed in black clerical robes with a cardinal's red garment beneath, one hand resting on an open book placed on a richly covered desk. Shelves of books behind him and the pendant cross at his collar identify him as a high-ranking ecclesiastic and bibliophile. The portrait by Bartolomeo Nazari is held at the Pinacoteca Querini Stampalia in Venice.
collection-of-beauty-plage-de-juan-les-p: From Monet's Antibes campaign on the Côte d'Azur, the canvas dissolves pines, sea and Alps into a high-keyed Mediterranean palette of pinks, mauves and turquoise. The artist complained the southern light was too bright to paint, yet returned with dozens of these luminous beach studies.
collection-of-beauty-plate-from-le-brun-: An engraved head labelled 'L'Attention' demonstrates one of the expressions catalogued by Charles Le Brun in his influential 1668 lecture on the passions of the soul. The plate comes from Carington Bowles's English edition published in London around 1785, and the impression belongs to the Wellcome Collection.
collection-of-beauty-po-vodam-1888: Christ, suffused in a luminous golden halo, walks above a dark and turbulent sea while huddled figures crouch on rocks in the foreground. Aivazovsky painted this biblical scene in 1888, weaving his career-long mastery of storm-lit marine subjects into a devotional composition he returned to several times across his career.
collection-of-beauty-polder-landscape-wi: Cattle are tended and milked by farmers in a broad Flemish meadow beneath a dramatic, cloud-filled sky. Rubens painted such pastoral subjects in the mid-1630s, around the time he acquired his country estate at Het Steen; the work is held in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich (Bavarian State Painting Collections, inv. 322).
collection-of-beauty-pont-argenteuil-mon: Sailing boats line the basin at Argenteuil beneath the highway bridge, their masts reflected in the broken blue water of the Seine. The picture belongs to the suburban riverscapes that defined the early Impressionist summers of 1872 to 1874.
collection-of-beauty-pont-neuf-1872-pier: Pedestrians and carriages cross Paris's oldest bridge under a clear summer sky, the Seine glittering between embankments. Renoir's brother Edmond reportedly delayed passersby in conversation so the painter could capture them in rapid, sun-drenched touches.
collection-of-beauty-pope-julius-ii: The aged della Rovere pope is seated in three-quarter view, beard untrimmed in mourning for the loss of Bologna, hands resting on the arms of his chair. Raphael's psychologically piercing portrait introduced a new informal type that would dominate papal imagery for over a century.
collection-of-beauty-pope-peter-pprubens: Saint Peter is shown in papal vestments holding the keys of heaven, his weathered features turned upward in devotion. Painted soon after Rubens's return from Italy, the half-length follows a Caravaggesque tradition of monumental, close-cropped apostle portraits.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-d-edmond-a: Seurat's friend, the painter Edmond Aman-Jean, is seen in profile against a darkened ground, modelled entirely in delicate hatchings of conté crayon on textured paper. The drawing was the first work Seurat exhibited at the Salon, in 1883, and it established the velvety tonal manner of his black-and-white sheets.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-d-homme-an: A bare-headed, middle-aged man in rich fantaisie drapery turns toward the viewer with an animated expression, rendered in Fragonard's characteristically rapid and fluid brushwork. Long catalogued at the Louvre as Diderot, the picture is now classed among Fragonard's figures de fantaisie, painted circa 1769 as virtuoso essays in informal costume portraiture.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-l-artis: Raphael places himself behind a foregrounded companion who turns to point outward, the two men linked by a cascade of hands and gazes. The double portrait is among the late, most psychologically intricate works produced in his Roman studio.

A bust-length self-portrait, the painter turned slightly with a heavy beard, set before a reversed landscape on the studio wall. Catalogued as FWN 434 and dated about 1875, the canvas was probably worked up in Armand Guillaumin's studio in Paris, whose own river view hangs behind the sitter.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-madame-: Henriette de Verninac, sister of Eugène Delacroix, is shown full-length, seated on a neoclassical chair in an Empire dress of white muslin with a gold-olive shawl, against a neutral grey ground. Jacques-Louis David painted this portrait in 1799; the Louvre acquired it in 1942 (RF 1942-16).
collection-of-beauty-portrait-de-victor-: The collector Victor Chocquet seen bust-length against patterned wallpaper, his greying hair and beard built up in close-keyed strokes. Chocquet, a customs official who amassed dozens of Impressionist canvases, was introduced to Cézanne by Renoir in 1875; the portrait dates from about 1876 to 1877.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-man-1: A bearded sitter in a dark coat is shown in profile, seated in a red chair, one hand resting in his lap, against a muted grey-blue ground. Edgar Degas painted this portrait in 1877; the work measures 79 by 59 cm and is held at the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute, Williamstown.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-man-a: Half-length portrait of an ecclesiastic in dark robes, his hand resting on a closed volume. Vasari identifies the sitter as a Canon of Pisa Cathedral and close friend of the painter, credited with helping Andrea secure his final commissions before his death in 1530.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-monk-: A young, bearded man in a dark brown habit is shown bust-length, his face lit directly against an earthy brown ground, meeting the viewer's gaze with quiet intensity. Rubens made such character studies as preparatory heads for his larger altarpieces, and this example is held in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (inv. 48.599).
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-a-woman: A bust-length likeness of a woman against a neutral ground, her face modelled with the smooth finish Boilly cultivated for small cabinet portraits. Oil on canvas, 22.2 by 17.5 cm, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Boilly produced hundreds of these compact heads for a Parisian middle-class clientele.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-alexand: A young girl in a teal silk dress holds a pink flower while resting her hand on a wooden birdcage containing a small dark bird. Attributed to François Boucher and dated 1749, the portrait depicts Alexandrine Le Normant d'Étiolles, daughter of Madame de Pompadour, painted during the period when Boucher was the family's favoured artist.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ann-for: Ann Ford sits in a fashionable Bath drawing room with her English guitar across her lap and a viola da gamba propped beside her chair. Painted in 1760 shortly after Gainsborough settled in Bath, the portrait celebrates Ford as a professional musician, a calling unusual for a woman of her class and one her father had tried to suppress.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-dr-will: Two King Charles spaniels owned by the anatomist Dr William Hunter sit alert on a stone ledge against a wooded background. Oil on canvas of around 1770, the picture is among the earliest known works by Gilbert Stuart, painted in his teens in Newport before he left for Scotland.

Two white-and-brown spotted spaniels stretch beneath a Newport Chippendale mahogany tea table, the larger asleep facing left and the smaller looking out at the viewer. Painted by the young Gilbert Stuart in Newport around 1770, the canvas is among the earliest surviving works by the future portraitist of George Washington.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-george-: This bust-length portrait shows George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham, in a dark doublet with a lace collar and the blue sash of the Order of the Garter. Long regarded as a later copy of a lost Rubens, dendrochronological and technical analysis of the panel subsequently confirmed an attribution to Rubens's studio, dating the support to the 1620s. The painting hung for generations at Pollok House before the attribution was revised.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-henri-m: The painter Henri Michel-Lévy stands in his studio leaning against his own canvases, a slack mannequin collapsed on the floorboards beside an open paintbox. Degas exhibited the 1878 portrait, now at the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon, at the fourth Impressionist exhibition under the title Artist in his Studio.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ida-rub: The dancer Ida Rubinstein reclines nude on a strip of blue cloth, her elongated limbs suggesting the flat profile of an ancient relief. Valentin Serov painted her in 1910 following her celebrated appearances in Diaghilev's Ballets Russes seasons, where she performed in Cléopâtre (1909) and Schéhérazade (1910). A green drape coils across the lower composition, its saturated colour contrasting with the spare, sandy ground.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-ivan-mo: The Moscow textile magnate Ivan Morozov sits at a table, his hands clasped before him, while a brilliantly coloured Matisse still life fills the wall behind his shoulder. Valentin Serov painted the portrait in 1910, the year before his own death; Morozov's renowned collection of French modern paintings was nationalised in 1918 and forms a core part of what is now held in Moscow's Pushkin Museum.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-la-faye: A bust portrait of Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, the officer who served in the American and French revolutions. Oil on canvas, dated 1788, formerly attributed to Henri-Pierre Danloux before being given to Boilly. The sitter is shown in civilian dress against a plain ground.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-margare: A half-length portrait of Margaret Gainsborough, née Burr, the artist's wife, shows her in a dark blue velvet shawl over a gold-brown dress with white lace at the throat. Gainsborough painted the canvas in 1778 with characteristically free brushwork, the features carefully observed against the loosely rendered drapery. The work is held by the Samuel Courtauld Trust at the Courtauld Gallery, London.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-mrs-the: Frances Deering Wentworth, painted at twenty in oil on canvas, holds a flying squirrel by a chain in a gesture borrowed from Copley's Pelham portrait of the same year. Married first to Theodore Atkinson Jr. and later to Governor John Wentworth, she sat to Copley in 1765 in Boston.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-peder-s: Tuxen's 1904 full-length portrait shows his Skagen colleague Peder Severin Krøyer standing on a sandy beach in a white summer suit and hat, a walking stick in one hand and what appears to be an artist's bag slung over his arm. The North Sea stretches behind him under a clear sky. The painting is held at the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest (inv. 191.B).
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-princes: The young princess is depicted as Iris, barefoot and airborne amid stormy clouds, a length of golden gauze billowing from her shoulder while she extends one arm as if pointing the way of the rainbow. Vigée Le Brun completed the large canvas in 1793 in Vienna, during her years of exile from revolutionary France. The work exemplifies the artist's synthesis of Neoclassical mythological allegory with the elegant portraiture of her royal and aristocratic clientele.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-sophia-: Sophia Shuvalova (1829–1912), later Countess Bobrinskaya, is shown in a white off-shoulder lace dress, holding a red flower against a lush garden background with trees and a bridge glimpsed beyond. Karl Bryullov painted the portrait in 1849, at a time when he was living abroad for his health, a few years before his death in Manziana in 1852.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-the-art: An early portrait by the teenage Vigée Le Brun shows her younger brother Étienne in elegant attire, his open expression rendered with the precocious assurance that would soon win her royal commissions. The handling already displays the porcelain finish and Rococo grace of her mature manner.
collection-of-beauty-portrait-of-the-wri: Maxim Gorky leans forward in a tieless dark shirt, his thin moustache and untidy hair signalling the workman writer he cultivated as a public persona. Serov painted the portrait in 1905, the year of the first Russian revolution, in which Gorky was briefly imprisoned for revolutionary agitation.
collection-of-beauty-portret-van-etienne: A three-quarter bust of a man in a blue-grey work jacket and matching cap, rendered with the short, hatched strokes Van Gogh absorbed from Seurat and Signac during his Paris years. The sitter, identified as Étienne-Lucien Martin, gazes slightly to the side against a cool blue-green ground. The portrait dates from 1887 and is held at the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (inv. s0125V1962).
collection-of-beauty-portret-van-willem-: William II, Prince of Orange, stands in full armour with a commander's baton beside his English wife Mary Stuart on a balcony, both shown full-length. Painted in 1647 for the Stadholder's court, the double portrait belongs to the Rijksmuseum (SK-A-871) and helped fix Honthorst's reputation as the dynasty's preferred image-maker.
collection-of-beauty-pozzi-samuel-par-sa: The celebrated Parisian gynecologist Samuel Pozzi stands full length in a flame-red dressing gown, fingers tugging at his collar and sash. Sargent's bravura essay in monochrome scarlet was painted in the sitter's own apartment and announced the young American's arrival in Parisian society.
collection-of-beauty-prado-los-desastres: Plate 4 of the Disasters of War, captioned 'The women give courage'. Goya shows female combatants resisting French troops during the Peninsular War, the etching and aquatint biting through the page in his characteristically stark contrasts of black and gnawed white.

Plate 46 of the Disasters of War, 'This is bad'. A friar is set upon amid scattered bodies, the scene drawn with the cramped, shallow space and bitten line that give the series its grim moral force. The plates were withheld until decades after Goya's death.

Plate 47 of the Disasters of War, captioned 'This is how it happened'. A robed figure kneels prostrate before a barred enclosure while armed men press in from above, the compressed space and harsh contrasts typical of Goya's documentary etching style. Part of the 80-print series created between 1810 and 1820 and held at the Museo del Prado, Madrid, it was not published until 1863.
collection-of-beauty-prayer-in-the-mosqu: Worshippers stand and prostrate themselves in prayer within a large colonnaded mosque interior, its striped arches and soaring nave rendered with Gérôme's characteristic precision. Pigeons wheel among the hanging lamps overhead. Painted in 1871, the work reflects Gérôme's direct study of Egyptian architecture and Islamic religious practice during his repeated travels in the region.
collection-of-beauty-prayers-at-sunset-u: Worshippers gather beneath the arches of a domed pavilion rising directly from the lake at Udaipur, its pale stone and gilded dome reflected in the deep blue water below. Bartlett's 1919 woodblock print, now in the Honolulu Academy of Arts, belongs to his Indian series and employs the flat areas of colour and atmospheric light characteristic of the shin-hanga movement.
collection-of-beauty-print-the-flight-in: An engraving showing the Virgin and Child on the donkey under a date palm, with angels shaking down its fruit while Joseph gathers the dates. Schongauer's fine, controlled burin work and tender narrative detail set the model for later northern printmaking, including the young Dürer.
collection-of-beauty-procesion-de-pascua: A vast religious procession winds across a sunburnt steppe, sweeping clergy, peasants, gendarmes, and crippled pilgrims into a single dust-clouded cross-section of imperial Russian society. Repin's panoramic canvas is a touchstone of Peredvizhniki social realism.
collection-of-beauty-promenade-sur-la-fa: A solitary figure stands on a grassy clifftop above the Normandy coast near Sainte-Adresse, a church visible to the left and a grey-green Channel stretching to the horizon. Painted in 1867, the canvas belongs to the Matsuoka Museum of Art, Tokyo, and reflects Monet's sustained engagement with the coastal landscape around his family's summer retreat at Le Havre.
collection-of-beauty-purfleet-and-the-es: Several vessels navigate a choppy reach of the Thames at Purfleet: a three-masted ship at left, sailing barges at centre, a hoy to the right, and a small rowboat with figures in the foreground. Painted in 1808, Turner's oil on canvas captures the heavy drama of an approaching storm set against patches of pale breaking sky, the flat Essex shore just visible in the distance.
collection-of-beauty-pythagoras-advocati: Rubens depicts the Greek philosopher gesturing toward a heap of fruit and grain as he urges his listeners to abstain from meat. The composition draws on Ovid's Metamorphoses, with abundant still-life passages painted in collaboration with Frans Snyders.
collection-of-beauty-qian-xuan-early-aut: A handscroll in ink and color on paper showing dragonflies, frogs, and aquatic plants beside a pond. Qian Xuan was a scholar-painter of the late Song and early Yuan, and the work pairs close natural observation with the lyric reserve of literati painting.
collection-of-beauty-quai-du-louvre-1867: An early Parisian cityscape, painted from a balcony of the Louvre overlooking the Seine. Bustling figures, carriages, and the dome of the Pantheon are rendered with the high vantage and bright daylight that anticipate Monet's mature Impressionist manner.
collection-of-beauty-quentin-matsys-a-gr: An elderly woman in a horned headdress and low-cut Burgundian bodice gazes from the frame, her features caricatured in a spirit of satirical grotesque. Painted around 1513 by Quinten Metsys and now in the National Gallery, London, the panel is traditionally identified as a pendant to a portrait of an old man and became the source for John Tenniel's Ugly Duchess in his illustrations to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
collection-of-beauty-quinten-massys-the-: The Virgin sits on a gilt Gothic throne holding the Christ Child, who clasps a book, while two angel musicians flank them at ground level and two more hover above in adoration. Painted between 1493 and 1497, the panel exemplifies the refined Flemish devotional mode Quinten Metsys established as Antwerp's leading master.
collection-of-beauty-quinten-metsys-head: An elderly bearded man in a plain, coarse garment turns in three-quarter view, his deeply furrowed brow and creased skin recorded with close physiognomic attention. Painted around 1525, the panel belongs to Metsys's late interest in expressive character heads, paralleling his more overtly grotesque caricature studies.
collection-of-beauty-rachel-strong-by-l-: Léon Bakst's 1924 portrait shows Rachel Strong — described in sources as the future Countess Henri de Buazhelen — standing outdoors in a dark dress with a white wrap, a cane in hand and a dog at her side. The golden-ochre landscape behind her reflects the warm palette of Bakst's late society portraiture.
collection-of-beauty-raffaello-madonna-c: The Virgin in a red dress and green mantle holds the Christ Child against a low Umbrian horizon, with distant buildings and a tower visible at the right. Known as the Small Cowper Madonna for its nineteenth-century English owner, this panel of around 1505 is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-raffaello-sanzio-ri: A portrait of the young Florentine banker Bindo Altoviti, who turns over his shoulder to meet the viewer's gaze. The cool palette, soft modeling, and elegant turn of the head exemplify Raphael's late Roman portrait style.
collection-of-beauty-raimondi-lucretia-s: An engraving after a design by Raphael showing the Roman matron Lucretia about to plunge a dagger into her breast. Raimondi's burin work helped establish reproductive printmaking as a vehicle for disseminating Italian Renaissance invention across Europe.
collection-of-beauty-raphael-fire-in-the: A fresco in the Vatican's Stanza dell'Incendio del Borgo, depicting the miraculous extinguishing of a fire in Rome's Borgo district by Pope Leo IV. Heroic nudes and a fleeing Aeneas-like figure carrying his father give the scene a deliberately classical cast.
collection-of-beauty-raphael-saint-georg: Saint George on a white horse drives his lance into the dragon while the rescued princess kneels in prayer at the right. Painted around 1506 as a diplomatic gift from Guidobaldo da Montefeltro to Henry VII of England, the small panel is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-raphael-the-alba-ma: In this tondo of around 1510, the Virgin sits in an open Italian landscape, supporting the Christ Child who holds a slender cross while the young Baptist looks on from the left. The Alba Madonna is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-raphael-the-miracul: A cartoon for the Sistine Chapel tapestry series commissioned by Pope Leo X, showing Christ blessing Peter and Andrew as their nets break under the weight of fish. The kneeling apostle and the cranes on the shore are among the most studied figures in Renaissance art.
collection-of-beauty-raphael-young-man-c: A red-chalk drawing of Aeneas carrying Anchises from burning Troy, made as a study for the figure group in the Fire in the Borgo fresco. The athletic torsion and confident hatching show Raphael's response to antique sculpture and to Michelangelo.
collection-of-beauty-reception-du-grand-: Louis XIV welcomes the Prince de Condé on the grand staircase at Versailles, the victorious general bowing as courtiers look on. Gérôme reconstructs the seventeenth-century scene with archaeological precision, marshalling marble, brocade and ceremonial hierarchy in the polished academic style he made famous.
collection-of-beauty-recoveredgleizes: A Cubist landscape of Meudon with a small figure threaded through faceted houses, trees, and a winding path. Gleizes exhibited Le Chemin (Paysage à Meudon) at the 1911 Salon des Indépendants, the show where the Salle 41 hang first announced Cubism as a public movement.
collection-of-beauty-red-cavalry-riding: A thin band of red horsemen gallops along the horizon against a vast pale sky, underpinned by bold horizontal stripes of red, black, green, blue, and cream — a Suprematist landscape painted between 1928 and 1932 by Kazimir Malevich. The work entered the State Russian Museum in Leningrad and stands as a rare bridge between Malevich's abstract language and recognisable Soviet iconography.
collection-of-beauty-red-fuji-southern-w: Better known as Red Fuji, this woodblock print captures the volcano flushed warm by dawn light during the late summer southerlies. Banded clouds and a near-abstract triangular silhouette make it a touchstone of the Thirty-six Views series.
collection-of-beauty-redoute-flowers01: A spray of cultivated flowers drawn life-size against an empty ground, each bloom and leaf described with botanical precision. A plate after Redouté, the botanist-painter attached to the Jardin des Plantes and to the Empress Joséphine's garden at Malmaison. Colour stipple engraving finished by hand, in the technique used throughout his folios.
collection-of-beauty-remaining-snow-at-i: A shin-hanga woodblock print of the wooded park at Inokashira in Tokyo, with patches of late snow lingering beside dark water. Hasui treats the season with the muted palette and atmospheric stillness that defined his landscape practice.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-abraham-e: An angel seizes Abraham's arm at the moment the knife slips from his grasp, while Isaac lies bound and bare-chested on the altar below. Signed and dated 1635, the canvas in the Hermitage in St Petersburg depicts the binding of Isaac at its most violent instant, with the blade caught in mid-fall — one of Rembrandt's most kinetic early narrative compositions.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-belsazar: The Babylonian king recoils as a glowing Hebrew inscription, MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN, appears on the wall during his blasphemous feast. Rembrandt stages the moment with theatrical lighting, overturned vessels, and a sumptuous gold-embroidered cloak.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-christ-in: The disciples struggle with sail and rigging on a heaving boat as Christ is roused to calm the sea. Rembrandt's only known seascape, it was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 1990 and remains missing.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-christus-: An etching, in its later state, of Pilate presenting the bound Christ to a crowd that demands his crucifixion. Rembrandt scraped away the foreground onlookers and replaced them with shadowed arches, intensifying the confrontation between judge and viewer.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-de-poolse: A young horseman in Eastern European costume rides a pale grey mount through a darkening landscape, bow and quiver at his back and a sabre at his side, with a fortified structure rising on the hill behind him. Attributed to Rembrandt and dated to around 1655, the canvas in the Frick Collection is among his most debated late works, its subject oscillating in scholarship between portrait, allegory, and historical type.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-girl-in-a: A young woman leans out of a painted frame, her hands resting on the illusory ledge in a sly play on the picture's own boundary. The trompe l'oeil device reflects Rembrandt's interest in animating the threshold between image and viewer.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-harmensz-: Andromeda stands chained to a rock face, her arms raised above her head and bound at the wrists, her lower body draped in white cloth, while water and reeds are visible in the distance behind her. Perseus and the sea monster are absent from the composition, which Rembrandt treats as an intimate nude study rather than a heroic confrontation. Painted around 1630 and held at the Mauritshuis in The Hague, the small panel is one of his earliest mythological works.

The philosopher Aristotle, in black robes and a gold chain bearing a portrait of Alexander, lays his hand on a marble bust of Homer. Commissioned in 1653 by the Sicilian collector Don Antonio Ruffo for 500 florins, the canvas was the first painting of a series the patron assembled around the philosopher and now hangs at the Metropolitan Museum.

Bathsheba sits naked after her bath, holding the letter from King David that summons her to him, her old servant drying her feet at the side. Signed and dated 1654, the canvas in the Louvre uses the body of Rembrandt's companion Hendrickje Stoffels for the biblical heroine caught between duty and complicity.
The evangelist pauses over his manuscript as an angel leans in to whisper at his ear. Rembrandt models both faces with a quiet warmth, treating divine inspiration as an intimate exchange.

Christ stands at the centre with the sick crowded to his right and parents pressing children toward him on the left, the dark archway opening onto Lazarus the leper. Known as the Hundred Guilder Print for the unprecedented price it fetched in Rembrandt's lifetime, the etching combines drypoint and engraving to compress several episodes from Matthew 19 into one nocturnal scene.

An elderly man, identified as St Bartholomew by the knife of his martyrdom resting on the surface before him, raises one hand to his chin in pensive contemplation. Signed and dated 1661, the canvas in the J. Paul Getty Museum is painted with the loose, expressive brushwork of Rembrandt's late period, giving the figure a worn, deeply human presence.

Aged Jacob, propped on his deathbed, crosses his arms to lay his right hand on the younger Ephraim while Joseph tries to redirect it, his wife Asenath watching at the side. Signed and dated 1656, the canvas in Schloss Wilhelmshöhe at Kassel reframes the Genesis scene as a tender domestic gathering rather than a formal blessing.

The aged prophet leans on a sumptuous gold vessel, head in hand, while the city of Jerusalem smokes in the dim distance behind him. Signed and dated 1630, the panel in the Rijksmuseum is among Rembrandt's earliest narrative pictures to wed Caravaggesque chiaroscuro to a deeply introspective biblical subject.

Lucretia stands in a white shift stained with blood, a dagger in one hand and a bell pull in the other, her eyes lowered in the moment after the self-inflicted wound. Signed and dated 1666, the canvas at the Minneapolis Institute of Art was the second and more restrained of Rembrandt's two paintings of the Roman heroine.

Long known as The Jewish Bride, the painting shows a couple in tender embrace, often identified with Old Testament pairs such as Isaac and Rebecca. Built up with thickly trowelled pigment, the gold sleeve and ruby skirt are among Rembrandt's most celebrated passages of paint.

The ragged son kneels before his aged father, who lays trembling hands on the bowed shoulders while elder figures watch from the shadowed background. Painted in Rembrandt's final years around 1668, the canvas now hangs in the Hermitage, its thick impasto and warm umber light marking the late style of his last decade in Amsterdam.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-harmenszo: A chalk drawing of a tame Asian elephant, the wrinkled hide rendered with close hatching and smudged strokes, the trunk extended as the animal walks. Signed and dated 1637, the sheet is one of several studies Rembrandt made of Hansken, a celebrated travelling elephant who visited Amsterdam and other Dutch cities during the 1630s.

Rembrandt presents himself at forty-six in a dark cloak and broad flat beret, gazing out with composed gravity against a neutral background. Painted in 1652 and now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, the large canvas belongs to the series of self-portraits that spans his entire career and marks a period of mounting financial pressure before the bankruptcy proceedings of 1656.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-lapidatio: Saul looks on from horseback as a knot of attackers raise stones above the kneeling deacon, who turns his face toward a beam of heavenly light. Signed and dated 1625, the canvas is Rembrandt's earliest documented painting, completed at nineteen in Leiden and now held by the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-portrait-: A half-length figure of a young woman in a rich crimson robe, her right hand raised and her left arm resting, her gaze directed slightly downward in warm, raking light. Traditionally identified as Hendrickje Stoffels, Rembrandt's companion in his later years, and painted around 1656, the picture now in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin belongs to a series of intimate figure studies from his mature period.

A portrait of the artist's wife shortly after their marriage, dressed in fanciful pastoral costume with a feathered hat. Rembrandt's warm light glances across pearls, embroidery, and her unguarded expression.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-portret-v: A bust-length portrait of a middle-aged woman in a black gown and wide pleated white ruff collar, set within a painted oval and turned slightly toward the viewer. Signed and dated 1634, the panel in the Rijksmuseum depicts Haesje Jacobsdr. van Cleyburg and is the pendant to a portrait of Dirck Pesser, together among the Amsterdam burgher commissions that established Rembrandt as the city's leading portraitist.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-scholar-a: A bearded scholar in a fur-trimmed gown and black cap sits at a writing table, quill in hand over an open book, caught in a moment of concentration. Painted in 1641 and now in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin, the canvas is the pendant to The Girl in a Picture Frame and is among the few Rembrandt pairs to have survived together.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-susanna-a: The chaste Susanna shrinks as the two elders intrude upon her bath, drawn from the Book of Daniel. Rembrandt focuses on her vulnerability and the elders' menace, modeling flesh and drapery with a soft, glowing chiaroscuro.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-the-abduc: Europa is borne away across the water on the back of Jupiter disguised as a white bull, while her companions react in alarm on the wooded shore beside an ornate carriage and white horses. Painted in 1632 and now in the J. Paul Getty Museum, the canvas brings an Ovidian subject into the idiom of a Dutch landscape, with a misty harbour and city walls receding into the left distance.
Rembrandt reimagines the classical myth as a startled, urinating infant snatched skyward by Jupiter's eagle. The unsettling realism breaks sharply with the idealized Italian tradition of the subject.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-the-anato: A group portrait of the Amsterdam Surgeons' Guild gathered around the dissected forearm of an executed criminal. Tulp's demonstration of the flexor tendons and the differentiated reactions of his colleagues turn a guild commission into a study of attention.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-the-artis: A small early panel showing a painter, dwarfed by an enormous panel on his easel, contemplating his work from across a bare studio. The image foregrounds thought rather than craft, framing painting as a fundamentally mental activity.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-the-windm: An etching of a stout post mill rising above a bastion, probably the bulwark known as 'Het Blauwhoofd' on the Amstel, etched by Rembrandt van Rijn in 1641. The composition places the mill and its adjoining low buildings close to the picture plane, with open countryside stretching behind. Rembrandt's drypoint reinforcements give the brickwork and timber a characteristic grainy luminosity prized by collectors of his prints.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-van-rijn-: Bust-length self-portrait of the painter facing right, wearing a gleaming steel gorget over a white collar and gazing back at the viewer. Long catalogued as a Rembrandt, the panel in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, was reassigned by the Rembrandt Research Project to a Leiden studio assistant copying a lost prototype of about 1629.

A bearded man in furred coat and a tall fur cap, a heavy gold chain across his chest, turning to meet the viewer's eye. Signed and dated 1637, the panel in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, belongs to Rembrandt's series of tronies of sitters in exotic and Eastern European costume rather than to commissioned portraiture.

A tronie, or character study, of an elderly bearded man in a fur cap and wide fur-collared coat, painted by Rembrandt van Rijn in 1630. The face is shown in three-quarter view, the light falling across deeply creased skin while the shaggy fur textures are rendered with close attention to surface variety. Works of this type — expressive head studies of anonymous figures in exotic costume — were a specialism of Rembrandt's early career.

Rembrandt van Rijn gazes outward in this 1642 self-portrait wearing a black flat cap and dark fur-trimmed coat, a gold chain visible at the chest. The face is lit from the upper left against a neutral grey-green ground. RCIN 404120 in the Royal Collection, the panel is among the most composed of Rembrandt's mid-career self-portraits.

Rembrandt's son Titus is shown in the brown habit and cowl of a Franciscan friar, his face turned downward in quiet introspection. Painted in 1660 and now in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, the picture employs the genre of the tronie to cast the young man in a devotional role rather than as a conventional portrait.

A late self-portrait of 1659, now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, in which Rembrandt faces the viewer in a dark beret and dark coat. The face, painted with broad and searching brushwork, records the accumulated marks of age with unsentimental directness. The painting is one of several large self-portraits from the artist's final decade in which he positioned himself with the gravitas of an Old Master.

A windmill stands silhouetted against a turbulent, luminous sky on a high earthen rampart above a quiet river. Long read as a brooding emblem of Dutch identity, the painting fuses topographical record with charged atmosphere.

An early self-portrait drawing of Rembrandt van Rijn, circa 1628–1629, in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Executed in pen, ink, and wash, the small work shows the young artist's curly-haired head in three-quarter view with energetic, searching line work. The informal medium and spontaneous handling distinguish it from the more finished self-portrait etchings and paintings of the same years.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-winterlan: A small winter landscape of 1646, now in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden, showing figures in a frost-bound village setting with bare trees and low farm buildings beneath a pale, luminous sky. The thinly brushed surface and cool, silvery palette are unusual among Rembrandt's works, placing this panel in a distinctly Dutch tradition of winter landscape painting.
collection-of-beauty-rembrandt-zelfportr: A self-portrait from the artist's later years, in which he sits frontally with a mahlstick and palette implied by his pose. Broad, loaded brushwork records a lined face that meets the viewer with sober self-knowledge.
collection-of-beauty-rembrant-self-portr: Rembrandt at fifty-four faces the viewer in a dark cap and brown jerkin, the face built up in thick, scraped layers of paint. Signed and dated 1660 and now in the Louvre, the canvas was painted the year he left his bankrupt house on the Jodenbreestraat for a smaller dwelling on the Rozengracht.
collection-of-beauty-remigius-van-leempu: Remigius van Leemput's 1667 oil copy of Holbein's lost dynastic mural for the Whitehall Privy Chamber shows Henry VIII standing in the foreground left and Jane Seymour in the foreground right, with Henry VII and Elizabeth of York disposed behind them flanking a central inscribed plinth. Painted for Charles II, the canvas is now in the Royal Collection (RCIN 405750) and is the primary record of Holbein's original composition.
collection-of-beauty-renoir-a-box-at-the: Two women in a theatre box, one in black lace resting her arm on the red velvet rail, the younger in white holding pink roses. Renoir reworked an earlier portrait into this image of spectators in 1880, oil on canvas, now in the Clark Art Institute, Williamstown.
collection-of-beauty-renoir-by-bazille: A portrait of the painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir seated with his knees drawn up, in a dark jacket and blue cravat. Oil on canvas, 62 by 51 cm, painted in 1867 and held by the Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Bazille and Renoir shared a studio that year and exchanged portraits.
collection-of-beauty-renoir-jeune-fille-: An intimate domestic scene of a young woman combing her hair, a recurring subject in Renoir's later years. The soft, feathery handling of flesh and fabric reflects his shift away from strict Impressionist plein-air practice toward a warmer, more classicizing manner influenced by Renaissance art.
collection-of-beauty-renoir-joseph-duran: Joseph Durand-Ruel, eldest son of Renoir's dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, shown as a young man against a leafy ground. Oil on canvas painted in 1882, the year Renoir also portrayed Joseph's younger brothers Charles and Georges. Joseph (1862 to 1928) went on to run the family gallery.
collection-of-beauty-renoir-pierre-augus: A bustling Sunday afternoon at a Montmartre dance garden, where dappled sunlight filters through the trees onto crowds of working-class Parisians. Renoir's loose, broken brushwork captures shifting light and lively conversation, treating modern leisure as a worthy subject for monumental painting.
collection-of-beauty-renoirgarden: A woman shaded by a parasol stands amid blossoming flowerbeds, her figure dissolving into the surrounding foliage. Renoir uses fragmented, comma-like brushstrokes and unmodulated touches of pure colour to fuse figure and garden into a single shimmering field of sunlight.
collection-of-beauty-repin-studying-exam: A student in uniform cap sits at a desk by a window, chin resting pensively on his hand while another figure reclines on a couch in the background. Painted in 1864, the work is an early genre study by Ilya Repin that captures the mood of examination preparation with careful tonal observation and controlled interior light.
collection-of-beauty-repin-turf-bench: Repin's wife Vera Alexeyevna, their daughters Vera and Nadya, and members of the Shevtsov family are gathered on a turf bench beneath leafy trees in an open-air setting. Painted in 1876, the work adapts the conventions of Russian realism to a relaxed plein-air group portrait bathed in warm summer light.
collection-of-beauty-reply-of-the-zaporo: A preparatory oil sketch for Repin's celebrated history painting, showing Cossacks erupting in raucous laughter as they dictate an obscene reply to the Ottoman sultan. The looser handling here preserves the immediacy and unbridled humour that the finished canvas would carry forward.
collection-of-beauty-reservist-of-the-fi: Cubo-Futurist fragments of a soldier's ear, moustache and cap collide with pasted printed paper, a postage stamp and a real thermometer affixed to the canvas. Malevich produced this assemblage in the autumn-winter of 1914 at 53.7 by 44.8 centimetres; it entered the Museum of Modern Art, New York, after the Berlin works left in Hugo Häring's care were acquired in 1935.
collection-of-beauty-retrato-de-juan-par: Velázquez painted this portrait of Juan de Pareja — his enslaved assistant and a painter of Moorish descent — in Rome in 1650 as a demonstration of his skill. The sitter's dignified bearing is rendered in a restrained palette of dark olive, grey, and brown, the face emerging with remarkable presence from the plain neutral background. Now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (inv. 1971.86), the portrait was exhibited at the Pantheon in Rome before Velázquez freed Pareja.
collection-of-beauty-retrato-de-la-espos: Elsbeth Binzenstock, Holbein's wife, sits with their children Philipp and Katharina, her face worn and watchful. Painted shortly after Holbein's 1528 return to Basel from his first English sojourn, the picture is identified through the Amerbach inventory of 1587 and now hangs in the Kunstmuseum Basel.
collection-of-beauty-retrato-del-papa-in: A famously unflinching state portrait of the pope, whose shrewd, suspicious gaze emerges from a cascade of crimson and white. Velázquez orchestrates a near-monochrome of vermilions and rose tones, using fluid brushwork to render lace, silk and satin with startling immediacy.
collection-of-beauty-reunion-de-famille-: Ten of the painter's relatives gathered on a shaded terrace at the family estate of Méric near Montpellier, most of them looking out at the viewer. Oil on canvas, 152 by 230 cm, painted in 1867 and held by the Musée d'Orsay, Paris, under inventory RF 2749. Bazille reworked the canvas before showing it at the Salon of 1868.
collection-of-beauty-reverend-robert-wal: A Church of Scotland minister glides across a frozen Edinburgh loch in elegant profile, arms folded against the chill. The silhouetted black figure on pale ice and misty hills became an emblem of the Scottish Enlightenment and a touchstone of Scottish national painting.
collection-of-beauty-ritratto-della-fami: Carl Joseph Begas assembled his extended family — including his wife, multiple children, and other relatives — in a spacious domestic interior for this large group portrait, painted in 1821. The figures are arranged across the room in animated domestic activity: a woman sews, a young woman plays guitar, children attend to a dog, and the father stands at centre holding a conductor's baton. Visible through an open window at right is a Gothic church tower.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-191: Faceted Parisian rooftops and the silhouette of the Eiffel Tower dissolve into a grid of prismatic colour. Painted across 1911-12 and now at the Guggenheim, Window on the City No. 3 belongs to Delaunay's Fenêtres series, the first sustained experiment in what Apollinaire would name Orphism.

A monumental synthesis combining the three Graces, the Seine and the Eiffel Tower into a single panorama of modern Paris. Delaunay fragments the city into faceted Cubist planes while introducing the prismatic colour rhythms that would define his Orphist style.

Cardiff rugby players leap for the ball beneath a Ferris wheel, an aeroplane, and a luminous advertising hoarding for Astra. Oil on canvas, 326 x 208 cm, the picture entered the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris as the largest of Delaunay's three Équipe de Cardiff variants from 1912-13.

A nude at her dressing table dissolves into wheeling discs of pure colour, the mirror and figure interpenetrating. Delaunay painted the 140 by 142 centimetre canvas in 1915 during his Iberian exile from the war; it is held by the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris and belongs to his Orphist series exploring simultaneous contrasts.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-193: Concentric arcs and rotating disc forms in bold primary and secondary colours fill this large canvas, painted in 1938 as a mural decoration for the Salon des Tuileries. The composition exemplifies Delaunay's mature Orphist language of simultaneous colour contrast, here brought to a monumental decorative scale. The work is held by the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-aut: Delaunay presents himself in a dark jacket with a patterned cravat against an animated background of bold colour strokes, painted between 1905 and 1906. The broad, unblended colour planes and vivid chromatic contrasts show the influence of Fauvism rather than Divisionism, marking an early stage of his exploration of colour relationships before his shift toward the Orphist work of the following decade.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-der: An early treatment of the iron tower that would obsess Delaunay for decades, viewed from below and toppling against a turbulent sky. The fractured planes and sharp diagonals translate Cubist analysis into a celebration of modern engineering.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-eif: Painted at the height of Delaunay's Cubist phase, the tower lurches and splinters as if seen simultaneously from multiple vantage points. Surrounding buildings collapse inward, dramatising the giddy modern experience of urban scale.

Delaunay shows the Eiffel Tower from a vertiginous overhead perspective, its ironwork base spread across a mosaic of green parkland and yellow pathways below. Painted in 1922 and now in the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, the canvas belongs to the series *La Tour Eiffel et Jardin du Champ de Mars*, in which Delaunay moved beyond his earlier Cubist fragmentation toward flatter, more geometric forms and vivid contrasting colour. The aerial viewpoint transforms the monument into an abstract plan embedded in the lush grounds of the Champ de Mars.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-jea: A close-up divisionist portrait of the painter Jean Metzinger, his face built from dense rectangular patches of green, yellow, violet, and pink applied in the manner of Neo-Impressionist pointillism. The background is a mosaic of multicoloured strokes, and the sitter faces the viewer directly. Painted by Robert Delaunay in 1906, the work demonstrates the artist's engagement with Chevreul's colour theory in the years before either painter turned to Cubism.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-l-h: A pre-Cubist portrait of fellow painter Jean Metzinger, holding a single tulip against a vivid mosaic of pure colour. The divisionist touch and saturated complementaries reveal Delaunay's debt to Neo-Impressionism on the eve of his turn to abstraction.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-nat: A still life of flowers and glass vases rendered in vivid divisionist strokes of pink, green, yellow, and blue, with what appears to be a brightly patterned parrot amid the botanical arrangement — as the title *Nature morte au perroquet* (Still Life with a Parrot) indicates. Painted in 1907, the canvas shows Delaunay at the height of his Neo-Impressionist phase, applying pure colour in small, mosaic-like touches under the influence of Chevreul and Seurat.
collection-of-beauty-robert-delaunay-ryt: Interlocking discs of blue, red, green, yellow, and black-and-white rotate against a light grey ground. Painted and signed in 1934, the canvas belongs to Delaunay's late *Rythmes* series, in which cascading arcs of pure colour generate a sense of kinetic rotation without any representational content. The work was displayed at the Centre Georges Pompidou's *Rythmes sans fin* exhibition (October 2014 – January 2015).
collection-of-beauty-robert-fulton-1806-: Robert Fulton is shown seated three-quarter length in a black coat and white cravat, a red curtain behind him and a marine scene — likely a reference to his torpedo and submarine experiments — visible through a window at left. Painted in London in 1806 by Benjamin West, the oil on canvas (36¼ × 28¼ in.) was gifted by Stephen C. Clark to the Fenimore Art Museum, Cooperstown, New York. The following year Fulton's steamboat Clermont made its celebrated first run on the Hudson River.
collection-of-beauty-rocks-at-mouthier-b: A close-up view of weathered limestone cliffs near the artist's native Franche-Comté, the river snaking through a narrow valley below. Courbet builds the rock face with palette-knife slabs of paint, asserting landscape as raw geological matter rather than picturesque scenery.
collection-of-beauty-rogier-van-der-weyd: A Netherlandish bust portrait of a young woman whose elaborate winged linen headdress frames a composed, downcast face. Rogier's precise contours, translucent skin and patient observation of folded cloth set the model for fifteenth-century Burgundian portraiture.

A stark devotional Crucifixion in which the swooning Virgin and grieving Saint John flank the cross against a flat red cloth and grey wall. Rogier strips the scene of landscape and narrative incident, concentrating the drama into sculptural silhouettes and restrained, almost monochrome colour.

A young woman in a starched linen headdress turns slightly to the left, her hands not yet finished in the drawing, the outline of one sketched at lower left. The silverpoint study, now in the British Museum, belongs to a small group of preparatory portrait drawings attributed to Rogier van der Weyden's Brussels workshop around 1440.

Christ on the Cross occupies the central panel, flanked by mourning figures including the Virgin Mary and Saint John; the wings show Saint Mary Magdalene (left) and Saint Veronica with her veil (right), all set against an open Flemish landscape of hills and towns beneath a blue sky. Mourning angels in deep blue hover at the top of each panel. Now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, the triptych exemplifies van der Weyden's command of precise drapery, restrained gesture, and narrative clarity in fifteenth-century Netherlandish devotional painting.

The Virgin Mary, clothed in saturated red, is seated within a Gothic stone arch and holds the Christ Child, who reaches toward the open pages of a book resting on her lap. An angel bearing a crown appears at the apex of the arch against a dark background. Dating from between circa 1435 and 1438, this panel — known as the Durán Madonna — demonstrates van der Weyden's mastery of finely modelled drapery and tender devotional intimacy, and is held in the Museo del Prado, Madrid.
collection-of-beauty-romaine-lacaux-by-p: Romaine Lacaux sits in a grey dress with white lace collar and sleeves trimmed in blue, holding a small bunch of red flowers, before a softly rendered backdrop with floral arrangements. Among Renoir's earliest signed canvases, the 1864 portrait already shows his sensitivity to reflected light on translucent fabrics and his previous training as a porcelain decorator in the delicate nuances of the young girl's complexion. The work is in the Cleveland Museum of Art (1942.1065).
collection-of-beauty-roman-charity-piete: An interpretation of the antique tale of Pero, who secretly nurses her imprisoned father Cimon to keep him alive. Rubens treats the moralising subject with characteristic warmth of flesh, dramatic chiaroscuro and a tender, tightly compressed embrace.
collection-of-beauty-rome-from-mount-ave: A panoramic view of the Eternal City bathed in golden Mediterranean haze, with the Tiber winding past domes and ruins toward distant hills. Turner exhibited this canvas after his Italian travels, dissolving topographical detail into atmospheric light worthy of Claude Lorrain.
collection-of-beauty-roses-vincent-van-g: A dense bouquet of white roses fills a terracotta vase against a pale green ground, painted at the asylum of Saint-Rémy in 1890, weeks before Van Gogh left for Auvers. The swirling impasto and rhythmic brushstrokes animate what might otherwise be a quiet still-life, turning it into a study in vitality. Now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.
collection-of-beauty-rubens-and-snyders-: The Achaean general Philopoemen is recognised by his hosts — an exemplum of stoic humility drawn from Plutarch — while a lavish kitchen table heaped with game, fowl, and produce fills the foreground. The still life is by Frans Snyders, a frequent collaborator who supplied naturalistic animal subjects, while Rubens painted the figures. The Recognition of Philopoemen, circa 1609, is held in the Museo del Prado.
collection-of-beauty-rubens-apostel-andr: From the Twelve Apostles series painted for the Duke of Lerma, Andrew is identified by the X-shaped saltire cross of his martyrdom. Rubens characterizes the fisherman-evangelist as a weather-beaten elder, modelled with the bold chiaroscuro he absorbed in Italy.
collection-of-beauty-rubens-apostel-paul: Paul appears as a forceful, full-haired elder gripping the sword of his beheading and cradling a book, in keeping with Counter-Reformation Pauline iconography. The half-length panel belongs to the Apostolado painted for the Duke of Lerma's collection, circa 1611, and is now in the Museo del Prado.
