kunstformen-images-haeckel-chiroptera: Bat heads arranged in frontal and lateral views, from the long-eared Plecotus auritus and leaf-nosed Megaderma to Chrotopterus auritus and the horseshoe bat Rhinolophus ferrumequinum, from Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904), plate 67. The plate lines up specialised noseleaves and ear funnels in multiple orientations to demonstrate the morphological diversity underlying echolocating sensory anatomy across fifteen species.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-ciliata: A survey of ciliate protozoa from Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904), plate 3, ranging from the vase-shaped tintinnid loricae of Codonella and Dictyocysta at the top to the large trumpet-shaped Stentor polymorphus and the branching colonies of Carchesium and Vorticella in the lower half. The plate moves from solitary microscopic shells to elaborate arborescent colonies, demonstrating the breadth of form within this single protozoan class.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-cirripedia: Goose barnacles in habit and dissection: Lepas anatifera intact, then with one valve cut away to reveal the feathered cirri and curled body. Conchoderma colonies are shown encrusting the whale-barnacle Coronula, a study in commensal stacking.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-coniferae: Conifer cones and foliage from monkey puzzle, Norway spruce, Santa Lucia fir, hinoki cypress, and Japanese thujopsis. Haeckel arranges scale-by-scale dissections beside intact cones to compare the geometry of seed-bearing structures across the group.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-copepoda: Planktonic copepods drawn with antennae and setae fanned out to fill the page, including the iridescent Calocalanus pavo with its peacock-tail furca. The plate celebrates ornamental setal arrays that drag through seawater for propulsion and sensing.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-crinoidea: Stalked sea lilies of the genera Endoxocrinus and Saracrinus, drawn full-length with feathery arms unfurled above jointed columns. Detail studies of stem ossicles emphasize the segmented, almost machined construction of these living fossil echinoderms.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-ctenophorae: Comb jellies suspended in implied current, their eight ciliated bands shown as iridescent ribbons running down translucent bodies. Haeckelia rubra appears from above and side, joined by Hormiphora and the winged Callianira bialata.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-cubomedusae: Box jellyfish in lateral view, the cuboidal bell of Chirodropus and Carybdea hung over trailing tentacle bundles. The plate isolates the rigid cubic geometry that distinguishes cubozoans from softer bell-shaped medusae.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-cyrtoidea: Radiolarian shells of the Cyrtoidea group, eleven mineralized lattices arranged in three rows. Helmet, bell, and tower forms display the silica skeletons that fascinated Haeckel from his Challenger expedition reports onward.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-cystoidea: Paleozoic cystoid echinoderms shown from above to display the polygonal calyx plating and pore-rhomb respiratory structures. Staurocystis, Glyptosphaerites, and Cystoblastus are arranged as a comparative key to early stalked echinoderm armor.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-decapoda: Decapod crustaceans in dorsal view, from the spiky Daldorfia horrida and long-eyed Podophthalmus vigil to the banded coral shrimp Stenopus hispidus. The plate revels in carapace ornament, spines, and elongated chelae across crab and shrimp morphologies.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-desmidiea: A plate of desmid green algae, single-celled freshwater organisms whose cell walls split into mirror-image semicells. Haeckel arranges Staurastrum and related genera to highlight their geometric symmetry, including views of mating cells in which two halves conjugate to form a zygospore.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-diatomea: An assembly of marine and freshwater diatoms, microscopic algae enclosed in silica frustules. Top and side views display the intricate punctate ornament of genera such as Auliscus, Cymbella and Campyloneis, drawn at a scale that turns optical microscopy into ornamental design.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-diatomea-4: Triangular and lyre-shaped diatom valves arranged in radial symmetry, including Triceratium and Lyrella species seen in valve view. The plate emphasises the lattice of areolae perforating the silica shell, a feature only resolvable under high magnification.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-discoidea: Radiolarians of the order Discoidea, single-celled marine plankton with star- and disc-shaped silica skeletons. Most figures derive from Haeckel's own 1887 Challenger Expedition monograph, where he described thousands of species from deep-sea sediment samples.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-discomedusae-: Studies of small disc jellyfish, with Linantha lunulata shown from above and in side profile alongside developmental stages of Palephyra. The plate documents both the radial gastrovascular canals visible from above and the bell musculature seen during swimming.

Multiple views of rhizostome jellyfish from the Toreuma group, with Toreuma bellagemma rendered from the side, oral surface, and aboral surface, alongside Toreuma thamnostoma and Cassiopeja cyclobalia. The arrangement presents each species from several angles to document mouth-arms, gonad position, and the gelatinous bell as a coordinated anatomical study. Plate 28 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).

Desmonema annasethe, a jellyfish Haeckel named after his late wife Anna Sethe, who died the year before he encountered the species. The trailing oral arms and tentacles, drawn in cascading filaments, are often read as a personal memorial within the scientific atlas.

Large rhizostome medusae including Pilema and Rhopilema shown from side, aboral and oral aspects. The plate captures the eight branched mouth-arms that replace a single central mouth in this group, filtering plankton through countless secondary openings.

Aurelia and related semaeostome jellyfish presented alongside the polyp stage budding off juvenile medusae by strobilation. Pairing adult and larval forms on one sheet illustrates the alternation of generations central to scyphozoan life cycles.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-echinidea: Sand dollars and sea biscuits including Clypeaster rosaceus and Encope emarginata, drawn with and without spines. Aboral views expose the five-petalled ambulacral pattern of the test, a hallmark of the irregular echinoids adapted to burrowing in sediment.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-echinidea-60: Cidaroid sea urchins including Cidaris tribuloides and Prionocidaris baculosa, with mouth and periproct regions shown stripped of spines to expose tubercles and plate sutures, alongside isolated pedicellaria, tube-foot endplates, and spine cross-sections from Centrostephanus, Phyllacanthus, and Sphaerechinus. Plate 60 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-filicinae: Staghorn ferns of the genus Platycerium, traced through successive frond stages from young plant to mature epiphyte. The shield-like sterile basal fronds and forked fertile blades are drawn to emphasise the dimorphism characteristic of the genus.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-filicinae-92: A composition of tropical ferns including tree ferns of Cyatheaceae, the bird's-nest fern Asplenium nidus and the eusporangiate Angiopteris. Habit drawings juxtapose growth forms ranging from arborescent trunks to ribbon-leaved Monogramma.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-flagellata: Choanoflagellates and related flagellate protists arranged as colonial branched assemblages, including Anthophysa, Cephalothamnium and Codonocladium. The collared cells on stalked rosettes anticipate the body plan of sponge choanocytes.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-florideae: Red algae of the Florideophyceae, with Chondrus crispus, the Irish moss of north Atlantic shores, given prominence. The plate displays the cartilaginous, repeatedly dichotomous thalli that produce carrageenan and were already commercially harvested in the nineteenth century.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-fucoideae: Brown seaweeds drawn at habit scale, including the giant Pacific kelp Nereocystis luetkeana, Cutleria and Cystoseira. The selection traces the morphological range from pneumatocyst-bearing kelps to bushy littoral species of the order Fucales.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-gamochonia: Coleoid cephalopods including Chiroteuthis, Histioteuthis and the common octopus, drawn from below and above. The plate sets pelagic deep-sea squids with hooked arms beside benthic octopuses to compare arm crowns, fins and chromatophore patterning.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-gorgonida: Gorgonian octocorals with skeletal spicules detailed beside whole polyps and branch fragments. Eunicella and Primnoella illustrate the eight-tentacled polyps and calcareous sclerites that stiffen the proteinaceous gorgonin axis of the colony.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-hexacoralla: Solitary and colonial stony corals of the Hexacorallia, including the cold-water reef-builder Lophelia prolifera. Skeletal views from above and the side reveal the six-fold symmetry of septa within each calcified corallite.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-hexacoralla-6: Reef corals from the genera Turbinaria, Pavona and Hydnophora arranged as a compositional bouquet. Lobate and frond-like growth forms are contrasted with branching morphologies to display the architectural variety produced by colonial scleractinian polyps.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-hexactinellae: Glass sponges of the class Hexactinellida, including the Venus's flower basket Euplectella aspergillum and the branching Farrea occa at centre. Whole-body drawings in the lower half are paired with magnified diagrams of isolated siliceous spicules — hexasters, amphidiscs, and plumicomes — arranged across the upper portion. Plate 35 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-lacertilia: A gathering of lizards including the flying dragon Draco volans, the Texas horned lizard Phrynosoma cornutum and a Trioceros chameleon. The plate compares cranial casques, dermal spines and gliding membranes as variations on a single squamate body plan.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-leptomedusae: Hydrozoan medusae of the order Leptothecata, including Aequorea and Zygocanna, depicted in blue from above and the side. The radial canals and frilled tentacle masses of the bell are emphasised throughout the composition. Plate 36 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904); Aequorea species are known in life for their bioluminescence, produced by the calcium-activated photoprotein aequorin.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-lichenes: A diverse assemblage of lichen species shown in growth habit on a dark ground, including branching and cup-bearing Cladonia, the large lobed Lobaria pulmonaria (Sticta pulmonaria in Haeckel's nomenclature), and several foliose Parmelia species. The plate surveys the breadth of lichen thallus architecture — fruticose, foliose, and crustose forms — across temperate and boreal habitats. Plate 83 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-melethallia: Coenobial green algae of the genus Pediastrum, whose flat plate-shaped colonies of polygonal cells float in fresh water. Arranged in concentric rings, the species illustrate how a fixed cell number per colony produces star-, wheel- and disc-shaped geometries.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-muscinae: A garden of mosses including Polytrichum commune, Sphagnum palustre and the dung moss Splachnum luteum with its inflated apophysis. Capsules, setae and leafy gametophytes are drawn at habit scale to compare bryophyte sporophyte architecture.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-mycetozoa: Slime moulds shown across their full life cycle, from amoeboid swarm cells emerging from spores to mature plasmodia of Badhamia and Trichia. The plate treats Mycetozoa as protists rather than fungi, reflecting Haeckel's broader reorganisation of the kingdoms of life.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-narcomedusae: Narcomedusan hydrozoans, deep-water jellyfish whose bell margin is scalloped into discrete lobes. Pegantha, Aeginura and Solmaris are shown from below to display the peripheral tentacles arising directly from the exumbrella, a defining feature of the order.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-nepenthaceae: The tropical pitcher plant Nepenthes gymnamphora, drawn with its modified leaves forming fluid-filled traps. Carnivorous insectivory had been confirmed only decades earlier, and the plate emphasises the lid, peristome and tendril that suspend each pitcher.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-nudibranchia: Sea slugs of multiple aeolid and dorid lineages, including the orange-tipped Facelina auriculata and the spotted Tritonia hombergii. Cerata, rhinophores and branchial plumes are rendered in colour to record pigmentation that fades from preserved specimens.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-ophiodea: Brittle stars arranged in radial symmetry across the plate, their slender, articulated arms fanning outward from small central discs. Haeckel emphasized the spiny ornamentation and pentaradial geometry of these echinoderms, drawing on specimens collected by the Challenger expedition.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-ophiodea-70: Basket stars and brittle stars displayed from multiple angles, including the branching, fractal-like arms of Astrophyton at center. The composition contrasts dense knotted limbs with the more sparse, whip-like rays of smaller ophiuroids to convey echinoderm diversity.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-orchidae: Tropical orchids rendered as a dense bouquet in plate 74 of Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904), including Odontoglossum, Oncidium, Cattleya, and Cypripedium (slipper orchid) species. The composition showcases the extraordinary diversity of floral form within the family — lipped labella, ruffled petals, hooded pouches, and long-spurred blossoms — drawn from horticultural specimens known to nineteenth-century collectors.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-ostraciontes: Boxfish and cowfish drawn from multiple angles to highlight their rigid carapace of fused scale plates. Haeckel sets the angular, polyhedral bodies against one another to underscore how these tropical reef fish trade flexibility for armored defense.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-pennatulida: Sea pens and sea pansies displayed as feather-like and disc-shaped colonies, with enlargements of individual polyps along the rachis. The plate documents the colonial architecture of these soft corals, showing how a single founding polyp gives rise to a polymorphic colony.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-peridinea: Marine dinoflagellates magnified to reveal their armored cellulose plates, flagellar grooves, and projecting horns. Species like Ceratium tripos and Ornithocercus magnificus dominate the composition, their delicate sail-like extensions translated into precise lithographic line.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-peromedusae: Crown jellies of the genus Periphylla shown from side and underside, the conical bell ringed by deep grooves and trailing tentacles. The plate captures the bioluminescent deep-sea medusae described from Challenger expedition hauls.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-phaeodaria-1: Microscopic radiolarians with siliceous skeletons constructed in geometric forms, including the icosahedral lattice of Circogonia and the radial spines of Haeckeliana. Haeckel renders these planktonic single-celled organisms as if they were architectural blueprints.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-phaeodaria-61: Detailed terminations of radiolarian spicules from the Aulographis group, each tip elaborated into candelabras, asterisks, or forks. The plate isolates these microscopic ornament details to show the structural inventiveness of phaeodarian skeletons.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-platodes: Plate 75 of Kunstformen der Natur (1904) surveys the diversity of parasitic flatworms, ranging from cercariae larvae with forked tails — including Cercaria dichotoma as studied by Johannes Müller — to adult monogeneans such as Diplozoon paradoxum (shown as a mated pair) and the mature proglottids and scolex of Taenia solium. Disc-shaped and elongated adult forms dominate the composition alongside the smaller larval stages, together illustrating the full span of platyhelminth body plans.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-polycyttaria: Colonial radiolarians shown as gelatinous spheres studded with individual cells and symbiotic zooxanthellae. The plate documents social plankton, where dozens of single-celled organisms cohabit in a shared transparent matrix.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-prosobranchia: Marine snails arranged as a still-life of shells, including the long-spired Murex pecten, the cone of Conus imperialis, and the harp-ribbed Harpa ventricosa. The plate functions as a survey of gastropod ornament, from spines to glossy enamel.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-rotatoria: Microscopic rotifers shown with their ciliated coronas and transparent bodies, including the trumpet-shaped Stephanoceros and the colonial Lacinularia. The plate freezes the spinning corona that gives these freshwater animals their name.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-sertulariae: Hydroid colonies branching like miniature ferns, with magnified hydrothecae and reproductive gonangia along each stem. The plate emphasizes how these cnidarians blur the line between plant-like growth form and animal anatomy.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-siphoneae: Plate 64 of Kunstformen der Natur (1904) presents the siphonous green algae — organisms in which the entire thallus is one continuous, multinucleate cell. Caulerpa species dominate the composition, their fronds ranging from grape-cluster (C. racemosa) to peltate discs and feathered pinnules; alongside them appear Acetabularia's parasol-like caps, the calcified cylinders of Neomeris, and the plume of Struvea, collectively demonstrating how a single cytoplasm can generate the visual complexity of an entire higher plant.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-siphonophorae: Porpema colonies shown with disc-like floats and trailing sexual polyps, set against magnified gas bladders. The plate documents how a siphonophore is not a single jelly but a coordinated colony of specialized zooids.

Physophora hydrostatica colonies arranged with central swimming bells and a skirt of stinging tentacles. Haeckel pairs an overall view with anatomical details of the gas float and individual nectophore to dissect the colonial body plan.

A Forskalia-like siphonophore dissected layer by layer, from intact colony to stripped polyp clusters. The sequence reveals the modular construction of a pelagic cnidarian, with each zooid specialized for swimming, feeding, or reproduction.

Mature and immature Epibulia and Rhizophysa colonies shown alongside cross-sections of their gas bladders. The plate emphasizes the apical pneumatophore that allows these chains of polyps to drift just below the sea surface.

Praya and Bassia colonies displayed as chains of paired swimming bells with trailing reproductive medusae. Haeckel uses the bilateral nectophores to convey the streamlined hydrodynamics of calycophoran siphonophores.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-spirobranchia: Brachiopod shells displayed in interior and exterior views, from Paleozoic fossil genera such as Spirifer, Cyrtina, and Rhynchonella alongside living forms including Lingula anatina and Magellania flavescens. Many specimens are opened to show the calcified spiral lophophore supports inside, while others are presented as detached animals without shells. Plate 97 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904), the plate serves as a comparative anatomy reference spanning geological time.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-spumellaria: Spherical and spindle-shaped radiolarian skeletons with concentric latticework and radiating spines. The plate isolates the polycystine forms whose silica architecture inspired Haeckel's broader argument that nature is intrinsically geometric.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-spyroidea: Two-chambered radiolarian skeletons rendered as miniature cages, each with a sagittal constriction and ornamental feet. The composition catalogs the helmet-like Nassellaria forms drawn from Challenger expedition microfossil samples.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-stauromedusae: Stalked jellyfish (Stauromedusae) rendered as goblet-shaped sessile medusae, including multiple views of Haliclystus auricula and Lucernaria species shown from the side, bottom, and in cross-section of the stalk. The goblet-and-stem body plan and the radiating tentacle clusters at the bell margin are illustrated against a plain ground. Plate 48 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-stephoidea: Ring-shaped radiolarian skeletons with single, double, or triple silica hoops, presented as crowns and lattices. The plate centers on simple-ringed Nassellaria, showing how minimal skeletal motifs can scaffold a living single cell.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-teleostei: Bizarrely formed bony fish, including seahorses, the leafy sea dragon Phycodurus eques, and the antennated frogfish Antennarius striatus. The plate emphasizes camouflage and modified fins that disguise these teleosts as drifting weed.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-tetracoralla: Solitary and colonial rugose corals shown as polished cross-sections and side views, including the horn-shaped Omphyma turbinata. The plate is essentially paleontological, displaying the four-fold septal symmetry of an extinct Paleozoic order.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-thalamophora-: Miliolid foraminifera arranged as porcelain-like shells with looping chambers, including Quinqueloculina and Cornuspira. The plate magnifies these microscopic shelled protists to reveal the sequential coiling that defines the order.

A diverse array of benthic foraminifera tests arranged against a dark ground, including flask- and spindle-shaped Lagena species ornamented with ribs and spines, alongside coiled Bulimina and Bolivina, the disc-like Rotalia calcar, and the elongate Cristellaria. The variety of chamber arrangements and surface textures — smooth, ribbed, granulate, and squamose — illustrates the morphological range within multilocular benthic forms. Plate 81 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-thalamphora: A comparative survey of foraminiferal diversity arranged against a dark ground, with forms ranging from the elongate stacked-chamber Nodosaria and flask-shaped Lagena to the planktonic globular Globigerina bulloides, the disc-like Nummulites, and the star-shaped Tinoporus and Calcarina. Cross-sections and top views accompany side views to reveal internal chamber sequences. Plate 2 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-thoracostraca: A symmetrical plate of malacostracan crustaceans and their larval stages, including the embryo (gastrula) of Lucifer typus, the nauplius larva of Penaeus, a mastigopus postlarva, zoea, alima, and phyllosoma larvae, alongside adult lobster and prawn forms. Haeckel arranges the developmental stages alongside the adults to juxtapose body plans across the life cycle. Plate 76 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-thuroidea: Sea cucumbers (Holothuroidea) and their microscopic skeletal elements arranged against a green ground: the adult bodies of Phyllophorus urna and Sporadipus botellus occupy the centre, flanked by successive auricularia and doliolaria larval stages of Synapta digitata and by a branching tree of Synapta tissue. Surrounding them are dozens of isolated spicules — anchor-, wheel-, and button-shaped — drawn from species across the class to illustrate the structural diversity of holothurian mineralised supports. Plate 50 of Ernst Haeckel's Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-tineida: A study of plume and leaf-mining moths in which Alucita and Pterophorus species spread their feathered wings into near-radial patterns. Magnified wing-scale details at the margins underscore the geometric microstructure beneath the apparently dusty surfaces.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-trachomedusae: Bell-shaped trachymedusae are drawn from above, beside, and beneath, with the long manubrium of Geryonia trailing like a clapper. The transparent tissues let internal gonads and radial canals show through, turning anatomy into a chandelier-like ornament.
kunstformen-images-haeckel-trochilidae: Twelve hummingbird species, including the Sword-billed Hummingbird and Booted Racket-tail, are arranged in a naturalistic composition against a sky-blue and leafy background, displaying iridescent gorgets, crests, and tail streamers. Haeckel's note records that the specimens were drawn from millinery skins, so the postures are decorative rather than observational, foregrounding plumage geometry over flight behaviour. The plate appears as number 99 in Kunstformen der Natur (1904).
kunstformen-images-haeckel-tubulariae: Solitary and budding hydromedusae such as Sarsia and Coryne float across the page, several shown in the act of releasing free-swimming medusae from polyp colonies. The plate compresses an entire alternating life cycle into a single ornamental field.
redoute-lilies-abama-ossifraga: Abama ossifraga, the bog asphodel, its narrow iris-like leaves rising to a cylindrical spike of six-parted yellowish-green flowers. The supplied text places it in the rush family (Joncées); the enlarged stamen and seed figures at the foot follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-agapanthus-umbellatus-004: Agapanthus umbellatus, its tuberous root throwing up a leafless stalk topped by an umbel of fifteen to twenty hyacinth-blue funnel-shaped blooms. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802); the plate dissections enlarge the stamens, ovary and style.
redoute-lilies-agapanthus-umbellatus-403: A second study of Agapanthus umbellatus, its blue umbel raised on a bare stalk above strap-shaped leaves. Redoute returned to the species for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1812 among the eight folio volumes printed between 1802 and 1816.
redoute-lilies-agava-yuccaefolia: Agave yuccaefolia, its narrow glaucous leaves — finely and irregularly toothed at the cartilaginous margins — gathered in a spreading rosette from which two tall slender stalks rise; the flowering individual documented in the source text reached three metres eight decimetres. The plates of Les Liliacées were stipple-engraved and hand-finished in watercolour, a technique Redouté used across the series issued between 1802 and 1816.
redoute-lilies-agave-spicata: Agave spicata, its stiff dark-green channelled leaves topped by a short crowded spike of fifteen to twenty greenish flowers with long protruding stamens. The supplied text places it in the bromeliad family (Broméliées); enlarged floral parts appear at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-albuca-cornuta: Albuca cornuta, its bulb sending up broad glaucous leaves and a bare stalk carrying a raceme of green-and-white flowers. The style here ends in three projecting horns, the feature that names the species. Drawn for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-albuca-fastigiata: Albuca fastigiata, a knotty green bulb throwing up ribbon-like channelled leaves and a central stalk crowned with a pyramidal raceme of twelve to fifteen flowers. The plate is from the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1814.
redoute-lilies-albuca-major: Albuca major, its bulb producing eight to ten upright leaves striped green and white, with a long raceme of nodding yellowish six-parted flowers on a stalk reaching nearly a metre. A botanist supplied the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
redoute-lilies-albuca-minor: Albuca minor, an Albuca recognised by its yellowish pendent flowers set in a loose spike on a stalk of four to five decimetres. Three of its six stamens are sterile, a trait of the genus; the dissection figures enlarge the flower's parts below.
redoute-lilies-albuica-abyssinica: Albuca abyssinica, distinguished by nearly stalkless flowers arranged in an elongated spike above narrow channelled leaves. The text records its Abyssinian origin; the plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1807.
redoute-lilies-aletris-fragrans: Aletris fragrans, a shrub two to four metres tall with a ringed stem and dark-green lance-shaped leaves, bearing an upright panicle of fragrant whitish flowers tinged violet. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, many of whose specimens were grown at Malmaison.
redoute-lilies-alisma-damasonium: Alisma damasonium, the star fruit, its long-stalked ovate leaves below whorls of pale lilac flowers whose six ovaries ripen into a star of capsules. The text places it in the water-plantain family (Alismacées); enlarged floral figures appear at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-alisma-natans: Alisma natans, a floating water-plantain with slender creeping stems and elliptical leaves resting at the surface, the small solitary flowers opening on long stalks and appearing white or very pale flesh-coloured. Drawn for the fifth volume of Les Liliacées, issued in 1809.
redoute-lilies-alisma-plantago: Alisma plantago, the common water-plantain, its ovate-pointed basal leaves on long petioles below a tall pyramidal panicle of whorled branches. The plates were printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate, then finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-alisma-ranunculoides: Alisma ranunculoides, its lance-shaped basal leaves below one or two umbels of lilac flowers with yellow claws, the many ovaries gathered into a bristly spherical head. The text places it in the water-plantain family (Alismacées), from the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-allium-album: Allium album, a small violet bulb producing a few flat green leaves and a stalk topped by a flattened umbel of large milk-white flowers. The plate shows the three-angled ovary and capsule below, each cell holding two black seeds. From the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-allium-ampeloprasum: Allium ampeloprasum, the wild leek, its fist-sized bulb of clustered cloves throwing up a stem to about a metre and a half crowned by a dense near-spherical umbel of small lilac flowers. The dissection figures below enlarge the flower's sexual parts.
redoute-lilies-allium-angulosum: Allium angulosum, an onion springing from a creeping woody rootstock, its glaucous channelled leaves often spiralled at the tip and its lilac flowers gathered in a half-spherical umbel. Drawn for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1809.
redoute-lilies-allium-arenarium: Allium arenarium, the sand garlic, its bulb sending up a slender glaucous stalk whose umbel is largely replaced by a head of small black bulblets among purple-violet flowers. The text assigns it to the asphodel family (Asphodèles), Linnaean Hexandria monogynia.
redoute-lilies-allium-biulcum: Allium bisulcum, an onion named for its half-cylindrical leaves grooved on both faces, bearing a full spherical umbel of pale-violet bell-shaped flowers. A botanist supplied the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plate in Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-allium-brachystemon: Allium brachystemon, a small-bulbed onion with few narrow leaves and a loose umbel of six to eight whitish flowers, the lance-shaped segments marked by a brown midline and notably short stamens. From the seventh volume of Les Liliacees, issued in 1812.
redoute-lilies-allium-carinatum: Allium carinatum, the keeled garlic, its channelled leaves on a slender stem and a loose umbel mixed with small green bulblets, the long thread-like stamens projecting well beyond the violet-red flowers. The plate dissections enlarge the floral parts below.
redoute-lilies-allium-carolinianum: Allium carolinianum, an oblong brown-tunicked bulb throwing up flat dark-green leaves and a globular umbel of twenty-five to thirty fragrant white flowers flushed rose. The plate enlarges the apricot-yellow anthers and the ovary below, from the second volume (1804).
redoute-lilies-allium-cernuum: Allium cernuum, the nodding onion, recognised by its pendent rounded umbel of pale-rose flowers on a stem curved at the top, with stamens projecting beyond the segments. The text assigns it to the asphodel family; enlarged floral figures appear at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-allium-chamae-moly: Allium chamae-moly, the smallest of the known garlics, with its rosette of narrow ground-hugging leaves and a short stem bearing an umbel of bell-shaped whitish flowers tinged red. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), the stem all but hidden in the leaf cluster.
redoute-lilies-allium-ciliare: Allium ciliare rises from a hazelnut-sized bulb to a smooth scape topped by a flat umbel of pure white, scentless flowers. The enlarged stamen and seed figures at the foot follow the botanical convention of the period, showing the violet-red anthers and the three-grooved ovary.
redoute-lilies-allium-denudatum: Allium denudatum, its angled scapes nodding before the flowers open, then straightening into a near-hemispherical umbel of small whitish blooms. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811); the species name refers to the early-falling spathe valves.
redoute-lilies-allium-flavum: Allium flavum, the yellow garlic, recognised at once by its loose pendent yellow flowers and the two long leaf-like valves of its spathe. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method Redoute used throughout the eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-allium-foliosum: Allium foliosum, close to the chive but carrying one leaf near the base of its stem, ending in a tight rounded head of pale violet flowers. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); a white-flowered variety was found on the high Pyrenean summits.
redoute-lilies-allium-fragrans: Allium fragrans, its sweetly scented flowers pink in bud then white with rose lines, set in an upright umbel above channelled basal leaves. The dissection figures below show the six stamens gathered into a cylinder around the pistil, a botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-allium-globosum: Allium globosum, its slender stems each ending in a globular umbel of bright pink bell-shaped flowers above thread-like leaves. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the enlarged figures show the brick-coloured anthers and the three-angled seed capsule.
redoute-lilies-allium-longispathum: Allium longispathum, its slender compressed scape carrying a loose rounded umbel of greenish flowers with red-veined segments. The species is named for its two long spathe valves, one reaching about a decimetre, the other half again as long, drawn for the sixth volume (1811).
redoute-lilies-allium-lusitanicum: Allium lusitanicum, the Portuguese garlic, with its fan of slender two-ranked leaves and a hemispherical umbel of some forty deep-lilac bell-shaped flowers. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); the dissection figures show the violet anthers holding pale blue pollen.
redoute-lilies-allium-moly: Allium moly, the golden garlic, with its broad flat leaves and a loose umbel of bright yellow star-shaped flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the technique Redoute used across the eight folio volumes of Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-allium-moschatum: Allium moschatum, the musk garlic, its flat umbel of about twenty white flowers veined brown-purple and carrying a fine scent. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the enlarged pistil figure shows the ovary marked with purple and green spots.
redoute-lilies-allium-mutabile: Allium mutabile, its loose umbel mixing small red star-shaped flowers with little white bulbils among the slender pedicels. The plate belongs to the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), the basal leaves channelled below and rolled bristle-like toward the tip.
redoute-lilies-allium-nigrum: Allium nigrum, largest of the garlics shown, its tall solid scape ending in a broad flat umbel of some fifty yellowish-white flowers. The dark green ovary turns almost black late in flowering, the trait that gives the species its name; drawn for the second volume (1804).
redoute-lilies-allium-nutans: Allium nutans, its flattened two-angled scape bearing a tight head-like umbel that nods in bud before straightening, the flowers pale lilac flushed rose. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the species is close to Allium senescens.
redoute-lilies-allium-obliquum: Allium obliquum, marked by its long stamens, obliquely set linear leaves and an axillary branch from the stem, ending in a nearly spherical umbel of small greenish flowers. The plate appeared in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812), the stamens nearly three times the perianth length.
redoute-lilies-allium-obtusiflorum: Allium obtusiflorum, its two unequal scapes each carrying a tight globular umbel of fifteen to twenty-five white flowers tinged rose and green-veined. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the dissection figures show the blunt, almost truncate perianth segments.
redoute-lilies-allium-pallens: Allium pallens, its spherical umbel of numerous whitish flowers forming small bell-like cups, the brown-veined segments pressed together. The plate belongs to the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), the long-pointed spathe valves drawn well beyond the umbel's width.
redoute-lilies-allium-paniculatum: Allium paniculatum, its slender stem ending in a loose terminal umbel of violet-red flowers, the outer pedicels recurved and pendent. The leaves are rolled into a channel with three rough toothed ribs; Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-allium-roseum: Allium roseum, its bulb shedding stalked offsets, the scape topped by a flat fifteen- to twenty-rayed umbel of pink flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the figures below show the yellow anthers and the rounded seed capsule.
redoute-lilies-allium-scorzoneraefolium: Allium scorzoneraefolium, with leaves like those of scorzonera and a loose umbel of four to six spreading yellow flowers, small reddish bulbils set among them. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the blooms resemble those of Allium moly.
redoute-lilies-allium-sphaerocephalon: Allium sphaerocephalon, the round-headed garlic, its tall slender scape ending in a dense spherical umbel of small purple-red flowers. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812); the figures show three inner stamens split into three points, a feature of the genus.
redoute-lilies-allium-striatum: Allium striatum, its channelled green leaves and a scape bearing an umbel of seven to ten white flowers grooved along each lobe. The dissection figures at the foot show the orange anthers and the awl-shaped filaments; the plate opens the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-allium-subhirsutum: Allium subhirsutum, its soft ciliate leaves and a flattened umbel of fragrant white flowers with narrow lance-shaped segments. The plate appeared in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811); two varieties are shown, one with hairy glaucous leaves, the other green and merely fringed.
redoute-lilies-allium-sulcatum: Allium sulcatum, the grooved garlic, with broad flat leaves and stiff triangular scapes ribbed and furrowed along their angles, ending in a tight umbel of snow-white scentless flowers. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814); the bulb is reddish-brown and hazelnut-sized.
redoute-lilies-allium-tataricum: Allium tataricum, its cylindrical leafy stalk rising about a metre to a flat umbel of white flowers veined in violet-purple. The dissection figures at the foot of the sheet enlarge the six purple-tipped stamens and the rounded ovary. Plate 98 appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-allium-triquetrum: Allium triquetrum, the three-cornered leek, its sharply triangular scape carrying a loose umbel of large white bells, each segment marked with a green midrib. The bulb sits in reddish coats, the leaves keeled like a sedge. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-allium-ursinum: Allium ursinum, wild garlic, recognised at a glance by its triangular stem and broad stalked leaves. The white star-shaped flowers form an open umbel above two or three lance-shaped blades on cylindrical petioles. This stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all eight volumes.
redoute-lilies-allium-victorialis: Allium victorialis, its rootstock wrapped in a netted sheath of dark fibres, sending up a slender scape to a tight spherical umbel of greenish-white flowers. The two or three broad elliptic leaves sheathe the stem at the base. Plate 265 belongs to the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-alstroemeria-ligtu: Alstroemeria ligtu, set apart by its fine foliage and an irregular flower mottled in pink and white. From a fascicle of tuberous roots rise simple angular stems ending in two or three flowers on naked stalks. The enlarged ovary and petal figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-alstroemeria-pelegrina: Alstroemeria pelegrina, the Pelegrina of Peru, its stems carrying three spreading flowers of pale purple marked with darker spots on the inner surface. The leaves are narrow, lance-shaped, and resupinate, twisted so the lower surface faces upward. Plate 46 belongs to the first volume of Les Liliacées (1802).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-atamasco: Amaryllis atamasco, the Virginia amaryllis, a single regular bloom on a slender scape rising from a rounded brown bulb, with narrow leaves spread along the ground. The text contrasts the one-flowered species with the irregular multi-flowered amaryllis. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-atamasco-b: A fruiting Amaryllis atamasco, drawn to record the seed capsule the earlier plate had lacked, with a smaller flower tinged rose outside and a short scape bent under the three-celled pod. The capsule splits into three valves holding black seeds. Plate 454 appeared in the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-aurea: Amaryllis aurea, its golden-yellow flowers crisped at the margins and gathered into an umbel of five to eight blooms on a stout compressed scape. The strap leaves are glaucous beneath, the corolla split into six narrow wavy segments. Plate 61 belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-belladonna: Amaryllis belladonna, its umbel of large rose-pink funnel flowers carried on a firm scape dusted grey-green, the broad strap leaves appearing here alongside the bloom. Each flower opens into six segments with six stamens shorter than the perianth. This plate belongs to the first volumes of Les Liliacées, published by Pierre-Joseph Redouté between 1805 and 1807.
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-brasiliensis: Amaryllis brasiliensis, its ribbon-like distichous leaves curving back in a half-circle and a violet-streaked hollow scape carrying four crimson flowers from a two-valved spathe. The ovate-lanceolate segments are thick and greenish at the claw. Plate 469 closes the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-broussonetii: Amaryllis broussonetii, distinguished by a compressed scape and a long-tubed flower borne only two to a spathe, the white segments crossed lengthwise by a purple band. The pleated leaves are bright green, the floral tube greenish below and purplish toward the top. Plate 62 appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-curvifolia: Amaryllis curvifolia, its scarlet umbel of about fifteen flowers on a scape rising five or six decimetres above a fascicle of sickle-curved glaucous leaves. The leaves open at the same time as the bloom and stay shorter than the scape. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-equestris: Amaryllis equestris, its bright red funnel flowers carried two to a scape, the curve of stalk, ovary and tube together suggesting an English saddle that gives the plant its name. The throat is bearded, the segments wavy with three broader outer lobes. Plate 32 belongs to the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-formosissima: Amaryllis formosissima, the Jacobean lily, its large nodding scarlet flower split so deeply that the three upreared and three drooping segments suggest two lips. The hollow reddish scape rises beside oblong two-ranked leaves. Plate 5 opened the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-humilis: Amaryllis humilis, a low plant with a fascicle of four or five narrow ribbon leaves and a slender scape bearing six or seven flowers in an umbel. The perigon opens irregularly into linear-lanceolate segments, wavy and recurved above the claw. Plate 450 belongs to the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-josephinae: Amaryllis josephinae, named for Empress Josephine, with the largest bulb of any known liliaceous plant supporting an umbel of some sixty flowers up to a metre across. The two-edged scape rises after the long sickle-curved leaves have dried. Redoute was flower painter to Josephine, and many specimens were grown at Malmaison.
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-longifolia: Amaryllis longifolia, its very long glaucous leaves curving over and pendent, with about twelve flowers in an umbel on a nearly cylindrical scape. The white segments carry a reddish-brown stripe, the three outer ones recurved at the tip. Plate 347 appeared in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-lutea: Amaryllis lutea, recalling the colchicum and crocus in habit, its solitary yellow bell-shaped flower seated in a membranous spathe above narrow two-ranked leaves. The stamens stand upright here, unusual among the amaryllis, the three outer ones nearly twice as long. Plate 148 belongs to the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-montana: Amaryllis montana, set apart by its slender leafy stem, linear leaves and regular blue flowers split to the ovary, the segments about three centimetres long. The blooms form an irregular panicle or umbel framed by lance-shaped bracts. Plate 241 appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-pallida: Amaryllis pallida, its umbel of five bell-shaped flowers nodding on unequal three-sided stalks, the white segments washed rose along the margins and back. The leaves appear only after the flowers, once the scape has withered. The botanical descriptions accompanying Redoute's plates were supplied by de Candolle and others.
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-reginae: Amaryllis reginae, the Mexican lily, its very large bright red flowers borne two to four on a scape shorter than the two-ranked leaves. The bell-shaped corolla has a bearded throat, the outer segments tipped with a green callus. Plate 9 belongs to the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-reticulata: Amaryllis reticulata, its tongue-shaped leaves marked with conspicuous longitudinal veins and a compressed glaucous scape carrying four pendent funnel flowers. The wide-spreading limb is yellowish within, the segments separating well above the ovary. Plate 424 belongs to the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-sarniensis: Amaryllis sarniensis, the Guernsey lily, its umbel of seven to ten vivid red flowers on a naked cylindrical scape, the segments spreading and curled back. Reddish membranous bracts wrap the base of the umbel. Despite the island name, the text notes the plant's structure and colour point to an origin outside Europe.
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-undulata: Amaryllis undulata, an ovoid bulb sending up narrow basal leaves and a smooth scape carrying an umbel of nine or ten small rose-pink flowers, their six narrow lobes wavy at the margins. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées (1804); the dissection details at lower left show the pistil and the bulbils that develop in place of seeds, following standard botanical illustration convention.
redoute-lilies-amaryllis-vittata: Amaryllis vittata, its tall hollow scape bearing four funnel-shaped flowers, each white segment marked with two longitudinal purple-red bands and crisped at the edges. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), stipple-engraved and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-anigosanthos-flavida: Anigosanthos flavida, the kangaroo paw, with sword-shaped leaves and branching stems ending in clusters of tubular flowers, the outside bristling with thick yellowish wool. Despite the title of Les Liliacées, Redouté's volumes ranged across many monocot families; this species is included from the family Haemodoraceae, native to Australia.
redoute-lilies-anthericum-aloides: Anthericum aloides, its thick fleshy aloe-like leaves giving rise to slender, somewhat pendulous scapes that carry elongated racemes of six-parted flowers, each segment with a green midrib. Redouté prepared the plate for Les Liliacées (1809); the source description confirms the characteristic charnu root and glaucous green leaves of this aloe-like species.
redoute-lilies-anthericum-annuum: Anthericum annuum growing in dense tufts, its awl-shaped grey-green leaves all basal and its flexuous scapes carrying a loose raceme of star-spread yellow flowers, each segment striped with a green longitudinal line. The plate was issued in the seventh volume of Les Liliacées (1812), stipple-engraved and finished by hand in watercolour in the standard technique of the series.
redoute-lilies-anthericum-frutescens: Anthericum frutescens, a half-woody species with a twisted creeping stem, a terminal cluster of fleshy half-cylindrical leaves, and a bare scape ending in a raceme of yellow flowers. The descriptive text accompanying Redoute's plates was supplied by botanists including A.P. de Candolle.
redoute-lilies-anthericum-longiscapum: Anthericum longiscapum, several tufts of fleshy half-cylindrical leaves on a short reddish trunk, with tall slender scapes carrying racemes of brown-and-yellow flowers. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814); the enlarged floral parts follow botanical convention.
redoute-lilies-anthericum-milleflorum: Anthericum milleflorum, named for its immense number of flowers borne in small clusters along slender spreading panicle branches, the white blooms tinged with lilac. Issued in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), the plate was stipple-engraved and coloured by hand.
redoute-lilies-antholyza-aethiopica: Antholyza aethiopica, its leafy stem rising from a tuberous root to a spike of bright red flowers set spirally along the axis, each with a long curved tube twisted at the base. The classification line places it among the Iridaceae; Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-antholyza-cunonia: Antholyza cunonia, its slender stem from a small bulb bearing a two-ranked spike of poppy-red flowers whose two-lipped corolla resembles a pea blossom. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), with the flower's parts enlarged in dissection below.
redoute-lilies-antholyza-praealta: Antholyza praealta, taller and broader-leaved than its Ethiopian relative, rising from a large flattened bulb wrapped in a net of crossed fibres, with sword-shaped leaves and numerous stalkless flowers in two ranks. The plate belongs to the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-aphyllanthes-monspeliensi: Aphyllanthes monspeliensis, forming small tufts of nearly leafless rush-like stems, each striped stem topped by one or two deep blue flowers wrapped in russet papery bracts. The classification places it among the rushes; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-aristea-cyanea: Aristea cyanea, with compressed sword-shaped leaves in fans and an angular stem ending in heads of blue six-parted flowers, each bloom set in an involucre of fringed bracts. The plate, from the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814), shows the plant with its characteristic three stamens, fibre-like filaments, and bilocular anthers as described in the accompanying botanical text.
redoute-lilies-asparagus-amarus: Asparagus amarus, a slender asparagus with pyramidal panicled branches bearing white triangular stipules and small drooping yellow-green bell-flowers in pairs or threes at each node. The plate belongs to the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814); the source description notes that new shoots of this species never exceed the thickness of an ordinary writing quill.
redoute-lilies-asparagus-horridus: Asparagus horridus, a woody bristling species whose spine-like leaves and angular branches almost hide its membership of the lily family, betrayed only by the small greenish flowers clustered in the leaf axils. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-asparagus-pectinatus: Asparagus pectinatus, a climbing slender vine whose narrow falcate leaves grow in threes along two opposite ranks, with few pendulous flowers on jointed stalks. The plate was issued in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-asparagus-sarmentosus: Asparagus sarmentosus, a climbing twining species reaching several metres, with slender short branches above a sharp spur and narrow leaves bearing tiny marginal teeth. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814); the small flowers come in short racemes.
redoute-lilies-asparagus-tenuifolius: Asparagus tenuifolius, long treated as a variety of common asparagus, with a pale green stem zig-zagging at the branch joints and threadlike leaves bunched fifteen to thirty together. The pendulous bell-flowers grow singly or in pairs; the plate belongs to the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-asparagus-tricarinatus: Asparagus tricarinatus, a hard woody climber rising to about five feet, with branches springing from apparent rosettes of six or seven leaves, the leaves and branch tips awl-shaped and bearing three grooves and three keels. Redouté drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814), placing it among the twining asparagus species that close out the series.
redoute-lilies-asphodelus-capillaris: Asphodelus capillaris, close to the yellow asphodel but distinct, with extremely numerous near-threadlike triangular leaves and a tall stem carrying an elongated raceme of yellow flowers, each segment green along the midline. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-asphodelus-fistulosus: Asphodelus fistulosus, with fibrous roots, slender awl-shaped hollow leaves, and a bare branching stem carrying loose racemes of white flowers, each segment crossed by a russet midrib. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805), stipple-engraved and coloured by hand.
redoute-lilies-asphodelus-luteus: Asphodelus luteus, the yellow asphodel, rising from a cluster of fleshy yellow roots, its stem nearly hidden by numerous linear leaves and topped by a long dense raceme of large yellow flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the round three-celled capsule is shown below.
redoute-lilies-asphodelus-ramosus: Asphodelus ramosus, growing from a bundle of spindle-shaped tubers, its glaucous channelled leaves below a tall stem carrying a long conical raceme of white flowers, each segment marked with a brown midrib. The plate belongs to the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-asphodelus-tauricus: Asphodelus tauricus, with cylindrical spindle-shaped roots and tufts of glaucous awl-shaped leaves, the single flowering stem rising beside sterile leaf-clusters to an elongated raceme of bracted flowers. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-belamcanda-chinensis: Belamcanda chinensis, the blackberry lily, its fan of sword-shaped leaves rising to branched spikes of spotted orange flowers. The plate places it in the iris family (Iridaceae); Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacees in 1805.
redoute-lilies-bromelia-ananas: Bromelia ananas, the cultivated pineapple, its broad spiny-edged leaves spreading at ground level and its flowers packed into a dense terminal cone topped by the familiar crown of foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, with enlarged figures of the six stamens and pistil at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-bromelia-karatas: Bromelia karatas, its stiff leaves nearly two metres long and armed along the margins with hooked brown spines, the flowers crowded into a globular head among coloured bracts. Redoute drew it for the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814), part of the bromeliad group the work includes despite its title.
redoute-lilies-bromelia-pinguin: Bromelia pinguin, the wild pineapple, its numerous linear leaves edged the whole length with strong recurved spines and a tall scape bearing a tight cylindrical raceme of flowers in clusters of four or five. The plates of Les Liliacees were stipple engravings printed in colour from a single plate, then finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-bulbocodium-vernum: Bulbocodium vernum, the spring meadow saffron, two or three lilac flowers sitting almost on the bulb among lance-shaped leaves, each bloom split to the base into six narrow segments. Redoute placed it near the colchicums and crocuses; the work was issued in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816.
redoute-lilies-butomus-umbellatus: Butomus umbellatus, the flowering rush, its triangular basal leaves below a tall scape ending in an umbel of fifteen to twenty rose-coloured flowers. The text notes it as the only known plant whose flower carries nine stamens and six styles, both shown enlarged in the dissection figures below.
redoute-lilies-canna-flaccida: Canna flaccida, its pale lance-shaped leaves sheathing an upright herbaceous stem topped by one to three large soft yellow flowers in a short spike. The text distinguishes it from the glaucous canna by its blooms, twice as large and fewer in number. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-canna-gigantea: Canna gigantea, a tall canna reaching some two metres, its large ovate-lanceolate leaves carried on arching petioles whose winged margins sheathe the stem. The accompanying text separates it from the Indian canna by its height, its long flower stalks, and the rounded ovary shown enlarged below.
redoute-lilies-canna-glauca: Canna glauca, its glaucous ovate leaves sheathing a stem about a metre high and its flowers set in pairs along an elongated terminal spike, yellow segments flecked with small red marks. A. P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates for Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-canna-indica: Canna indica, the Indian shot, with thick creeping roots, ovate pointed leaves, and red flowers washed with yellow in a loose terminal spike. The plate places it in the canna family (Cannaceae); the enlarged stamen and style figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-colchicum-alpinum: Colchicum alpinum, the alpine meadow saffron, one or two rose-coloured flowers on slender tubes rising from a bulb, the six segments veined and spotted with violet. The text notes the linear-lanceolate leaves appear at a different season than the flowers; Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-colchicum-autumnale: Colchicum autumnale, the autumn crocus, its pale lilac flowers rising in autumn on long tubes that serve as stalks, the leaves and capsule following in spring. The plate shows the six stamens and three long styles enlarged below, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-colchicum-autumnale-latif: Colchicum autumnale, the autumn crocus shown here in a broad-leaved form, its bell-opening flowers borne from a tubular spathe that lengthens to reach the soil surface. Redoute placed it in the Colchicaceae; the work was issued in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816.
redoute-lilies-colchicum-variegatum: Colchicum variegatum, the wavy-leaved meadow saffron, its flower segments marked with small white and lilac squares set like a chequerboard. The text likens this tessellated colouring to that of the snake's head fritillary; flowers appear in autumn, the wavy leaves in spring.
redoute-lilies-commelina-africana: Commelina africana, its lance-shaped leaves on a glabrous jointed stem and its flowers held within a folded heart-shaped bract, the three inner segments a soft matt yellow. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), the source text noting the similarities and differences between the outer calyx-like lobes and the larger, delicate inner segments.
redoute-lilies-commelina-communis: Commelina communis, the Asiatic dayflower, its lance-shaped leaves on a hollow ascending stem and its flowers enclosed in a heart-shaped spathe, the two upper inner segments a clear blue. The text describes six unequal stamens, three of them bearing fertile anthers, shown enlarged at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-commelina-dianthifolia: Commelina dianthifolia, with fusiform tubers and a slender jointed stem to six or eight decimetres, its narrow five-veined leaves finely ciliate at the margin. The flowers rise from a lance-shaped heart-based involucre folded along its length; Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-commelina-dubia: Commelina dubia, close to the tuberous dayflower but lower in stature, its ovate-lanceolate leaves five- to seven-veined and reddish at the cartilaginous margins. The flowers form small terminal clusters, each wrapped in a heart-shaped bract folded along its midrib. The plates were printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-commelina-persicariaefoli: Commelina persicariaefolia, named for a leaf resembling that of the persicaria, its ovate-lanceolate blades rising from ciliate tubular sheaths on upright stems. The flowers emerge in clusters at the stem tips, each group held in a folded heart-shaped spathe with pale blue inner segments.
redoute-lilies-commelina-rubens: Commelina rubens, with reddish hairy stems trailing below and rising above, its lance-shaped leaves slightly waved near the tip. The flowers form terminal umbels of three or four, each wrapped in a heart-shaped folded spathe. The text notes the genus is large and poorly characterised, making the species hard to fix.
redoute-lilies-commelina-ruberosa: Commelina tuberosa, the tuber dayflower, its tubercled root sending up herbaceous stems banded with hairs and bearing wavy-margined lance-shaped leaves. Four to six flowers sit in a terminal umbel hidden in a boat-shaped spathe, each bloom opening for only a few hours. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-commelina-zanonia: Commelina zanonia, a dayflower with broad lance-shaped leaves clasping jointed, sheathed stems and small three-petalled white flowers opening at the upper nodes. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées, the plate dating from between 1807 and 1809.
redoute-lilies-convalaria-japonica: Ophiopogon japonicus, shown here as Convallaria japonica, a low tufted plant of grassy linear leaves with a short raceme of small white flowers half-hidden among them. The text places it near the asparagus family; the six stamens and tiny ovary are enlarged in the figures below.
redoute-lilies-convallaria-majalis: Convallaria majalis, lily of the valley, its two glossy lance-shaped leaves beside a leafless arching scape hung with five or six nodding white bells. The plate notes the fruit as a red three-celled berry. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and the work appeared in eight folio volumes between 1802 and 1816.
redoute-lilies-crinum-americanum: Crinum americanum shown with broad strap-shaped leaves and an umbel of ten to twenty white flowers, the long perianth tube opening into six narrow spreading lobes. The plate belongs to Les Liliacées, Redouté dating it between 1811 and 1813; the source text confirms the distinctive flattened, triangular flower stalk.
redoute-lilies-crinum-asiaticum: Crinum asiaticum, drawn for Les Liliacees with its bulb sending up long strap leaves and an umbel of long-tubed white flowers. Redoute printed the work in eight folio volumes, this one in 1811; the colour was laid down from a single stipple plate and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-crinum-commelini: Plate 322 shows Crinum commelini, its six to eight channelled basal leaves rising from a buried bulb beside a cylindrical green scape bearing three or four white flowers with long perianth tubes. Like all the plates, it was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-crinum-erubescens: Crinum erubescens, named for the purple-red wash across the outer surface of its fragrant white flowers, four to seven borne on a flattened stalk above lance-shaped leaves. The plate opened the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), set in the amaryllis family of the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-crinum-giganteum: Crinum giganteum drawn for Les Liliacées, its large bulb sending up broad leaves and an umbel of wide white trumpet flowers with open, spreading lobes. The plate dates from between 1807 and 1809 and appears in the fourth volume of the series.
redoute-lilies-crinum-taitense: Plate 408 shows Crinum taitense, distinguished by its sharply two-edged compressed scape carrying an open hemispherical umbel of roughly thirty flowers above metre-long leaves. The plate appears in the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812).
redoute-lilies-crocus-biflorus: Crocus biflorus, two or three blooms to a tuft, the whitish segments marked outside with broad violet lines and the corm wrapped in smooth brown scales. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); it sits in the iris family on the classification line.
redoute-lilies-crocus-luteus: Plate 196 shows Crocus luteus, its flattened corm sending up tufts of grassy leaves and a yellow bell of six lobes streaked outside with brown or violet lines, the three style branches enlarged below. Each plate was stipple-engraved, printed in colour, and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-crocus-minimus: Crocus minimus, a dwarf saffron rarely reaching ten centimetres, its narrow almost thread-like leaves overtopping the small flower. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804) and places the plant in the iris family of the Jussieu arrangement.
redoute-lilies-crocus-sativus: Crocus sativus, the cultivated saffron, its corm raising narrow grassy leaves and a large purple flower with prominent orange-red stigmas — the source of the spice saffron. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées, the plate dating between 1805 and 1807.
redoute-lilies-crocus-susianus: Plate 293 shows Crocus susianus, its orange-yellow segments recurving and rolling outward at opening, the three outer ones backed with violet lines, above narrow grooved leaves. The plate appears in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), in the iris family.
redoute-lilies-crocus-vernus: Crocus vernus, a solitary flower of six lance-shaped segments ranging from white to violet or blue, the corm sheathed in netted brown fibres and the leaves marked with a white midrib. Redoute, flower painter to Empress Josephine, drew it for the fifth volume (1809).
redoute-lilies-curcuma-longa: Plate 473 shows Curcuma longa, the turmeric, its sheathing petioles forming an upright stem with broad lance-shaped leaves and a loose pale-green cone of imbricate bracts holding the flowers. The plate closes the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), in the Cannaceae of Jussieu.
redoute-lilies-cyanella-capensis: Cyanella capensis, its depressed whitish bulbs sending up a slender branched stem with dark ciliate leaves and loose racemes of six-parted flowers, here a pale lilac. The plate sits in the asphodel family of the Jussieu line and appears in the seventh volume (1812).
redoute-lilies-cypripedium-calceolus: Cypripedium calceolus, the lady's slipper orchid, shown here bearing two flowers on a leafy stem, each with four spreading maroon outer divisions surrounding an inflated yellow pouch. Redouté drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacées (1802), and the accompanying text notes it as a European orchid that resists cultivation.
redoute-lilies-cypripedium-flavescens: Cypripedium flavescens, close to the alpine slipper orchid but with an entirely pale-yellow flower, the upper division spotted with small red points and finely veined. The supplied text gives it as native to North America; the plate appears in the first volume (1802).
redoute-lilies-cyrtanthus-angustifolius: Plate 388 shows Cyrtanthus angustifolius, two narrow upright leaves from an egg-shaped bulb and a scape bearing two to five scarlet tubular flowers, slightly nodding, with six short lobes. The plate belongs to the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812), in the amaryllis family.
redoute-lilies-cyrtanthus-obliquus: Cyrtanthus obliquus, its fist-sized bulb raising obliquely twisted glaucous leaves in two ranks and a scape of about twelve pendent trumpet flowers, yellow at the base and red beyond. The plate appears in the seventh volume (1812); enlarged floral parts sit at the foot.
redoute-lilies-cyrtanthus-vittatus: Cyrtanthus vittatus, drawn for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807), showing a bulb with strap leaves and a scape of flowers whose open white petals are striped pink-red on the reverse, alongside slender pink-flushed buds. The plate belongs to the amaryllis family of the Jussieu classification.
redoute-lilies-daisia-graminifolia: Plate 163 shows Diasia graminifolia, reaching three or four decimetres, with grass-like leaves sheathing iris-fashion and a loose panicle of slender divergent branches. The flowers, whitish and often marked with a red line on the midrib, sit in the iris family of the classification line.
redoute-lilies-daisia-iridifolia: Diasia iridifolia, a tuberous bulb the size of a hazelnut raising a slender branched stem with flattened iris-like leaves and scattered sessile flowers. The yellowish corolla, each segment marked with a purple line, divides into six deep lobes; the plate opened the first volume (1802).
redoute-lilies-dianella-coerulea: Plate 79 shows Dianella coerulea, set apart from the sword-leaved species by its azure-blue flowers borne in a loose panicle on a tall stalk, the wheel-shaped corolla of six reflexed lobes contrasting with yellow anthers. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-dianella-ensifolia: Dianella ensifolia, its iris-like striate leaves rising from fibrous roots to a leafless scape bearing a loose panicle of small flowers with six spreading petals and yellow-tipped stamens. The plate opened the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802); the dissection figures follow period convention.
redoute-lilies-dracoena-reflexa: Plate 92 shows Dracaena reflexa, a shrub with spirally set lance-shaped leaves that bend and arch toward the ground, topped by a large panicle of seven or eight simple racemes of whitish flowers. The plate sits in the Asparagaceae of Jussieu and appears in the second volume (1804).
redoute-lilies-dracoena-terminalis: Dracaena terminalis, a small shrub whose foliage shifts from dark green to reddish, drawn with its ringed stem and a branching panicle of pale flowers. Redoute placed it among the asparagus family (Asperges) for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804); the cultivated specimens reddened in the glasshouse much as wild ones do in the Moluccas.
redoute-lilies-drimia-elata: Drimia elata rising from a scaly greenish bulb half out of the soil, its bare scape carrying a loose raceme of pendent flowers above narrow glaucous leaves. The text places it in the asphodel family; the enlarged stamen figures below follow the period's botanical convention. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume (1814).
redoute-lilies-echeandia-terniflora: Echeandia terniflora, its grassy ribbed leaves and slender scapes ending in a long raceme of bright yellow flowers borne three to each bract. The fused anthers form a hollow cone like that of the composite family, an unusual detail Redoute recorded for the sixth volume (1811) of Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-epidendrum-aloifolium: Epidendrum aloifolium, a stiff-leaved orchid with a spike of seven or eight white flowers banded in reddish bronze, the lip ridged and three-lobed. Despite the work's title, Les Liliacees covers many monocot families beyond true lilies, here an orchid as the Jussieu classification line shows.
redoute-lilies-epidendrum-bifidum: Epidendrum bifidum, an orchid with jointed stems carrying two sheathing leaves and a terminal raceme of purple-red flowers, the corolla split into six segments. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). Enlarged dissection figures at the foot of the sheet show the flower's parts.
redoute-lilies-epidendrum-ciliare: Epidendrum ciliare, a large white-flowered orchid named for the long fringe on the side lobes of its lip, set above firm dark green leaves on noded stems. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used throughout the eight folio volumes.
redoute-lilies-epidendrum-cochleatum: Epidendrum cochleatum, an orchid rising from almond-shaped green pseudobulbs to a nodding scape of three to six flowers. A twist in the pedicel turns the heart-shaped lip upright like a standard, a feature Redoute noted for the sixth volume (1811). Pale green segments hang below the resupinate bloom.
redoute-lilies-epidendrum-sinense: Epidendrum sinense, with linear leathery leaves and a stiff scape of five or six erect flowers, the outer segments dull yellow marked with seven red lines. A.P. de Candolle and others supplied the descriptive text accompanying Redoute's plates, here for the second volume (1804).
redoute-lilies-eriospermum-lanceaefolium: Eriospermum lanceaefolium, a tuberous-rooted plant with a single ovate-lanceolate leaf dusted with fine points and a slender scape bearing a loose raceme of small green-and-white flowers. The text assigns it to the asphodel family; the enlarged stamen figures below follow the botanical convention of the day.
redoute-lilies-erythronium-dens-canis: Erythronium dens-canis, the dog's-tooth violet, named for its tooth-shaped bulb segments, with two mottled basal leaves and a solitary nodding flower whose six segments reflex sharply upward. Redouté depicted two specimens for the fourth volume (1807), both in the pink-purple range; the source text also notes a yellow variety C among the colour forms known for this lily-family plant.
redoute-lilies-eucomis-punctata: Eucomis punctata, its long wavy leaves spotted beneath with small black points and a cylindrical raceme topped by a tuft of leafy bracts. The plate notes its close resemblance to the royal eucomis figured in the third volume; this one appeared in the fourth (1807) of Les Liliacees.
redoute-lilies-eucomis-regia: Eucomis regia rising from a bulb nearly the size of a fist, its broad green leaves crisped and lightly crinkled at the edges and a dense spike of sessile greenish flowers crowned with a pineapple-like tuft of leafy bracts. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805); Redouté, who served as flower painter to Empress Joséphine, drew numerous bulbous plants from living specimens for the series.
redoute-lilies-ferraria-ferrariola: Ferraria ferrariola, with a fibrous root and a simple leafy stem ending in clustered flowers held within a green two-valved spathe. The text contrasts it with the tuberous, fetid-flowered Ferraria undulata of plate 28; this scentless iris-family species appeared in the eighth volume (1814).
redoute-lilies-ferraria-undulata: Ferraria undulata growing from a rounded tuber like a cyclamen's, with sword-shaped leaves and bizarre brown-purple flowers whose six spreading segments have markedly crisped, undulate margins. An iris-family plant, it opened the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-flagellaria-indica: Flagellaria indica, a climbing plant whose leaf tips coil into circinately coiled tendrils, depicted with its small flowers arranged in terminal branched panicles. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacées (1809) and includes botanical dissection figures at the foot of the sheet.
redoute-lilies-fritillaria-imperialis: Fritillaria imperialis, the crown imperial, its tall leafy stem topped by a ring of pendent saffron flowers beneath a tuft of crowning leaves, each petal cupping a silvery nectar drop at its base. The lily-family plant was familiar even to non-botanists; Redoute drew it for the third volume (1805).
redoute-lilies-fritillaria-latifolia: Fritillaria latifolia, a close relative of the snake's-head fritillary with broader, flatter leaves clustered toward the upper stem and a solitary nodding flower whose outer surface is yellowish, the inner face purple with greenish chequering. The plate, in the first volume (1802), sets out the leaf and marking differences that separate this species from F. meleagris, with which it had long been confused.
redoute-lilies-fritillaria-meleagris: Fritillaria meleagris, the snake's-head fritillary, rising from a solid bulb on a slender stem with narrow glaucous leaves and a nodding bell-shaped flower marked in a purple-and-white chequer. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume (1807); colour variants run from pure white to almost wholly purple.
redoute-lilies-fritillaria-persica: Fritillaria persica, set apart by its oblique spiralled leaves and a long raceme of many small bractless flowers in dull green-tinged purple. The plate appeared in the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804). A callous tubercle replaces the bract at the base of each pedicel.
redoute-lilies-furcraea-gigantea: Furcraea gigantea, a giant agave-like plant with stiff, lance-shaped, toothed leaves and a towering flowering stalk bearing an immense panicle of more than a thousand greenish-white flowers. The plate appeared in the eighth volume (1814) of Les Liliacées, drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
redoute-lilies-galanthus-nivalis: Galanthus nivalis, the common snowdrop, with an ovoid bulb sending up two narrow leaves and a slender scape bearing a single nodding white flower. Its three outer segments are shorter, notched, and green-tipped, while the three inner segments are milky white and oblong. Redouté placed it among the narcissus family (Narcisses); the plate appeared in the fourth volume (1807) of Les Liliacées.
redoute-lilies-galaxia-ixiaeflora: Galaxia ixiaeflora, an iris-family plant resembling an Ixia but set apart by stamens fused into a cylindrical column. Its short spike carries two to five flowers tinted cinnamon at the base and lilac to purple above. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-galaxia-ovata: Galaxia ovata, a small iris-family plant with ovate leaves and short-tubed flowers, its three stamens joined at the filaments. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), a stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
