redoute-lilies-polygonatum-sibiricum: Polygonatum sibiricum, an angular stem with narrow whorled leaves hooked at the tips, the small greenish-white flowers on forked stalks ringed by two opposite bracts at the division. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811). The enlarged floral figures below follow the botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-verticillatum: Polygonatum verticillatum, a slender stem set with crowded whorls of five or six lanceolate-linear leaves, the small whitish pendulous flowers borne from the middle and lower whorls. The plate, from the fifth volume (1809), records the round violet three-celled berry. The genus sits in the asparagus family on the Jussieu line.
redoute-lilies-polygonatum-vulgare: Polygonatum vulgare, Solomon's seal, a strongly angled stem with eight to ten ovate leaves and solitary or paired white pendulous flowers on arched axillary stalks. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809). The dissection figures at the foot of the sheet show the flower's parts enlarged.
redoute-lilies-pontederia-cordata: Pontederia cordata, an aquatic plant of still waters with long-petioled heart-shaped leaves and a spike of blue almost two-lipped flowers held above the surface. The text notes a variety gathered by Fraser in South Carolina. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-sagittaria-ovata: Plate 411 shows Sagittaria ovata, its long-stalked oval leaves rising from the water beneath a loose pyramidal panicle of three-whorled monoecious flowers, male blooms above and female below. The classification line places it in the Alismataceae, the water-plantain family.
redoute-lilies-sagittaria-sagittifolia: Sagittaria sagittifolia, the common arrowhead, with its triangular arrow-shaped leaves on stout air-filled petioles and a simple terminal raceme of whorled flowers. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809); the lower stalks usually stand submerged in water.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-carnea: Sanseviera carnea, its two-ranked linear-lanceolate leaves rising from a horizontal rhizome to a loose spike of pink flowers, each tubular bloom opening into six recurved segments. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811), placed by Jussieu among the asparagus family.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-guineensis: Plate 330 shows Sanseviera guineensis, the bow-string hemp of Guinea, with stiff dark-banded leaves and a green scape bearing a dense raceme of white tubular flowers paired along its length. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the stamens and floral parts, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-lilies-sanseviera-zeylanica: Sanseviera zeylanica, the Ceylon bow-string hemp, with fleshy channelled leaves marked by transverse bands and a thick scape carrying a crowded raceme of greenish-white flowers in clusters of four or five. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-scilla-amoena-130: Scilla amoena, with channelled basal leaves and angular scapes each ending in one to three amethyst-blue flowers larger than those of other squills. The source describes the flowers as bell-shaped in bud, opening to six spreading segments with a longitudinal nerve and two small white spots at the base. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
redoute-lilies-scilla-amoena-298: Plate 298 shows Scilla amoena again, an ovoid bulb sending up channelled leaves and slender scapes bearing four to six pale-blue flowers in a loose raceme, each segment marked with two whitish elongated spots at the base. Dissection figures at the foot of the sheet enlarge the stamen and fruit. Redouté drew this plate for the fifth volume of Les Liliacées (1809).
redoute-lilies-scilla-autumnalis: Scilla autumnalis, the autumn squill, with narrow almost thread-like leaves and slender scapes carrying a loose raceme of pale-blue or rosy flowers, the dissection figures showing ovary, capsule and black seeds. The plate appeared in the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-scilla-bifolia: Scilla bifolia, the two-leaved squill, with a pair of opposite sheathing leaves and a short terminal raceme of blue flowers whose perianth splits to the base into six spreading segments. The bulb, leaves, and multiple scapes bearing flowers at various stages are shown together. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacées (1809), drawn by Pierre-Joseph Redouté.
redoute-lilies-scilla-campanulata: Plate 435 shows Scilla campanulata, the bell-flowered squill, its lanceolate arching leaves below a slightly conical raceme of twelve to twenty pale-blue bell-shaped flowers, each pedicel set with two coloured bracts. It appeared in the eighth and final volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-scilla-italica: Scilla italica, the Italian squill, with soft linear leaves and a short crowded terminal raceme of small pale greyish-blue flowers, each carried on a stout pedicel with a membranous bract longer than the pedicel. The plate appeared in Les Liliacées (published 1811–1813) by Pierre-Joseph Redouté, depicting the plant with its ovoid bulb and spreading basal leaves.
redoute-lilies-scilla-lilio-hyacinthus: Scilla lilio-hyacinthus, notable for a scaly fleshy bulb resembling that of a true lily, with bright-green oblong leaves and a slender scape ending in five or six soft-blue flowers. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807); the fruit is a three-angled capsule.
redoute-lilies-scilla-lingulata: Scilla lingulata, set apart by its bracts divided through their entire length into two or three linear shreds, with lanceolate leaves reflexed in their upper portion and a fairly tight raceme of pale-blue flowers. Redouté drew it for Les Liliacées (published 1811–1813), depicting the plant with its hazelnut-sized rounded bulb and short scape rising to eight or sixteen centimetres.
redoute-lilies-scilla-maritima: Plate 116 shows Scilla maritima, the sea squill, recognised by its spherical bulb larger than a fist that often sits half out of the ground, sending up a tall scape with a long raceme of white star-opening flowers. Its bracts carry a basal appendage found in no other squill.
redoute-lilies-scilla-non-scripta: Scilla non-scripta, the English bluebell, with linear basal leaves and an arched scape ending in a short one-sided nodding raceme of fragrant blue bell-shaped flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-scilla-obtusifolia: Scilla obtusifolia, a blunt-leaved squill, drawn with its rounded bulb, short broad basal leaves, and two scapes each bearing a raceme of pink flowers. The plate appeared in Les Liliacées (published 1807–1809) by Pierre-Joseph Redouté, and includes small dissection figures at the margins.
redoute-lilies-scilla-patula: Scilla patula, the spreading squill, with broad leaves lying on the ground and an upright ovoid raceme of blue bell-shaped flowers that nod once fully open, each pedicel set with two awl-shaped blue bracts. The plate appeared in the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-scilla-peruviana: Plate 167 shows Scilla peruviana, with linear leaves spread in a wide rosette and a stout scape ending in a dense conical raceme of many blue-violet flowers. The lower dissection figures show the stamens and the three-angled, three-celled capsule typical of the squills.
redoute-lilies-scilla-pomeridiana: Scilla pomeridiana, with a large fibrous-coated bulb and lanceolate leaves bearing a prodigious quantity of very fine white points on their surface, the branching stem rising to about one metre and carrying widely spaced pale white-pink flowers along divergent branches nearly at right angles. Redouté drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814–1816).
redoute-lilies-scilla-umbellata: Scilla umbellata, set apart by its low habit and few pale-blue flowers arranged in a false umbel, with linear channelled leaves shorter than the scape. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Liliacees (1805); the dissection figures show the stamens and three-celled capsule.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-bermudiana: Sisyrinchium bermudiana, with a flattened two-edged stem, iris-like fan of sheathing leaves, and wheel-shaped flowers of blue mixed with yellow clustered within spathes. Jussieu's line places it among the Iridaceae; the three stamens are joined by their filaments into a cylindrical tube.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-collinum: Sisyrinchium collinum, a small iris-relative drawn with its flattened stem, narrow fan of leaves and wheel-shaped flowers within their spathes. The plate appeared in the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809), the stipple engraving printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-convolutum: Plate 47 shows Sisyrinchium convolutum, with sword-like glaucous leaves and a wheel-shaped yellow flower deeply cut into six segments that roll up on themselves after blooming. It appeared in the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), classed by Jussieu among the Iridaceae.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-elegans: Sisyrinchium elegans, growing from a small ovoid bulb to a slender stem bearing a long sword-shaped leaf and a single large six-segmented flower with a yellow centre, the segments marked with a longitudinal greenish blotch. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805–1807); the plate includes a dissection showing the flattened open perianth and the pistil.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-gramineum: Sisyrinchium gramineum, its grass-like sword-shaped leaves flanking flattened winged stems that end in small clustered flowers held in a two-valved spathe. The plate belongs to the iris family in Jussieu's system; Redoute drew it for Volume 5 of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-palmifolium: Sisyrinchium palmifolium, growing from an oval red-scaled bulb and bearing pleated lance-shaped leaves below white star-flowers enclosed in a green spathe. Redoute drew it for the sixth folio volume of Les Liliacees (1811), the stamen figures at the foot of the sheet enlarged in the manner of the period.
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-striatum: Sisyrinchium striatum, its cylindrical iris-like stems carrying a long spike of pale yellowish flowers veined in brown or purple. Printed as a stipple engraving in colour and finished by hand, the plate appeared in Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-sisyrinchium-tenuifolium: Sisyrinchium tenuifolium, forming a turf of slender flattened stems among very narrow sword-shaped leaves, with yellow six-parted flowers opening one at a time from each terminal umbel. The plate belongs to the iris family and appeared in Volume 5 of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-smilacina-racemosa: Smilacina racemosa, its arching stem set with ovate ribbed leaves and tipped by a branched raceme of small white flowers that give way to red-speckled berries. The work places it among the asparagus family of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 4 of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-smilacina-stellata: Smilacina stellata, an asparagus-family plant whose leafy stem ends in small white star-shaped flowers. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), printed as a stipple engraving in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-sowerbaea-juncea: Sowerbaea juncea, its tufts of slender rush-like leaves giving rise to bare scapes topped by rounded umbels of lilac-pink flowers within a reddish collar of bracts. The plate places it among the asphodels of Jussieu and appeared in Volume 6 of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-strelitzia-reginae: Strelitzia reginae, its long leathery leaves on cylindrical petioles set beside the spathe from which the brilliant crested flower emerges. The text records it as a Cape of Good Hope introduction much admired in European gardens; Redoute drew it for Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-streptopus-amplexifolius: Streptopus amplexifolius, a slender plant with clasping heart-based leaves and solitary white bell-flowers hanging on sharply bent stalks. The work assigns it to the asparagus family of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 5 of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-tigridia-pavonia: Tigridia pavonia, its single bell-shaped flower opening to six petals spotted crimson and flame at the centre, set above sword-shaped pleated leaves. The plate belongs to the iris family and led off the very first volume of Les Liliacees (1802), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-tofieldia-palustris: Tofieldia palustris, its sword-shaped basal leaves below a narrow terminal raceme of small white six-parted flowers, with the three-horned ovary shown enlarged at the foot. The plate places it among the Colchicaceae of Jussieu and appeared in Volume 5 of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-tofieldia-pubescens: Tofieldia pubescens, its iris-like flattened leaves beneath a slender bristly stem carrying a narrow raceme of small whitish flowers grouped in threes. Redoute drew it for the sixth folio volume of Les Liliacees (1811), each plate a stipple engraving printed in colour.
redoute-lilies-tradescantia-discolor: Tradescantia discolor, recognised by leaves green above and deep red-purple beneath, with a head of small whitish flowers cradled in two reddish boat-shaped bracts. The work places it among the rushes of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-tradescantia-erecta: Tradescantia erecta, an upright branching plant with sheathing ovate leaves and tight terminal clusters of nodding flowers whose three inner segments are deep blue. The plate appeared in Volume 4 of Les Liliacees (1807), printed as a stipple engraving and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-tradescantia-rosea: Tradescantia rosea, a small species with narrow channelled leaves and a simple umbel of pink flowers on stalks longer than the floral leaves. The work places it among the rushes of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-tradescantia-virginica: Tradescantia virginica, its grassy leaves below clustered flowers of rich violet-purple, the colour for which the plant was sought in gardens. The accompanying text notes pale-violet and white-flowered variants as well as hairy forms; the plate appeared in Volume 2 of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-trillium-rhomboideum: Trillium rhomboideum, growing from a thick rhizome to a whorl of three rhomboidal leaves from which a single stalked flower rises on a short scape. The work places it among the Asparagaceae of Jussieu and distinguishes it from Trillium sessile by its stalked bloom; the plate appeared in Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-trillium-sessile: Trillium sessile, growing from a thick horizontal rhizome, its whorl of three broad mottled leaves — marked with dark and glaucous green — bearing a single erect flower of deep crimson-red above them on a visible peduncle. The text distinguishes it from related trilliums by its variegated foliage, likened in colour to that of the dog's-tooth violet. Redouté drew it for Volume 3 of Les Liliacées (1805).
redoute-lilies-tritoma-media: Tritoma media, its long drooping keeled leaves below a stout scape ending in a dense raceme of tubular flowers shading from pale yellow to orange-red. The text notes the colour varies with season, redder in spring blooms; the plate appeared in Volume 3 of Les Liliacees (1805).
redoute-lilies-tritoma-uvaria: Tritoma uvaria, its stiff keeled leaves with finely toothed margins around a stout bare scape carrying a dense raceme of pendent tubular flowers, saffron-yellow below and scarlet toward the tip. The work places it among the asphodels of Jussieu and appeared in Volume 5 of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-tulipa-celsiana: Tulipa celsiana, a small wild-type tulip with narrow channelled leaves and a solitary upright yellow flower, faintly scented and smaller than the common species. The plate belongs to the true lilies of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-tulipa-clusiana: Tulipa clusiana, its solitary white bell-flower marked with bright red-violet on the outer face of the three larger segments, appearing wholly violet when closed. The plate belongs to the true lilies and appeared in Volume 1 of Les Liliacees (1802), printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-tulipa-cornuta: Tulipa cornuta, a tall slender tulip whose six narrow segments draw out into long horn-like points, the bud forming a sharp inverted cone before opening. The plate places it among the Liliaceae of Jussieu; Redoute drew it for the eighth and last volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-tulipa-gesneriana-dracont: Tulipa gesneriana var. dracontia, the dragon tulip, its large solitary terminal flower carried on a stout smooth stem above three broad half-clasping leaves; the six petals are deeply lacerated along their margins, giving the bloom its distinctive feathered appearance in yellow banded with red. A small schematic of the bulb appears to the lower left. Redouté drew this variety for the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814), and the accompanying text describes the annual renewal of the bulb through offsets on a common basal plate.
redoute-lilies-tulipa-gesneriana-luteo-r: Tulipa gesneriana, the garden tulip, its single large terminal flower of six vivid yellow petals streaked with broad converging red bands, rising above three oblong half-clasping leaves on a smooth stem. The source text notes that the varieties of this species are too numerous to catalogue in full. Redouté drew this yellow-and-red variety for the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814).
redoute-lilies-tulipa-oculus-solis: Tulipa oculus-solis, its large solitary flower of six deep-red petals each bearing a prominent blackish basal blotch edged by a pale zone — the eye-of-the-sun marking that gives the species its name. The outer three petals taper to a distinct point, a feature the accompanying text uses to distinguish it from Tulipa gesneriana. Redouté drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacées (1807).
redoute-lilies-tulipa-suaveolens: Tulipa suaveolens, the scented tulip, its single fragrant bloom of six pointed petals in vivid red shading to yellow at the margins. The stem and upper leaf surfaces are downy, a trait the French text uses to separate it from the garden tulip. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-lilies-tulipa-sylvestris: Tulipa sylvestris, the wild tulip, its single yellow flower held upright when fully open, the six oblong segments slightly bearded at their tips; the three outer segments carry a greenish tinge on their exterior face. A small engraving of the stamens and pistil appears to the lower right. Redouté drew it for the third volume of Les Liliacées (1805), the accompanying text noting that the bud nods before opening but the flower stands erect once in bloom.
redoute-lilies-uvularia-perfoliata: Uvularia perfoliata, the perfoliate bellwort, its pale drooping flowers hung from a slender stem that pierces the clasping leaves. Despite the title Les Liliacees, the work ranges across many monocot families, as the Jussieu classification line on each plate shows. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume (1807).
redoute-lilies-veltheimia-capensis: Veltheimia capensis, the Cape veltheimia, its tubular pink-spotted flowers nodding in a dense ovoid spike above a fan of wavy-edged glaucous leaves. The botanical text places it in the asphodel family. Redoute drew it for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807).
redoute-lilies-veltheimia-glauca: Veltheimia glauca, its short ovoid spike of pendent flesh-coloured flowers carried on a scape above glaucous channelled leaves. The plate notes the three-winged seed capsule, each cell holding two seeds. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-velthemimia-abyssinica: Veltheimia abyssinica, drawn for the fourth volume of Les Liliacees (1807), a bulbous plant of the asphodel family with a scape of tubular nodding flowers above strap-shaped leaves. The plates were printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-lilies-veratrum-album: Veratrum album, the white hellebore, its tall stem set with broad pleated alternate leaves and topped by a long branching raceme of small pale greenish-yellow flowers whose segments are marked with darker green veins on a pale ground. Redouté drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacées (1814); the botanical text describes the plant's fistular stem, its many-nerved leaves, and the dimorphic stamens whose filaments are inserted opposite the perianth divisions.
redoute-lilies-veratrum-nigrum: Veratrum nigrum, the black hellebore, its metre-high stem bearing pleated leaves and a very long raceme of small flowers, each segment a blackish purple with a bright basal spot. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812); the dissection figures show the stamens at the petal base.
redoute-lilies-vieusseuxia-glaucopis: Vieusseuxia glaucopis, its flower of six divisions, the three outer white with a fine blue blotch at the base, the inner three narrow and tipped with three points. The stamen filaments unite in a column around the style, shown enlarged below. Redoute drew this iris-family plant for the first volume of Les Liliacees (1802).
redoute-lilies-wachendorfia-thyrsiflora: Wachendorfia thyrsiflora, its golden-yellow flowers gathered into an upright oblong raceme above pleated lance-shaped leaves arranged like those of an iris. The French text places it near the iris family on an ovoid tuber whose flesh turns red when cut. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Liliacees (1804).
redoute-lilies-witsenia-corymbosa: Witsenia corymbosa, a shrubby iris-family plant whose angular stem bears fans of stiff sword-shaped leaves and flowers gathered in a corymb, each pair enclosed in a multi-valved spathe. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814), the stem ringed with scars where old leaves have fallen.
redoute-lilies-witsenia-maura: Witsenia maura, an iris-family shrublet from the Cape, its woody jointed stem carrying fans of stiff narrow leaves and flowers with a pink-purple tube and yellow lobes, each pair emerging from overlapping brown scaly spathes. Redouté drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacées (1809); dissection figures at lower left show the short-filament stamens and elongated style.
redoute-lilies-witsenia-maura-latifolia: Witsenia maura, its shrubby jointed stem bearing distichous fan-arranged leaves and short spikes of paired flowers set among overlapping ovoid scales. The text notes its close kinship to Witsenia corymbosa within the iris family. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-lilies-yucca-aloifolia: Yucca aloifolia, the aloe-leaved yucca, its woody trunk topped by a dense rosette of stiff spine-tipped leaves and a tall branched panicle of pendent flowers. Redoute drew it for the seventh volume of Les Liliacees (1812); the text records stems reaching three or four metres.
redoute-lilies-yucca-filamentosa: Yucca filamentosa, distinguished by its lack of a stem, with numerous radical leaves whose margins fray into white curling threads. The tall scape carries a pyramidal panicle of whitish nodding flowers shaped somewhat like tulips. Redoute drew it for the fifth volume of Les Liliacees (1809).
redoute-lilies-yucca-gloriosa: Yucca gloriosa, the entire-leaved yucca, a near-shrub whose short woody trunk bears terminal clusters of stiff brown-edged leaves and a metre-high pyramidal panicle. The text counts it among the few lily-family plants that grow on a true woody trunk. Redoute drew it for the sixth volume of Les Liliacees (1811).
redoute-lilies-zigadenus-glaberrimus: Zigadenus glaberrimus, its triangular two-to-three-foot stem rising from a creeping rootstock and ending in a pyramidal panicle of wheel-shaped flowers with six spreading lance-shaped segments. The classification line places it among the rushes. Redoute drew it for the eighth volume of Les Liliacees (1814).
redoute-roses-rosa-aciphylla: Rosa aciphylla, a low shrub under three feet with stiff dark-brown branches and sparse hooked prickles, its small flowers carrying five tiny petals of white faintly tinged with pink. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three folio volumes; this plate belongs to the 1821 volume.
redoute-roses-rosa-alba-cymaefolia: A form of Rosa alba, the white rose, its pale blooms set among grey-green foliage on an upright shrub. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used across all three volumes.
redoute-roses-rosa-alba-flore-pleno: The double white rose, Rosa alba flore pleno, its many-petalled bloom packed above pale foliage. The botanist Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates for Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-alba-foliacea: Rosa alba foliacea, a branching shrub nearly free of prickles, its full white corolla over three inches across with five or six ranks of heart-notched petals above grey-backed leaves. Two of the calyx lobes stay simple while three are leafy, a trait noted in Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-alba-regalis: Rosa alba in its royal form, a very large bloom of many petal ranks in white shading toward flesh-pink, borne several together at the branch tips. The French text likens it to the Cuisse de Nymphe and names it the English maiden's blush.
redoute-roses-rosa-alpina-flore-variegat: A variegated form of the Alpine rose, Rosa alpina, its smallish petals streaked bright red on a pink ground, the thornless shrub reaching three or four feet. Redoute drew it for Les Roses (1817-1824); this plate is from the 1821 volume.
redoute-roses-rosa-alpina-laevis: Rosa alpina in its smooth form, a four- or five-foot shrub with reddish thornless stems and single flowers of five vivid red petals paling toward the claw, set above doubly toothed leaves. The stems are wholly without prickles, a mark of the Alpine roses noted by Thory.
redoute-roses-rosa-alpina-pendulina: Rosa alpina pendulina, its long thornless stems carrying nodding single flowers of five rose-violet petals above oval doubly toothed leaflets, the elongated ovaries curving down after pollination. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; this plate appeared in the 1817 volume.
redoute-roses-rosa-alpina-vulgaris: The common Alpine rose, Rosa alpina vulgaris, its pink flowers borne on smooth thornless stems above toothed foliage. Les Roses documents species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid.
redoute-roses-rosa-andegavensis-118: Rosa andegavensis, the Anjou rose, a tall hedge shrub whose flowers open pale pink and fade to white, carrying a faint scent of strawberry above oval pointed leaflets. The calyx tube and stalk bristle with gland-tipped hairs, a distinguishing trait recorded in Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-andegavensis-59: Rosa andegavensis, the Anjou rose, with five-petalled flowers that begin pale pink and turn white, the gland-bristled calyx and stalk shown beneath sharply toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; this plate belongs to the 1821 volume.
redoute-roses-rosa-arvensis: Rosa arvensis, the field rose, a trailing shrub with reddish arching branches and fragrant white flowers gathered at the tips of short side-shoots. The plate notes the fused styles forming a slender central column, distinctive to the species.
redoute-roses-rosa-banksiae: Rosa banksiae, the Lady Banks rose, a rampant near-thornless climber bearing small sweetly scented flowers in primrose-like umbels of ten or more on long stalks. The leaflets are glossy on both faces; Redoute drew the rose for the 1821 volume of Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-berberifolia: Rosa berberifolia, the barberry-leaved rose, a small two-foot shrub with simple alternate leaves and solitary canary-yellow flowers, each petal marked with a purple blotch at the claw. The bristly ovary and lobed calyx appear below the bloom in this 1817 plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-bifera-alba: A white form of Rosa bifera, the four-seasons rose, its full pale bloom set among toothed foliage. The botanist Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the text that accompanied Redoute's plates for Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-bifera-officinalis: Rosa bifera in its perfumers' form, a four- or five-foot bush bearing very fragrant rose-pink flowers of four or five petal ranks above oval toothed leaflets. Known as the Puteaux rose, it was the variety most used in the perfume trade.
redoute-roses-rosa-bifera-pumila: Rosa bifera pumila, a dwarf four-seasons rose barely a foot high, its pale-pink double flowers clustered in upright corymbs above small dark-green leaflets. The stalks and funnel-shaped calyx tubes are coated with rose-scented glandular hairs, with red pear-shaped hips at the foot.
redoute-roses-rosa-bifera-variegata: Rosa bifera variegata, a four-seasons rose whose nearly round leaflets are blotched with irregular yellowish marks, its fragrant near-double flowers gathered in an upright corymb. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; this plate is from the 1824 volume.
redoute-roses-rosa-biserrata: Rosa biserrata, the mountain rose, a three- or four-foot shrub with curved prickles, doubly toothed leaflets each ending in a gland, and pale-pink solitary flowers. It was found on Mont Valerien near Paris by Dr Merat, whose description Thory reproduced.
redoute-roses-rosa-bracteata: Rosa bracteata, the Macartney rose, a trailing shrub with slender hairy branches and glossy leaflets, its fragrant white flowers wrapped at the base by overlapping fringed bracts. The petals are broad and heart-notched, tipped with a small point.
redoute-roses-rosa-brevistyla-leucochroa: Rosa brevistyla, the short-styled rose, a dense six- to eight-foot bush with reddish hooked prickles, its faintly scented yellowish-white flowers borne three or four together in a short corymb. The fused styles rise as one short glabrous column from the centre of the bloom.
redoute-roses-rosa-campanulata-flore-alb: A white-flowered form of Rosa campanulata, the bell rose, its pale blooms set among toothed foliage. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the most celebrated rose collection of the age, from which Les Roses grew.
redoute-roses-rosa-candolleana-elegans: Rosa candolleana, the Candolle rose, a graceful four- or five-foot shrub with red-brown stems thick with small prickles, its five white petals banded outside with bright-pink stripes. An ovoid red hip ripens after flowering, shown in this 1821 plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-canina-burboniana: Rosa canina burboniana, the Bourbon Island dog rose, a vigorous bushy shrub with strong reddish hooked prickles and glossy leaflets, its sweet-scented flowers of three or four petal ranks in brilliant rose. Red ovoid hips ripen at the foot of the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-canina-grandiflora: A large-flowered dog rose, Rosa canina grandiflora, its five soft-pink petals paler toward the claw and yellowish at the base, set above glabrous leaflets and hooked prickles. The branching shrub bears nearly round hips that ripen red, drawn for Les Roses (1817-1824).
redoute-roses-rosa-canina-nitens: Rosa canina, the wild dog rose, with pale-pink single flowers, toothed leaflets, and arching stems set with curved prickles. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, the most famous rose iconography ever made and the record of species roses before the modern hybrid.
redoute-roses-rosa-carolina-corymbosa: Rosa carolina in its corymb-flowered form, light-pink petals notched at the tip above ovate leaflets and reddish stems with scattered prickles. Claude-Antoine Thory, who wrote the text, treats it as a variety of Michaux's R. caroliniana rather than the species Willdenow named.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia: The hundred-petalled cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia, its rounded bloom packed with rose-pink petals that deepen toward the centre, above doubly toothed dark-green leaflets and bristly ovaries. Thory noted the rose had already been figured by Clusius and earlier botanists.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-anemonoide: An anemone-flowered cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia anemonoides, its pink corolla in five or six ranks with the short inner petals folded and cupped like an anemone. The variety can be kept only by grafting, then layered to raise own-root plants, per Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-anglica-ru: A red-flowered cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia in the form called the Cumberland rose, its full double bloom above toothed leaflets and prickled stems. The plate is a stipple engraving printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-bipinnata-: Rosa centifolia in its celery-leaved form, the leaflets cut and divided so the foliage resembles celery, with the usual rose-pink double flower of the cabbage rose. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.

A celery-leaved cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia bipinnata, its finely divided leaflets set below a full pink double flower. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the rose collection from which Les Roses grew.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-bullata: Rosa centifolia bullata, the cabbage rose with puffed, blistered leaflets that swell and curl back on themselves, above a rounded pink double bloom. Thory records it as the lettuce-leaved rose propagated by the nurseryman Dupont.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-carnea: The Vilmorin rose, a cabbage rose with nearly full flowers of a transparent flesh-pink, borne singly or in twos and threes above light-green woolly-backed leaflets. Thory notes the variety, kept by grafting, was named for the nurseryman who first distributed it.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-caryophyll: The carnation rose, a cabbage rose variety with a small pink corolla above ovate pointed leaflets, woolly beneath, and stems set with unequal reddish prickles. The variety can be multiplied only by grafting or layering, according to Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-crenata: A crenate-leaved cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia crenata, with rounded leaflets deeply scalloped and heart-shaped at the base, below a many-petalled pink flower whose inner petals are crumpled. Thory records the bloom as scented, though less so than the common cabbage rose.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-flore-simp: A single-flowered cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia flore simplici, showing five pink petals around a boss of stamens rather than the usual full double bloom. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-foliacea: A leafy-bracted cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia foliacea, its pink double flower set among enlarged leaf-like bracts at the calyx. Les Roses was issued in three folio volumes between 1817 and 1824, this plate in the second.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-minor: The Bordeaux rose, a small cabbage rose forming a bush about a foot and a half high, its flowers in fours and sixes with seven or eight ranks of pink petals smaller than the common centifolia. The leaflets are nearly round and woolly beneath, per Thory's description.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-mutabilis: Rosa centifolia in the form called the Unique rose, its full bloom shading from white toward pink across the petals. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses, issued in 1817.
redoute-roses-rosa-centifolia-prolifera-: A cabbage rose that carries two variations on one plant, the leafy-bracted and the proliferous forms, with a pink flower growing through from its own centre. Thory notes the foliage otherwise matches the many centifolias already figured in the work.
redoute-roses-rosa-cinnamomea: The cinnamon rose, Rosa cinnamomea, with scented red-tinged single flowers gathered in a corymb above seven-leaflet leaves and smooth flowering shoots. Thory records that it flowers in May and grows wild across southern Europe.
redoute-roses-rosa-cinnamomea-majalis: Rosa cinnamomea in its May-flowering form, single flowers of five heart-notched petals washed red above ovate leaflets and stems crowded with short prickles below. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, and Les Roses grew out of her Malmaison collection.
redoute-roses-rosa-clynophylla: Rosa clynophylla, a smooth climbing shrub whose alternate leaves droop in a marked way, bearing solitary white flowers with petals yellowish toward the claw. The stems and the entire calyx are covered in a short silky whitish down, per Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-collina-fastigiata-12: Rosa collina in its fastigiate form, soft-pink five-petalled flowers in a loose umbel above ovate-lanceolate leaflets, glossy above and woolly beneath. The strong hooked prickles are broadly swollen at the base, and the styles are free and glabrous.
redoute-roses-rosa-collina-fastigiata-61: A hill rose, Rosa collina fastigiata, nearly scentless pink flowers arranged in an umbel above singly toothed leaflets on a shrub seven or eight feet high. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the flower's parts, a botanical convention of the period.
redoute-roses-rosa-collina-monsoniana: Lady Monson's rose, Rosa collina monsoniana, with clear-pink five-petalled flowers notched at the tip and slender stems set with strong hooked prickles. The hips ripen to an orange-red, and Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the accompanying text.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena: The damask rose, Rosa damascena, its five notched petals white faintly washed with pink opening from a deep-red bud, the flowers two or three together in a loose panicle. Hairy glandular pedicels and an elongate pinnatifid calyx complete the sheet, drawn for Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena-aurora: Rosa damascena in its Aurora form, a full bloom of six or seven rows of petals in rose tinted toward yellow, clustered in an umbel above five rounded leaflets. The strongly arching petiole sets this variety apart. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena-celsiana: Rosa damascena, the damask rose grown as the Rosier de Cels, its pink double flower set above grey-green foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena-coccinea: A damask rose grown as the Portland rose, its faintly scented flowers borne three or four to a branch tip in a loose umbel. The corolla holds two or three rows of deep purple petals notched at the apex, above five or seven oval leaflets. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena-italica: Rosa damascena italica, the autumn-flowering Quatre-Saisons of Italy, its soft pink flowers carried in threes above bright green oval leaflets. An elongated red hip appears at maturity. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-damascena-variegata: The York and Lancaster rose, a damask whose four or five rows of petals are most often white streaked and spotted with pink, the same shrub also throwing all-pink and all-white flowers. The sticky red-glanded stems and calyces are fragrant. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-dumetorum: Rosa dumetorum, a wild rose of woods and hedges near Paris, its small five-petalled flowers of very pale pink clustered in a short tight corymb. A spherical hip ripens bright red. The shrub rises to six feet, the flower small for its vigour, with hooked prickles paired near the stipules.
redoute-roses-rosa-eglanteria: Rosa eglanteria, a tall rose to twelve feet whose large single flowers carry five jonquil-yellow petals nearly two and a half inches across, the styles tipped with purple stigmas. The crushed leaves smell of ripe apple while the flowers are fetid. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued between 1817 and 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-eglanteria-luteola: Rosa eglanteria luteola, a smaller many-branched form of the yellow eglantine to about three feet, with seven to eleven small near-round leaflets. The five canary-yellow petals are notched at the apex and the flower carries a disagreeable scent. The stipple plate was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-eglanteria-punicea: Rosa eglanteria in its red form, the Austrian copper known in gardens as the Rose Capucine or Rose d'Autriche, the same plant sometimes bearing yellow and red flowers on one stock. The globular hip stays constant across the species. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-eglanteria-subrubra: Rosa eglanteria subrubra, the cherry eglantine, its solitary flowers showing five heart-notched petals pale cherry-red within and canary-yellow without. Seven small glaucous leaflets sit above a nearly thornless flowering branch. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-farinosa: Rosa farinosa, a much-branched shrub whose three to seven leaflets are covered both sides with a soft whitish down. Five very pale pink petals form each flower, gathered in a terminal corymb above an egg-shaped hip that ripens dull red. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-foetida: Rosa foetida, a shrub to six feet whose small near-scentless flowers carry five soft pink petals that the sun quickly fades, usually borne singly. The ovoid orange-red hips give off a fetid smell when crushed. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica: Rosa gallica as the common Provins rose, its large semi-double flowers of fine purple-red borne singly or in pairs at the branch tips. Oval pointed leaflets sit on bristly petioles set with glands and small hooked prickles. The descriptive text accompanying the plate was written by Claude-Antoine Thory.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-agatha-delphi: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Enfant de France, its many close-set petals of deep rose folded over one another like a military pompon, hiding the calyx lobes. A pear-shaped hip ripens red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-agatha-parvul: An Agatha variety of the Provins rose, its very double flower of dark violet-purple packed with tight rolled petals like a ranunculus. The shrub barely reaches a foot and a half, with pear-shaped hips that hold through much of winter. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-agatha-prolif: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica, a proliferous rose from whose softer-pink flower a second bloom emerges, sometimes a third from the centre of that. The flattened stalk often carries leafy bracts in tiers. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-agatha-regali: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Agathe Royale, its very double corolla of bright rose petals rolled and crumpled at the centre and wedged between calyx and styles. The flower carries no stamens. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-agatha-uncarn: An Agatha form of Rosa gallica grown as the Agathe Carnee, its many close-set petals a softer pink than the Agathe Prolifere. Firm dark-green leaflets, downy beneath, sit below flowers borne several together at the branch tips, and the hip is rarely seen. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-aurelianensis: Rosa gallica aurelianensis, the Duchesse d'Orleans, a gallica to four feet whose lightly scented flowers carry five or six rows of deep rose petals, usually borne in threes. Large firm leaflets sit on glandular-bristly stalks, and the hips ripen red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-coerulea: Rosa gallica grown as a Provins rose, its rose-purple bloom set above the toothed leaflets of the French rose. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's celebrated rose collection at Malmaison, where he served as her flower painter.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-flore-marmore: Rosa gallica in a marbled form, its nearly scentless flowers above three inches wide carrying two or three rows of pale pink petals spotted with a deeper rose that reads as marbling. Numerous stamens surround a sessile half-globular head of stigmas. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-giganteo: Rosa gallica in a giant-flowered Provins form, its lightly scented corolla more than five inches across with several rows of fine rose petals, those at the centre rolled and crumpled over the spent stamens. A large nearly round hip ripens red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-granati: Rosa gallica grown as the Rosier de France, a deep-toned French rose set above its coarsely toothed leaflets. The stipple plate was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-gueriniana: Rosa gallica gueriniana, the Rosier Guerin, a French rose shown in flower above its toothed leaflets. Les Roses documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid, and Redoute drew this plate for the third volume, published in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-latifolia: Rosa gallica latifolia, the broad-leaved Provins rose, with deep-pink double flowers of five or six petal ranks notched at the tip and unusually large dark-green leaflets. The fruit ripens almost ellipsoid and bright red. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all three folio volumes.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-maheka-flore-: Rosa gallica maheka in a near-single form, a Provins variety carrying broad pink to crimson petals above toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, the most famous rose iconography ever made, which documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the modern hybrid.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-pontiana: Rosa gallica pontiana, the rose of Andre du Pont, a bushy Provins shrub bearing large bright-red flowers of seven or eight petal ranks with a light fragrance. Its leaflets are firm and finely double-toothed on hairy stalks. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-purpurea-velu: Rosa gallica purpurea velutina parva, a low Provins variety with trailing branches and medium flowers of three petal ranks, brilliant purple shading to a velvety violet over golden stamens. It was raised from seed by the nurseryman Van Eeden of Haarlem, who used it to plant the gardens of Malmaison in 1810.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-purpuro-viola: Rosa gallica purpuro-violacea magna, the rose called l'Eveque, an old Provins variety with broad purple-violet petals heart-notched at the tip and gathered around a central tuft of styles. Its leaves carry five firm ovate leaflets, hairless above and downy beneath. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-regalis: Rosa gallica regalis, the Royal Provins, a semi-double rose of four or five petal ranks in a pink deeper than the common cabbage rose, its blooms often more than three inches across. A few central stamens have turned into small crumpled petals. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-rosea-flore-s: Rosa gallica rosea in a single form, five rose-pink petals more than three inches across and heart-notched at the tip, above large leaflets downy beneath. The fruit ripens globular and red. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-stapeliae-flo: Rosa gallica stapeliae-flora, a Provins shrub with five large concave petals of fairly deep purple marked with many small tawny-yellow spots set in longitudinal lines. The numerous stamens surround a convex head of styles, and the fruit ripens from reddish to black. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-gallica-versicolor: Rosa gallica versicolor, the striped rose of France, always semi-double and never full, its soft-pink petals streaked with brighter red. The leaves bear seven oblong leaflets downy beneath, and the fruit is round and reddish at maturity. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's rose collection at Malmaison.
redoute-roses-rosa-geminata: Rosa geminata, the twin-flowered rose, with branches that arch and lie along the ground like the field rose, bearing five large satin-white petals tinged faintly with pink. The calyx tube swells at the middle between the forms of the white and damask roses. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-hispida-argentea: Rosa hispida argentea, a dense shrub reaching six or seven feet, its branches covered in stiff bristles and scattered straight prickles. The flowers carry six or seven ranks of concave silvery-white petals, and the round fruit is bristly and reddish when ripe. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-hudsoniana-salicifoli: Rosa hudsoniana salicifolia, the willow-leaved Hudson rose, with smooth thornless green stems and narrow leaflets resembling those of the osier willow. Its flowers, gathered in a loose cyme, show five petals of a pretty deep pink, often pointed at the tip. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-hudsoniana-scandens: Rosa hudsoniana scandens, a climbing Hudson rose able to cover arbours, its smooth red-brown branches free of prickles. The solitary or paired flowers carry three or four ranks of soft pink petals and open in May. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plates.
redoute-roses-rosa-hudsoniana-subcorymbo: Rosa hudsoniana subcorymbosa, a Hudson rose of two or three feet with thornless reddish branches and elliptical leaflets, green above and glaucous beneath. Its flowers gather in a loose corymb and show five or six ranks of soft pink petals around a sessile head of stigmas. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica: Rosa indica, the China rose described by Linnaeus, forming bushes of about two feet with nearly thornless branches and five simply toothed leaflets. Its solitary flowers show five heart-notched petals ranging from the softest pink to deepest purple. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-acuminata: Rosa indica acuminata, a small China rose of about two feet with leaflets washed a wine tint beneath, its lightly scented solitary flowers carrying five always-pointed petals of white flushed with pink. The long stamens curl back over the styles as in all the India roses. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-autumnalis: Rosa indica autumnalis, the autumn Bengal rose, a China cultivar bearing rose-pink double flowers above smooth toothed foliage. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which documented species roses and early garden cultivars before the rise of the modern hybrid. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the flower's parts.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-caryophillea: Rosa indica caryophillea, the carnation Bengal, an elegant China rose under twenty inches with eight to ten ranks of deep rose petals, some crossed by a white line, that crimp and ruffle so the open flower resembles a carnation. The fruit is ovoid and smooth. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-cruenta: Rosa indica cruenta, a Bengal rose, a China cultivar carrying deep crimson flowers above glossy toothed leaflets. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the most celebrated rose collection of the age, and Les Roses grew out of it. The dissection figures at the foot enlarge the flower's parts.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-dichotoma: Rosa indica dichotoma, a China rose to two feet or more under glass, its forked branches armed with scattered hooked prickles and glossy five to seven leaflets. The scented flowers gather at the branch tips on repeatedly forking peduncles. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-fragrans: Rosa indica fragrans, the fragrant China rose, its very large nodding flowers often more than two and a half inches across, a flesh-tinged white that looks almost transparent. The globular ovary and calyx lobes are smooth. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-fragrans-flore: Rosa indica fragrans in a single form, the tea-scented rose, with five fairly large heart-notched petals of soft pink that carry a sweet fragrance far. The long stamens fold back over the styles as in all India roses, and the fruit ripens from red to black. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-multipetala: Rosa indica multipetala, a Bengal rose forming a bushy shrub of three or four feet, its green branches armed with strong reddish hooked prickles. The double flowers, deeper pink than the common China rose, open from a bright-red bud, the crumpled central petals nearly hiding the stamens. The plate was printed in colour from a single stipple-engraved plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-pannosa: Rosa indica pannosa, the Bengal bichonne, a China cultivar under a foot and a half with concave frizzled petals of purple streaked in paler tones that give a marked cinnamon scent as they open. It was raised from seed about a dozen years earlier by Gauche, a Paris florist-gardener, who introduced it to foreign nurseries.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-pumila: Rosa indica in its dwarf Bengal form, a low shrub under a foot tall with sparse straight prickles and solitary pink flowers of four or five ranks of notched petals. Thory's text notes it was raised from seed and flowers without pause from mid-May to the first frosts.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-pumila-flor-si: A single-flowered dwarf Bengal rose, its five white petals washed with pink rounded at the tip above small glossy leaflets, with oval pale-red hips. Redoute drew it for Les Roses; the stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-sertulata: Rosa indica sertulata, a bushy Bengal rose carrying five or six flowers together in a kind of bouquet, the petals white at the claw and tender pink at the tip. The plate appeared in the third volume of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-stelligera: Rosa indica stelligera, a Bengal rose with rose-pink bloom and toothed leaflets on a slender branching stem. The plate belongs to the third volume of Les Roses, published in 1824; Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose Malmaison garden seeded the work.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-subalba: Rosa indica in a near-white Bengal form, its pale petals set above glossy leaflets on a slender stem. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-subviolacea: Rosa indica in a crimson-violet form, its nearly full corolla gathered in an umbel at the branch tips above five or seven pointed leaflets edged in colour. The text marks it as a sub-variety of the crimson-flowered Indian rose, set apart by its deep violet-crimson tone.
redoute-roses-rosa-indica-vulgaris: Rosa indica vulgaris, the common Indian rose, with smooth green canes four to six feet tall, glossy leaflets and semi-double soft-pink flowers borne several together in a loose panicle. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-inermis: Rosa inermis, the thornless rose, a dense bush four or five feet high with smooth green branches free of prickles and soft-pink double flowers two inches or more across. Thory's text notes it as one of the first roses to flower in the garden each year.
redoute-roses-rosa-kamtchatica: Rosa kamtchatica, a two to three foot bush bristling with numerous straight whitish prickles, bearing large fragrant flowers of orange-red tinged violet and rounded red-brown hips. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, which grew out of Empress Josephine's rose collection at Malmaison.
redoute-roses-rosa-leucantha: Rosa leucantha, a tall leafy bush with strong red hooked prickles and large flowers of five white petals faintly pink at the top, notched at the heart, gathered in a corymb. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Roses, issued in 1817.
redoute-roses-rosa-lheritieranea: Rosa lheritieranea, a climbing rose laden with flowers whose four or five ranks of petals curl back over the stamens, violet-pink and white toward the claw, each often crossed by a pale line. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-longifolia: Rosa longifolia, the peach-leaved rose, with long acuminate leaflets and ten to twelve uneven soft-pink petals sometimes flecked white, the inner ones crumpled and rolled at the centre, and an oval reddening hip. Thory's text reports it native to the East Indies, where its near-thornless stem grows tall.
redoute-roses-rosa-lucida: Rosa lucida, the glossy rose, a thick bush five or six feet high with smooth canes and glossy leaflets, bearing light-pink flowers three or four together in terminal corymbs and flattened globular red hips. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses, published in 1817.
redoute-roses-rosa-malmundariensis: Rosa malmundariensis, the Malmedy rose, a bush six or seven feet tall with mixed straight and hooked prickles and five very pale-pink petals notched at the heart, with large rounded red hips. Thory's text records that Dr Le Jeune found it on the mountains near Malmedy.
redoute-roses-rosa-mollissima-flore-subm: Rosa mollissima, a four-foot rose of the soft-leaved group whose oval leaflets are so downy they feel like fine cloth, bearing flowers of four ranks of petals in a softened carmine and white. The plate belongs to the second volume of Les Roses, issued in 1821.
redoute-roses-rosa-montezumae: Rosa montezumae, a wild rose with pink bloom and toothed leaflets on a thorned stem. The plate comes from the first volume of Les Roses, published in 1817; the stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-moschata: Rosa moschata, the musk rose, with strong broad hooked prickles, oblong dark-green leaflets and faintly scented white flowers borne in a panicle on slender glandular stalks. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-moschata-flore-semi-p: A semi-double musk rose, its white corolla of three or four ranks of petals above leaflets woolly beneath, differing from the single form only in its fuller flower and sparser prickles. Thory's text recounts the rose's musk scent and its use in distilling attar of roses in the East.
redoute-roses-rosa-mucosa-alba: A white form of the moss rose, its petals a white washed with very tender pink, otherwise matching the ordinary moss rose in habit and the glandular growth that names it. Thory's text notes the flower is never truly white, despite the name it was given.
redoute-roses-rosa-mucosa-anemone-flora: An anemone-flowered moss rose, an upright eighteen-inch bush thick with straight prickles, its four or five ranks of deep-pink petals converging toward the centre, some flecked with paler pink. Thory's text records it was raised from seed by M. Lemeunier and named for his town, La Fleche.
redoute-roses-rosa-multiflora-carnea: Rosa multiflora in a flesh-pink form, its many small flowers clustered along arching canes above toothed leaflets. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-multiflora-platyphyll: Rosa multiflora in a broad-leaved purple form, its flowers larger than the pink type and its leaflets three or four times bigger, rounded and broad. Thory's text records that Noisette introduced it to France, having found it near London grown from seed received from Japan.
redoute-roses-rosa-muscosa: Rosa muscosa, the moss rose, a two to three foot bush with straight prickles, its stalks, hips and pinnatifid calyx lobes bristling with long glandular hairs that look like a mass of moss, the five-petalled light-pink flowers sweetly scented. The plate appeared in the first volume of Les Roses, issued in 1817.
redoute-roses-rosa-muscosa-multiplex: A very double moss rose, its many ranks of petals crumpled and rolled at the centre, barely showing the spreading styles, the bloom sometimes more than three inches across. The moss-like glandular growth on the calyx names the rose; Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text.
redoute-roses-rosa-nivea: Rosa nivea, a thornless shrub barely two feet high with glossy three-part leaves and large, scentless, snow-white flowers about three inches across above pointed white buds. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-noisettiana: Rosa noisettiana, a tall shrub bearing clusters of pale rose-washed double flowers that open in succession at the branch tips, set among five to seven leaflets. Named for Philippe Noisette, it carried as many as a hundred and thirty blooms in a single panicle. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-noisettiana-purpurea: A rose-flowered Noisette, smaller in every part than the Philippe Noisette type, its bright pink petals deepening rather than fading as they age. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824), the descriptive text supplied by Claude-Antoine Thory.
redoute-roses-rosa-orbessanea: Rosa orbessanea, the Rosier d'Orbessan, shown in flower with its foliage on a single folio sheet. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in three volumes between 1817 and 1824; the plate was stipple-engraved, printed in colour, and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-parviflora-flore-mult: Rosa parviflora, a low North American shrub reaching about two feet, its double flowers a pretty rose colour paler at the centre than the edge, above five-leaflet foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-pimpinellifolia-flore: Rosa pimpinellifolia in a white double form, the burnet rose with small leaflets and pale blooms. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821); Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the accompanying botanical text.

A red double form of Rosa pimpinellifolia, a dense bush about a foot and a half high with rounded leaflets and soft-rose, lightly scented flowers, its small cherry-sized hips ripening from red to black. The corolla varies from five to seven rows of petals. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses (1817).
redoute-roses-rosa-pimpinellifolia-inerm: Rosa pimpinellifolia inermis, a thornless burnet rose to three feet bearing single five-petalled flowers that range from light to deeper red, above leaves of up to eleven rounded leaflets. The young branches carry a few prickles that vanish as they grow. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-pimpinellifolia-major: A sub-variety of the burnet rose with five large petals irregularly streaked in greyish-white, pale rose, and deeper pink, yellow toward the claw, above leaflets in sevens to elevens. The branches bristle with many fine, nearly straight prickles, and the small hips ripen from red to black. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text.
redoute-roses-rosa-pimpinellifolia-maria: Rosa pimpinellifolia, the burnet rose, reaching three to four feet in cultivation with prickly reddish stems and large fragrant white flowers tinged yellow at the claw. Its black hips hang nodding at maturity. Redoute drew it for the first volume of Les Roses (1817).
redoute-roses-rosa-pimpinellifolia-pumil: A small burnet rose barely a foot high, the plate showing a single shoot cut near the root, its brown stems crowded with straight prickles and bearing white, heart-notched five-petalled flowers that hold a cupped form. The hips ripen from red to black. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-pomonia-flore-subsimp: A nearly single form of the pompon rose, a slender shrub under two feet with flowers of six or seven petals, less prickly than the double pompon. Its small elongated red hips often abort before ripening. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821).
redoute-roses-rosa-pomponia: Rosa pomponia, the pompon rose, a low branchy bush with five wrinkled grey-green leaflets and sweetly scented double flowers in a pretty rose that deepens toward the centre. The pedicels and calyx carry sticky black stalked glands. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-pomponiana: Rosa pomponiana, a fairly bushy sub-shrub under a metre with five oval leaflets and small, usually double flowers of deep purple-red, long confused with the Pompon de Bordeaux. The botanist De Candolle described it in the Flore Francaise, the source Thory reproduced for this plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-pomponiana-muscosa: A mossy pompon rose under a foot high, its stem crowded with small prickles mixed with glandular hairs and its pedicels and calyx coated in sticky branched growth like moss. The corolla runs to eight or ten rows of petals in the colour of the ordinary pompon. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
redoute-roses-rosa-pumila: Rosa pumila, a German sub-shrub to about a foot and a half with firm five-part leaves and fragrant flowers of five large petals, whitish outside and light purple within, above pear-shaped hips that turn reddish or orange and persist through winter. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-rapa-flore-semipleno: Rosa rapa in a semi-double form, the Rosier Turneps, shown in flower with its foliage. Redoute drew it for the second volume of Les Roses (1821); the stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-reclinata-fleures-sim: Rosa reclinata in its single-flowered form, a near-thornless climber with seven-leaflet leaves and soft pink, heart-notched petals, the buds bending toward the ground before opening then straightening. Its hips are nearly round and red. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
redoute-roses-rosa-reclinata-fleurs-pres: Rosa reclinata in its near-double form of about twenty petals, otherwise identical to the single Rosier a Boutons Renverses, a tall climber whose buds nod earthward before rising to open. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes.
redoute-roses-rosa-redutea-glauca: Rosa redutea glauca, a shrub to about three feet with glaucous five-part leaves rose-tinged beneath and white petals washed with pink, marked inside with dark red dots and striped outside with reddish bands. The name honours Redoute himself, flower painter to Empress Josephine. The plate was drawn for the first volume of Les Roses (1817).
redoute-roses-rosa-redutea-rubescens: Rosa redutea in its rubescens form, shown in flower with its foliage on a single sheet. Named for Redoute, the plate appeared in the first volume of Les Roses (1817); it was stipple-engraved, printed in colour, and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-rosenbergiana: Rosa rosenbergiana, a very bushy shrub to about three feet with yellowish prickles, oval crenate leaflets, and umbel-like clusters of many-petalled white flowers tinged rose at the centre. The turbinate calyx tubes bristle with small prickles like the branches. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text for the plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubifolia: Rosa rubifolia, the bramble-leaved rose, to three or four feet with reddish hooked prickles, soft crisped leaflets, and clusters of five-petalled flowers in soft rose that fade to white. Its styles are fused into a smooth column as in Rosa arvensis. Redoute drew it for the third volume of Les Roses (1824).
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa: Rosa rubiginosa, the sweetbriar, a hedgerow rose to five or six feet with hooked prickles and rough leaflets whose glandular undersides give off a winey scent when crushed. Its flowers gather two to five at the branch tips on bristly stalks. The stipple engraving was printed in colour and finished by hand.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-aculeatiss: Rosa rubiginosa in a densely prickled form, its branches bristling with unequal straight spines below seven-leaflet foliage and small pale-pink five-petalled flowers borne in twos and threes. Claude-Antoine Thory supplied the botanical text that accompanied Redoute's plate.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-anemone-fl: An anemone-flowered sweetbriar, Rosa rubiginosa, its purple flowers tinged with violet and arranged in a corymb above wine-scented leaves, with red hips that darken in autumn cold. Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-cretica: Rosa rubiginosa, the sweetbriar of Crete, shown with its prickled stems and glandular foliage. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand, the method used across all three volumes of Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-nemoralis: Rosa rubiginosa in its woodland eglantine form, a tall briar with hooked spines, five pale-green leaflets and small soft-pink flowers notched at the petal tips. The ovoid hips ripen red and keep a few of the bristles from the young calyx tube.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-vaillantia: A sweetbriar variety, Rosa rubiginosa vaillantiana, its five-petalled flowers opening faintly washed with pink then settling to a pure matt white that lasts until the petals fall. This colour shift sets it apart from the redder roses of the rubiginosa group, which hold their hue to the end.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubiginosa-zabeth: Rosa rubiginosa, here the form named for Queen Elizabeth, with its glandular sweetbriar foliage and prickled stems. Redoute was flower painter to Empress Josephine, whose garden at Malmaison held the rose collection from which Les Roses grew.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubininosa-flore-semi: A semi-double sweetbriar, Rosa rubiginosa, nursery-grown as the small Hesse rose, its tender-pink flowers carrying ten to twenty notched petals above apple-scented leaves. The orange-red hips stay nearly smooth at maturity and persist a long time.
redoute-roses-rosa-rubrifolia: Rosa rubrifolia, a tall briar reddish and glaucous throughout, its flowers red in bud and opening to greenish-white in clustered heads above oval wine-tinted leaflets. Redoute drew it for Volume 1 of Les Roses, published in 1817.
redoute-roses-rosa-sempervirens: Rosa sempervirens, the evergreen climbing rose, its stems reaching fifteen feet to clamber over shrubs and trees, with firm glossy leaflets and fragrant white five-petalled flowers in small clusters. The styles fuse into a short bristled column and the small round hips ripen red into winter.
redoute-roses-rosa-sempervirens-globosa: A globose-hipped form of Rosa sempervirens, the evergreen climber, with glossy persistent leaflets and fragrant white flowers whose styles join in a single bristled column. Redoute drew it for Volume 3 of Les Roses, issued in 1824.
redoute-roses-rosa-sempervirens-latifoli: Rosa sempervirens in a broad-leaved form, the evergreen climbing rose with its glossy persistent foliage and white flowers. Claude-Antoine Thory wrote the descriptive text that accompanied Redoute's plates throughout Les Roses.
redoute-roses-rosa-sepium-flore-submulti: A near-double form of Rosa sepium, the hedge rose, its small spaced leaflets glandular beneath and four or five ranks of pale-red petals whitening toward the claw. The styles gather almost smooth in a bundle, and the ovoid calyx tube is hairless.
redoute-roses-rosa-sepium-myrtifolia: Rosa sepium in a myrtle-leaved form, its small glossy leaflets recalling myrtle on slender drooping branches armed with strong hooked spines. The five whitish petals soon flush red in sunlight, and the elliptical fruit ripens red then blackens.
redoute-roses-rosa-sepium-rosea: A pink-flowered hedge rose, Rosa sepium, tall and branching with whitish hooked spines and small leaflets glandular beneath. The five petals open soft pink but lose colour and whiten within hours, especially in full sun, above smooth ovoid hips.
redoute-roses-rosa-smpervirens-leschenau: A variety of Rosa sempervirens named for the traveller Leschenault, who found it on a high mountain in southern Asia; its violet branches and foliage carry a glaucous bloom like hoarfrost. Large pure-white heart-notched petals surround many stamens and a bristled column of fused styles topped with violet stigmas.
redoute-roses-rosa-spinulifolia-dematrat: Rosa spinulifolia, a shrub with red-brown branches bearing long straight solitary spines and leaflets set beneath with many small hooked prickles along the veins. The single soft-pink flowers stand at the branch tips on bristly glandular stalks, with the styles free.
redoute-roses-rosa-stylosa: Rosa stylosa, the field rose, a shrub with twisting greyish branches and serrated glossy leaflets, its soft-pink flowers borne several together and whitening quickly in sun. The styles fuse into a short column, as in Rosa arvensis, and the elliptical hip ripens red.
redoute-roses-rosa-sulfurea: Rosa sulfurea, the sulphur-yellow rose, its stem set with fine yellowish subulate spines and seven-leaflet wings, the solitary scentless flowers a pale yellow on short smooth stalks. Among its earlier illustrators were Clusius, Besler and Andrews, listed in Thory's text.
redoute-roses-rosa-tomentosa: Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, its leaflets clothed both sides with soft pressed hairs and its pale-pink flowers above elongated ovoid hips. Josephine Redoute discovered it near Paris in the woods of Meudon in 1817, where it had escaped earlier botanists.
redoute-roses-rosa-tomentosa-flore-multi: A many-petalled form of Rosa tomentosa, the downy rose, with its softly haired leaflets and full pink flowers. The stipple engraving was printed in colour from a single plate and finished by hand in watercolour.
redoute-roses-rosa-turbinata: Rosa turbinata, the Frankfort rose, a shrub whose calyx tube narrows and swells into the shape of a spinning top, below tomentose leaflets and sweet-scented double flowers in small corymbs. The young flower stalks bristle with stiff glandular hairs.
redoute-roses-rosa-ventenatiana: Rosa ventenatiana, a low briar with crowded straight prickles whose upper leaves persist around the bud so the open flower seems to rest on a bed of leaves. The fragrant blooms carry four or five ranks of soft-pink petals yellowish toward the claw, above a thimble-shaped calyx tube.
redoute-roses-rosa-villosa: Rosa villosa, the soft-haired apple rose, known by the grey down on its leaflets and the large bristly hips that earned it the name Rosier a Pommes. Its lightly scented flowers carry five heart-notched petals, light red in cultivated plants and dirty white in wild ones.
redoute-roses-rosa-villosa-evrathiana: A vigorous variety of Rosa villosa reaching ten feet, nearly spineless, with very large dark-green leaflets and flowers hung in a pendent panicle on bristly glandular stalks. The buds open rarely, and those that do show seven or eight ranks of soft-pink petals.
redoute-roses-rosa-villosa-terebenthina: Rosa villosa in its turpentine-scented form, a bushy shrub bearing small five-petalled flowers that are red above and pale toward the base, set among large oval leaflets edged with sticky glandular hairs. The crushed foliage gives off a strong turpentine odour. Redoute drew it for Les Roses, issued in folio volumes between 1817 and 1824.
